Finally, hostility also shows temporal structure, with coercive openings front-loading the first turn while affective hostility accumulates over a session. We release the lexicon, the detector cross-validation pipeline, and all derived tables.

</details>


### [25] [FLoKD: Adaptive Knowledge Distillation for Federated Low-Rank LLM over Wireless Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13580)
*Xinlu Zhang,Na Yan,Yang Su,Yansha Deng,Toktam Mahmoodi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FLoKD: An adaptive knowledge-distillation framework for federated LoRA fine-tuning of LLMs over wireless networks that reduces communication overhead by 50-65% while maintaining competitive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated learning for LLMs faces communication bottlenecks in wireless networks. Existing approaches like LoRA still have scaling communication costs, while knowledge distillation with token-level logits incurs high overhead due to sequence length and vocabulary size. Reducing logits lowers cost but degrades accuracy.

Method: FLoKD framework uses intermediate LoRA activations as distillation signals instead of logits or full parameters. Proposes transformer block importance scoring to selectively transmit the most informative blocks, and two dataset selection strategies: discarding public samples deviating from local data distribution and prioritizing most informative samples for distillation.

Result: Extensive experiments across WikiText-103, PTB, and Dialog datasets demonstrate 50-65% reduction in communication overhead while achieving rapid convergence to competitive perplexity compared to baselines.

Conclusion: FLoKD effectively addresses the communication bottleneck in federated LLM fine-tuning over wireless networks by combining adaptive knowledge distillation with selective transmission strategies, enabling efficient collaborative training without compromising performance.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across a wide range of natural language processing tasks. However, conventional fine-tuning typically relies on centralized data collection, bringing in privacy concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative LLM fine-tuning without sharing raw client data, but its deployment over bandwidth-constrained wireless networks is hindered by the communication overhead of model-parameter transmission. Although Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduces the number of trainable parameters, its communication cost still increases with model scale. Knowledge distillation avoids parameter sharing via output logits, but token-level logits in LLMs incur high communication cost due to sequence length and vocabulary size. Reducing logits lowers the cost but weakens supervision and degrades accuracy. To address these limitations, we propose FLoKD, an adaptive knowledge-distillation framework for federated LoRA fine-tuning of LLMs over wireless networks, which communicates intermediate LoRA activations as the distillation signal rather than logits or full parameters. Since transmitting all blocks over the entire public dataset remains costly, we further propose a transformer block importance scoring framework that selectively transmits the most informative blocks, and two dataset selection strategies that discard public samples deviating from the local data distribution and prioritise those most informative for distillation. Extensive experiments across multiple generative language datasets, including WikiText-103, PTB, and Dialog, demonstrate that our proposed framework reduces communication overhead by 50-65% while achieving rapid convergence to competitive perplexity compared to baselines.

</details>


### [26] [$τ$-Elicitation: Benchmarking multi-turn entity extraction in voice agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13602)
*Soham Ray,Victor Barres*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A benchmark for voice agents shows they struggle with exact entity capture; text agents outperform them, and structured recovery strategies help but increase call time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Voice agents need to collect personal information (names, addresses, dates, etc.) accurately, but existing benchmarks don't reveal where exactly these capture failures occur.

Method: Introduced τ-Elicitation benchmark with 200 tasks across 10 entity types, varying difficulty levels, caller realism scenarios, and three environments. Compared voice vs. text agents, and tested verification strategies and recovery scaffolds.

Result: Text agents passed all tasks, while voice agents achieved only 0.14 to 0.41 exact success rates. Agents verified hard/unfamiliar entities but not weak caller voices; only 24-37% of verified errors were repaired. Structured scaffolds improved performance but added 21-28 seconds per call.

Conclusion: Strategy selection and successful recovery are the main bottlenecks in exact spoken entity collection; realism factors have minimal impact on exact success but affect repair effort.

Abstract: Voice agents often need to collect names, addresses, identifiers, dates, and times exactly, yet end-to-end benchmarks obscure where capture fails. We introduce $τ$-Elicitation, a 200-task voice benchmark spanning 10 entity types, controlled difficulty, caller realisms, and three environments. A matched text agent passes all tasks, but four voice configurations achieve robust exact success from 0.14 to 0.41. Agents increase verification for hard and unfamiliar entities and sometimes for incorrect captures, but not for their weakest caller voice; only 24 to 37 percent of verified errors are repaired. A scaffold that prescribes spelling, read-back, correction, and confirmation raises robust Pass$^3$ by 14 to 31 points, at a cost of 21 to 28 seconds per call. Realisms such as spelling variations and restarts do not detectably affect exact success; mispronunciation increases repair effort. These results identify strategy selection and successful recovery as the central bottlenecks in exact spoken entity collection.

</details>


### [27] [Solar Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13648)
*Jyotsna Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Solar Intelligence is a unified framework combining solar analytics, evidence-based Q&A, and ML forecasting to solve fragmentation in solar decision support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current solar decision support is fragmented across dashboards (data without explanation), research papers (slow to parse), and general-purpose LLMs (not domain-specific and lack evidence). There's no unified system for solar analytics, scientific Q&A with evidence, and forecasting.

Method: Hybrid retrieval-augmented framework integrating: 1) Structured solar analytics with NASA POWER & Biosphere 2 data via DuckDB SQL, 2) Scientific Q&A using hybrid retriever (BM25 + ChromaDB embeddings via Reciprocal Rank Fusion) with evidence grounding via llama3.2:3b, and 3) ML forecasting with XGBoost model for irradiance, temperature, wind speed predictions.

Result: Developed Solar Intelligence platform with integrated solar data analytics, evidence-grounded scientific question answering, and machine learning forecasting capabilities accessible via FastAPI, Streamlit, and MCP server interfaces.

Conclusion: Solar Intelligence provides a unified solution that bridges the gap between fragmented solar decision support tools, enabling students, researchers, and energy analysts to access comprehensive solar analytics, evidence-based scientific answers, and reliable forecasts through multiple interfaces.

Abstract: Solar energy decision support is fragmented across dashboards that provide data without explanation, research papers are slow to parse, and general-purpose language models are not solar domain specific and answer without evidence. This paper introduces Solar Intelligence, a hybrid retrieval-augmented framework that unifies structured solar analytics, evidence-grounded scientific question answering, and machine learning forecasting in one system. The platform integrates daily NASA POWER solar and meteorological data, Biosphere 2 ground-sensor readings, and a curated corpus of research papers and institutional reports. Structured queries use DuckDB SQL; scientific questions are answered by a hybrid retriever that fuses BM25 and ChromaDB dense embeddings via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, with responses grounded through a language model (llama3.2:3b). An Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model produces daily forecasts of irradiance, temperature, and wind speed. The system is exposed via FastAPI, Streamlit, and an MCP server, so it can be used as an application, an API service, or an agent tool - by students, researchers, and energy analysts.

</details>


### [28] [Safety as a Constraint: Fine-Tuning a LLM Recommender to Explain Itself](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13657)
*Jiashu He,Emma Yanyang Kong,JJ Tan,David Fagnan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Fine-tuned LLM generates faithful, non-harmful personalized explanations for video recommendations without compromising core recommendation performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional recommender systems predict what users will interact with but not why, while personalized explanations enhance service quality and user engagement. Frontier-model solutions add cost and latency, creating need for integrated solution.

Method: Train a recommender LLM to generate personalized explanations based on user watching history. Train two LLM-judge reward models covering three criteria (faithfulness to show elements, non-harmfulness), and use constrained GRPO to incorporate these criteria during fine-tuning.

Result: Fine-tuned model improves all-three-criteria PASS rate from 0.649 to 0.956 (internal judges) and from 0.677 to 0.931 (independent judge), while frontier generator performs similar to untuned baseline. Model maintains original language and recommendation abilities.

Conclusion: LLM-based recommender can be fine-tuned for complex tasks like explanation generation without compromising original recommendation performance, enabling single-model agentic user interfaces.

Abstract: Traditional recommender systems are typically trained to predict what item users will interact with next, but not why. However, offering personalized evidence for why a user might like the predicted item is an important way to enhance the service and to raise the likelihood that the user will be genuinely interested in the recommendation. This service can be delivered by integrating a frontier-model call into the member-facing pipeline, but it will add extra cost and latency. In this paper, we train a recommender LLM to generate personalized explanations for its reccomendation, based on the user's watching history at a large video streaming service. We impose two requirements on the generated explanation: it must be faithful to the elements of the shows it links, and it must be strictly non-harmful to the user. To this end, we first train two LLM-judge reward models covering three specific criteria, and propose constrained GRPO to incorporate these different criteria. On a held-out real-world testing set, our fine-tuned model improves the all-three-criteria PASS rate rises from 0.649 to 0.956 under our own judges and from 0.677 to 0.931 under an independent judge, where as the frontier generator performs similar to the untuned recommender baseline. We conduct further experiments to show that the model's language and recommendation abilities remain unchanged. Based on these results, we conclude that an LLM-based recommender can be fine-tuned on other complex tasks without compromising its original recommendation performance, thus provide insights for further agentic user interface powered by a single model.

</details>


### [29] [FedV-KGQA in Practice: Design Lessons and an Interactive Prototype](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13661)
*Md Saikat Islam Khan Bappy,Oshani Seneviratne*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FedV-KGQA enables multi-hop question answering over vertically partitioned knowledge graphs where different organizations hold disjoint relation types, using federated learning without sharing raw triples or relation embeddings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In practice, knowledge graphs are often vertically partitioned across organizations that share entity identifiers but have disjoint relation types. No single party can see complete reasoning chains, making traditional centralized KGQA approaches infeasible while preserving data privacy.

Method: Each silo (organization) enriches its local graph and trains knowledge graph embeddings on its own triples. A server concatenates silo-specific entity views, anchors projected questions at topic entities, and ranks candidates by similarity while keeping raw triples and relation embeddings private within each silo.

Result: Three key findings: 1) Federated fusion recovers most centralized accuracy while single silos recover little, 2) Anchoring and enrichment matter more than embedding model choice, 3) Cheapest encoder depends on target accuracy rather than parameter count.

Conclusion: FedV-KGQA demonstrates viable federated KGQA over vertically partitioned graphs with practical design lessons, enabling collaborative question answering while preserving data privacy across organizations.

Abstract: Knowledge graph question answering usually assumes that one system can reach the whole graph. In practice, facts are often held by organizations that share entity identifiers but own disjoint relation types, so no single party sees a complete reasoning chain. This poster presents the empirical findings of FedV-KGQA on multi-hop question answering over such vertically partitioned graphs. Each silo enriches its local graph and trains a knowledge graph embedding on its own triples. A server then concatenates the silo-specific entity views, anchors the projected question at the topic entity, and ranks candidates by similarity. Raw triples and relation embeddings never leave a silo. Comparing the FedV-KGQA experiments with one another yields three results. First, federated fusion recovers most of the centralized accuracy, while a single silo recovers little. Second, anchoring and enrichment matter more than the choice of embedding model. Third, the cheapest encoder depends on the target accuracy rather than on parameter count. This poster paper contributes that cross-experiment comparison, four design lessons drawn from it, and an interactive prototype that runs real inference and traces the full pipeline, per question, on released checkpoints.

</details>


### [30] [Cost Characterization of Vertically Partitioned Federated Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13664)
*Md Saikat Islam Khan Bappy,Oshani Seneviratne*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes vertical partitioning strategies for federated knowledge graphs across organizational silos, finding that the design space reduces to a trade-off between cross-silo path length and load balance, with practical guidance for deployments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Knowledge graphs are distributed across autonomous organizations that share entities but have disjoint relation subsets (vertical partitioning). Multi-hop queries require combining facts from multiple silos, making partitioning strategy a critical decision affecting communication, indexing, load balance, and query latency, but the costs of different strategies remain insufficiently studied.

Method: Formalizes vertical partitioning as a design space and compares four strategies: semantic domain grouping, frequency-balanced partitioning, co-occurrence graph-cut partitioning, and random partitioning. Evaluates using five metrics: communication cost, candidate index size, cross-silo path length, load balance, and end-to-end query latency. Experiments on MetaQA and PathQuestion datasets using a fixed federated knowledge graph QA architecture based on TransE embeddings and frozen BERT encoder across three silo configurations, keeping the learning model unchanged to isolate partitioning effects.

Result: Three of the five evaluation metrics (communication cost, candidate index size, and end-to-end query latency) are determined by the graph structure and silo count rather than the specific partition. This reduces the design problem to two conflicting axes: cross-silo path length and load balance. The trade-off between locality and balance holds only when each silo can hold several relations, and weakens as the number of silos increases.

Conclusion: The study provides practical guidance for deployments constrained by cross-silo reasoning or silo load limitations. By isolating the effect of partitioning strategies while keeping the learning model constant, the research shows that partitioning design essentially involves balancing cross-silo path length against load distribution, with important implications for distributed knowledge graph management.

Abstract: Knowledge graphs are increasingly distributed across autonomous organizations that share an entity space but own disjoint subsets of relations, forming a vertical partition. Answering a multi-hop query may require combining facts from several silos, making the partitioning strategy a key data management decision that affects communication, indexing, load balance, and query latency. However, the costs associated with different partitioning strategies remain insufficiently studied. We formalize vertical partitioning as a design space and compare four strategies: semantic domain grouping, frequency-balanced partitioning, co-occurrence graph-cut partitioning, and random partitioning. We evaluate them using five metrics: communication cost, candidate index size, cross-silo path length, load balance, and end-to-end query latency. Three of the five prove to be determined by the graph and the silo count rather than by the partition, which reduces the design problem to two conflicting axes, cross-silo path length and load balance. Experiments on MetaQA and PathQuestion use a fixed federated knowledge graph question-answering architecture based on TransE embeddings and a frozen BERT encoder across three silo configurations. By keeping the learning model unchanged, we isolate the effect of partitioning and show that the trade-off between locality and balance holds only where each silo can hold several relations, weakening as the number of silos increases. The study provides practical guidance for deployments constrained by cross-silo reasoning or by silo load.

</details>


### [31] [GeoSkill:Experience-Driven Hierarchical Skill Learning with Collaborative Revision forGeospatialAgents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13667)
*Han Luo,Xian Xu,Yinhe Liu,Yanfei Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GeoSkill is a hierarchical skill learning framework that helps geospatial agents transform historical execution experience into reusable planning and tool-usage skills, improving task accuracy and tool reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Geospatial agents need to handle recurring and evolving analytical tasks, but existing memory-augmented approaches struggle to summarize long-horizon tool-chain orchestration experience and tool-level constraints. LLM self-reflection for updating experience often leads to misattribution and unreliable revisions.

Method: GeoSkill has two core components: 1) Hierarchical Skill Bank (HSB) with Planning Skill Bank (high-level task planning) and Tool Skill Bank (tool usage constraints), and 2) Collaborative Trace-driven Skill Revision (CTSR) mechanism where Judge, Critic, and Refiner collaboratively identify errors, localize skill-level defects, and perform targeted modifications.

Result: Experiments on EarthBench and ThinkGeo datasets show GeoSkill effectively transforms historical execution experience into reusable hierarchical skills, improving both end-to-end task accuracy and tool-execution reliability in geospatial tasks.

Conclusion: GeoSkill provides a structured framework for geospatial agents to distill and reuse procedural knowledge from historical executions, addressing the limitations of existing memory-augmented approaches and enabling more reliable and accurate geospatial analysis.

Abstract: Geospatial agents are increasingly expected to support recurring and evolving analytical tasks rather than execute isolated workflows. In such settings, effective agents must distill prior execution experience into reusable geospatial procedural knowledge to guide future planning and tool use. However, existing memory-augmented paradigms struggle to summarize both long-horizon tool-chain orchestration experience and tool-level invocation constraints in geospatial analysis, while directly relying on LLM self-reflection to update experience often leads to misattribution and unreliable revisions. To address these challenges, we propose GeoSkill, an experience-driven hierarchical skill learning framework for geospatial agents. GeoSkill comprises two core components: (i) a Hierarchical Skill Bank (HSB), consisting of a Planning Skill Bank and a Tool Skill Bank, which respectively distill high-level task-planning experience and tool usage constraints, enabling structured representation and cross-task reuse of historical execution experience; and (ii) a Collaborative Trace-driven Skill Revision (CTSR) mechanism, where Judge, Critic, and Refiner collaboratively perform error identification, skill-level defect localization, and targeted modification, preventing misattributed and unreliable revisions from polluting the skill bank. GeoSkill learns and validates skills from historical executions during development, and freezes the skill bank for retrieval-only guidance on unseen tasks during deployment. Extensive experiments on EarthBench and ThinkGeo demonstrate that GeoSkill effectively transforms historical execution experience into reusable hierarchical skills, improving both end-to-end task accuracy and tool-execution reliability in geospatial tasks.

</details>


### [32] [Enhancing Event Candidate Acquisition for Event Linking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13670)
*Ziyang Zhang,Yinan Liu,Boyi Xue,Yingxuan Huang,Bin Wang,Xiaochun Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MACE improves event linking by using specialized LLM agents to refine event structure before candidate acquisition, enhancing accuracy without modifying the linking model itself.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing event linking methods have weaknesses in candidate event acquisition due to: (1) short ambiguous mentions, (2) noisy arguments, and (3) evidence that is unevenly useful for retrieval. These limitations reduce the quality of candidate events fed to linking models.

Method: MACE (Multi-Agent Candidate Event acquisition) uses evidence-specialized LLM agents to acquire time, location, participant, and event-type evidence. The system exposes intermediate queries to candidate-event lookup tools and has a coordinator revise the evidence set before final candidate construction. This refines event structure prior to linking.

Result: Experiments on two event linking benchmarks show that adding MACE to different event linking models consistently improves accuracy. The improvement demonstrates better candidate event acquisition without requiring modifications to the underlying event linking model architecture.

Conclusion: MACE successfully addresses weaknesses in candidate event acquisition through multi-agent refinement of event evidence, providing a generalizable approach to improve event linking performance across different models.

Abstract: Event linking associates event mentions in text with entries in a knowledge base (KB), or identifies them as out-of-KB events. Although existing methods use different architectures, candidate event acquisition can still be weakened by short ambiguous mentions, noisy arguments, and evidence that is unevenly useful for retrieval. We present MACE, a Multi-Agent Candidate Event acquisition method that refines event structure before linking. MACE uses evidence-specialized LLM agents to acquire time, location, participant, and event-type evidence, exposes intermediate queries to candidate-event lookup tools, and lets a coordinator revise the evidence set before final candidate construction. Experiments on two event linking benchmarks show that adding MACE to different event linking models consistently improves accuracy. These results show that MACE improves event linking through better candidate event acquisition without modifying the event linking model.

</details>


### [33] [Recoverability as a System Primitive for Long-Horizon AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13672)
*Zhihui Zhang,Wei Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Recoverability is introduced as a system primitive that makes reuse an explicit decision, requiring selection of supported starting points and permitted recovery actions, with behavioral contracts binding choices to evidence and validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI agent systems lack proper mechanisms for handling interruptions during multi-step tasks. Restarting from scratch wastes completed work, while continuing from unverified or outdated progress can propagate earlier errors forward.

Method: A reference architecture connects persistence, validation, and control with complementary runtime instances testing distinct responsibilities. The approach includes behavioral contracts binding recovery choices to supporting evidence, execution, and independent checks.

Result: Four deterministic and 20 paired file challenges show that accurate restoration and successful completion can conceal disallowed starting points. Event-time tests demonstrate that permission must also constrain actions, and independently held policy evidence can expose violations even after effects occur.

Conclusion: Recovery decisions need their own evaluation beyond restored bytes and final task success. Within supplied policies and declared trust models, the contribution is a common, testable interface for retaining justified progress and making reuse conditions explicit and enforceable.

Abstract: AI agents can be interrupted while editing files, calling tools, or carrying out multi-step tasks. Restarting repeats completed work, but continuing from unverified or outdated progress can carry earlier errors forward. A saved state is not necessarily a suitable place to resume. We introduce recoverability as a system primitive that makes reuse an explicit decision: select a supported starting point and a permitted recovery action, or withhold automatic continuation. Its behavioral contract binds that choice to supporting evidence, execution, and independent checks. A reference architecture connects persistence, validation, and control, with complementary runtime instances testing distinct responsibilities. Four deterministic and 20 paired file challenges demonstrate that accurate restoration and successful completion can conceal disallowed starting points. Progress controls attribute retained work to shared restoration. Event-time tests show that permission must also constrain the action, and that independently held policy evidence can expose violations even after an effect occurs. These findings establish why recovery decisions need their own evaluation, beyond restored bytes and final task success. Within supplied policies and a declared trust model, the contribution is a common, testable interface for retaining justified progress and making the conditions for its reuse explicit and enforceable.

</details>


### [34] [Windowed A-K-MDP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13676)
*Xiangwen Yang,Frankie Cho,Iadine Chades*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Windowed A-K-MDP algorithm fixes A-K-MDP's binary search flaw by evaluating all distinct feasible partitions within a divisor window, improving interpretable MDP generation for conservation management.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MDPs are valuable for conservation decision-making but produce policies that are difficult for managers to interpret, even with small state spaces. The K-MDP approach aims to create simpler, interpretable MDPs but previous A-K-MDP algorithm can miss better abstract states due to its binary search approach.

Method: Proposed Windowed A-K-MDP algorithm that generates every distinct feasible partition induced within a declared divisor window, then evaluates candidates until reaching ideal value loss (J = 0) or exhausting the family of candidates. This avoids the problem where binary search in A-K-MDP can skip better abstract states.

Result: Across 33 K-MDP instances, Windowed A-K-MDP improved 25 cases and tied 8 cases compared to the original A-K-MDP algorithm, demonstrating consistent improvements without any regressions.

Conclusion: Windowed A-K-MDP effectively fixes the binary search flaw in A-K-MDP, providing a more reliable method for generating interpretable MDPs for conservation management by systematically evaluating all feasible partitions within a defined window.

Abstract: Markov decision processes (MDPs) are used to support decision-making in conservation of biodiversity, but policies, even over small state spaces, can be difficult to interpret for conservation managers. K-MDP methods address this problem by building simpler MDPs with at most K abstract states. We show that the previously proposed A-K-MDP algorithm that relies on selecting a discretisation divisor using binary search can skip better abstract states. To fix this issue, we propose Windowed A-K-MDP, an algorithm that generates every distinct feasible partition induced within a declared divisor window and evaluates candidates until reaching the ideal value loss (J = 0) or exhausting the family of candidates. Across 33 K-MDP instances, Windowed improved 25 and tied 8.

</details>


### [35] [Drift-Constrained Optimization: Only Direction Matters in Fine-Tuning Instruct Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13680)
*Fei Yuan,Changjiang Gao,Yilei Tu,Yifeng Liu,Shujian Huang,Yu Qiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Fine-tuning with controlled behavioral drift: Specify a drift budget first, then maximize target performance within it by selecting optimal update directions, revealing that direction matters more than magnitude of change.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuning instruct models often causes behavioral drift that degrades existing capabilities; instead of treating this as an uncontrolled side effect, the authors propose to specify a behavioral drift budget upfront and maximize target-task performance within that constrained space.

Method: Frame fine-tuning as a direction-selection problem: Behavioral drift induces a shared geometry anchored at the reference model, with drift budget defining a boundary. The approach compares fine-tuning updates through directional efficiency and tests predictions in a stringent QA-only setting where models are fine-tuned only on final answers but must generate multi-step reasoning at inference.

Result: Coarse layer-selective probes reveal effective directions that improve target performance while preserving reasoning and general capabilities. Across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, these directions substantially improve scientific reasoning and multilingual translation, matching or outperforming dedicated translation systems across 100+ languages and providing stronger initialization for RL.

Conclusion: Fine-tuning is not just about how much a model changes, but how that change is spent - strategic direction selection within a drift budget can qualitatively alter outcomes and preserve existing capabilities while improving target performance.

Abstract: Fine-tuning instruct models often improves target performance while inducing behavioral drift from the reference model, which can degrade existing capabilities. Rather than treating this drift as an uncontrolled consequence of optimization, we specify a behavioral drift budget before optimization and ask how to boost the target-task performance within it. Locally, behavioral drift induces a shared geometry anchored at the reference model, with the drift budget defining a boundary within this space. In this space, drift determines distance from the reference, leaving update direction as the remaining degree of freedom. Fine-tuning updates can therefore be compared through their directional efficiency, naturally reformulating fine-tuning as a direction-selection problem. This reformulation makes a concrete prediction: changing the accessible directions can qualitatively alter the outcome of fine-tuning. We test this prediction in a stringent QA-only setting, where strong instruct models are fine-tuned only on final answers but must still generate multi-step reasoning at inference. Despite this mismatch, a coarse layer-selective probe reverses the failure of QA-only fine-tuning and reveals the existence of effective directions, with multiple neighboring configurations improving target performance while preserving reasoning and general capabilities. Across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, these directions substantially improve scientific reasoning and multilingual translation. Over more than 100 languages, the resulting models match or outperform dedicated translation systems and provide a stronger initialization for subsequent reinforcement learning. Our results suggest that fine-tuning is not just about how much a model changes, but how that change is spent. https://github.com/CONE-MT/DCO and https://huggingface.co/collections/LLaMAX/dco

</details>


### [36] [Degraded but Not Entirely Ineffective: PE-Based Deformable Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13712)
*Jinhua Wu,Xinliang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes PEBDSAM/PEBSAM, a deformable position encoding-based module that addresses multiple GNN limitations (over-smoothing, over-compression, fixed neighborhoods, heterophily issues) in one step through flexible spatial aggregation beyond first-order neighbors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional GNNs have fundamental limitations: depth causes over-smoothing, long-range dependencies cause over-compression, fixed neighborhoods restrict receptive fields, and on heterophilous graphs, topological neighbors introduce noise. While individual solutions exist, few address all these challenges simultaneously.

Method: Proposed Position Encoding-Based Deformable Spatial Aggregation Module (PEBDSAM) uses deformable mechanism in position space to identify relevant nodes beyond first-order neighbors. After diagnostic experiments showed offset failures, streamlined to Position Encoding-Based Spatial Aggregation Module (PEBSAM) and PEBSAM-Speed for large datasets. Module is plug-and-play.

Result: Diagnostic experiments revealed current offsets fail but model performance still improves, pointing to future research. Applied to GCN, GAT, GIN, and GraphSAGE, achieving good results on three homophilous and six heterophilous graph datasets.

Conclusion: PEBSAM successfully addresses multiple fundamental GNN limitations in one step through flexible position-based aggregation, works across various GNN architectures and datasets (both homophilous and heterophilous), and provides insights for future deformable mechanism research.

Abstract: Many real-world scenarios can be represented using graph-structured data. However, traditional GNNs that transmit messages based on first-order neighbors have long faced several fundamental contradictions: increasing depth leads to over-smoothing, long-range dependencies cause over-compression, fixed neighborhoods restrict the receptive field, and on heterophilous graphs, topological neighbors become a source of noise. Although many works have addressed these issues individually, few mechanisms can simultaneously alleviate all of these challenges. To address the aforementioned problems, we propose a Position Encoding-Based Deformable Spatial Aggregation Module (PEBDSAM) that solves them all in one step. Specifically, we utilize a deformable mechanism in the position space to identify relevant nodes to supplement the original first-order neighbor information of GNNs, allowing traditional GNNs to adapt to heterophilous scenarios. Through diagnostic experiments, we obtained several major findings: current offsets fail to have any effect; subsequently, we analyzed the causes of offset failure and why model performance still improves even after offset failure, pointing out future research directions. Based on these diagnostic experiments, we streamlined the original PEBDSAM, resulting in a simplified version, which we call the Position Encoding-Based Spatial Aggregation Module (PEBSAM). In addition, we propose a PEBSAM-Speed to adapt to large datasets. Finally, we designed the module to be plug-and-play and applied it to GCN, GAT, GIN, and GraphSAGE, achieving desirable results on three homophilous datasets and six heterophilous graph datasets.

</details>


### [37] [JaxAHT: A JAX-Based Library for Ad Hoc Teamwork](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13716)
*Caroline Wang,Rolando Fernandez,Zelal Su Mustafaoglu,Montek Kundan,Jiaxun Cui,Lingyun Xiao,Zhihan Wang,Di Yang Shi,Aditya Madhan,Johnny Liu,Arrasy Rahman,Peter Stone*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JaxAHT is a new JAX-based open-source library that accelerates Ad Hoc Teamwork research by providing standardized benchmarks, diverse teammate suites, and massive parallelization with 95x speedup over PyTorch.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ad Hoc Teamwork research faces three major challenges: prohibitive computational costs, lack of standardized benchmark implementations, and absence of diverse, validated evaluation teammate suites. These bottlenecks hinder progress in the field.

Method: Developed JaxAHT, a JAX-based library leveraging hardware acceleration and massive parallelization. The library provides a unified framework for teammate generation, ego agent training, and evaluation against unseen teammates. Also created diverse evaluation teammate suites across Level-Based Foraging, Overcooked, and Hanabi domains.

Result: Achieved approximately 95x wall-clock speedup over PyTorch counterparts. Using the framework, conducted a large-scale benchmark study comparing teammate generation and AHT agent learning methods. Found that no algorithm consistently performs best, and that agent modeling primarily benefits role-based scenarios with diverse teammates.

Conclusion: JaxAHT successfully addresses key bottlenecks in AHT research by accelerating computational workflows, providing standardization, and enabling large-scale evaluation. The framework reveals important insights about algorithm performance and the limited benefits of agent modeling to specific scenarios.

Abstract: Ad Hoc Teamwork (AHT) addresses the challenge of designing agents capable of coordinating with novel partners without prior coordination. However, progress in the field is hindered by the prohibitive computational cost of the AHT research lifecycle, the lack of standardized benchmark implementations, and the absence of a diverse, validated evaluation teammate suite. In this work, we introduce JaxAHT, the first open-source, JAX-based library designed to accelerate and standardize the AHT research lifecycle. Leveraging JAX's hardware acceleration and massive parallelization capabilities, JaxAHT provides a unified framework for teammate generation, ego agent training, and evaluation against unseen teammates, achieving approximately 95x wall-clock speedup over PyTorch counterparts. Alongside the library, we contribute a diverse suite of evaluation teammates across the domains of Level-Based Foraging, Overcooked, and Hanabi. To illustrate the value of the framework, we use it to conduct a large-scale, compute-controlled benchmark study comparing teammate generation and AHT agent learning methods, finding that no algorithm consistently performs best, and that agent modeling primarily offers benefits in role-based scenarios with diverse teammates.

</details>


### [38] [MANAS-2: Constrained Reconstruction for EEG Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13717)
*Arvasu Kulkarni,Aditya Ray Mishra,Mahir Jain,Parshva Runwal,Lakshya Saini,Siddharth Panwar,Sandeep Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MANAS-2 introduces Constrained Reconstruction (ConRec), a physics-based regularizer for EEG foundation models that improves spectral organization and transfer learning by penalizing unnatural energy fluctuations in reconstructed waveforms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard masked reconstruction for EEG foundation models often focuses on low-SNR waveform reconstruction, which doesn't necessarily produce optimal latent representations for downstream tasks. The authors aim to create more useful and spectrally organized latent spaces.

Method: Combines a Raw-Band Hybrid (RBH) masked autoencoder with Constrained Reconstruction (ConRec). RBH reconstructs both temporal waveform patches and spectral-band targets. ConRec is a physics-motivated regularizer that penalizes differences in RMS energy between adjacent short windows of the reconstructed temporal waveform, encouraging organization of oscillatory-envelope information.

Result: Adding ConRec improved frozen ridge recovery of six-band spectral power from R^2=0.860 to 0.906 and inter-patch band-energy dynamics from R^2=0.283 to 0.354. MANAS-2 outperforms leading EEG foundation models on most downstream knowledge-transfer tasks and shows architecture-independent improvements even when applied to temporal-only models.

Conclusion: Physically motivated constraints imposed through the decoder can create more spectrally organized and transferable latent spaces. MANAS-2 demonstrates that constrained reconstruction can shape representation quality rather than just reconstruction quality, providing a new approach for EEG foundation models.

Abstract: Masked reconstruction is widely used for EEG foundation models, but optimizing reconstruction on low-SNR waveforms does not necessarily produce the most useful latent representation. We introduce MANAS-2, a new EEG foundation model that combines a Raw-Band Hybrid (RBH) masked autoencoder with Constrained Reconstruction (ConRec), a physics-motivated regularizer. RBH jointly reconstructs temporal waveform patches and compact spectral-band targets, while ConRec acts only on the temporal decoder output, penalizing differences in RMS energy between adjacent short windows of the reconstructed waveform. ConRec is intended to shape the encoder by biasing it toward the organization of oscillatory-envelope information. Across seven held-out EEG datasets, adding ConRec to an otherwise identical RBH model increases frozen ridge recovery of six-band spectral power from mean R^2=0.860 to 0.906 and recovery of inter-patch band-energy dynamics from R^2=0.283 to 0.354, while temporal waveform information remains highly recoverable from the frozen latents. Applied to a temporal-only masked autoencoder, ConRec also improves frozen downstream transfer and frequency-dependent latent geometry despite receiving no spectral targets: i.e., the effects of ConRec are architecture-independent. MANAS-2 also outperforms leading EEG Foundation Models on most downstream knowledge-transfer tasks. From the effects of ConRec, we see that a physically motivated constraint imposed through the decoder can make for a more spectrally organized and transferable latent space. MANAS-2 therefore provides a new EEG foundation model built around constrained reconstruction as a mechanism for shaping representation--rather than reconstruction--quality.

</details>


### [39] [IBBench-Light: A Paired Evaluation of Task-Conditioned Responses to External Directives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13725)
*Kainan Zhou,Gangzhen Qian,Zhaoyi Li,Hang Xiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IBBench-Light is a benchmark that tests instruction models on both procedural execution and text processing tasks using the same records, using paired exact-contract accuracy to measure performance more accurately than marginal averages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to create a more accurate benchmark for instruction-following models that tests both execution and processing tasks against the same records, addressing limitations of traditional metrics that use marginal averages which can mask performance issues when both types of tasks need to be performed correctly.

Method: IBBench-Light uses 12 semantic bases to create 144 matched pairs per model, testing both procedure execution and text processing. It employs Paired Exact-Contract Accuracy (PECA) requiring both task types to satisfy output contracts. The study includes auditing literal-target exposure, case normalization, adding 1,722 CPU generations as controls, testing within-base wording changes, generation stopping, and comparing with IHEval using the same SmolLM2 checkpoint.

Result: Results show Qwen succeeds on 132 execution and 109 processing prompts individually, but only 97 complete pairs, revealing what marginal averages omit. Changing EOS sets in Phi models dramatically changes exact paired success from 0/144 to 62/144, showing the critical importance of generation stopping policies on benchmark performance.

Conclusion: The benchmark effectively measures conditional task and output-contract success, revealing that performance evaluation must consider both task margins and paired counts together with stopping policies, as models may perform well on individual tasks but fail when both need to be performed correctly from the same records.

Abstract: An external record may contain a procedure to apply or text to read, depending on the user's request. IBBench-Light tests both uses against the same record. Twelve semantic bases yield 144 matched pairs per model; four quantized instruction models produced 1,152 archived greedy responses. Paired exact-contract accuracy (PECA) requires both members to satisfy their output contracts. Qwen succeeds on 132 execute and 109 process prompts, but only 97 complete pairs, showing what marginal averages omit. We audit literal-target exposure and case normalization, then add 1,722 logged CPU generations to test directive-absent controls, twelve additional semantic bases, within-base wording changes, and generation stopping. In the pinned Phi rerun, changing the end-of-sequence (EOS) set changes exact paired success from 0/144 to 62/144. A bounded IHEval comparison uses the same SmolLM2 checkpoint and output budget while preserving its published instruction roles and scorer. The benchmark measures conditional task and output-contract success. Its task margins and paired count need to be read together with the stopping policy.

</details>


### [40] [Trustworthy Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Cybersecurity and Systems Survey on Threat Landscapes, Defense Architectures, and Open Challenges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13731)
*Seyedakbar Mostafavi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Survey paper developing a comprehensive security framework for autonomous AI agent systems, covering threat analysis, defense architectures, and governance mapping.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The transition from passive foundation models to autonomous agentic AI systems introduces unprecedented security risks as these systems gain execution authority across various infrastructure while using natural language as both data and control code, creating a Turing-complete blast radius where untrusted data becomes executable instructions.

Method: The authors conducted a comprehensive survey synthesizing 206 foundational studies and regulatory standards. They formalized agent architecture as a stateful 5-tuple, established a 6-dimensional trustworthiness taxonomy, systematically analyzed threat surfaces, formulated multi-layered defense-in-depth architecture, reviewed standardized evaluation benchmarks, and mapped controls to international AI governance frameworks.

Result: Developed a complete systems-security reference framework for trustworthy agentic AI that includes formal architectural definitions, comprehensive threat analysis, a zero-trust defense architecture with components like Dual-LLM isolation, Capability-Based Access Control, kernel eBPF probes, sandboxed runtimes, and connections to international governance standards.

Conclusion: The paper provides a foundational security framework for the emerging field of autonomous AI agents, addressing critical gaps in securing systems that combine recursive reasoning, persistent memory, tool execution, and multi-agent collaboration, with proposed solutions spanning technical controls to governance alignment.

Abstract: The transition from passive foundation models to autonomous, goal-directed agentic AI systems has introduced unprecedented capabilities by coupling recursive cognitive reasoning loops, persistent memory architectures, live tool execution planes, and multi-agent collaboration topologies. However, granting probabilistic neural cores execution authority across filesystems, networks, and cloud infrastructure dissolves classical security perimeters: natural language simultaneously serves as input data, internal control code, and communication protocols, exposing a Turing-complete blast radius where untrusted data represents executable instructions. This survey delivers a comprehensive systems-security reference framework for trustworthy agentic AI, synthesizing 206 foundational studies and regulatory standards. We formalize the general agent architecture as a stateful 5-tuple and establish a 6-dimensional trustworthiness taxonomy covering security, safety, privacy, explainability, fairness, and accountability. We systematically analyze threat surfaces across intra-execution loops and interaction planes, formulate a multi-layered zero-trust defense-in-depth architecture integrating Dual-LLM isolation, Capability-Based Access Control, kernel eBPF probes, and sandboxed runtimes, review standardized evaluation benchmarks, and map technical controls to international AI governance frameworks.

</details>


### [41] [How Many Thoughts Can a Vector Hold? The Capacity of Reasoning by Superposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13747)
*Hongyu Gu,Chang Liu,Jingwen Fu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Cumulative superposition of full reasoning history in continuous thought representations can require lower dimensions than frontier-only approaches, enabling more reliable latent reasoning with fixed capacity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent methods move partial computations into fixed-dimensional latent states for continuous reasoning, raising a fundamental design question: what should continuous thoughts preserve as reasoning proceeds? Intuition suggests discarding past computations and keeping only the current frontier to avoid dilution, but this intuition may be incorrect.

Method: Theoretical analysis of superposition in latent reasoning states, comparing cumulative superposition (retaining full reasoning history) versus frontier-only superposition (holding only current alternatives). Proves that under identical downstream computations, cumulative superposition can require lower representational dimensions. Also addresses memory weighting in reusable weighted superpositions.

Result: Cumulative superposition retaining full reasoning history can require lower representational dimensions than frontier-only approaches. At fixed hidden width, this allows latent reasoners to retain more valid evidence, distinguish more plausible downstream outcomes, and delay unreliable state compression. Uniform cumulative weighting is proven minimax-optimal for robust future reasoning, avoiding bottlenecks from prioritizing recent or salient items.

Conclusion: Balanced cumulative memory turns superposition from an observed effect into a design principle: a fixed representational budget can support more reliable, reusable computations through cumulative superposition rather than frontier-only approaches. This provides theoretical foundations for designing more effective continuous reasoning systems.

Abstract: Large language models solve hard problems through intermediate computations across multi-step reasoning. Traditional chain-of-thought encodes these computations as tokens. Recent continuous and recurrent methods instead move partial computations into fixed-dimensional latent states, where a single thought can superpose multiple alternatives. This raises a fundamental design question:what should continuous thoughts preserve as reasoning proceeds? An intuitive approach discards past computations and keeps only the current reasoning frontier. Storing more items seems to dilute states and waste limited representational capacity. We show this intuition can be incorrect. Under identical downstream computations, cumulative superposition retaining full reasoning history can require lower representational dimensions than frontier-only superposition holding only current alternatives. At fixed hidden width, this advantage allows latent reasoners to retain more valid evidence, distinguish more plausible downstream outcomes, and delay the point where compressed states turn unreliable. This counter-intuitive effect emerges because informative historical components coherently reinforce each other, while unrelated alternatives bring random interference. This perspective also answers a practical design question: how should models weight memories accumulated inside latent states when their future use is unknown? Across reusable weighted superpositions, prioritizing a small set of recent or salient items produces weakly-represented memories that bottleneck subsequent attention. Uniform cumulative weighting avoids this flaw, and we prove it is minimax-optimal for robust future reasoning. Our results turn superposition from an observed latent-space effect into a design principle: balanced cumulative memory lets a fixed representational budget support more reliable, reusable computations.

</details>


### [42] [Positioning manuscripts in the scientific landscape with agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13760)
*Jiawen Chen,Zichen Zhang,Bingxuan Li,Quan Sun,Yiyan Zhang,Edric Tam,Jinjie Lin,Didong Li,Yun Li,Bingxin Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PASS (Publication-oriented Agentic Scientific System) is an AI agent that predicts suitable publication venues for research manuscripts by analyzing content and literature context, achieving 50.3% Top-1 and 86.1% Top-5 accuracy across biomedical fields.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The publication process is time-consuming, stressful, and uncertain. Recent LLM advances show promise for scientific tasks, but there's a need for AI systems that can help researchers navigate publication by reliably predicting suitable venues based on manuscript content and literature context.

Method: PASS positions manuscripts within their domain-specific literature context by: 1) reconstructing local scientific neighborhoods, 2) tracing topic trajectories, and 3) reasoning over field-specific journal spaces. It uses a literature retrieval module as a key component, evaluated on leakage-audited benchmark of 2,000+ preprints across 16 biomedical fields.

Result: PASS achieved 50.3% Top-1 and 86.1% Top-5 accuracy, outperforming SOTA LLM baselines and journal-selection tools. Literature retrieval module was strongest performance contributor. System maintained near-full performance from abstracts alone (vs. baselines needing full text). Quality scores aligned with independent publication outcome measures. Human evaluation showed strong researcher agreement.

Conclusion: Agentic AI systems like PASS can effectively help researchers navigate publication by understanding manuscripts in literature context and predicting suitable venues, with strong performance and researcher agreement. The public platform (ratemypaper.ai) provides broad access to this capability.

Abstract: Publishing a research manuscript is a routine yet demanding part of scientific life: time-consuming, stressful, and often uncertain in outcome. Recent advances in large language model (LLM)-based agentic AI have shown promise across a range of scientific tasks, and here we ask whether agentic AI can help researchers navigate the publication process itself by reliably inferring a manuscript's eventual publication venue from its content and literature context. We introduce PASS (Publication-oriented Agentic Scientific System), an agentic system that understands manuscripts within their domain-specific literature context and predicts top-matched publication venues. PASS positions each manuscript within its surrounding literature landscape by reconstructing its local scientific neighborhood, tracing its topic trajectory, and reasoning over field-specific journal spaces. Evaluated on a leakage-audited benchmark of over 2,000 preprints across 16 biomedical fields, PASS achieved Top-1 accuracy of 50.3% and Top-5 accuracy of 86.1%, outperforming state-of-the-art LLM baselines and established journal-selection tools. PASS-produced quality scores, such as impact potential and novelty, aligned with independent measures of publication outcome. We also found that the designed literature retrieval module is the strongest performance contributor, particularly for positioning manuscripts relative to nearby work, and that PASS maintained near-full performance from the abstract alone, whereas LLM baselines required the full manuscript text. An independent human evaluation found strong researcher agreement with PASS's manuscript understanding and recommendation rationale. PASS has been released as a public platform (https://ratemypaper.ai/) for broad researcher access.

</details>


### [43] [Homeostatic Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13771)
*Yue Jin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes "Homeostatic Continual Learning" - a method for AI agents to learn continuously in changing environments without catastrophic forgetting by detecting and adapting to outliers in environmental data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for AI agents to learn continuously in changing environments without catastrophic forgetting, which is a fundamental challenge in continual learning where neural networks tend to forget previously learned knowledge when exposed to new data.

Method: "Homeostatic Continual Learning" method that enables agents to detect outliers in environment data when experiencing outliers in their output. The method helps agents gradually complete their model and policy by adapting to new contexts while retaining previous knowledge.

Result: The method enables AI agents to perform well in increasingly diverse contexts by avoiding catastrophic forgetting. The paper also discusses extending this approach to build a world model where agents factorize objects into features, abstract objects into comparable concept instances, and map concepts to intents through features.

Conclusion: The Homeostatic Continual Learning method provides a promising approach to continual learning without catastrophic forgetting. The paper discusses practical implementation considerations, connections to various AI fields, and broader implications of the method for developing more robust and adaptable AI systems.

Abstract: In this paper, I formulate a Continual Learning problem and propose a method named "Homeostatic Continual Learning" that enables an AI agent to learn continuously in a changing environment without catastrophic forgetting. The core of the method is to find outliers in the environment data when the agent experiences an outlier in its output. Through this method, the agent gradually completes its model and policy and performs well in more and more contexts. I also suggest that we may use the method to build a world model where the agent factorizes the objects in the world into features, abstract objects into comparable instances of concepts and map concepts to intents through features. I discuss the works needed to render the method practical, the connections to many fields in Artificial Intelligence and the broader implications of the method.

</details>


### [44] [Surprising Effectiveness of Self-Demonstrations in Enhancing Schema-Ontology Mapping with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13776)
*Siddhesh Thombre,Manasi Patwardhan,Sunita Sarawagi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A self-demonstration-driven neuro-symbolic approach that combines task decomposition and pattern-guided demonstration generation achieves SOTA performance for schema-ontology mapping, outperforming existing methods by 25 F1 points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The persistent challenge of integrating heterogeneous relational databases into centralized ontologies due to semantic heterogeneity, cryptic schema naming, missing metadata, and the abstraction gap between relational schemas and ontological models.

Method: A self-demonstration-driven approach with two key strategies: (1) neuro-symbolic decomposition of the task into cascaded sub-tasks using symbolic constraints to structure search space and LLMs for semantic reasoning in each sub-task, and (2) self-generated demonstrations guided by domain-agnostic patterns to supervise each sub-task.

Result: Experiments on three most challenging scenarios from RODI benchmark show state-of-the-art performance, substantially outperforming traditional schema-to-ontology mapping techniques and recent LLM-based approaches by 25 percentage points F1 improvements.

Conclusion: The proposed approach effectively addresses schema-ontology integration challenges through neuro-symbolic task decomposition and pattern-guided self-demonstrations, demonstrating significant performance gains over existing methods.

Abstract: Integrating heterogeneous relational databases into a centralized ontology remains a persistent challenge in enterprise knowledge representation, primarily due to semantic heterogeneity, cryptic schema naming, missing metadata, and the abstraction gap between relational schemas and ontological models. Although large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic reasoning capabilities, we show that directly applying them through one-shot prompting or naive multi-stage pipelines leads to poor performance for schema-ontology mapping. This paper presents a self-demonstration-driven approach that combines a neuro-symbolic task decomposition with a novel mechanism for automatically generating pattern-guided, dependency-aware demonstrations to address this integration challenge. Our approach incorporates two key strategies to achieve substantial accuracy gains over existing LLM-based schema integration methods: (i) a neuro-symbolic decomposition of the task into cascaded sub-tasks, where symbolic constraints structure the search space and LLMs perform semantic reasoning within each focused sub-task, and (ii) self-generated demonstrations guided by domain-agnostic patterns to supervise each sub-task. Experiments on three of the most challenging scenarios from the RODI benchmark show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, substantially outperforming (25 percentage points F1 improvements) both traditional schema-to-ontology mapping techniques and recent LLM-based schema-to-ontology and schema matching approaches. Ablation studies further reveal the significant benefits of pattern-guided self-demonstrations and the complementary benefits of neuro-symbolic task decomposition.

</details>


### [45] [Partition Scores Are Not System Scores: Deployment-Fidelity Gaps in Decomposed Algorithm Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13785)
*Jiachen Zhang,Yu Tang,Li Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper examines the "deployment-fidelity gap" in decomposed algorithm selection, showing that partition-level oracle scores overestimate deployable performance, and proposes reporting both partition and end-to-end scores alongside diagnostic corrections.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Oracle-style quantities in algorithm selection (like virtual best solvers) are widely reported as upper bounds, but in decomposed algorithm selection, partition-level oracle scores don't reflect what's achievable by deployable systems, creating a gap between reported bounds and actual deployable performance.

Method: Defined the deployment-fidelity gap G(R) as difference between partition-level and deployable end-to-end utility; derived mathematical conditions for deployment optimality; conducted empirical evaluation across five public algorithm-selection benchmarks covering tabular AutoML and combinatorial CSP/SAT problems; implemented a training-side validation gap-correction diagnostic.

Result: Every decomposed pipeline showed positive deployment-fidelity gap (ranging from 0.012 to 0.13). Four of ten decomposed-versus-flat decisions had sign-changing point estimates (partition advantage reversed in end-to-end). On PROTEUS-2014, a 33-point partition advantage shrunk to 20-point end-to-end advantage. The diagnostic successfully recovered the deployable sign on all sign-changing cases.

Conclusion: Partition-level reports alone are insufficient for certifying deployable performance; both partition and end-to-end scores should be reported side-by-side; the proposed gap-correction diagnostic helps but doesn't replace direct end-to-end evaluation.

Abstract: Oracle-style quantities, including virtual best solvers, selected-portfolio VBS, virtual-best encodings, and best-in-family summaries, are widely reported as upper bounds on what a deployable selector could achieve. In decomposed algorithm selection, an analogous partition-level score grants an oracle choice of the best algorithm within the selected family; once the family selector is fixed, the deployable system must replace that within-family oracle with a learned within-family selector.
  We define the deployment-fidelity gap G(R) as the difference between partition-level and deployable end-to-end utility and derive two accounting consequences: a per-instance margin-regret stability condition that tells us when a partition-time family choice is deployment-optimal, and a sharp partition-only identification interval that, when it strictly crosses zero, prevents the partition-level report from certifying the deployable winner.
  Across five public algorithm-selection benchmarks spanning tabular AutoML and combinatorial CSP/SAT, every decomposed pipeline has positive G(R), ranging from 0.012 on TabZilla to 0.13 on PROTEUS-2014. Four of ten decomposed-versus-flat decisions have sign-changing point estimates; on PROTEUS-2014, a 33-point partition advantage shrinks to a 20-point end-to-end advantage. A training-side validation gap-correction diagnostic recovers the point-estimate deployable sign on all four sign-changing cells; it is a reporting aid, not a substitute for direct end-to-end evaluation. Partition and end-to-end scores should be reported side by side.

</details>


### [46] [Do Not Restart: Residual Completion for Stateful Agent Handoffs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13800)
*Runzhi Deng,Yiming Zhong,Fang Zhao,Pan Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CFRC is a method for efficient AI tool-agent routing that reduces inference costs by 66-78% while maintaining comparable accuracy to full-task agents, through commitment-constrained residual completion with stateful handoffs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Routing and cascades between models can reduce tool-agent costs, but stateful handoffs must preserve choices, effects, and obligations. Current approaches need better mechanisms to ensure correct transfer of control while maintaining commitments.

Method: CFRC (Commitment-Frontier Residual Completion) enforces three constraints: target-before-proposal, whole-proposal-before-authority, and live-evidence-before-success. It freezes residual contracts from accepted progress, closes successor continuations into evidence-linked graphs, and admits execution only when the remainder is covered by live receipts that discharge obligations.

Result: CFRC achieves 22.0%-34.6% of the inference cost of full-task agents while maintaining comparable macro accuracy across five environments and two same-provider model pairs. Cross-provider results show broader transfer capability.

Conclusion: CFRC provides a formal approach to commitment-constrained residual completion that enables efficient model routing with proven contract-relative partial correctness, extending to original residual requests under complete contract construction, offering significant cost savings with maintained accuracy.

Abstract: Routing and cascades reduce tool-agent cost by transferring control across models, but stateful handoffs must preserve accepted choices, realized effects, and unfinished obligations. We formulate this as commitment-constrained residual completion and introduce Commitment-Frontier Residual Completion (CFRC). CFRC enforces target-before-proposal, whole-proposal-before-authority, and live-evidence-before-success: it freezes a residual contract from accepted progress, closes the successor continuation into an evidence-linked graph, and admits execution only when the remainder is covered, with live receipts discharging obligations. We establish contract-relative partial correctness, which extends to the original residual request under complete contract construction. Across five environments and two same-provider model pairs, CFRC achieves comparable macro accuracy to strong full-task agents at only 22.0%-34.6% of their inference cost, with additional cross-provider results demonstrating broader transfer.

</details>


### [47] [LLM-Enhanced Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Unified Electric Vehicles-Charging Station-Grid Optimization in Public Charging Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13805)
*Yang Zhang,Lindong Xie,Chongyu Wang,Gaojunjie Li,Siqi Bu,Edward Chung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes an LLM-enhanced Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework for optimizing electric vehicle charging scheduling in IoT environments, addressing multi-objective optimization challenges for grid stability, EV satisfaction, and station profitability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MARL approaches struggle with high-dimensional IoT data states and conflicting stakeholder interests (EV charging satisfaction, station profitability, grid stability), creating a complex multi-objective optimization problem that needs better interpretability and adaptive balancing.

Method: The authors propose a novel LLM-enhanced MARL framework that integrates Large Language Models to address two key bottlenecks: interpretable feature selection from real-time IoT sensing data and adaptive multi-objective balancing through semantic reasoning. The framework simultaneously optimizes Grid, EVs, and Stations in a unified loop.

Result: Extensive experiments show the framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving superior market efficiency while reducing training time by over 70%. It offers improved performance in balancing profit, user satisfaction, and grid load.

Conclusion: The LLM-enhanced MARL framework provides a scalable, transparent solution for efficient and sustainable IoT-enabled urban charging infrastructure management, successfully addressing the complex multi-objective optimization challenge through interpretable feature selection and adaptive objective balancing.

Abstract: In the era of the Internet of Things (IoT), coordinating connected electric vehicle (EV) charging scheduling to balance EV charging satisfaction, station profitability, and smart grid stability presents a complex multi-objective challenge. Existing Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) approaches often struggle with high-dimensional state spaces generated by massive IoT sensing data and conflicting stakeholder interests. This paper proposes a novel LLM-enhanced MARL framework that, for the first time, simultaneously optimizes the Grid, EVs, and Stations within a unified loop. By integrating Large Language Model (LLM), we address two critical bottlenecks: interpretable feature selection and adaptive multi-objective balancing. The LLM analyzes real-time IoT-collected environmental states to extract physically significant features and dynamically assigns weights to conflicting objectives-including profit, user satisfaction, and grid load-using semantic reasoning instead of complex manual tuning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving superior market efficiency while reducing training time by over 70%. This approach offers a scalable, transparent solution for efficient and sustainable IoT-enabled urban charging infrastructure management.

</details>


### [48] [Bypass Observation: A Conceptual Design of a Non-Intrusive Layer-Wise Semantic Extraction Architecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13807)
*Haibin Tong,Jiang Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Bypass Observation introduces a non-intrusive readout architecture for Transformer models that attaches observation heads to selected layers without affecting the main computation flow, enabling monitoring of hidden states during reasoning with minimal overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models reason in high-dimensional hidden-state spaces that are opaque to users, who only see final outputs. There's a need to make model computation more observable without disrupting the main inference process.

Method: Proposes a non-intrusive layer-wise readout architecture with three variants: shared LM head across layers, layer-specific heads, and layer- or step-adaptive head. The approach attaches read-only observation heads to selected Transformer layers without feeding outputs back into the backbone. Discusses optimizations including sparse observation, low-rank factorization, reduced vocabularies, top-k readout, and selective positions to reduce overhead.

Result: Derived a closed-form overhead approximation governed primarily by V/(12d), with representative estimates ranging from about 30% to 240%. Distinguished bypass chain-of-thought from conventional chain-of-thought, where bypass readouts remain causally external at inference time. Proposed applications to looped and recurrent-depth Transformers for iteration-wise readout of convergence, oscillation, and halting signals.

Conclusion: Bypass Observation can make model computation more observable while remaining a partial and potentially misleading projection of hidden states. The approach is conceptual and analytical, with systematic empirical validation needed as future work. The architecture enables monitoring without disrupting inference and has potential applications in analyzing model reasoning processes.

Abstract: Large language models reason in high-dimensional hidden-state spaces, while users observe only final outputs. We introduce Bypass Observation, a non-intrusive layer-wise readout architecture that attaches read-only observation heads to selected Transformer layers without feeding their outputs back into the backbone. We consider three variants: a shared LM head across layers, layer-specific heads, and a layer- or step-adaptive head. For full-vocabulary readout, we derive a closed-form overhead approximation governed primarily by V/(12d), with representative estimates ranging from about 30% to 240%, and discuss cost reductions via sparse observation, low-rank factorization, reduced vocabularies, top-k readout, and selective positions. We argue that Bypass Observation can make model computation more observable while remaining only a partial, potentially misleading projection of hidden states. We further distinguish bypass chain-of-thought from conventional chain-of-thought: conventional reasoning tokens enter the autoregressive computation, whereas bypass readouts remain causally external at inference time, although they can still provide training signals in reinforcement learning. Finally, we discuss applications to looped and recurrent-depth Transformers, where iteration-wise readout may expose convergence, oscillation, and potential halting signals. The proposal is conceptual and analytical; systematic empirical validation remains future work.

</details>


### [49] [ViperQ: Order Flow Pattern Recognition via Auction Market Theory for Reinforcement Learning Trading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13825)
*Asser Moustafa,Rares-Mihail Neagu,Jugal Kalita*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ViperQ is a reinforcement learning trading system that uses Auction Market Theory features as state representation and achieves strong returns on Tesla and NVIDIA with zero leverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL trading systems rely on price-aggregate OHLCV bars or limit-order-book features, leaving practitioner microstructure pattern theories like Auction Market Theory without computational instantiation in academic literature.

Method: ViperQ uses Auction Market Theory primitives (Volume Point of Control, Value Area position, Low Volume Node flags, Cumulative Volume Delta divergence, tape-velocity signatures) assembled into 20D Z-normalized vector. Two Proximal Policy Optimization agents trained with prospect theory-grounded asymmetric reward function using Kahneman-Tversky loss-aversion coefficient.

Result: On held-out 12-month institutional tick data: +163.6% ROI on TSLA (-27.5% max drawdown, 27,019 trades) and +116.5% ROI on NVDA (-47.8% max drawdown, 12,892 trades) with zero leverage.

Conclusion: Auction Market Theory features are tractable structured inputs for sequential decision-making on financial time series, motivating further work on microstructure-aware policy learning.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning trading systems published in the academic literature overwhelmingly rely on price-aggregate state representations (OHLCV bars) or limit-order-book depth features, leaving microstructure pattern theories from the practitioner literature, namely Auction Market Theory and Market Profile, without a peer-reviewed computational instantiation. We present ViperQ, a reinforcement learning system whose state representation is built explicitly from Auction Market Theory primitives: Volume Point of Control, Value Area position, Low Volume Node flags, Cumulative Volume Delta divergence, and tape-velocity signatures, assembled into a 20-dimensional Z-normalised vector. Two Proximal Policy Optimisation agents are trained with a prospect theory-grounded asymmetric reward function that penalises losing holds at a magnitude consistent with Kahneman and Tversky's loss-aversion coefficient. Evaluated on a held-out twelve-month partition of institutional tick data the agents have never seen, ViperQ achieves +163.6% ROI on TSLA (-27.5% max drawdown, 27,019 trades) and +116.5% ROI on NVDA (-47.8% max drawdown, 12,892 trades) under zero leverage. The results establish Auction Market Theory features as a tractable structured input modality for sequential decision-making on financial time series and motivate further work on microstructure-aware policy learning.

</details>


### [50] [UniCAR-RL: Seeing Better before Thinking Deeper in Visual Mathematics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13849)
