*Yuzhe Li,Hao Yan,Hao Wang,Xingchen Liu,Ya-Qi Yu,Jihao Wu,Minghui Liao,Wei Chen,Yuliang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UniCAR-RL is a novel RL framework that decouples perception and reasoning optimization in MLLMs to address visual hallucinations in mathematical reasoning, using three synergistic branches to achieve targeted improvement without expensive annotation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLMs struggle with complex mathematical visual reasoning due to fine-grained perception deficiencies, where initial visual hallucinations trigger cascading reasoning failures. Traditional RL approaches fail to separate perceptual errors from logical mistakes, while perception-enhanced CoT fine-tuning is costly and still suffers from hallucinations.

Method: UniCAR-RL consists of three branches: 1) Caption-RL branch optimizes perception through verifier-guided reasoning validation; 2) Reasoning-RL branch performs logical reasoning using gold image descriptions to prevent cascading errors; 3) QA-RL branch maintains end-to-end alignment for robust QA performance. The framework explicitly decouples perception and reasoning optimization during training.

Result: Experiments show UniCAR-RL substantially improves MLLMs' mathematical and visual reasoning using only raw short-answer data. It also demonstrates strong generalization across diverse architectures and scales.

Conclusion: UniCAR-RL provides an effective annotation-free RL framework that isolates and optimizes both perception and reasoning capabilities in MLLMs, addressing the core challenge of visual hallucinations in mathematical visual reasoning while maintaining broad applicability.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often struggle with complex mathematical visual reasoning primarily due to a lack of fine-grained perception, causing initial visual hallucinations to directly trigger cascading reasoning failures. In traditional end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL), sparse rewards fail to decouple perceptual hallucinations from logical missteps, hindering targeted perception optimization. Alternatively, fine-tuning with perception-enhanced CoT data incurs high costs and hallucinations. In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing UniCAR-RL, an annotation-free RL framework. By explicitly decoupling the optimization of perception and reasoning during the training process, it achieves isolation and optimization of both capabilities. Specifically, UniCAR-RL consists of three synergistic branches: 1) a Caption-RL branch that optimizes perception capabilities through verifier-guided reasoning validation; 2) a Reasoning-RL branch that performs logical reasoning based on a gold image description to halt cascading errors; 3) a QA-RL branch that retains native end-to-end alignment to ensure robust question-answering performance. Experiments show that UniCAR-RL substantially improves MLLMs' mathematical and visual reasoning using only raw short-answer data. Furthermore, it demonstrates strong generalization across diverse architectures and scales.

</details>


### [51] [ClinAgent: A ReAct-Based Agent for Conversational Access to Clinical Trial Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13860)
*Antonino Vaccarella,Riccardo Cantini,Domenico Talia,Paolo Trunfio,Marianna Talia,Rosamaria Lappano,Marcello Maggiolini*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ClinAgent is an agentic RAG system using LLMs to enable natural language querying of clinical trial registries with multi-turn conversational interaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Querying clinical trial registries is currently manual and error-prone, requiring navigation of large volumes of semi-structured data without natural language interaction or cross-source synthesis capabilities.

Method: An LLM agent following the ReAct paradigm with integrated tools including ClinicalTrials.gov search, PubMed module, and Python-based analyzer on locally cached structured trial data. Evaluated three LLM backends (Gemini 3.0 Flash, DeepSeek V3.2 thinking/non-thinking) using operational effectiveness, planning quality, tool-use efficiency, and expert judgment metrics.

Result: DeepSeek (thinking mode) excels in planning quality, while Gemini achieves highest overall performance and strongest expert ratings. The system demonstrates complementary strengths among different LLM backends.

Conclusion: Agentic AI systems like ClinAgent have potential to improve accessibility and synthesis of clinical trial information, supporting more efficient and user-centered biomedical research workflows.

Abstract: Querying clinical trial registries remains a manual and error-prone process, requiring researchers to navigate large volumes of semi-structured data without support for natural language interaction or cross-source synthesis. To address this, we introduce ClinAgent, a conversational system based on agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) that enables clinicians and researchers to query clinical trial information in plain language and receive grounded, up-to-date responses across multi-turn interactions. The system centers on a Large Language Model (LLM) agent following the ReAct paradigm, which iteratively reasons over queries, selects among a set of integrated tools, and refines its actions based on intermediate outputs. These tools include a ClinicalTrials.gov search interface, a PubMed module, and a Python-based analyzer operating on a locally cached structured dataset of clinical trials. We evaluate the system using a three-phase framework assessing operational effectiveness, planning quality, tool-use efficiency, and expert qualitative judgments, comparing three LLM backends: Gemini 3.0 Flash and two variants of DeepSeek V3.2 (thinking and non-thinking). Results reveal complementary strengths, with DeepSeek (thinking mode) excelling in planning quality, while Gemini achieves the highest overall performance and strongest expert ratings. Overall, our findings highlight the potential of agentic AI systems to improve the accessibility and synthesis of clinical trial information, supporting more efficient and user-centered biomedical research workflows.

</details>


### [52] [Map Users and Mapmakers: The Scope of Cognitive Attribution from Acquired Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13879)
*Yiling Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper develops a framework for specifying how acquired representations enlarge cognitive systems, distinguishing five types of attribution to clarify what capacities are actually established versus what requires additional support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the need to precisely specify how acquired representations enlarge cognitive systems without automatically transferring the capacities used to produce those representations. There's a concern about attributing broader cognitive repertoires than what has actually been demonstrated.

Method: The authors develop a five-part attribution table framework distinguishing: effective tracking, application of acquired structures, acquisition from explicit specifications, acquisition from identifying observations, and retention and reuse. Each entry identifies positive capacity commitments and further claims requiring support. The argument grants meaningful content, causal efficacy, and productive inference upfront.

Result: The framework shows why complete application competence doesn't determine acquisition capacity, and why acquiring criteria from descriptions differs from finding them in examples. When applied to Andrew Ng's Othello-GPT world-model and machine concept discussions, the framework preserves demonstrated recognition, classification, inference, and qualified acquisition while specifying what remains unestablished about criterion discovery and accumulation.

Conclusion: The analysis concerns the scope of cognitive attribution rather than constitutive conditions of concept possession: cognitive achievements deserve credit only for capacities they actually establish, without silently importing broader repertoires through the labels attached to them.

Abstract: An acquired representation can enlarge a system's cognitive repertoire without transferring the capacities exercised in producing that representation. This paper develops a framework for specifying that enlargement and its limits. Its central contribution is a five-part attribution table distinguishing effective tracking, application of acquired structures, acquisition from explicit specifications, acquisition from identifying observations, and retention and reuse. Each entry identifies a positive capacity commitment and a further claim requiring additional support. The argument deliberately grants meaningful content, causal efficacy, and productive inference, so that its conclusion does not depend on treating representations as inert encodings. Map and category examples show why even complete application competence leaves acquisition capacity undetermined, and why acquiring a criterion from its description differs from finding it in examples. Short formal proofs appear in an appendix. The framework is applied to Andrew Ng's world-model interpretation of Othello-GPT and to the specific indicators discussed in contemporary accounts of machine concepts. It preserves demonstrated recognition, classification, inference, and qualified acquisition while specifying what remains unestablished about criterion discovery and accumulation. The result concerns the scope of cognitive attribution rather than the constitutive conditions of concept possession: cognitive achievements deserve credit for the capacities they establish, without silently importing a broader repertoire through the labels attached to them.

</details>


### [53] [LoRA Fine-Tuned Models for Control Systems Course Q\&A: A Multidimensional Evaluation of Model Scale and Rank Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13918)
*Shaowen Lu,Chengxu Liu,Ping Zhou,Tao Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-3B and 7B models with LoRA on control-systems course data improves similarity to reference answers and structured-output consistency, with 7B-r16 achieving best performance but r=8 offering better parameter efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs used in specialized university courses (especially control systems) produce inconsistently structured responses that are hard to verify. Control-systems questions require coordinated terminology, notation, derivations, and stepwise explanations which general-purpose LLMs don't consistently provide.

Method: Built supervised fine-tuning dataset of 360 system-user-assistant conversations from Linear Control Systems course exercises. Applied LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) to Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct models. Tested LoRA ranks r=4, 8, and 16. Evaluated with identical data splits, inference settings, and protocols using ROUGE, BERTScore, and structured-output features measuring reference-answer similarity and Solution-Method-Teaching Points format stability.

Result: LoRA improved both similarity and structured-output stability at both model sizes. 7B-r16 achieved highest ROUGE-L (0.4093) and BERTScore-F1 (0.8643). r=8 offered better balance between performance and parameter efficiency. Bootstrap resampling showed statistically significant ROUGE-L gains: 0.0764 for 3B-r16 and 0.0874 for 7B-r16.

Conclusion: LoRA can align open-source instruction-tuned models more closely with course-specific language and pedagogical organization. However, current metrics mainly capture textual similarity and formatting consistency, not domain-specific reasoning or mathematical correctness, which require expert assessment and task-specific rubrics.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in specialized university courses, but control-systems questions require coordinated terminology, notation, derivations, and stepwise explanations. Direct general-purpose responses may be inconsistently structured and hard to verify. Using exercises and reference solutions from a Linear Control Systems course, we built a supervised fine-tuning dataset of 360 system-user-assistant conversations. We applied LoRA to Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. With identical data splits, inference settings, and evaluation protocols, we compared base and fine-tuned models and tested LoRA ranks r=4, 8, and 16. Evaluation used ROUGE, BERTScore, and structured-output features to measure reference-answer similarity and stability of the Solution-Method-Teaching Points format. LoRA improved both similarity and structured-output stability at both sizes. On the current test set, 7B-r16 achieved the highest ROUGE-L (0.4093) and BERTScore-F1 (0.8643), while r=8 offered a better balance between performance and parameter efficiency. Bootstrap resampling showed ROUGE-L gains of 0.0764 [0.0613, 0.0915] for 3B-r16 and 0.0874 [0.0687, 0.1042] for 7B-r16; both intervals exceeded zero, indicating stable textual-similarity improvements on the current test set. These results suggest LoRA can align open-source instruction-tuned models more closely with the language and pedagogical organization of course reference answers. However, the metrics mainly capture textual similarity and formatting consistency, not domain-specific reasoning or mathematical correctness, which require expert assessment and task-specific rubrics.

</details>


### [54] [SAILOR: Solver-Assisted Interactive LLM-based Optimization Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13945)
*Shaghayegh Sadeghi,Stephen L. Smith,David C. Del Rey Fern'andez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SAILOR is a system that detects missing numerical values in natural-language optimization problems, asks targeted follow-up questions to get required values, and updates the model before solving, with priority based on uncertainty and solver estimates of value importance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Natural-language descriptions of optimization problems often have incomplete or vague numerical information (costs, capacities, demands, bounds, penalties) that solvers need. Language models can translate descriptions to code, but when required values are missing, they must either stop or guess arbitrarily.

Method: SAILOR detects unsupported numerical choices, asks users targeted follow-up questions, and updates optimization models. Questions are prioritized using uncertainty measures and solver-derived estimates of how strongly each missing value affects the current model. Evaluation uses 1,723 instances from seven masked benchmarks with an idealized simulator returning ground-truth values.

Result: Exact objective-value agreement ranges from 27.0% to 87.6% across datasets, requiring 1.4-5.7 questions per instance on average. Results establish feasibility under controlled branch-and-reveal feedback but don't measure performance with human users or general structural model repair.

Conclusion: SAILOR demonstrates a feasible approach to handle incomplete numerical information in optimization problem descriptions through targeted question-asking and model updating. The system addresses a key limitation in natural-language-to-code translation for optimization, though real-world human interaction and broader model repair capabilities remain unexplored.

Abstract: Natural-language descriptions of optimization problems may be incomplete or vague about numerical information that a solver requires, including costs, capacities, demands, bounds, and penalties. A language model can translate the description into code, but when a required value is absent it must either stop or guess. We present SAILOR, a proof-of-concept system that detects such unsupported numerical choices, asks the user targeted follow-up questions, and updates the optimization model before returning a solution. Questions are prioritized using uncertainty and solver-derived estimates of how strongly each missing value affects the current model. We evaluate the pipeline on 1,723 instances from seven masked benchmarks using an idealized simulator that returns ground-truth values. Exact objective-value agreement ranges from 27.0% to 87.6% across datasets, with 1.4--5.7 questions per instance on average. These results establish feasibility under controlled branch-and-reveal feedback; they do not measure performance with human users or general structural model repair. Code is available at: https://github.com/sshaghayeghs/SAILOR.

</details>


### [55] [Synthetic Data in Marketing Research: How to Evaluate and When to Trust](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13995)
*Oded Netzer,Rajan Sambandam*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper examines when synthetic data from LLMs works best for marketing research, distinguishing three types of synthetic respondents, developing a taxonomy of accuracy measures, and introducing the forgotten question problem with a diagnostic tool.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The debate about synthetic data in marketing research has polarized between extreme positions - either claiming LLMs make human respondents obsolete or advocating complete avoidance. The authors argue this polarization obscures the more useful question: not whether synthetic respondents work, but when they work effectively.

Method: 1) Distinguish three types of synthetic data: ungrounded LLM responses, segment-level personas, and individual-level digital twins, mapping each to appropriate decision support. 2) Develop a taxonomy of four families of accuracy measures to explain varying reported twin accuracy. 3) Introduce the "forgotten question problem" and propose an ex-ante answerability diagnostic (R^2 of random forest predicting twin outputs from construction data). Tested across 108 attitude questions from a nationally representative survey (N=3,063).

Result: Across 108 attitude questions, screening at R^2 above 0.7 raised the mean twin-human individual-level correlation by 15% and reduced the share of poorly answered questions from 25.9% to 4.3%. Embedding similarity and experienced-researcher judgment provided correlated but weaker screening performance.

Conclusion: The paper moves beyond the polarized debate about synthetic data by providing practical frameworks for determining when different types of synthetic respondents work effectively. The proposed diagnostic tool helps identify when digital twins can reliably answer omitted questions, offering a principled approach to synthetic data use in marketing research.

Abstract: Debate over synthetic data in marketing research has polarized between claims that large language models (LLMs) make human respondents obsolete and calls to avoid them entirely. We argue that both positions obscure the more useful question: not whether synthetic respondents work, but when. Building on Brand, Israeli, and Ngwe (2026), we make three contributions. First, we distinguish three types of synthetic data (ungrounded LLM responses, segment-level personas, and individual-level digital twins) and map each to the decisions it can support. Second, we develop a taxonomy of four families of accuracy measures and suggest that the wide range of reported twin accuracy, from near-perfect to near-chance, largely reflects differences in what is being measured rather than in method quality. Aggregate measures often perform well even when little information is supplied to the LLM, and can mask a complete absence of respondent-level differentiation. Third, we introduce the forgotten question problem, in which a question is omitted from a fielded study, as a setting for twin-based augmentation of existing data. We propose an ex-ante answerability diagnostic that requires no ground truth: the R^2 of a random forest predicting twin outputs from the data used to construct the twins. Across 108 attitude questions from a nationally representative survey (N = 3,063), screening at R^2 above 0.7 raises the mean twin-human individual-level correlation by 15% and reduces the share of poorly answered questions from 25.9% to 4.3%. Embedding similarity and experienced-researcher judgment provide correlated but weaker screens.

</details>


### [56] [Convergent Emergence of In-Context Learning Across Modalities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14011)
*Nathan Breslow,Seungwook Han,Daniel Hyunsoo Lee,Aayush Mishra,Anqi Liu,Daniel Khashabi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Few-shot in-context learning (ICL) emerges across six different modalities (language, genome, integer sequences, time series, images, proteins) with correlated task difficulty patterns, supporting the Convergent Emergence Hypothesis in five out of six modalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While few-shot ICL has been studied extensively in language models and recently in genomic models, it's unclear whether ICL emerges broadly across different domains and what common structure might be shared across modalities.

Method: Developed a controlled cross-modality framework that instantiates the same task suite across multiple modalities (language, genome, integer sequences, time series, images, proteins) to test the Convergent Emergence Hypothesis - that tasks benefiting from ICL in one modality tend to benefit in others.

Result: Paired-mapping ICL emerges across all six tested modalities, surpasses controlled baselines, and shows correlated per-task effects across five of the modalities, but not all.

Conclusion: The results provide support for the Convergent Emergence Hypothesis in some modalities but not all, suggesting that while ICL emerges broadly across domains, the shared structure may not be universal across every modality tested.

Abstract: Few-shot in-context learning (ICL), the capacity of a model to infer abstract patterns from input-output examples provided in its prompt and apply them to new inputs, has been extensively studied in large language models trained for next-token prediction on human text. Recently, few-shot ICL has been demonstrated in autoregressive genomic models as well. This raises a question: does ICL emerge broadly across domains, and if so, what common structure is shared?
  To address both, we develop a controlled cross-modality framework that instantiates the same task suite in a variety of modalities to test what we call the Convergent Emergence Hypothesis: the idea that few-shot ICL, when it emerges, shares a common cross-modality difficulty profile - i.e., tasks that benefit from ICL in one modality tend to benefit in others. We show that paired-mapping ICL emerges across six modalities (language, genome, integer sequences, time series, images, and proteins), surpasses controlled baselines, and has correlated per-task effects across five of them. Together, these results provide support for the Convergent Emergence Hypothesis in some modalities, but not all.

</details>


### [57] [Schizophrenia Detection from EEG Signals: A Transformer Framework with Spectrogram Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14015)
*Abtin Shafiei,Mohsen Hooshmand,Majid Ramezani*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An EEG-based schizophrenia classification framework using time-frequency representations and both traditional ML and deep learning models achieves competitive performance with careful subject-level data partitioning to prevent data leakage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Schizophrenia diagnosis remains primarily clinical and subjective. EEG provides a non-invasive way to study brain activity, but existing EEG-based classification studies suffer from small datasets, inconsistent preprocessing, and inadequate prevention of subject-related data leakage in evaluation protocols.

Method: Transform preprocessed EEG recordings into time-frequency representations using Short-Time Fourier Transform to create spectrogram images. Classify these images using both conventional ML algorithms (SVM, Random Forests, XGBoost) and deep learning models (convolutional architectures and CNN-Transformer hybrids). All data partitions are performed at the subject level to ensure reliable evaluation.

Result: The proposed approach achieves competitive classification performance: CNN-Transformer (CT-SZ) achieves AUC-ROC of 88.41%, and CNN + Squeeze and Excitation + Transformer (CST-SZ) achieves AUC-ROC of 92.88% on independent test set.

Conclusion: The EEG-based framework using time-frequency representations with careful subject-level data partitioning and modern deep learning architectures shows promising results for automated schizophrenia detection, addressing limitations of previous studies.

Abstract: Schizophrenia is a serious psychiatric disorder that affects millions of people worldwide, and its diagnosis remains primarily dependent on clinical assessment. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive approach to investigate brain activity and has shown potential to support automated Schizophrenia detection. However, existing EEG-based classification studies often suffer from limitations including small datasets, inconsistent preprocessing strategies, and evaluation protocols that may not adequately prevent subject-related data leakage. In this study, we propose an EEG-based Schizophrenia classification framework that transforms preprocessed EEG recordings into time-frequency representations using the Short-Time Fourier Transform. The generated spectrogram images are classified using both conventional Machine Learning algorithms, including Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, and XGBoost, and Deep Learning models, including convolutional architectures and CNN-Transformer hybrids. To ensure reliable evaluation, all data partitions are performed at the subject level. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves competitive classification performance, with the CNN-Transformer (CT-SZ) model achieving an AUC-ROC of 88.41% and the CNN + Squeeze and Excitation + Transformer (CST-SZ) achieving an AUC-ROC of 92.88% on the independent test set.

</details>


### [58] [VeriDx: Earning the Right to Diagnose with Disease-Centric Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14018)
*Zhong Cao,Shuying Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VeriDx is a disease-centric verification framework that evaluates medical LLMs by tracking whether diagnostic hypotheses satisfy clinical obligations (evidence checking, alternative ruling out, contradiction resolution, test consideration, closure justification), exposing failures beyond simple answer correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluations of medical LLMs focus on final answers, local steps, or isolated facts, missing hypothesis-induced commitments and obligations that arise during clinical reasoning, such as checking key evidence, ruling out alternatives, and resolving contradictions.

Method: VeriDx links free-form diagnostic reasoning to structured disease profiles, tracking whether each hypothesis satisfies, leaves unresolved, or violates its clinical obligations. The framework is instantiated for complex respiratory diagnosis using guideline-derived disease profiles and expert-annotated longitudinal cases.

Result: Many diagnostic errors are not isolated mistakes but broken commitments made earlier in the reasoning process. The framework exposes failures like missing critical tests, unresolved differentials, ignored contradictions, unsupported claims, and premature closure.

Conclusion: A disease-centric verification approach like VeriDx provides more comprehensive evaluation of medical LLMs by capturing the complex obligations inherent in clinical reasoning, moving beyond simple answer correctness to assess the quality of the diagnostic process itself.

Abstract: A correct diagnosis can still be reached for the wrong reasons. In clinical reasoning, every disease hypothesis creates obligations: key evidence must be checked, alternatives must be ruled out, contradictions must be resolved, useful tests must be considered, and closure must be justified. Current evaluations of medical LLMs mostly focus on final answers, local steps, or isolated facts, and therefore miss these hypothesis-induced commitments. We introduce \textbf{VeriDx}, a disease-centric verification framework that links free-form diagnostic reasoning to structured disease profiles. VeriDx tracks whether each hypothesis is satisfied, unresolved, or violated its clinical obligations, exposing failures such as missing critical tests, unresolved differentials, ignored contradictions, unsupported claims, and premature closure. We instantiate VeriDx for complex respiratory diagnosis using guideline-derived disease profiles and expert-annotated longitudinal cases. Our results show that many diagnostic errors are not isolated mistakes, but broken commitments made earlier in the reasoning process.

</details>


### [59] [Semantic Knowledge Technologies: what the Semantic Web lost sight of, and what it never had](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14121)
*Achille Zappa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper critiques the Semantic Web's limitations and proposes "Semantic Knowledge Technologies" as an extended framework that addresses missing elements (conditions, operations, coverage) to achieve true machine understanding through a 7-layer architecture and measurable tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The Semantic Web successfully created standards for machine-interpretable information but failed to deliver the promised machine competence. Current AI systems (like language models) answer questions but lack inspectable knowledge structures. The paper argues the original goal was correct but the technical program was incomplete.

Method: The paper analyzes what's missing from Semantic Web standards (conditions for claims, operational grounding, declared coverage), defines five measurable tests for "understanding" (check, connect, derive, act, delimit), proposes a seven-layer architecture, and introduces key concepts like Large Knowledge Models, SLKMs, and Semantic AGI.

Result: The paper presents a comprehensive research agenda with: 1) A diagnosis of Semantic Web limitations, 2) A framework for Semantic Knowledge Technologies, 3) A 7-layer architecture for cognitive capabilities, 4) New definitions (LKM, SLKM, Semantic AGI), and 5) A graded ladder approach replacing "general" intelligence with testable criteria.

Conclusion: Semantic Knowledge Technologies offer a path forward by extending the Semantic Web's core principles to address its fundamental omissions. The paper provides a falsifiable research agenda with measurable tests for machine understanding, moving beyond untestable claims about general intelligence toward a more rigorous, implementable framework.

Abstract: The Semantic Web set out to give information a machine-interpretable form so that software could integrate and reason over it. Its standards became scientific knowledge infrastructure, but the machine competence it promised did not follow, and the systems now answering questions over scientific knowledge are language models holding no inspectable account of what they know. This paper argues the original goal was right and the technical programme incomplete, states what is missing, and names the extended programme Semantic Knowledge Technologies: the same technical core carried out of its web-publishing origin and applied to knowledge wherever held. The diagnosis is that the standards formalised truth while omitting three things: the conditions under which a claim holds, the operations its terms permit, and any account of what a base covers. Without conditions, contradiction and applicability cannot be judged; without operational grounding, holding a statement confers no ability; without declared coverage, a system cannot recognise the boundary of its own content, which under the open-world assumption cannot be inferred. The paper fixes the word understanding to five measurable tests (check, connect, derive, act, delimit) and sets out a seven-layer architecture in which the first three layers are enabling and the rest the cognitive capabilities they make possible. It then defines three terms the programme implies: Large Knowledge Model, a model whose unit of output is a reference to an addressable claim, not a token; SLKM, the knowledge base an agent builds for itself from declared sources; and Semantic Artificial General Intelligence, stated as a falsifiable position about necessary conditions, not a system. A graded ladder replaces the untestable word general. It is offered as a research agenda, with its weakest points and refutation condition named.

</details>


### [60] [MOSCOPT: Mixture-of-Skills Collective Optimization for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14399)
*Zhenyu Zhang1,Jiudong Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MOSCOPT is a parameter-free algorithm that jointly optimizes multiple complementary skills and a gating skill for LLM-based agents, achieving monotonic improvement through three-phase interleaved updates without gradient tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing prompt and skill optimization methods only optimize a single text template, missing the synergy among multiple complementary strategies. There's a need for methods that can leverage multiple skills dynamically.

Method: Proposes MOSCOPT: a text-native, parameter-free algorithm that jointly optimizes a pool of N skills and a gating skill G that dynamically selects K skills per step. Uses EditAdam with internally maintained dual states and three-phase interleaved updates (skills pool, gating skill, and global reward) to achieve monotonic improvement without gradient or parameter tuning.

Result: Extensive experiments across 5 benchmarks and 3 target LLMs demonstrate that MOSCOPT consistently outperforms all baselines. Both the mixture-of-skills architecture with selective activation and the collective evolution with three-phase interleaving are essential to its superior performance.

Conclusion: MOSCOPT successfully addresses the limitation of single-template optimization by enabling joint optimization of multiple skills with dynamic selection, achieving state-of-the-art performance through its parameter-free, gradient-free approach that leverages complementary skill synergies.

Abstract: Natural language prompts and skills serve as the strategic backbone of LLM-based agents. Recent advances in prompt and skill optimization have achieved notable gains, yet all existing methods optimize a \emph{single} text template---missing the synergy among multiple complementary strategies. We propose MOSCOPT, a text-native, parameter-free algorithm that jointly optimizes a pool of $N$ skills and a gating skill $G$ that dynamically selects $K$ skills per step. To effectively optimize the skills, we build the EditAdam with internally maintained dual states. Through the three-phase interleaved updates with EditAdam, the system monotonically improves without gradient or parameter tuning. Extensive experiments and detailed ablations across 5 benchmarks and 3 target LLMs demonstrate that MOSCOPT consistently outperforms all baselines, and confirm that both the mixture-of-skills architecture with selective activation and the collective evolution with three-phase interleaving are essential to its superior performance. Code is released https://github.com/zhangzhenyu13/SummerClaw/tree/master/summerclaw/agent_trainer/algorithms/moscopt.

</details>


### [61] [Dynamic Learning Solutions: A System for Personalized Educational Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14408)
*Siddhanth Sridhar,Shreya Chaurasia,Baddela Sai Yaswantha Reddy,Deepak Parmar,Shylaja S S*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Automated pipeline converts NCERT textbooks into interactive video explanations using RAG, Stable Diffusion, animation, and speech synthesis to answer user queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To transform static educational materials from NCERT textbooks into engaging, interactive video-based explanations that directly respond to user questions, creating a more dynamic and personalized learning experience.

Method: 1. User uploads PDF and asks question
2. RAG model optimized for NCERT textbooks retrieves relevant content
3. Generates multi-scene script with narrative explanations and visual prompts
4. Stable Diffusion module generates contextually relevant images with layer-by-layer implementation for interpretability
5. DynamiCrafter animates the sequences
6. Google Text-to-Speech generates synchronized narration with time-based control

Result: The system successfully produces coherent video explanations integrating animation, narration, and textbook-aligned visuals. The RAG model performs best on NCERT textbook content, demonstrating the pipeline's effectiveness in transforming static educational material into interactive, engaging learning content.

Conclusion: The pipeline demonstrates a scalable approach to personalized digital education by combining multi-modal document retrieval, generative visual models, animation frameworks, and speech synthesis, creating an effective system for interactive educational content delivery.

Abstract: We present an automated pipeline that converts NCERT textbooks into interactive video explanations that respond directly to user queries. A user uploads a PDF and asks a question; the system then generates a video-based explanation as output, handling both text and visual elements from the PDF for multi-modal retrieval and response generation. The pipeline combines a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) model with generative multimedia components. The RAG stage is optimized for the structure of NCERT textbooks and performs best on content from those books. Given a user query, the RAG model retrieves relevant content from the PDF and generates a multi-scene script containing narrative explanations and structured visual prompts aligned with the textbook's explanatory style. These prompts are passed to a Stable Diffusion module, implemented layer by layer for interpretability and control, which generates contextually relevant images. The images are then processed by DynamiCrafter to produce animated sequences. Finally, a Google Text-to-Speech module generates synchronized narration, aligning speech with the visual scenes through time-based control. The result is a coherent video explanation integrating animation, narration, and textbook-aligned visuals, transforming static educational material into an engaging learning experience. By combining multi-modal document retrieval, generative visual models, animation frameworks, and speech synthesis, this pipeline demonstrates a scalable approach to delivering interactive, personalized digital education content.

</details>


### [62] [Question's Gambit: The First Move Matters in Agentic Deep Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14412)
*Radin Hamidi Rad,Amin Bigdeli,Negar Arabzadeh,Sajad Ebrahimi,Charles L. A. Clarke,Benjamin C. M. Fung,Ebrahim Bagheri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Question's Gambit is a first-move retrieval module for deep research agents that decomposes questions into clues, runs complementary searches, and reranks results before the main search-and-reasoning loop begins.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep research agents often fail to connect evidence documents to gold answers even when lexical retrieval surfaces high-quality evidence. The first retrieval move is identified as a critical design decision that can significantly impact agent performance.

Method: Question's Gambit decomposes questions into sets of clues, reformulates them into complementary searches, consolidates retrieved results, and reranks the candidate pool before the agent's main iterative search-and-reasoning process begins.

Result: On BrowseComp-Plus, Question's Gambit improves retrieval recall and downstream agent accuracy from 83.1% to 90.5% with GPT-5.5 over Pi-Serini, the strongest reported agentic baseline. Benefits also transfer to MultiHop-RAG, a more conventional multi-hop question structure.

Conclusion: Effective agentic deep research depends not only on tools inside the reasoning loop, but also on the quality of the initial retrieval move. First-move design significantly impacts overall agent performance.

Abstract: Deep research agents answer complex questions through iterative loops of searching, reading, and reasoning. Recent work on reasoning-intensive benchmarks such as BrowseComp-Plus shows that well-configured lexical retrieval can surface high-quality evidence, yet agents may still fail to connect documents carrying evidence to the gold documents. We identify a deep research agent's first retrieval move as an important design decision for this setting. We introduce Question's Gambit, a first-move retrieval module that decomposes the question into a set of clues, reformulates them into complementary searches, consolidates the retrieved results, and reranks the candidate pool before the agent begins its iterative search-and-reasoning process. This produces an opening context designed to support both clue aggregation and final-answer verification. We further evaluate on MultiHop-RAG to test whether these benefits transfer beyond BrowseComp-Plus to a more conventional multi-hop question structure. Experiments on BrowseComp-Plus show that Question's Gambit improves retrieval recall and downstream agent accuracy over strong baselines, improving answer accuracy from 83.1% to 90.5% with gpt-5.5 over Pi-Serini, the strongest reported agentic baseline. Our results confirm that effective agentic deep research depends not only on the tools available inside the loop, but also on the quality of the first move. We published our implementation publicly at https://github.com/radinhamidi/Question-s-Gambit.

</details>


### [63] [Safety Signals to Verify NetOps Agents with Action-Level Granularity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14422)
*Tobias Labarta,Frederik Pahde,Novak Boskov,Maximilian Dreyer,David Birkenberger,Manzoor Ahmed Khan,Sebastian Lapuschkin,Wojciech Samek*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a ground truth framework for evaluating NetOps agents' action impacts, showing that agent internal signals better predict harmful/progressive actions than observable signals alone, with potential for safety applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic NetOps agents need long-horizon reliability for autonomous network control, especially in critical settings like datacenter fabrics. Current benchmarks lack per-action ground truth to evaluate action impacts, making it hard to determine when agents should abstain from risky actions that could cause downtime.

Method: Constructs ground truth for network repair tasks in NetArena using symbolic replay of emulated networks. Validates against environment to get exact value of every action, then derives two pre-execution targets: whether action reduces repair distance (progress) and whether it increases it (harm). Tests 10 agent models to compare internal signal-based verifiers against observable signal baselines.

Result: Agent verifiers leveraging internal signals predict both harm and progress more reliably than baselines using only observable signals. The internal signals show better performance for both detecting harmful actions and identifying progressive actions.

Conclusion: The proposed ground truth framework enables better evaluation of NetOps agent safety. The findings suggest internal agent signals provide valuable predictive information about action impacts, which could be used as safety feedback in agent harnesses to prevent risky actions and protect critical network systems.

Abstract: Agentic Network Operations (NetOps) are an emerging paradigm promising to enable workload-aware, self-adjustable, and reliable autonomous networks. While agents have proven their value in incident summarization and telemetry signal extraction, their effectiveness as autonomous control-loop engines heavily relies on their long-horizon reliability. One such setting is the datacenter fabric, where an agent must respond to alarms and operator intents while abstaining from high-risk actions that may cause or extend downtime. Abstention, however, presupposes that an action's impact is known pre-execution, which necessitates a per-action ground truth that NetOps agent benchmarks do not provide. We construct such a ground truth for the network repair task of NetArena. A symbolic replay of the emulated network, validated against the environment at every turn, yields the exact value of every action. From the action-level value, we derive two pre-execution targets, namely whether an action reduces the repair distance (progress) and whether it increases it (harm). We show across 10 agent models, that agent verifiers leveraging internal signals predict both harm and progress more reliably than a baseline using observable signals only. Perspectively, we aim to use these signals as safety feedback to an agent harness to abstain from risky actions and protect the target system.

</details>


### [64] [When does a scaling result justify a different allocation? A critical review of resource-allocation evidence for AI systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14500)
*Seyed Morteza Emadi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper provides a critical framework for evaluating AI scaling studies that combine multiple components (pretrained models with retrieval, search, verification, tools, interaction), focusing on how to determine when scaling results support resource-allocation decisions rather than just measuring performance improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI scaling studies often show better performance with larger budgets, but don't clarify where additional resources should be optimally allocated. The paper aims to address this gap by developing a framework to determine when scaling evidence actually supports resource-allocation decisions across different system components.

Method: The paper conducts an integrative review comparing evidence across pretraining, test-time computation, retrieval, and agent evaluation. It introduces two key concepts: (1) a "capability surface" that expresses performance as a function of budgets, mechanisms, and available information, and (2) a "resource envelope" that provides a structured record of task characteristics, development/run-time resources, information access, and procedures. The method includes analytical examples demonstrating how evaluation metrics, deployment volume, selection rules, and stopping policies can alter allocation conclusions.

Result: The review identifies three recurring mismatches in existing scaling evidence: (1) success counted before answer selection, (2) information that deployed systems won't have access to, and (3) costs omitted from comparisons. The paper shows through worked examples that allocation conclusions can change based on evaluation metrics, deployment volume, selection rules, and stopping policies. When applied to published comparisons, the resource envelope framework reveals which conclusions the evidence actually supports and which deployment questions remain unresolved.

Conclusion: The framework provides structured comparisons needed to choose among feasible AI systems under resource constraints, motivating experiments on transfer of allocation rules across tasks and operating conditions. The paper deliberately avoids proposing universal scaling laws or inferring general intelligence from benchmark gains, instead focusing on practical resource-allocation decision support.

Abstract: AI scaling studies increasingly evaluate systems that combine a pretrained model with retrieval, search, verification, tools, and interaction. Yet a higher score under a larger budget does not by itself show where additional resources are best spent. This critical integrative review asks when a reported scaling result supports a resource-allocation decision. It compares evidence across pretraining, test-time computation, retrieval, and agent evaluation, distinguishing the performance of a tested procedure from the best performance achievable under a resource limit. The synthesis shows that three mismatches recur across this evidence: success counted before an answer is chosen, information a deployed system will not have, and costs left out of the comparison. A capability surface expresses performance as a function of budgets, mechanisms, and available information. Worked analytical examples show how the evaluation metric, deployment volume, selection rule, and stopping policy can alter an allocation conclusion. A resource envelope provides a structured record of the task, development and run-time resources, information access, and procedure behind a reported score. Its application to a published comparison illustrates which conclusions the evidence supports and which deployment questions remain unresolved. The resulting framework specifies the comparisons needed to choose among feasible systems and motivates experiments on the transfer of allocation rules across tasks and operating conditions. It does not propose a universal scaling law or infer general intelligence from benchmark gains.

</details>


### [65] [Beyond Scene Description: Multi-Agent Orchestration for Non-visual Access to Virtual Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14512)
*Toqeer Ali Syed,Ali Akarma,Adeel Ahmad,Danial Hameed*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MetaBlind proposes an AI agent-based architecture with eight specialized modules and an orchestrator to manage nonvisual access to virtual worlds, dynamically selecting relevant information to avoid auditory overload for blind users.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current assistive tools for blind/visually impaired users in virtual worlds work in isolation, solving single tasks like object naming or route planning. Virtual environments present complex simultaneous interactions (obstacles, speakers, gestures, chat, slides, notifications) that overwhelm traditional single-agent narration approaches, trading visual barriers for auditory ones.

Method: MetaBlind uses eight specialized AI agents (perception, navigation, social interaction, object interaction, communication, safety/trust, memory, personalization) that publish information to a shared accessibility context. An Accessibility Orchestrator scores candidates on six dimensions (safety relevance, goal relevance, urgency, confidence, user relevance, estimated listening load) and selectively releases relevant information through speech, structured audio, or haptic output.

Result: The paper presents MetaBlind at the design stage with formal specification of the selection process, orchestration algorithm, and evaluation protocol against single-agent assistants. No prototype measurements or user studies are reported yet - the protocol defines what outcomes would support or refute the design.

Conclusion: MetaBlind offers a structured, multi-agent approach to nonvisual access in virtual environments that could address the simultaneous, complex nature of modern virtual interactions while preventing auditory overload through intelligent orchestration and filtering of information.

Abstract: Virtual worlds now host classrooms, meetings, conferences, shops, and social venues, and nearly every interaction they expose assumes a user who can scan a three-dimensional scene, follow avatars, and read floating panels. Blind and visually impaired (BVI) users are left with assistive tools that each solve one task in isolation: naming an object, reading text, describing a scene, or planning a route. A live virtual room defeats that model: obstacles, speakers, gestures, chat, slides, and notifications arrive together, and a tool that narrates all of them trades a visual barrier for an auditory one. This paper presents MetaBlind, an architecture that distributes nonvisual access across eight specialized agents, spanning perception, navigation, social and object interaction, communication, safety and trust, memory, and personalization, and that places an Accessibility Orchestrator between those agents and the user. Agents publish candidate information into a shared accessibility context instead of speaking to the user directly. The orchestrator scores each candidate on safety relevance, goal relevance, urgency, confidence, user relevance, and estimated listening load, then releases only the items it judges relevant at that moment through speech, structured audio, or haptic output. We give the selection step a formal statement, specify the orchestration cycle as an algorithm, and define an evaluation protocol against a single-agent assistant. MetaBlind is reported at the design stage, with no prototype measurement or user study, and the protocol states which outcomes would support the design and which would refute it.

</details>


### [66] [OptoAgent: A Trustworthy Multi-Agent Framework for Opportunistic Vision Micro-Screening in Classroom Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14514)
*Toqeer Ali Syed,Ali Akarma,Adeel Ahmad,Hammad Muneer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SightSentinel is an architecture that turns educational displays into continuous vision screening sites using embedded optotype probes and specialized agents to detect vision problems in children without requiring scheduled tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Children with vision problems often don't report difficulties and adapt by moving closer. Traditional school screening is scheduled, staff-dependent, and separate from classroom moments where issues appear. Existing digital tests still require someone to initiate testing.

Method: An architecture that embeds short calibrated optotype probes in ordinary educational content on wall displays. Eight specialized agents: perception agents measure viewing distance, recognition accuracy, approach behavior, gaze stability, response latency, and interocular difference; a quality agent filters bad observations; a longitudinal agent accumulates evidence against baselines; an orchestrator reports Vision Concern Score through a safety gate.

Result: The paper presents the formulation, architecture, and a four-stage validation protocol against clinical reference standards. It explores whether many cheap, noisy, well-gated encounters can achieve referral decisions that scheduled tests might miss or delay.

Conclusion: The approach aims to provide continuous, embedded vision screening in educational settings without disrupting normal activities, but includes conditions under which it should be rejected and emphasizes it excludes diagnosis, refraction, prescription, and reassurance.

Abstract: A child with reduced distance vision often does not know that anything is wrong. Children adapt, move closer, and rarely report the difficulty, so the problem can survive years of schooling before an adult notices. School screening addresses part of this, but it runs on a schedule, depends on staffing, and is separated from the classroom moments where the difficulty appears. Smartphone and web-based acuity tests have widened access, yet every one of them still needs somebody to start a test. We present SightSentinel, an architecture that turns a wall display a child already reads from into a recurring screening site. Ordinary educational content carries short calibrated optotype probes, and eight specialized agents divide the work. Perception agents recover viewing distance, recognition accuracy, approach behavior, gaze stability, response latency, and interocular difference from each encounter. A quality agent discards observations taken under bad geometry, poor lighting, or inattention. A longitudinal agent accumulates only the surviving evidence against the child's own baseline, and an orchestrator reports a Vision Concern Score routed through a safety gate whose output range excludes diagnosis, refraction, prescription, and reassurance. The design question is whether many cheap, noisy, well-gated encounters can reach a referral decision that one scheduled test reaches late or misses. We state the formulation, the architecture, a four-stage validation protocol against clinical reference standards, and the conditions under which the approach should be rejected.

</details>


### [67] [AI Deployment Accountability Engineering: A Vision for Accountable AI in Safety-Critical Socio-Technical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14592)
*Murat Kantarcioglu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ADAE is a proposed AI engineering discipline focused on continuous accountability for deployed AI systems in real-world socio-technical environments, moving beyond traditional model-centric evaluation to address system-level risks during operation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI evaluation practices are model-centric and insufficient for deployed systems operating in dynamic socio-technical environments with distribution shifts, human feedback loops, privacy constraints, and multi-agent interactions. These systems need ongoing accountability after deployment.

Method: Proposes AI Deployment Accountability Engineering (ADAE) as a new subdiscipline treating accountability as a deployment-layer property rather than just a model property. Focuses on four pillars: context-dependent failure mode discovery, privacy-preserving measurement, system-level risk analysis for agentic AI, and translating technical failures to operational/institutional risks.

Result: Introduces a research agenda and conceptual framework for ADAE that would provide measurable, continuous, actionable accountability for deployed AI systems, enabling identification of failure contexts, attribution across technical/human components, and timely intervention.

Conclusion: ADAE addresses the gap between pre-deployment model evaluation and real-world system operation, establishing foundational principles, mathematical tools, and system architectures for accountable AI deployment across safety-critical domains like healthcare and finance.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are rapidly becoming critical components in healthcare, finance, public services, and other safety-critical domains. Yet the engineering practices used to evaluate these systems remain predominantly model-centric, emphasizing properties such as accuracy, robustness, fairness, and interpretability before deployment. These properties are necessary but insufficient once an AI system operates within an ever changing socio-technical environment characterized by distribution shifts, institutional constraints, human feedback loops, privacy requirements, and interactions among multiple AI agents.
  This vision paper introduces AI Deployment Accountability Engineering (ADAE), a proposed AI engineering subdiscipline concerned with establishing measurable, continuous, and actionable accountability for deployed AI systems. ADAE treats accountability as a deployment-layer property rather than solely as a property of an individual model. It seeks to determine whether an AI-enabled system continues to operate within acceptable risk limits, identify the contexts in which failures emerge, attribute failures across interacting technical and human components, translate technical failures into downstream consequences, and support timely intervention.
  We articulate a research agenda built around four interconnected pillars: structured discovery of context-dependent failure modes, privacy-preserving accountability measurement, system-level risk analysis for agentic AI, and translation of technical failures into operational, and institutional risks. The broader goal is to establish foundational principles, mathematical tools, and system architectures for accountable AI deployment across safety-critical applications.

</details>


### [68] [A note on goal-based hierarchical RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14605)
*Kevin Murphy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper unifies and extends prior work on agent-centric general value functions and belief-based agents using hierarchical hidden Markov models to handle partially observable environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The ACGVF framework from prior work allows agents to choose their own goals and decide when goals are finished, but assumes fully observable environments. Meanwhile, belief-based agent designs handle partial observability but assume externally provided goals. The authors aim to unify these two approaches.

Method: The authors use hierarchical hidden Markov models (HHMM) to unify and extend the ACGVF framework and belief-based agent designs, enabling goal autonomy in partially observable environments.

Result: The paper presents a unified framework that combines goal autonomy (choosing goals and when to finish them) with belief-based state estimation for partially observable environments, addressing limitations of both prior approaches.

Conclusion: The HHMM-based unification provides a more comprehensive framework for reinforcement learning, control, and planning that handles both goal autonomy and partial observability, potentially advancing agent design in cognitive science and AI.

Abstract: The agent-centric general value function (ACGVF) construction of
  \citet{tasse2026goal} lets the agent make two decisions that are
  normally imposed by the environment or agent designer: which goal to
  pursue and when to declare a goal as finished (in addition to
  choosing the action). This is a very general framework that
  subsumes almost all prior work on reinforcement learning, control
  and planning, as well as more general formalisms proposed in the
  cognitive sciences. However, it assumes the environment is fully
  observed, i.e., that the observation is a sufficient statistic. In
  \citet{murphy2025rl}, a general agent design was proposed where the
  policy is based on an internal belief state $z_t$ and an internal
  goal; however, the goals were assumed to be externally provided. In
  this note, we unify and extend these two approaches using the
  formalism of hierarchical hidden Markov models (HHMM) \citep{murphy2001hhmm}.

</details>


### [69] [DynSTEER: Dynamic Stage-wise Trajectory Evaluation and Execution-time Review for Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14637)
*Zhichao Shi,Wenjie Zhang,Xuhui Jiang,Xiaojun Wu,Cehao Yang,Chengjin Xu,Jian Guo,Yuanzhuo Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DynSTEER is a dynamic stage-wise trajectory evaluation framework that addresses limitations in current LLM agent evaluation by segmenting rollouts into stages, using path-tolerant milestone graphs, and enabling early termination of failed executions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation paradigms for LLM agents have three major limitations: 1) terminal-only assessment ignores intermediate processes and struggles to localize errors efficiently, 2) single-reference matching penalizes valid alternative solution paths, and 3) post-hoc trajectory judging incurs high costs without early termination of failed runs.

Method: DynSTEER segments agent rollouts into stages anchored by key completed actions, creating a path-tolerant milestone graph from public task views that respects diverse legitimate strategies without leaking ground truth. It adaptively routes evaluation queries across multi-tier judges and halts unrecoverable executions online.

Result: Experiments show DynSTEER improves evaluation discriminability across LLM agents by 85.2% over native evaluation, separates all model pairs with statistical significance, and saves 34.51% of execution steps on failed rollouts.

Conclusion: DynSTEER provides a more effective framework for evaluating long-horizon task execution by LLM agents, addressing key limitations in current evaluation methods through dynamic stage-wise assessment, path-tolerant milestone tracking, and early termination of failed executions.

Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed for long-horizon task execution. However, current evaluation paradigms face three major limitations: terminal-only assessment ignores intermediate processes and struggles to localize errors efficiently and accurately, single-reference matching penalizes valid alternative solution paths, and post-hoc trajectory judging incurs high costs without the ability to halt failed runs early. To address these issues, we propose DynSTEER, a dynamic stage-wise trajectory evaluation framework for agents. DynSTEER segments rollouts into stages anchored by key completed actions, focusing evaluation on essential milestones with adequate context while enabling targeted strategy adjustments. It compiles a path-tolerant milestone graph from public task views to respect diverse legitimate strategies without leaking ground truth. Furthermore, it adaptively routes evaluation queries across multi-tier judges and halts unrecoverable executions online to curb resource waste. Experiments demonstrate that DynSTEER improves evaluation discriminability across LLM agents by 85.2\% over native evaluation, separates all model pairs with statistical significance, and saves 34.51\% of execution steps on failed rollouts.

</details>


### [70] [Diffusion-Based Generation of Gait Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14642)
*Damian Benasco,Juan Carballeira-Lopez,Jaime Ramos-Rojas,Julio S. Lora-Millan,Antonio J. Del-Ama,David Rodriguez-Cianca,Pablo Lanillos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Conditional diffusion models can generate realistic, controllable lower-limb joint-angle trajectories for personalized gait synthesis in assistive robotics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generation of patient-specific musculoskeletal gait trajectories is challenging but essential for wearable robotics and rehabilitation. Current approaches using hand-crafted templates or optimization procedures don't scale well across subjects and walking conditions.

Method: The authors explore conditional diffusion models for generating lower-limb joint-angle trajectories conditioned on gait parameters like step length. They compare a baseline transformer diffusion model with a controllable diffusion transformer variant incorporating adaptive normalization and classifier-free guidance.

Result: Experiments on a dataset of 4,590 gait cycles show that diffusion models can generate realistic periodic gait trajectories while enabling controllability over gait characteristics.

Conclusion: Diffusion models show promising potential for personalized gait synthesis in assistive robotics by generating adaptable, biomechanically realistic trajectories conditioned on patient-specific parameters.

Abstract: Generation of musculoskeletal gait trajectories conditioned on patient-specific parameters remains a key challenge for wearable robotics and rehabilitation. Assistive systems such as lower-limb exoskeletons require reference trajectories that adapt to individual morphology and therapeutic goals while preserving biomechanical realism. Traditional approaches rely on hand-crafted gait templates or optimization procedures that scale poorly across subjects and walking conditions. In this work, we explore conditional diffusion models for generating lower-limb joint-angle trajectories conditioned on gait parameters such as step length. We compare a baseline transformer diffusion model with a controllable diffusion transformer variant incorporating adaptive normalization and classifier-free guidance. Experiments on a dataset of 4,590 gait cycles show that diffusion models can generate realistic periodic gait trajectories while enabling some controllability variation in gait characteristics, highlighting their potential for personalized gait synthesis in assistive robotics.

</details>


### [71] [Lightning Weave: Improving the Accuracy-Efficiency Frontier of Reasoning Models through Capability Composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14708)
*Yecheng Wu,Song Han,Han Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Lightning Weave is a post-training framework that extracts and composes independently learned accuracy and efficiency capabilities from specialist models into a single student model through on-policy distillation, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Jointly improving reasoning accuracy and inference efficiency is challenging because these objectives often favor different reasoning behaviors, creating tension between the two goals in reasoning systems.

Method: The framework uses on-policy distillation to extract policy shifts from specialist models (accuracy-focused and efficiency-focused) relative to the base model, then composes these capabilities by aligning log-ratio shifts at shared student token states using Tilted-Target DOPD to create stable learning targets.

Result: Significant improvements across mathematics and code benchmarks: Qwen3.5-4B achieves 64.0% accuracy on HMMT 2025 (vs 59.2%) with 10.7% fewer tokens, and 54.2% on LiveCodeBench v5 (vs 41.7%) with 9.6% fewer tokens, establishing a strong accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier.

Conclusion: Lightning Weave provides a practical route to efficient reasoning through capability composition, successfully combining independently learned strengths in accuracy and efficiency into unified models while maintaining computational efficiency during training.

Abstract: A core goal of efficient reasoning is to improve the accuracy-efficiency frontier. However, jointly improving reasoning accuracy and inference efficiency can be challenging, as the two objectives can favor different reasoning behaviors. Independently post-trained models already offer distinct strengths in accuracy and efficiency. We introduce Lightning Weave, a post-training framework that extracts and composes these independently learned capabilities in a single student through on-policy distillation. Each acquired capability is represented by the policy shift from the model before post-training to the resulting specialist. Lightning Weave combines aligned log-ratio shifts at shared student token states and uses Tilted-Target DOPD to convert the cached signals into a stable learning target. Each anchor pair scores the cached trajectories once, enabling subsequent student training without serving multiple live anchor models concurrently. Across diverse student models and benchmarks in mathematics and code, Lightning Weave substantially improves upon the base students and achieves a state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency frontier. On Qwen3.5-4B, it raises HMMT 2025 accuracy from 59.2% to 64.0% with 10.7% fewer response tokens, and LiveCodeBench v5 accuracy from 41.7% to 54.2% with 9.6% fewer response tokens. Adjusting the relative strengths of the anchor signals yields a strong empirical accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier. These results establish Lightning Weave as a new practical route to efficient reasoning through capability composition. Code will be released soon.

</details>


### [72] [Depth and Scale in the Sub-150M Regime: JugnuLM-53M vs JugnuLM-110M](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14715)
*Dushyant Rajput,Nirdesh Chauhan,Siddharth Kosaraju*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Scaling a conventional 53.5M parameter model to 109.7M with deeper architecture improves performance across benchmarks while using fewer training tokens, establishing a baseline for ablation studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To create a clean scaling control experiment by increasing model capacity (from 53.5M to 109.7M parameters) while keeping the training method and data fixed, to isolate the effects of architecture scaling from other factors.

Method: Scaled the model from 53.5M to 109.7M parameters using a deep-and-thin 23-layer x 576-hidden design while maintaining Qwen3-style decoder architecture with grouped-query attention, RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, QK-Norm, and z-loss. Trained on FineWeb-Edu data and conducted systematic ablation studies (R0-R4) evaluating value residuals, Muon optimizer, diverse data blend, and logit distillation.

Result: The 110M model improved performance across benchmarks: BLiMP 78.1→81.3, ARC-Easy 51.4→52.5, WikiText-2 perplexity 2.04→1.95, matching GPT-X2-125M performance with 12% fewer parameters and 33% fewer training tokens. Value residuals (R1) and Muon optimizer (R2) provided additional ARC-Easy gains (+3.6 points) while maintaining BLiMP performance. Diverse data blending and distillation showed limited benefits.

Conclusion: Increasing model capacity through deeper architecture (without changing data or training method) significantly improves performance, with gains attributable to model capacity rather than data quantity. Value residuals and Muon optimizer provide meaningful improvements, while data blending and distillation offer limited benefits in this parameter regime.

Abstract: We scale our conventional sub-150M pretraining recipe from 53.5M to 109.7M parameters, holding the method fixed (Qwen3-style decoder with grouped-query attention, RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, QK-Norm, and a z-loss; FineWeb-Edu data) and changing only the geometry to a deep-and-thin 23-layer x 576-hidden design. The larger model improves across the board -- BLiMP 78.1 -> 81.3, ARC-Easy 51.4 -> 52.5, WikiText-2 byte-perplexity 2.04 -> 1.95 -- and its 81.3% BLiMP essentially matches GPT-X2-125M (81.28) at about 12% fewer parameters. Notably the 110M model achieves this on fewer training tokens (about 8B vs 12B), so the gain is attributable to capacity and depth, not more data. Both models are deliberately conventional; this report is a clean scaling control and the baseline rung (R0) of an ablation study of what further improves models in this regime. An ablation ladder follows: value residuals (R1) and the Muon optimizer (R2) lift ARC-Easy by a cumulative +3.6 (52.5 -> 56.1) at a near-flat BLiMP and are kept; a diverse data blend (R3) and two logit-distillation settings (R4a/R4b) are not kept -- honest negatives. R3 pins ARC-Easy to FineWeb-Edu's educational filtering rather than raw diversity; distillation from a 1.7B teacher can reach the class-leading ARC-Easy (56.99, matching GPT-X2-125M) but only at a perplexity cost that dialing KD down then erases -- so R2 remains the best kept stack.

</details>


### [73] [Moral Rebel Agents: Decision-Making Under Conflicting Obligations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14716)
*Hector Munoz-Avila,David W. Aha,Paola Rizzo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates "moral rebellion" in autonomous agents - the ability to deviate from user-assigned tasks when morally justified. It proposes and evaluates five agent architectures with different moral reasoning approaches in a search-and-rescue domain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous agents are typically required to follow user-assigned tasks, but strict obedience may conflict with moral obligations that arise during execution. There's a need to investigate when and how agents should deviate from assigned tasks for moral reasons.

Method: The authors formalize five agent architectures: 1) amoral agent (task-focused without moral consideration), and four moral rebel agents: 2) utilitarian (maximize outcomes), 3) deontic (enforce norms), 4) utilitarian-deontic (UD, combines both), and 5) dutiful (preserves task commitments). They implement these within a hierarchical task network planning framework and evaluate them in a Mini Search-and-Rescue domain.

Result: The agents exhibit distinct trade-offs among rescue results, assigned-task completion, and norm compliance. The preservation of task commitments emerges as important - UD and dutiful agents produce substantially different behaviors despite shared foundations. Commitment-aware moral reasoning produces different outcomes in morally consequential environments.

Conclusion: Moral rebellion is a necessary capability for autonomous agents, and commitment-aware moral reasoning is crucial for agents operating in morally consequential environments. Different moral frameworks lead to different trade-offs between task completion, moral obligations, and norm compliance.

Abstract: Autonomous agents are typically obliged to follow user-assigned tasks. However, strict obedience may conflict with moral obligations that arise during execution. This paper investigates \textbf{moral rebellion}: the ability of an autonomous agent to deviate from a user-assigned task when morally justified. We formalize five agent architectures: an \textit{amoral agent} that pursues assigned tasks without considering moral obligations, and four forms of \textbf{moral rebel agency}: (1) \textit{utilitarian agents} that opportunistically maximize task outcomes; (2) \textit{deontic} agents that enforce normative constraints; (3) \textit{utilitarian-deontic} (UD) agents that combine deontic constraints with utilitarian reasoning; and (4) \textit{dutiful} agents that additionally preserve commitments to assigned tasks. We implement these architectures within a hierarchical task network planning framework and evaluate them in a Mini Search-and-Rescue domain that exposes trade-offs among assigned-task completion, opportunistic rescue, and norm compliance. Our empirical results show that the proposed agents exhibit distinct trade-offs among rescue results, assigned-task completion, and norm compliance. In particular, the preservation of task commitments emerges as an important dimension of moral rebellion, for which the UD and dutiful agents produce substantially different behaviors despite their shared utilitarian and deontological foundations. These findings highlight the importance of commitment-aware moral reasoning for autonomous agents operating in morally consequential environments.

</details>


### [74] [Bayesian Intelligence from the Outside](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14724)
*Alex Smolin,Bryan Wilder*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper develops a Bayesian theory of intelligence for AI agents, showing that agents are Bayesian-rational if their reports aren't fully contradictory, explores intelligence ordering based on informational access, and reveals aggregation challenges for coarse reports.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to establish a formal foundation for inferring intelligence from observable behavior in AI systems like language models, addressing the fundamental challenge of determining when agents' behavior is genuinely intelligent versus merely pattern-matching.

Method: The authors develop a Bayesian framework where agents update priors based on internal experiments induced by prompts and faithfully report posteriors. They use mathematical analysis to derive necessary and sufficient conditions for Bayesian rationality, characterize intelligence ordering through information access, and analyze report aggregation using theoretical models.

Result: Key results: 1) Agents are Bayesian if and only if their reports aren't fully contradictory (some state remains possible across all reports). 2) Report frequencies and probability magnitudes impose no additional restrictions. 3) An intelligence order can be characterized by access to more informative experiments. 4) Aggregating coarse reports can lead to arbitrary weighting of unexcluded states.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a mathematical foundation for assessing AI intelligence through Bayesian rationality, showing it's difficult to reject Bayesian explanations of behavior, and highlighting challenges in aggregating imperfect reports from intelligent agents.
