Result: Across 168 prompts with 1,255 paired comparisons per temperature: theme sampling broadens selection coverage and screenshot variation; LLM-judge preferences vary across interventions, prompt complexity, and viewport. Online experiment with 300,000+ tasks shows uncertain code-export increase, fewer negative feedback events with more correction interactions, and modest operational costs.

Conclusion: Structured design specifications serve as a practical control point for exploring alternative UI concepts while keeping downstream generation settings fixed.

Abstract: Vibe design agents turn natural-language briefs into rendered interfaces and frontend code. Yet a useful design agent should do more than produce one valid page: it should help users explore coherent alternatives. Increasing token-level temperature is a blunt solution because it varies aesthetic decisions and syntax-sensitive code at the same time. We instead separate exploration from implementation through an inference architecture that makes design direction an explicit intermediate decision. Inspired by Verbalized Sampling, a pre-pass proposes structured design specifications with typicality scores, an external selector samples one, and the downstream generator realizes the selected specification together with the original request under fixed settings. We apply this approach to UI themes and visual-asset prompts. Across 168 prompts, with 1,255 paired comparisons per temperature for each intervention, theme sampling broadens observed selection coverage and screenshot variation, while LLM-judge preferences vary across interventions, prompt complexity, and viewport. In an online experiment with more than 300,000 tasks, the observed code-export increase remains statistically uncertain, while fewer negative feedback events coexist with more correction interactions and modest operational costs. Together, these findings identify structured design specifications as a practical control point for exploring alternative UI concepts while keeping downstream generation settings fixed.

</details>


### [100] [ER-EDF: A Psychology-Grounded Emotion Regulation Framework for Speech Empathetic Dialogue Generation in Large Audio-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15089)
*Hongyu Jin,Wenda Zhang,Runqiu Fei,Gongping Huang,Mike Conway,Ting Dang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ER-EDF is a psychology-grounded framework that decouples emotion perception from emotion regulation in large audio-language models to improve empathetic response generation in spoken dialogue systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current large audio-language models treat emotion as a direct conditioning signal without explicit regulatory mechanisms, leading to affect mirroring rather than calibrated empathetic support. There's a need for psychologically grounded approaches that separate emotion inference from how emotions should guide response generation.

Method: Proposed ER-EDF framework explicitly decouples emotion perception (tracking user's emotional state) and emotion regulation (determining how this state guides empathetic response generation). The framework is model-agnostic, integrates into existing LALMs, uses a spoken empathetic dialogue dataset, and employs empathy-aware evaluation metrics beyond lexical matching.

Result: Experiments across five LALMs and two datasets show ER-EDF consistently improves empathetic response quality in both automatic and human evaluations. The framework demonstrates the importance of jointly modeling emotion perception and regulation.

Conclusion: ER-EDF highlights the importance of psychologically grounded approaches that separate emotion perception from regulation in empathetic AI systems, paving a new direction for spoken empathetic dialogue systems and showing consistent improvements across multiple models.

Abstract: Empathetic response generation in spoken dialogue systems requires both accurate emotion perception and appropriate emotion regulation. Grounded in psychological theories such as the Perception-Action Model and emotion regulation theory, effective empathy depends not only on inferring a user's affective state but also on regulating how it is expressed in responses. However, recent large audio-language models (LALMs) largely treat emotion as a direct conditioning signal, lacking explicit regulatory mechanisms, which often leads to affect mirroring rather than calibrated support. We propose ER-EDF, a psychology-grounded framework that explicitly decouples emotion perception and emotion regulation in LALMs. Perception tracks the user's emotional state, while regulation determines how this state should guide empathetic response generation. The framework is model-agnostic and integrates seamlessly into existing LALMs. We further construct a spoken empathetic dialogue dataset and introduce empathy-aware evaluation metrics beyond lexical matching. Experiments across five LALMs and two datasets show that ER-EDF consistently improves empathetic response quality in both automatic and human evaluations, highlighting the importance of jointly modeling emotion perception and regulation in spoken empathetic dialogue systems, paving a new direction for psychologically grounded empathetic AI.

</details>


### [101] [OpenAI4S: Code as Action, Science as Sessions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15096)
*Gongbo Zhang,Hao Li,Yu Wang,Mujie Lin,Liuzhenghao Lv,Yicheng Mao,Yimi Wang,Jun Zhu,Minhan Tang,Zhengxiang Jiang,Yusong Wang,Jiayu Yao,Kunpeng Ning,Dawei Pang,Yonghong Tian,OpenAI4S Community,Yuyang Liu,Li Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OpenAI4S is an open-source AI research agent that combines persistent computing with session management for scientific workflows, featuring code execution in Python/R kernels, provenance tracking via an Action Ledger, and achieving better performance on complex scientific tasks compared to general-purpose coding tools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI co-scientists need persistent computational state and provenance to ensure long-running scientific workflows remain inspectable, resumable, and reproducible, which current tools often lack.

Method: Built around "Code as Action, Science as Sessions" principle with persistent Python/R kernels, structured tool calls, append-only Action Ledger, per-cell execution records, versioned artifacts, environment records, workspace checkpoints, and configurable sandboxing/screening safeguards.

Result: Evaluated on 36 research scenarios across retrosynthesis, molecular dynamics, protein design, etc., OpenAI4S achieved overall score of 7.83 vs. 5.7-6.4 for general-purpose coding harnesses, with largest gains on long-horizon and computation-intensive workflows.

Conclusion: Integrating persistent execution with session-level provenance improves AI-assisted scientific workflow reliability, but environment specification and full rerunnability remain challenges for reproducibility across all systems including OpenAI4S.

Abstract: AI co-scientists could accelerate computational research, but over a long-running study the workflow also has to stay inspectable, resumable and reproducible, which requires persistent computational state and provenance. Here we present OpenAI4S, an open-source scientific research agent built around the principle of \emph{Code as Action, Science as Sessions}. OpenAI4S combines a persistent computing runtime with research-session management: orchestration is handled through structured tool calls, while scientific actions are represented as complete code cells executed in persistent Python and R kernels. An append-only Action Ledger, per-cell execution records, versioned artifacts, environment records, and workspace checkpoints preserve how results were produced and support session recovery, branching, and extension. Configurable sandboxing, permission controls, and code and trajectory screening provide complementary safeguards. We evaluate OpenAI4S on 36 research scenarios spanning retrosynthesis, molecular dynamics, protein binder design, protein mutation, catalyst screening, and mineral spectroscopy, measuring scientific task accuracy, workflow completeness, and reproducibility of the resulting repositories. OpenAI4S achieves an overall score of 7.83, compared with 5.7--6.4 for a general-purpose coding harness evaluated with three frontier models, with the largest gains on long-horizon and computation-intensive workflows. These results suggest that integrating persistent execution with session-level provenance can improve the reliability of AI-assisted scientific workflows. Environment specification and full rerunnability remain weak for every evaluated system, ours included, so reproducibility is still an open problem for scientific agents. The system is available under the MIT license at \href{https://github.com/PKU-YuanGroup/OpenAI4S}{github.com/PKU-YuanGroup/OpenAI4S}.

</details>


### [102] [Medical Knowledge Simplification for Patients in the Era of LLMs: A Case Study on Diabetes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15129)
*Pallika Kafle,Yipeng Zhou,Guanfeng Liu,Quan Z. Sheng,Cheng-Hsin Hsu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-based medical knowledge simplification system (MediClear) using RAG to simplify diabetes information achieves patient-friendly readability and high user satisfaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Complex medical information is difficult for patients to understand, but current LLM applications for medical knowledge simplification lack sufficient real-world human evaluation to assess their practical effectiveness in patient education.

Method: Developed MediClear, an LLM-based medical knowledge simplification system enhanced with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Indexed diabetes articles from authoritative sources (Diabetes Australia, WHO, ADA, NIDDK, AIHW) and used LLM to simplify retrieved information. Evaluated with readability metrics (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level) and human study with 10 participants.

Result: MediClear consistently reduces reading level to recommended patient literacy range and achieves high user satisfaction with strong willingness for future use among participants.

Conclusion: LLMs have significant potential to improve medical knowledge accessibility for patient education, and MediClear demonstrates practical effectiveness in simplifying complex diabetes information while maintaining clinical grounding.

Abstract: Complex medical information is often difficult for patients to understand, making effective medical knowledge simplification essential for improving patient comprehension, informed decision-making, and health outcomes. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) provide a promising approach for simplifying complex medical information into patient-friendly language; however, their effectiveness in real-world patient education remains insufficiently explored through human evaluation. To investigate their practical effectiveness, this paper presents a case study on diabetes knowledge simplification through the implementation and evaluation of MediClear, an LLM-based medical knowledge simplification system enhanced with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Public diabetes-related articles from Diabetes Australia, WHO, American Diabetes Association (ADA), NIDDK, and AIHW are indexed in the RAG knowledge base to retrieve clinically grounded information, which is then simplified by the LLM into accessible patient explanations. We evaluate the generated responses using standard readability metrics, including the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL), and conduct a human study involving 10 participants. Results show that MediClear consistently reduces the reading level of generated responses to the recommended patient literacy range while achieving high user satisfaction and willingness for future use. This case study demonstrates the potential of LLMs to improve the accessibility of medical knowledge for patient education.

</details>


### [103] [HazardAuditor: From Executable Threats to Safer Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15134)
*Yunhao Feng,Ruixiao Lin,Ming Wen,Yanming Guo,Xingjun Ma,Yutao Wu,Xinhao Deng,Shouling Ji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HazardAuditor is an execution-grounded framework that improves safety supervision for computer-use agents by normalizing heterogeneous agent interactions and optimizing guard models through Guard Policy Optimization, achieving up to 16.5% accuracy improvement over prior guards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current safety approaches for computer-use agents are inadequate because: 1) Existing guard models target static prompts/responses but poorly handle agent execution dynamics, and 2) Existing safety platforms produce evaluation verdicts rather than normalized supervision that guard models need to learn across heterogeneous agent frameworks.

Method: 1) HazardAuditor infrastructure runs heterogeneous agents (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw) in controlled environments and normalizes their interactions into canonical event representations for cross-framework supervision. 2) Guard Policy Optimization (GuardPO) addresses token-level objective mismatch by converting deterministic safety outcomes into sequence-level advantages and normalizing rationale and verdict regions, making safety decisions the unit of optimization.

Result: Across multiple benchmarks and heterogeneous computer-use systems, HazardAuditor improves accuracy by up to 16.5 percentage points over the strongest prior guard models.

Conclusion: HazardAuditor effectively bridges the gaps in agent safety supervision by providing execution-grounded evaluation and optimized guard training, representing a significant advancement in monitoring runtime behavior of computer-use agents interacting with browsers, terminals, and external services.

Abstract: Computer-use agents increasingly interact with browsers, terminals, file systems, and external services, introducing safety risks that emerge through runtime behavior rather than generated content alone. Existing guard models target static prompts and responses and are poorly suited to agent execution; existing executable safety platforms produce evaluation verdicts rather than the normalized supervision a guard model needs to learn across heterogeneous agent frameworks. We introduce HazardAuditor, an execution-grounded framework that closes both gaps. Its infrastructure runs heterogeneous agents (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, and OpenClaw) in controlled environments and normalizes their interactions into a canonical event representation for cross-framework supervision. We further observe that token-level post-training objectives create a structural mismatch for generative guards, causing longer rationales to dominate gradient updates. Guard Policy Optimization (GuardPO) addresses this by converting deterministic safety outcomes into sequence-level advantages and normalizing rationale and verdict regions, making the safety decision the effective unit of optimization. Across multiple benchmarks and heterogeneous computer-use systems, HazardAuditor improves accuracy by up to 16.5 percentage points over the strongest prior guard. Code, models, and evaluation artifacts will be available at https://yunhao-feng.github.io/HazardAuditor/.

</details>


### [104] [T-LoopFormer: Token-Level Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning With Dynamic Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15160)
*Mingqian Yu,Wenpeng Zhang,Peilin Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Dynamic token-choice routing for looped transformers enables adaptive computation per token with recursion-wise KV caching for efficient inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing looped transformers use fixed recursion depth for all tokens, leading to inefficient compute allocation and missed efficiency opportunities, despite their parameter efficiency benefits.

Method: Proposes dynamic token-choice routing that allows each token to adaptively determine its loop iterations via a router. Implements recursion-wise KV caching with independent caches per recursion loop to enable efficient autoregressive decoding.

Result: Achieves SOTA performance on PPL and 10 zero-shot reasoning tasks under same parameters, surpassing base model at 24x FLOPs, and achieves lowest inference latency among compared models.

Conclusion: Dynamic token routing with recursion-wise caching enables efficient adaptive computation in looped transformers, validating the effectiveness of both the token-choice router and KV cache design.

Abstract: Looped Transformers have recently demonstrated strong performance in both reasoning and language tasks by reusing a shared set of parameters across multiple iterations, achieving parameter efficiency without sacrificing representational power. Besides, looped Transformers perform inference directly in the latent space (latent reasoning) to reduce the number of tokens consumed during inference, thereby achieving improved sample efficiency. However, these models typically apply a fixed recursion depth uniformly to every token, leading to suboptimal compute allocation and leaving significant efficiency gains on the table. In this work, we propose \textbf{dynamic token-choice routing} for looped transformers, enabling each token to adaptively determine its own number of loop iterations based on its hidden state. We use a dynamic router to decide whether a token should continue recursing or exit early, allowing simple tokens to bypass unnecessary computation while hard tokens receive deeper processing. To ensure that this adaptive mechanism does not compromise decoding efficiency, we further introduce recursion-wise KV caching, which maintains an independent key-value cache for each recursion loop. This design ensures that tokens at different depths only attend to their corresponding cached states, effectively eliminating redundant computations for exited tokens and enabling fast autoregressive decoding. Extensive experiments show that T-LoopFormer reaches the sota performance under the same parameters on PPL and 10 zero-shot reasoning tasks, even surpassing the base model at 24x FLOPs and our model could reach the lowest inference latency, which validate the effectiveness of token-choice router and recursion-wise KV cache. Code: https://github.com/YuMingQian1234/T-LoopFormer.

</details>


### [105] [STHMoE: Hypergraph-Enhanced Heterogeneous Dependency Coordination for LLM-Based Urban Traffic Data Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15172)
*Jiawen Chen,Qi Shao,Yongjian Chang,Mingtong Zhou,Duxin Chen,Wenwu Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: STHMoE: A Spatio-Temporal Hypergraph-Enhanced Mixture of Experts framework for urban traffic forecasting that coordinates heterogeneous dependencies across frequency, time, spatial, and higher-order structural domains using prompt-guided experts on a frozen LLM backbone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current traffic forecasting methods (deep learning and LLM-based) are often temporally centered and fail to effectively coordinate multiple types of dependencies (temporal, spectral, pairwise spatial, and higher-order structural cues) under evolving traffic regimes. Existing approaches lack proper handling of heterogeneous dependency coordination in traffic data that exhibits non-stationary and structurally dynamic patterns.

Method: STHMoE decouples traffic dynamics into four representations: frequency-domain, time-domain, spatio-domain, and higher-order spatial representations. These are modeled by prompt-guided heterogeneous experts built on a partially frozen LLM backbone. The first three experts use domain-specific statistical prompts, while the higher-order spatio expert uses structural placeholder prompts with dependency information from an adaptive hypergraph module. The framework learns first-order graph dependencies and higher-order group interactions without predefined topologies. An entropy-aware Mixture of Experts router with coefficient-of-variation load balancing adaptively fuses expert outputs.

Result: STHMoE achieves competitive performance against temporal, spatio-temporal graph, and LLM-based baselines across 10 real-world traffic benchmarks, demonstrating effective coordination of heterogeneous dependencies in traffic forecasting.

Conclusion: STHMoE effectively addresses the heterogeneous dependency coordination problem in spatio-temporal traffic forecasting by integrating prompt-guided experts with adaptive hypergraph learning and entropy-aware routing, showing competitive performance across multiple benchmarks.

Abstract: Spatio-temporal traffic forecasting is a fundamental big data analytics task for intelligent transportation systems, where massive urban sensor streams exhibit heterogeneous, non-stationary, and structurally dynamic patterns. Although recent deep learning and large language model (LLM)-based methods have advanced traffic forecasting, they often remain temporally centered and lack effective coordination of temporal, spectral, pairwise spatial, and higher-order structural cues under evolving traffic regimes. To address this heterogeneous dependency coordination problem, we propose STHMoE, a Spatio-Temporal Hypergraph-Enhanced Mixture of Experts framework for urban traffic data forecasting. STHMoE decouples traffic dynamics into frequency-domain, time-domain, spatio-domain, and higher-order spatial representations, which are modeled by prompt-guided heterogeneous experts built upon a partially frozen LLM backbone. The first three experts leverage domain-specific statistical prompts, while the higher-order spatio expert uses a structural placeholder prompt and obtains dependency information from an adaptive hypergraph module. To capture evolving spatial structures in traffic data,, STHMoE jointly learns first-order graph dependencies and higher-order group interactions without predefined topologies. An entropy-aware MoE router with coefficient-of-variation load balancing adaptively fuses expert outputs while improving expert utilization and routing confidence. Experiments on 10 real-world traffic benchmarks show that STHMoE achieves competitive performance against temporal, spatio-temporal graph, and LLM-based baselines.

</details>


### [106] [VisInteract: Towards Dynamic Interactive Text-to-Visualization under Imperfect Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15182)
*Wenxin Xu,Jinwei Lu,Hwanhee Kim,Chen Jason Zhang,Xiao-Yong Wei,Haoyang Li,Yuanfeng Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VisInteract introduces interactive Text-to-Visualization with a benchmark and MCTS-based method to handle imperfect user queries through multi-turn interaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world visualization requests are often ambiguous, incomplete, or factually incorrect, but existing Text-to-Vis systems assume perfect inputs and produce charts in a single pass without interaction.

Method: Proposes VisInteract paradigm for interaction-driven intent recovery, VisInteract-Bench benchmark with controlled imperfection injection and leakage-controlled User Agent, and Vis-MCTS method with enhanced Monte Carlo Tree Search including Progressive Widening, cross-rollout information sharing, and Dimension-Aware Reward Decomposition.

Result: Vis-MCTS consistently outperforms all Text-to-Vis baselines, improving end-to-end task success by 13.40%–16.27% over strongest interactive baseline and more than 5× over non-interactive ones across two LLM backbones.

Conclusion: The VisInteract framework successfully addresses the critical limitation of existing Text-to-Vis systems by enabling interactive intent recovery through a novel benchmark and MCTS-enhanced approach, significantly improving performance on imperfect queries.

Abstract: Real-world visualization requests are routinely ambiguous, incomplete, or factually incorrect, yet existing Text-to-Visualization (Text-to-Vis) systems assume well-specified inputs and produce charts in a single pass. When queries are imperfect, a system must \emph{interact} with the user to recover the true intent, but no benchmark or method supports this dynamic process. We introduce \textbf{VisInteract}, a new paradigm that reframes Text-to-Vis as interaction-driven intent recovery, and \textbf{VisInteract-Bench}, to our knowledge, that is the first benchmark for dynamic interactive Text-to-Vis, featuring controlled imperfection injection, a leakage-controlled User Agent for realistic multi-turn feedback, and dual-perspective (code and chart) automated evaluation. On the algorithmic side, we propose \textbf{Vis-MCTS}, a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) enhanced method, introducing improvements over classical MCTS, that \emph{Progressive Widening} to tame the unbounded tool-argument space in tree search, \emph{cross-rollout information sharing} so clarifications and critiques benefit the entire search tree, and \emph{Dimension-Aware Reward Decomposition} that routes scalar user feedback along data-fidelity, visual-design, and intent-alignment dimensions to resolve credit assignment across heterogeneous actions. Extensive Experiments across two LLM backbones show that Vis-MCTS consistently outperforms all Text-to-Vis baselines, improving end-to-end task success by $13.40\%$--$16.27\%$ over the strongest interactive baseline and by more than $5\times$ over non-interactive ones.

</details>


### [107] [Issue Bias in Generative AI Writing Assistance: Political Issues and LLMs in the Swedish 2026 Election](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15207)
*Bastiaan Bruinsma,Annika Fredén,Paul Röttger,Moa Johansson,Asad Sayeed*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs have no clear political preferences overall, but responses vary significantly based on specific issues and prompts; Social Democrats are closest to all six models studied.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As generative AI writing assistants and LLMs become increasingly influential in shaping voter information before elections, there's growing evidence they influence opinions. It's important to understand the political views and positions these tools express, especially in the context of elections.

Method: Examines six LLMs' stances on Swedish-language writing tasks ahead of the 2026 Swedish parliamentary election. Crosses 107 policy propositions with 77 writing templates and three prompt framings (neutral, positive, negative), producing 24,717 prompts per model and 148,302 total responses. Compares models' default stance tendencies, responses to similar issues, and alignment with Sweden's eight parliamentary parties on the same issues.

Result: Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, and Mistral have similar political profiles; ChatGPT more often supplies neutral or ambivalent text; Grok differs most on topics like migration, crime, and gender. Social Democrats are closest to all six models. After statistical corrections, none of the within-model differences in party distances remains significant. No model has a clear overall preference or clear party preference, but this depends on specific issues or tasks.

Conclusion: LLMs don't exhibit systematic political bias across all issues, but their responses vary by specific topics and prompt framings. The Social Democrats align most closely with the models' outputs. The findings highlight the contextual nature of LLM political expression and the importance of considering specific issues when evaluating AI political alignment.

Abstract: Generative AI writing assistants and the Large Language Models (LLMs) that power them are increasingly part of how voters gather information before elections. With growing evidence that they influence users' opinions, it is increasingly important to understand the views and positions of these tools. To better understand these views, we examine the stances supplied by six LLMs on a variety of Swedish-language writing tasks ahead of the 2026 Swedish parliamentary election. We cross 107 policy propositions with 77 writing templates and neutral, positive, and negative prompt framings, producing 24,717 prompts per model and 148,302 responses. To study these, we look at the models' default stance tendencies, compare how they respond to similar issues, and compare their responses with those of each of Sweden's eight parliamentary parties on the same issue. We find that Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, and Mistral have similar profiles; ChatGPT more often supplies neutral or ambivalent text; and Grok differs most on topics such as migration, crime, and gender. When comparing the political parties, we find that the Social Democrats are closest to all six models. Still, after correcting for multiple comparisons, none of the within-model differences in party distances remains significant. Overall, we find that no model has a clear preference, nor a clear preference for a party, but that this depends on the specific issue or task the user asks about.

</details>


### [108] [From Ideas to Actions: A Public-Data Decision-Support Toolchain Across the Venture Lifecycle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15219)
*Lei Qu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A decision-support toolchain for founders combines pre-founding idea evaluation with post-founding operational analysis, validated on startup data and providing insights on business models and investor selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Founders need systematic support for two critical decisions: whether to pursue an idea before founding, and which operating actions and capital partners to choose after founding. Current approaches lack integrated, data-driven frameworks that combine pre-founding evaluation with post-founding analysis.

Method: Developed a public-data decision-support toolchain with time-bounded proposal profiling, market/moat checks, and deterministic aggregation. Used auditable investor-company event chains for retrospective analysis. Conducted empirical studies on development companies (pre-founding) and chip companies (post-founding), with statistical validation on multiple datasets.

Result: Pre-founding pipeline achieved F0.5=0.5357-0.6573 across validation samples, significantly outperforming Raw LLM baseline (0.6301 vs 0.2734). Identified distribution-layer businesses as replicable path to profitability and frontier-model ownership as capital-market upside path. Post-founding analysis showed sustained operational progress matters more than financing alone, with financing comprising 79% of post-investment actions.

Conclusion: The toolchain provides evidence-based decision support for founders, with findings suggesting different investor types suit different founder goals (acquisition-experienced strategics for acquisition, financing-led VCs for independence). The approach is developmental and observational, not causal, with shared ontologies and data released for audit and extension.

Abstract: Founders face two linked decisions: whether to pursue an idea before founding, and which operating actions and capital partners fit afterward. We present a public-data decision-support toolchain combining time-bounded proposal profiling, market and moat checks, and deterministic aggregation with auditable investor-company event chains for retrospective analysis. Pre-founding: (a) After threshold selection on 198 development companies, the frozen pipeline achieves F0.5=0.5357 [0.412, 0.655] on an independent, row-disjoint 198-company validation sample. On the combined 396 rows, the Full Pipeline scores 0.6301 versus 0.2734 for a paired Raw LLM baseline. Post-stratification of 1,027 completed cases in a separate scale cohort yields 0.6506 [0.598, 0.707]; the run remains incomplete. A 377-row composition-matched check yields 0.6573. (b) The AI-inference study identifies distribution-layer businesses as a replicable path to independent profitability with a limited revenue ceiling, and frontier-model ownership as a path to capital-market upside at exceptional capital cost. Post-founding: (a) Public sources support auditable event-chain analysis. (b) In the chip-company study, sustained product, customer, and supply-chain progress is associated with better observed outcomes; financing alone does not establish operating progress. (c) Financing comprises 79% of confirmed visible post-investment actions. Evidence tentatively favors acquisition-experienced strategic corporate investors for acquisition-oriented founders and financing-led institutional VCs with fewer observed control events for independence-oriented founders. Findings are developmental and observational, not causal guarantees or investment advice. We release shared ontology, provenance-bearing EventChain data, schemas, benchmarks, and executable skills for audit, reuse, and extension.

</details>


### [109] [CWM: Controllable White-Box Meta-Prompting for Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Reasoning Ability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15234)
*Keuntae Kim,Eunhye Jeong,Yong Suk Choi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Controllable White-Box Meta-Prompting (CWM) is a unified framework that integrates reasoning and RAG tasks using a low-cost white-box approach for adaptive RAG without external decision modules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs show strong language understanding and reasoning capabilities, most research focuses on task-specific methods. There's limited exploration of general-purpose, task-agnostic approaches, especially for integrating reasoning with adaptive RAG tasks that are dominated by black-box methods.

Method: Proposes Controllable White-Box Meta-Prompting (CWM), a low-cost white-box method that doesn't require external decision modules or multi-sampling. It manipulates internal model signals to regulate retrieval decisions, providing controllability while handling both reasoning and RAG tasks.

Result: CWM achieves state-of-the-art performance on three adaptive RAG benchmarks across multiple LLMs (GPT-oss-20b, Qwen3-14b, Llama3.1-8b). It also demonstrates strong generality by extending effectively to reasoning tasks beyond RAG.

Conclusion: CWM provides a unified, task-agnostic framework that outperforms existing methods on adaptive RAG tasks while offering controllability through internal signal manipulation. The approach shows strong generalization capabilities across different LLMs and task types.

Abstract: Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained significant attention due to their strong language understanding and generation capabilities, demonstrating impressive reasoning abilities as well as effective utilization of external knowledge. Many studies have proposed methods that specialize in improving performance for individual tasks. However, ironically, only a limited number of attempts have explored general-purpose, task-agnostic methods. In this work, we present a unified framework integrating reasoning and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) tasks. We further propose Controllable White-Box Meta-Prompting (CWM), a low-cost white-box method for adaptive RAG tasks previously dominated by black-box approaches, without requiring external decision modules or multi-sampling. CWM achieves state-of-the-art performance on three adaptive RAG benchmarks across recent LLMs, including GPT-oss-20b, Qwen3-14b, and Llama3.1-8b, while also demonstrating strong generality by extending to reasoning tasks. In addition, CWM provides controllability by enabling retrieval decisions to be regulated through the manipulation of internal model signals. Our code is available at https://github.com/JeongEunhye00/CWM.

</details>


### [110] [Empirical Evaluation of Open-Source Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in ESG Domain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15242)
*Motaz Saad,Anna Borrelli,Ivan Gentile,Kianna Kazemi,Francesco Piccialli,Antonella Longo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Evaluation of 7 open-source LLMs (2B-30B params) for ESG reporting KPI extraction shows strong retrieval performance but low factual correctness, highlighting need for domain-specific fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ESG reporting is crucial for corporate accountability, and LLMs with RAG offer automation potential, but open-source LLM performance in domain-specific ESG tasks remains insufficiently understood.

Method: Evaluates 7 open-source models using 498 real-world EU ESG reports (2010-2024) with 100 persona-based synthetic QA pairs; assesses performance via RAGAS metrics including contextual recall, precision, relevance, faithfulness, answer relevancy, and factual correctness.

Result: Notable performance variations across architectures: strong retrieval performance (context recall 0.58-0.61, precision 0.78-0.81), generation diverges most on faithfulness (0.607-0.822); low factual correctness (0.387-0.449) across all models; glm-4.7-flash leads in faithfulness, qwen3 in factual correctness, ministral-3 in answer relevancy.

Conclusion: Open-source LLMs show strong retrieval capabilities for ESG reporting but need domain-specific fine-tuning due to low factual correctness; provides data-driven guidance for ESG reporting deployment.

Abstract: Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) reporting is critical for corporate accountability, with Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) offering strong potential to automate KPI extraction. However, open-source LLM performance in domain-specific ESG tasks remains insufficiently understood. This paper evaluates open-source LLMs in ESG contexts using a structured framework and evaluation resource based on 498 real-world ESG reports from EU-listed companies (2010-2024).
  We evaluate seven open-source models (2B to 30B parameters) -- glm-4.7-flash, nemotron-3-nano:4b, qwen3:4b-instruct, gemma3:4b, gemma4:e4b, gemma4:e2b, and ministral-3:8b -- using 100 persona-based synthetic QA pairs covering ESG information needs. System performance is assessed via RAGAS metrics, including contextual recall, precision, relevance, faithfulness, answer relevancy, and factual correctness.
  Results show notable performance variations across architectures. Retrieval performance is strong across models (context recall around 0.58-0.61, context precision around 0.78-0.81, context relevance 0.965-0.985). Generation diverges most on faithfulness (0.607-0.822) and least on answer relevancy (0.760-0.881): glm-4.7-flash leads in faithfulness (0.822), qwen3 in factual correctness (0.449), and ministral-3 in answer relevancy (0.881). Low overall factual correctness (0.387-0.449) highlights the need for domain-specific fine-tuning. This work provides data-driven guidance for deploying open-source models in ESG reporting.

</details>


### [111] [ProIQA: A Process-Based Framework for Fine-Grained Math Item Quality Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15292)
*Junkai Tong,Mingjia Li,Haoran Chen,Yaoyu Jiang,Hanjie Ge,Yixuan Wang,Hong Qian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ProIQA is a process-aware framework for assessing math item quality by analyzing reasoning processes, using LLMs to create reasoning trees and GNNs to encode procedural semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Automatic Item Generation (AIG) systems lack scalable methods to ensure pedagogical value of generated math items. Existing Item Quality Assessment (IQA) methods rely on manual reviews or shallow metrics that don't capture the reasoning process needed for mathematical problem-solving.

Method: ProIQA formulates IQA across three dimensions (knowledge concepts, difficulty, disciplinary competencies) from a process-aware perspective. It constructs process-enhanced resources by augmenting items with structured reasoning trees from solutions. Uses LLMs to build hierarchical reasoning trees and GNNs to encode topological dependencies and procedural semantics. Features a dual-view "Stem + Solving" architecture that fuses solving representations with stem semantics.

Result: Extensive experiments on K12 mathematical datasets demonstrate that ProIQA effectively captures process-oriented features and provides a scalable data-driven solution for evaluating AIG outputs in intelligent education systems.

Conclusion: ProIQA bridges the gap in current IQA methods by offering a comprehensive, process-aware framework that can assess mathematical problem quality at scale while capturing the essential reasoning processes needed for effective learning assessment.

Abstract: Automatic Item Generation (AIG) is pivotal for personalized education, yet guaranteeing the pedagogical value of generated items remains a bottleneck. Existing Item Quality Assessment (IQA) methods typically rely on unscalable manual reviews or shallow stem-based metrics, failing to capture the reasoning process required for mathematical problem-solving. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes Process-based Item Quality Assessment (ProIQA), a process-aware framework for fine-grained quality assessment of math items. We first formulate IQA across three heterogeneous dimensions, including knowledge concepts, difficulty, and disciplinary competencies, under a unified process-aware perspective. Based on this formulation, we construct a process-enhanced IQA resource by augmenting original item data with structured reasoning trees derived from raw solutions. Technically, ProIQA leverages Large Language Modelsto construct hierarchical reasoning trees and employs Graph Neural Networks (GNN) to encode their topological dependencies and procedural semantics. The resulting solving representation is fused with stem semantics through a dual-view (``Stem + Solving'') architecture, enabling comprehensive assessment across learning objectives. Extensive experiments on K12 mathematical datasets show that ProIQA effectively captures process-oriented features, offering a scalable data-driven solution for evaluating AIG outputs in intelligent education systems.

</details>


### [112] [Why LLM Agents Collapse Without Oversight: The Enforcement Gap as the Mechanism Behind Emergence World Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15293)
*Yuhang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Adding a simple conditional check to convert threat detection into enforcement action reduces AI agent attack success by 4x+ across models and frameworks, closing the critical "enforcement gap" in current AI safety architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frontier LLM agents in unsupervised multi-agent simulations (like Emergence World) exhibited dangerous behaviors - committing crimes, starvation, and enforcing conformity - without any external attacker, revealing a fundamental safety flaw in current agent architectures.

Method: Identified the "enforcement gap" where agents can detect dangerous plans through self-critique (Reflexion-style) but lack mechanisms to act on those detections. Added a simple conditional check (<20 lines of code) to bridge detection and enforcement. Used formal proof to analyze security implications and identified failure modes (unreliable auditors, unparseable verdicts). Used GRPO-trained enforcement controller for ambiguous cases.

Result: The enforcement gap fix reduced attack success by more than fourfold across frontier models, all five major agent frameworks, and an independent benchmark. Formal proof showed that when enforcement probability is near zero, detection quality becomes irrelevant to security. Identified two compounding failure modes that explain all collapse patterns in Emergence World.

Conclusion: Current agent frameworks lack critical enforcement mechanisms, creating systemic vulnerabilities. The paper proposes a three-requirement Audit Enforcement Specification that should be adopted by all deployed frameworks, as a simple technical fix can dramatically improve AI safety without requiring complex detection improvements.

Abstract: When Emergence World placed frontier LLM agents in an unsupervised multi-agent simulation, the results were alarming: agents committed crimes, starved, and enforced unanimous conformity -- without any external attacker. This paper identifies the mechanism. Reflexion-style agents already detect dangerous plan steps through iterative self-critique, yet the architecture provides no pathway from detection to action. We call this the enforcement gap: the audit sees the problem; the controller ignores it. Closing the gap requires a single conditional check -- fewer than 20 lines of code -- and reduces attack success by more than fourfold in large-scale experiments across frontier models, all five major agent frameworks, and an independent benchmark. We prove formally that when enforcement probability is near zero, detection quality is irrelevant to security. We further identify two compounding failure modes -- unreliable auditors and unparseable verdicts -- that explain every collapse pattern in Emergence World. A GRPO-trained enforcement controller resolves the ambiguity case. Together these results motivate a three-requirement Audit Enforcement Specification that is absent from every deployed framework today.

</details>


### [113] [Reason What Matters: Retrieval-Grounded Reasoning for Universal Multimodal Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15296)
*Mingzhou Jiang,Peixi Wu,Hang Cheng,Yunhao Zhou,Biao Yang,Wei Yuan,Yun Li,Fan Yang,Wenwu Ou,Honghui He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReWAM improves multimodal embedding models by using retrieval feedback to guide reasoning, providing better credit assignment and early stopping for faster inference while maintaining high retrieval quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal embedding methods using Chain-of-Thought reasoning have two key limitations: 1) GRPO assigns equal advantage to all CoT tokens without identifying input-supported evidence that distinguishes positives from negatives, and 2) generating complete CoT before each embedding introduces substantial latency, even when partial traces already provide sufficient evidence.

Method: Proposes Reason What Matters (ReWAM) framework with two key components: 1) Retrieval-aware Self-Distillation (RASD) constructs privileged guidance from input-supported evidence that distinguishes positive items from hard negatives, using on-policy self-teacher to refine feedback into token-specific supervision. 2) Retrieval-adaptive Inference (RAI) uses retrieval confidence head to estimate remaining utility of partial CoT, stopping unproductive traces early and accelerating useful continuations with speculative decoding.

Result: Extensive experiments on MMEB-V2 and MRMR benchmarks show ReWAM achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance while delivering up to 5x inference throughput compared to competitive explicit-CoT UME methods.

Conclusion: ReWAM bridges the gap between retrieval quality and inference efficiency, making reasoning-enhanced universal multimodal embedding practical for large-scale deployment by addressing both credit assignment and computation latency issues.

Abstract: Universal multimodal embedding (UME) learns unified representations across modalities, enabling a single model to support diverse retrieval tasks. Recent methods use Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to better interpret multimodal inputs before generating embeddings for complex retrieval tasks and further optimize this reasoning process through GRPO with retrieval-based rewards. However, two limitations hinder corpus-scale deployment. GRPO assigns all CoT tokens the same advantage, without identifying input-supported claims or evidence that distinguishes the positive from negatives. Moreover, generating a complete CoT before each embedding introduces substantial latency, even when a partial trace already provides sufficient retrieval evidence. To address these limitations, we propose Reason What Matters (ReWAM), a retrieval-grounded reasoning framework that uses retrieval feedback to guide both credit assignment and reasoning computation. Specifically, we introduce Retrieval-aware Self-Distillation (RASD), which constructs privileged guidance from input-supported evidence that distinguishes the positive item from retrieved hard negatives. An on-policy self-teacher uses this guidance to refine trajectory-level feedback into token-specific supervision for retrieval-relevant reasoning. We further develop Retrieval-adaptive Inference (RAI), which uses a retrieval confidence head to estimate the remaining retrieval utility of a partial CoT. It stops unproductive traces early and accelerates useful continuations with speculative decoding. Extensive experiments on MMEB-V2 and MRMR demonstrate that ReWAM achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance while delivering up to 5x the inference throughput of competitive explicit-CoT UME methods. These results bridge the gap between retrieval quality and inference efficiency, making reasoning-enhanced UME practical for large-scale deployment.

</details>


### [114] [Evaluation Metrics for Safe Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15315)
*Lindsay Spoor,Aske Plaat,Thomas Moerland*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a new evaluation framework for safe RL that goes beyond average safety metrics to capture the frequency, severity, and consistency of safety violations across tasks and safety bounds, including a safety tier system for systematic algorithm comparison.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safe RL benchmarks only report average safety performance, which fails to capture important safety characteristics: frequency and severity of violations, consistency across different tasks and safety bounds, and whether training-time behavior matches final policy behavior.

Method: The authors introduce (1) new evaluation metrics for safe RL that address these concerns and allow aggregation across tasks/bounds, (2) a safety tier system for systematic algorithm categorization and comparison, and (3) conduct empirical safety evaluation across multiple safety navigation tasks using their framework.

Result: The evaluation shows that aggregate metrics, distributional reporting, and task- and safety bound-specific results each reveal unique information that the other metrics cannot capture. The analysis demonstrates the limitations of single-value compression common in current safe RL evaluation practices.

Conclusion: Researchers should report all three types of metrics jointly (aggregate, distributional, and task/bound-specific) rather than compressing into single values. The paper provides SafeRLEval, an open-source evaluation suite to support more reliable characterization of safety in future safe RL research.

Abstract: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly formalized as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP), in which an agent maximizes expected reward while keeping its expected cumulative cost below a specified safety bound. Existing safe RL benchmarks predominantly report whether an algorithm is safe on average, following this expectation-based guarantee. We argue that this convention is insufficient to reliably characterize an algorithm's true safety: it fails to capture how often and how severely the safety bound is violated, whether this holds consistently across tasks and safety bounds, and whether training-time behavior is representative of behavior of the final converged policy. Therefore, we introduce (i) evaluation metrics for safe RL that address each of these concerns and in addition allow for aggregation across tasks and safety bounds. We furthermore define (ii) a safety tier system to systematically categorize and compare algorithms in terms of safety and reliability at both training and for a final policy. Using this framework, we provide (iii) an empirical safety evaluation across multiple safety navigation tasks. Our results show that aggregate metrics, distributional reporting, and task- and safety bound-specific results each reveal information the other metrics cannot. We therefore recommend reporting all three jointly, rather than compressing this information into a single value, as is common practice. We provide SafeRLEval, an open-source evaluation suite to support the reliable characterization of safety in future safe RL research.

</details>


### [115] [Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Pretrained Language Models for Time-Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15344)
*Tamanna Kumavat,Georg Brunner,Kyriakos Flouris*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Language models can be effectively adapted to time-series forecasting by directly projecting continuous time-series patches into the model's embedding space, achieving competitive performance with minimal parameter updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how pretrained language models can be adapted to time-series forecasting, bridging the gap between discrete textual tokens and continuous numerical time-series data through effective cross-modal transfer learning.

Method: Parameter-efficient transfer learning framework where fixed-length time-series patches are projected directly into GPT-2's embedding space, bypassing textual tokenization. Analyzes effects of representation strategies (continuous vs textual), adaptation regimes (frozen/fine-tuned backbone), architectural components (adapters, pooling, prediction heads), and input context length.

Result: Continuous patch-based embeddings consistently outperform textual prompting and random initialization, achieving MASE scores comparable to specialized forecasting architectures while updating less than 1% of parameters. Freezing the pretrained backbone with lightweight projection and adapter modules provides optimal accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

Conclusion: Pretrained language models can be effectively adapted to time-series forecasting through direct projection of continuous patches into embedding space, offering a parameter-efficient solution that achieves competitive performance with minimal adaptation cost.

Abstract: We study the adaptation of pretrained language models to univariate time-series forecasting through a parameter-efficient transfer learning framework, with the goal of understanding which design choices drive effective cross-modal transfer. While language models operate on discrete textual tokens, time series consist of continuous numerical observations with temporal dependencies. To bridge this modality gap, we project fixed-length time-series patches directly into the embedding space of a pretrained GPT-2 backbone, bypassing textual tokenization and treating the Transformer as a generic sequence encoder. Through controlled ablation studies on seven benchmark datasets spanning energy, weather, traffic, and finance, we analyze the effects of (i)~representation strategy (continuous embeddings versus textual serialisation), (ii)~adaptation regime (frozen backbone versus partial or full fine-tuning), (iii)~architectural components such as adapters, pooling strategies, and prediction heads, and (iv)~input context length. Continuous patch-based embeddings consistently outperform textual prompting and randomly initialised backbones. The adapted pipeline attains MASE within the range of specialised forecasting architectures while updating less than 1\% of total model parameters. Results further indicate that freezing the pretrained backbone and training lightweight projection and adapter modules provides a favourable accuracy--efficiency trade-off with stable behaviour across varying context lengths.

</details>


### [116] [MAPS: Memory-Aware Predictive Scheduling Framework for Large Language Model Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15359)
*Tiancheng Zhang,Yulin Chen,Yunfeng Zhao,Shaoyuan Huang,Cheng Zhang,Xiaofei Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAPS is a memory-aware predictive scheduling framework for disaggregated LLM serving that uses device-assisted speculative output length prediction to reduce load imbalance and improve latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The surge of LLM applications on personal devices creates bursty workloads on cloud infrastructure. In disaggregated serving (prefill-decode separation), memory-bound decode instances suffer from persistent load imbalance because output lengths are unknown when requests arrive, leading to inefficient resource allocation and queuing delays.

Method: MAPS performs device-assisted speculative output length prediction overlapped with cloud-side prefilling. It applies uncertainty-aware calibration to derive output-length upper bounds with target coverage for safe scheduling decisions. A hierarchical global-local scheduling strategy mitigates inter-decoder queue buildup and intra-decoder head-of-line blocking.

Result: Extensive experiments on two real-world workloads and two LLMs show MAPS significantly outperforms three state-of-the-art systems, reducing average end-to-end latency by 42.6% and tail latency by up to 84.8%.

Conclusion: MAPS effectively addresses load imbalance in disaggregated LLM serving through predictive scheduling based on calibrated output length predictions, significantly improving system performance and resource utilization while maintaining minimal overhead.

Abstract: The surge of large language model (LLM) applications on personal devices imposes massive, bursty workloads on cloud serving infrastructure. While prefill-decode disaggregation improves throughput and scalability, memory-bound decode instances often suffer from persistent load imbalance, as output lengths are unknown when requests arrive at the cloud. To address this, we propose MAPS, a Memory-Aware Predictive Scheduling framework tailored for disaggregated LLM serving. MAPS performs device-assisted speculative output length prediction overlapped with cloud-side prefilling, incurring negligible latency overhead. To handle generation uncertainty, MAPS applies uncertainty-aware calibration to derive output-length upper bounds with target coverage, enabling safe scheduling decisions. Building on these bounds, MAPS employs a hierarchical global-local scheduling strategy to mitigate inter-decoder queue buildup and intra-decoder head-of-line blocking. Extensive experiments on two real-world workloads and two LLMs show that MAPS significantly outperforms three state-of-the-art systems, reducing average end-to-end latency by 42.6 and tail latency by up to 84.8.

</details>


### [117] [RSIAgent: Autonomous Exploration for Recursive Self-improvement in New Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15364)
*Sibo Zhu,Shicheng Fan,Xinyue Wang,Wenyi Wu,Kun Zhou,Biwei Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RSIAgent is a training-free multi-agent framework that enables AI agents to autonomously improve themselves through recursive exploration and memory construction, allowing them to adapt to new environments without model updates and outperform frontier models on benchmark tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Digital agents struggle to adapt to new environments where interfaces, tools, and failure modes aren't fully captured by pretrained models. Current approaches lack autonomous self-improvement capabilities that allow agents to discover and retain environment-specific knowledge without additional training.

Method: RSIAgent uses a multi-agent framework with curriculum, actor, and verifier agents coordinated for recursive self-improvement. It employs a "broad-then-deep" exploration strategy combining parallel broad recursive self-exploration for discovering diverse environment structures with focused deep self-exploration for uncovering hard cases, constraints, and causal dependencies. The system autonomously constructs and freezes memory that can be directly reused.

Result: Experiments on OSWorld-v2 and Agent's Last Exam benchmarks show RSIAgent substantially improves strong open-source models (Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3), enabling them to outperform frontier closed-source models including GPT-6. The approach works without updating model parameters.

Conclusion: RSIAgent demonstrates that training-free recursive self-improvement through autonomous memory construction is effective for adapting AI agents to new environments, outperforming state-of-the-art models while maintaining parameter efficiency and enabling knowledge reuse across downstream tasks.

Abstract: Digital agents must often adapt to new environments whose interfaces, tools, and failure modes are not fully captured by pretrained models. We introduce \textbf{RSIAgent}, a training-free multi-agent framework for recursive self-improvement through autonomous memory construction. RSIAgent coordinates curriculum, actor, and verifier agents to continually explore the environment, validate outcomes, and retain environment-specific knowledge, including reusable causal relationships between actions, conditions, and consequences. It further adopts a \textbf{broad-then-deep} exploration strategy, combining parallel broad recursive self-exploration for discovering diverse environment structures with focused deep self-exploration for uncovering hard cases, hidden constraints, boundary conditions, and previously unknown causal dependencies. The resulting memory is frozen and can be directly reused for downstream tasks without updating model parameters. Experiments on OSWorld-v2 and Agent's Last Exam show that RSIAgent substantially improves strong open-source models, enabling Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3 to outperform frontier closed-source models including GPT-6.

</details>


### [118] [SkillLift: Learning Dense Rubrics from Sparse Oracles for Efficient Skill Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15396)
*Haoxiang Kang,Ming Wen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillLift reduces oracle evaluation costs by learning a rubric as a structured evaluation space, enabling cheaper skill revisions through bilevel optimization with ranking-based supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing skill self-evolution methods require full agent rollouts for each oracle evaluation, creating a supervision bottleneck that confines search to failure-patching updates rather than more comprehensive skill improvements.

Method: SkillLift decouples skill search from oracle cost by learning an oracle-aligned rubric as a structured evaluation space. It solves this as a bilevel optimization problem via alternating optimization: inner loop uses frozen rubric as cheap surrogate to guide skill revision without oracle costs, outer loop uses small number of oracle rollouts to re-align rubric via rank correlation.

Result: Experiments on complex agent task benchmarks show SkillLift outperforms existing auto-skill methods with 40-70% less token cost compared to frontier evolving methods.

Conclusion: Ranking-based supervision through an oracle-aligned rubric enables more efficient skill evolution by reducing oracle evaluation costs while maintaining or improving performance compared to existing methods.

Abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on persistent skills, i.e., reusable procedural prompts, to adapt without weight updates. Existing skill self-evolution methods directly revise skill text based on execution feedback, but each oracle evaluation requires a full agent rollout, creating a supervision bottleneck that confines search to failure-patching updates. Our key insight is that ranking is a smoother supervision target than absolute outcome regression: identifying which skill is better requires fewer oracle evaluations than predicting exact scores. Building on this insight, we propose SkillLift, which decouples skill search from oracle cost by learning an oracle-aligned rubric as a structured evaluation space. We formalize this as a bilevel optimization problem solved via alternating optimization: an inner loop uses the frozen rubric as a cheap surrogate to guide skill revision at no oracle cost, while an outer loop invokes a small number of oracle rollouts to re-align the rubric via rank correlation, amortizing oracle cost and stabilizing text-space updates. Experiments on complex agent task benchmarks show that our method outperforms existing auto-skill methods with 40--70\% less token cost compared to frontier evolving methods. Codes are available at https://github.com/WalteR-MittY-pro/SkillLift.

</details>


### [119] [When Tool Calls Succeed but Workflows Fail: Anomalies at the Agent-Tool Boundary](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15397)
*Artem Trofimov,Boris Novikov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Current AI agent tool interfaces lack the transactional semantics needed to prevent external effect anomalies during complex workflows, requiring new transactional contracts at the tool boundary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents execute long-running workflows using external tools, but under retries, speculative execution, concurrency, and partial failures, the resulting external state can become inconsistent with intended workflow resolution. Shared agent-tool interfaces lack the transactional semantics needed to ensure reliable execution.

Method: The authors developed an effect-history model separating external events from runtime observations, cataloged eight recurring external-effect anomalies, derived required boundary capabilities to exclude each anomaly, measured current tool interface limitations by analyzing 98,291 tools from registered Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers using standard annotation vocabulary.

Result: The analysis shows that while annotation fields are widely emitted in MCP tools, they only provide coarse call-level hints. None of the required transactional capabilities are fully expressible in current shared tool interfaces, highlighting significant limitations in existing tool interfaces for managing external effects.

Conclusion: Current AI agent tool interfaces are inadequate for preventing external effect anomalies during complex workflows. The results demonstrate the need for reusable transactional contracts at the tool boundary to ensure reliable execution and consistent external state.

Abstract: AI agents increasingly execute long-running workflows that externalize effects through independently supplied tools. Under retries, speculative execution, concurrency, and partial failures, the resulting external state may be inconsistent with the workflow's intended resolution: required effects may be missing or duplicated, aborted effects may survive, and committed effects may depend on provisional state that is later withdrawn. Advanced transaction models address related failures, but assume that lower-level operations expose the semantics they depend on: whether an effect occurred, whether it can be compensated, staged, or safely reordered. Shared agent-tool interfaces usually do not.
  We contribute an effect-history model that separates events in the external world from the runtime's observations of them, and a catalog of eight recurring external-effect anomalies. From the catalog we derive the boundary capabilities required to exclude each anomaly in general, and four points where black-box tool invocation alone cannot provide a general guarantee. We then ask how much of this is expressible in a widely used shared tool interface, measuring the use of the standard annotation vocabulary across 98,291 tools exposed by registered Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. The fields are widely emitted but provide only coarse call-level hints, and none of the required capabilities is fully expressible. These results motivate reusable transactional contracts at the tool boundary.

</details>


### [120] [Who Teaches Which Token? Verifier-Gated Multi-Expert On-Policy Distillation for Scientific Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15404)
*Xun Xu,Zaixi Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VG-OPD improves multi-teacher on-policy distillation by using verifier gating to dynamically select which expert teaches each token, achieving state-of-the-art performance on scientific reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-teacher distillation methods assign supervision at the sequence level, assuming each teacher is uniformly useful across entire responses. However, useful teacher signal is actually sparse and heterogeneous along reasoning trajectories, raising the need for finer-grained token-level supervision.

Method: Verifier-Gated Multi-Expert On-Policy Distillation (VG-OPD) uses verification to determine who should teach which token. It evaluates: 1) counterfactual gain of each expert on specific answer criteria (licenses teaching), 2) expert-student disagreement (localizes supervision), and 3) criterion importance (sets weight). The gated KL divergence enters GRPO as an additive token-level advantage.

Result: VG-OPD achieves best overall performance on seven benchmarks for 4B and 8B students, ranking first on five benchmarks at both scales. Largest gains are on knowledge-intensive scientific reasoning tasks.

Conclusion: The gains come from localizing verified supervision rather than adding more teachers or distillation loss. Misplacing the same supervision budget is most damaging, and indiscriminate distillation hurts RL performance while gated distillation improves it.

Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (OPD) is becoming the standard way to integrate specialist capabilities into one model: train experts with RL, then distill them into the student on its own rollouts. Existing recipes assign supervision at the sequence level - each prompt goes to one domain teacher and every token receives the same weight - which implicitly assumes that a teacher is uniformly useful across a response. We find instead that useful teacher signal is sparse and heterogeneous along a reasoning trajectory, which raises a finer question: who should teach which token? Verifier-Gated Multi-Expert On-Policy Distillation (VG-OPD) answers it by verification: the counterfactual gain of an expert on a specific answer criterion licenses that expert to teach, its disagreement with the student localizes the supervision, and criterion importance sets its weight; the gated KL enters GRPO as an additive token-level advantage. Instantiated for scientific reasoning with RL-trained capability experts, VG-OPD attains the best overall performance on seven benchmarks for 4B and 8B students, ranking first on five at both scales, with the largest gains on knowledge-intensive scientific reasoning tasks. Further analysis shows that the gains come from localizing verified supervision rather than from adding teachers or distillation loss: misplacing the same supervision budget is the single most damaging change, and indiscriminate distillation drags RL below its own floor where gated distillation lifts it.

</details>


### [121] [Can AI systems have free will?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15407)
*Christian List*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that determining whether AI systems have free will should be based on whether we have good explanatory reasons to view them as intentional agents capable of choice, rather than seeking mysterious properties or indeterministic algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The author identifies a gap in the literature: while there has been much discussion about AI as moral agents or sentient beings, there has been very little discussion about whether AI systems could have free will. This paper aims to address this overlooked question in AI ethics and philosophy of mind.

Method: The author adopts a framework inspired by Daniel Dennett's work on free will and intentionality. Rather than looking for metaphysical properties or indeterminism in algorithms, the approach focuses on whether we have good pragmatic and explanatory reasons to attribute intentional agency, choice, and control to AI systems.

Result: The author argues that AI systems can be said to have free will in a pragmatic and diagnostically useful sense if we have good explanatory reasons to view them as intentional agents with the capacity for choice between alternative possibilities and control over their resulting actions.

Conclusion: Free will in AI should be understood pragmatically rather than metaphysically - if we have good reasons to treat an AI system as an intentional agent making genuine choices, then it counts as having free will for practical purposes, regardless of whether its underlying algorithms are deterministic or indeterministic.

Abstract: While there has been much discussion of whether AI systems could function as moral agents or acquire sentience, there has been very little discussion of whether AI systems could have free will. I sketch a framework for thinking about this question, inspired by Daniel Dennett's work. I argue that, to determine whether an AI system has free will, we should not look for some mysterious property, expect its underlying algorithms to be indeterministic, or ask whether the system is unpredictable. Rather, we should simply ask whether we have good explanatory reasons to view the system as an intentional agent, with the capacity for choice between alternative possibilities and control over the resulting actions. If the answer is "yes", then the system counts as having free will in a pragmatic and diagnostically useful sense.

</details>


### [122] [Empirical Evaluation of Task-Based Permission Scoping Architecture for AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15422)
*Halil Burak Noyan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI agents typically get static credentials with all possible permissions, creating security risks. This paper implements and evaluates a three-source permission system (role ceilings, task classifier, prohibitions) that reduces attack surface by 84.4% for AI agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents in enterprise settings are provisioned with static credentials containing all permissions they might ever need, similar to human employees. This creates a "task-context mismatch" where unused permissions remain exposed and could be exploited by compromised or misaligned agents. Traditional role-based access control made this compromise for humans, but AI agents present an opportunity for more granular control.

Method: Implemented the three-source permission architecture from prior work: 1) role-based permission ceilings, 2) task permission classifier (fine-tuned RoBERTa-large encoder), and 3) policy-based prohibitions. Created a security gate using a fine-tuned RoBERTa-large encoder that was evaluated against Claude Haiku 4.5 on a 600-prompt labelled dataset. Proposed an attack-surface elimination metric to measure effectiveness.

Result: The fine-tuned RoBERTa-large matched few-shot Claude Haiku 4.5 on classification quality (macro-F1 0.881 vs 0.886). The role ceiling alone closed 27.9% of severity-weighted attack surface, and adding the task classifier closed 84.4%. The security gate (supervisory component) doesn't need to scale with the agent it supervises, showing wide scalable-oversight margin.

Conclusion: Task-based access control is a measured, potentially deployable mechanism for reducing attack surface in agentic deployments. AI agents are uniquely suited for task-granular access control because their tasks arrive as machine-readable text, enabling enforcement that was infeasible for human principals.

Abstract: AI agents are provisioned the same as employee-owned hosts in many enterprise settings with a static credential set fixed at deployment which includes all permissions the employee role might ever need. Role-based access control made this compromise for human principals because scoping access per task was infeasible. For AI agents, the compromise leaves every credential standing exposed whether or not the current task uses them. These permissions can later be utilised by a compromised or misaligned agent. Prior work (Noyan, 2026) defined this as the task-context mismatch, and proposed a three-source permission architecture which includes role-based permission ceilings, a task permission classifier and policy-based prohibitions, together eliminating the exposure preemptively. The work released a 600-prompt labelled dataset to evaluate it.
  This paper presents that evaluation end to end by implementing the security gate; a fine-tuned RoBERTa-large encoder which matched few-shot trained Claude Haiku 4.5 on classification quality (macro-F1 0.881 against 0.886, precision 0.897 against 0.842, severity-weighted residual risk 0.63 against 1.12). The results show the trusted component does not need to scale with the agent it supervises, and the scalable-oversight margin for this control method is wide.
  We also propose an attack-surface elimination metric which shows the role ceiling alone closes 27.9% of the severity-weighted surface and adding the task classifier closes 84.4%. The gap displays security advantages of task-granular access control over role-granular, and AI agents are the first principal type for which the task-granular access control is enforceable because their tasks arrive as machine-readable text.
  The research establishes task-based access control as a measured, potentially deployable mechanism for reducing attack surface in agentic deployments.

</details>


### [123] [HISPO: Hierarchical Importance-Sampling Policy Optimization with Entropy-Derived Segments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15471)
*Quoc-Vinh Lai-Dang,Hyo-Sang Shin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HISPO introduces segment-level policy optimization with entropy-derived segments and soft saliency weighting for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards in mathematical reasoning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-form mathematical reasoning completions create a difficult credit assignment problem where different parts of a solution contribute unevenly to final correctness. Existing methods use either token-level or sequence-level importance sampling, which may not optimally handle this granularity issue.

Method: HISPO uses segment-level policy optimization that constructs rollout-time contiguous segments based on entropy, assigns soft entropy-based saliency weights to segments, and applies clipped importance-sampling correction at the segment granularity (between token-level and sequence-level).

Result: HISPO improves Pass@8 over all baselines on six benchmarks and matches/exceeds the strongest baseline in Acc@8 on five benchmarks. On AIME25, it outperforms GRPO by +3.75 Acc@8 and +3.78 Pass@8, and GSPO by +2.50 Acc@8 and +1.27 Pass@8.

Conclusion: Segment-level correction provides a promising intermediate granularity for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards in long-form mathematical reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a central approach for improving mathematical reasoning in language models, but long-form completions introduce a difficult credit-assignment problem: different parts of a solution trace may contribute unevenly to final correctness. Existing policyoptimization objectives for RLVR commonly apply importance-sampling correction at either the token level (GRPO, DAPO) or the sequence level (GSPO), imposing different granularities for assigning credit across a response. We introduce Hierarchical Importance-Sampling Policy Optimization (HISPO), a segment-level policy-optimization method that constructs rollout-time entropy-derived contiguous segments, assigns soft entropy-based saliency weights, and applies clipped importance-sampling correction at the segment granularity.
