Method: The paper introduces Never Give Up (NGU), an adaptive sampling method that continues generating samples for a problem until one is correct. By leveraging asynchronous RL, NGU naturally uses fewer samples to filter out easy problems while allocating more compute to solving harder ones. The authors investigate design choices affecting NGU (such as off-policy robustness) and develop best practices for implementation.

Result: On the math benchmark Deepscaler, NGU improves performance per compute, especially on harder problems. On the coding task Manufactoria, where standard GRPO with per-test reward fails to solve problems with mixed easy and difficult tests, NGU iteratively improves, solving increasingly harder tests until it learns to fully solve coding problems.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that modern RL methods exacerbate the Matthew Effect by inefficiently allocating compute to easy problems, and that adaptive methods like NGU which dynamically reallocate compute to harder problems can significantly improve performance efficiency, particularly on challenging tasks.

Abstract: We demonstrate that training LLMs with RL does not improve performance equally across a dataset. RL shows large improvements on easy problems that an LLM is already good at solving, but small improvements on hard problems. We call this the Matthew Effect in RL for LLMs, after the phenomenon of cumulative advantage from economics and network science summarized as "the rich get richer". The naive explanation is that hard problems require more compute to find a solution. We argue that modern RL methods are exacerbating the issue by wasting too much compute on easy problems and instead should dynamically reallocate how they use compute. We introduce Never Give Up (NGU), a simple adaptive sampling method that keeps generating samples for a problem until one is correct. By leveraging asynchronous RL, this naturally uses fewer samples to filter out easy problems and allocates more compute to solving harder problems. We investigate the design choices that affect NGU, such as off-policy robustness, and develop a set of best practices. On the math benchmark Deepscaler, NGU improves performance per compute, especially on harder problems. On a recent coding task, Manufactoria, standard GRPO with a per-test reward fails to fully solve problems that have a range of easy and difficult tests. NGU iteratively improves, solving harder and harder tests, until it learns to fully solve coding problems.

</details>


### [174] [A Machine Learning API for Earth Observation Data Cubes Based on openEO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13453)
*Brian Pondi,Jonas Hurst,Rolf Simoes,Jonas Starke,Marius Appel,Edzer Pebesma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a machine learning specification for openEO to standardize ML workflows on Earth Observation data cubes across cloud platforms, addressing the mismatch between spatio-temporal EO data organization and ML method requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a fundamental mismatch between how Earth Observation data is organized (as spatio-temporal data cubes) and how machine learning methods operate (on tabular feature matrices or structured tensor inputs). This forces platform-specific transformations that are difficult to reproduce or transfer across different cloud infrastructures. While openEO provides a unified interface for EO data access and processing, it lacks standardized ML integration.

Method: The authors propose a process-level ML specification for openEO structured into three stages: 1) model initialization, 2) model actions (training, tuning, inference, validation), and 3) model management. The specification supports both classical algorithms (Random Forest, SVM) and deep learning architectures for time-series and spatial patch-based modeling (TempCNN, Temporal Attention Encoders, foundation model inference). They developed three prototype implementations in R and Python to demonstrate feasibility.

Result: Three prototype implementations demonstrated feasibility across diverse technology stacks. A crop type mapping use case showed cross-backend interoperability by submitting identical process graphs to independent R and Python backends, with comparable predictions and evaluation metrics. Two additional use cases demonstrated deep learning on time series and foundation model inference. However, the prototypes revealed that full cross-backend portability requires deeper harmonization of serialization formats and execution semantics beyond the process level, as backend library versions and preprocessing conventions also affect reproducibility.

Conclusion: The proposed specification advances the reproducibility, portability, and accessibility of ML workflows on EO data cubes across cloud platforms. However, achieving full cross-backend portability requires addressing both process-level standardization and backend-specific factors through explicit backend conformance profiles, which represents the most important near-term direction for improvement.

Abstract: Earth Observation (EO) data are increasingly organized as spatio-temporal data cubes, while machine learning (ML) methods operate on tabular feature matrices or structured tensor inputs. This mismatch forces platform-specific transformations that are difficult to reproduce or transfer across cloud infrastructures. The openEO specification provides a unified interface for EO data access and processing across heterogeneous backends, but lacks a standardized approach for ML integration.
  We propose a process-level ML specification for openEO structured into three stages: model initialization, model actions (training, tuning, inference, validation), and model management. It supports classical algorithms such as Random Forest and SVM, as well as deep learning architectures for time-series and spatial patch-based modeling, including TempCNN, Temporal Attention Encoders, and foundation model inference. Three prototype implementations in R and Python demonstrate feasibility across diverse technology stacks. A crop type mapping use case demonstrates cross-backend interoperability by submitting an identical process graph to independent R and Python backends and comparing predictions and evaluation metrics.
  Two further use cases demonstrate deep learning on time series and foundation model inference, each executed on a dedicated backend. The prototypes reveal, however, that full cross-backend portability requires deeper harmonization of serialization formats and execution semantics than the process level alone can enforce; backend library versions and preprocessing conventions outside the specification's boundary also affect reproducibility. Addressing both through explicit backend conformance profiles represents the most important near-term direction. The specification advances the reproducibility, portability, and accessibility of ML workflows on EO data cubes across cloud platforms.

</details>


### [175] [On the Potential of Multi-Task Learning in Predictive Process Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13477)
*Lukas Kirchdorfer,Keyvan Amiri Elyasi,Heiner Stuckenschmidt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MTL in Predictive Process Monitoring shows promise for improving next-activity prediction and addressing class imbalance compared to traditional single-task approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most current deep learning approaches in Predictive Process Monitoring use single-task learning (training separate models per task), which increases maintenance effort and overlooks potential synergies between related tasks. Multi-task learning offers a promising alternative but its effectiveness in PPM remains underexplored.

Method: The authors conducted the first comprehensive empirical study of MTL for PPM, evaluating various task combinations, neural architectures, and optimization methods to understand when and how MTL improves upon STL in PPM.

Result: MTL shows substantial improvements for next-activity prediction and inherently mitigates class imbalance issues. Task balancing is especially critical under low-capacity models, and certain task combinations show particularly strong synergies.

Conclusion: Multi-task learning represents a strong paradigm for Predictive Process Monitoring, offering benefits over single-task learning approaches, particularly for next-activity prediction and class imbalance problems, with proper task balancing being crucial for optimal performance.

Abstract: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) forecasts how ongoing organizational processes unfold, enabling information systems to move beyond execution support toward proactive analysis and monitoring. Although deep learning has improved prediction accuracy in PPM, most approaches follow a single-task learning (STL) setup, training a separate model per task. This increases maintenance effort and overlooks potential synergies. Multi-task learning (MTL), which jointly learns multiple prediction targets in one model, offers a promising alternative, yet its effectiveness in PPM remains underexplored. It remains unclear whether and under which settings MTL improves upon STL, which prediction tasks benefit most from joint learning, which task combinations are particularly synergistic, and if and how tasks should be balanced. To fill this gap, we present the first comprehensive empirical study of MTL for PPM, evaluating a variety of task combinations, neural architectures, and optimization methods. Overall, our results position MTL as a strong paradigm for PPM: we see substantial improvements in next-activity prediction and inherent mitigation of class imbalance using MTL, while task balancing is especially critical under low-capacity models.

</details>


### [176] [One Spectrum, Two Resources: Data-Memory Scaling in Autoregressive Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13500)
*Chiwun Yang,Xiaoyu Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Paper establishes a fundamental law connecting data and memory resources via a predictive-energy spectrum, with a minimax rate law showing how data resolution and memory capacity combine through an optimal bit allocation process.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the fundamental relationship between learned memory capacity and available data volume, and to characterize how these two resources interact to determine prediction performance in autoregressive retrieval sources.

Method: Theoretical analysis using a positive-entropy autoregressive retrieval source model, energy spectrum characterization, minimax analysis, and experimental validation including masked query-key attention head implementation, bit allocation strategies, and quantization experiments across pretrained models.

Result: Proved the minimax law relating data (n) and memory (B) through the energy spectrum μ, showing how optimal bit allocation determines the tradeoff, with empirical validation recovering the predicted collapse and coupling exponents across model scales.

Conclusion: Data and memory resources are fundamentally coupled through a predictive-energy spectrum, with optimal performance requiring coordinated bit allocation between routing information and value precision, and energy-dimension pairing being essential for determining resource requirements.

Abstract: How much learned memory is needed to benefit from more data? We show that the two resources are governed by one predictive-energy spectrum in a positive-entropy autoregressive retrieval source. Each coordinate contributes its query probability times the squared radius of its unknown logit. Writing $μ$ for the resulting energy spectrum, we prove the minimax law $\mathfrak R^*_{\rm value}(n,B)\asymp_R Φ_μ(n^{-1})+Φ_μ(τ_B), Φ_μ(t)=\int\min\{x,t\}\,μ(\mathrm dx),$ for $n$ prediction blocks and a learned state with at most $2^B$ values. Data set the resolution $1/n$; memory sets the level $τ_B$ reached by optimal bit allocation. The complete curve also recovers the positive spectrum. Energy-dimension pairing is essential: two causal sources with identical block-energy and block-dimension marginals have different data and memory exponents. A masked query-key attention head learns the route and values, realizing the law with explicit routing, format, and arithmetic errors. Further results give exponent-adaptive allocation, finite-precision realization, and compute-precision laws under two-sided arithmetic assumptions. Experiments recover the data-memory collapse and coupling exponents, explain the routing and allocation mechanisms, and examine weight-only quantization across six pretrained-model scales.

</details>


### [177] [Pretraining for Sample-Efficient Neural Interfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13507)
*Ben Tang,Zachary Spalding,Gregory B. Cogan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MAPA is a masked autoencoder with spatial encodings that learns transferable neural representations from heterogeneous iEEG data, enabling accurate cross-subject decoding with far less labeled data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Brain-computer interfaces require large labeled datasets per subject for training decoders, which is costly and time-consuming. Self-supervised learning could help by using unlabeled recordings, but this is challenging for intracranial EEG due to anatomical and electrode placement differences between subjects.

Method: MAPA (Masked Autoencoder with Spatial Encodings) is a vanilla masked autoencoder enhanced with two spatial encodings: 1) anatomical region embedding, and 2) relative positional encoding. These enable learning neural representations that transfer across subjects despite heterogeneity in contact placement and neuroanatomy.

Result: MAPA achieves state-of-the-art performance across all three regimes of the Neuroprobe benchmark without fine-tuning: within-session, cross-session, and cross-subject. Most impressively, for cross-subject decoding, only ~164 labeled trials are needed with MAPA features to reach accuracy that would normally require 3,500 trials without pretraining - a 21x reduction in labeled data.

Conclusion: Self-supervised pretraining with spatial encoding (MAPA) can effectively scale across heterogeneous iEEG recordings and dramatically reduce the labeled data needed for accurate decoding in new subjects, making BCIs more practical and accessible.

Abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) decode neural activity to restore lost function. Typically, training a high-performance neural decoder requires a large labeled dataset to be collected from every new subject. One way to reduce the labeled data cost is self-supervised pretraining, which learns general neural representations from unlabeled recordings that accumulate across subjects. However, for intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) recordings, self-supervised learning has been challenging due to differences in contact placement and neuroanatomy between subjects. We propose MAPA, an otherwise vanilla masked autoencoder with two spatial encodings, an anatomical region embedding and a relative positional encoding, which together enable it to learn neural representations that transfer to unseen subjects and across various tasks. MAPA sets a new state of the art across all three regimes of the Neuroprobe benchmark without fine-tuning: within-session, cross-session, and cross-subject. In the cross-subject regime, a linear probe on MAPA's features needs only ${\sim}164$ labeled trials to reach the accuracy that takes 3,500 without pretraining. Our results show that self-supervised pretraining can scale across heterogeneous iEEG recordings and reduce the labeled data needed for accurate decoding in new subjects.

</details>


### [178] [A Three-Axis Stress Test of LLM vs Classical ML for Network Intrusion Detection under Distribution Shift and Adversarial Evasion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13511)
*Muhammad Ebad Atif,Muhammad Haider Ali*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: No universal winner between XGBoost and RoBERTa-LoRA for NIDS - performance depends on evaluation axis (same-dataset, cross-dataset transfer, or adversarial robustness).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarking of LLMs against classical ML for network intrusion detection relies on incomplete same-dataset evaluation protocols that don't capture real-world robustness challenges.

Method: Evaluated XGBoost and RoBERTa-LoRA on two independently collected NetFlow v2 networks across three axes: same-dataset performance, cross-dataset transfer, and adversarial evasion. Conducted staged feature-leakage ablation study.

Result: Models statistically tied on same-dataset; XGBoost wins by 15 F1 points on cross-dataset transfer; RoBERTa-LoRA wins by ~17 F1 points under adversarial evasion. Cross-dataset transfer is strongly directional, and feature leakage is distributed across representation.

Conclusion: NIDS model evaluation requires testing across multiple independent robustness axes with multiple metrics per axis, not just same-dataset accuracy. Model recommendation depends entirely on which axis is tested.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly benchmarked against classical machine learning for network intrusion detection (NIDS), almost always using same-dataset evaluation, and that protocol turns out to be incomplete. Evaluating XGBoost and RoBERTa-LoRA on two independently collected NetFlow v2 networks across three axes (same-dataset performance, cross-dataset transfer, and adversarial evasion) reveals no universal winner. The two models are statistically tied same-dataset. XGBoost wins decisively under cross-dataset distribution shift, by 15 points of F1 and 25 points of balanced accuracy; on the target network RoBERTa-LoRA's false positive rate reaches 0.78, leaving it barely above chance despite a superficially moderate F1. RoBERTa-LoRA wins decisively under adversarial evasion, by roughly 17 points of F1 at a representative mid-range perturbation strength, while both models hold false positive rates below 0.01 throughout. The model an evaluator would recommend therefore depends entirely on which axis is tested, not on same-dataset accuracy alone. A staged feature-leakage ablation improves cross-dataset transfer non-monotonically, indicating the leakage signal is distributed across the feature representation rather than confined to a few columns, and cross-dataset transfer between our two networks is strongly directional. These results argue for evaluating NIDS models along multiple independent robustness axes, and with more than one metric per axis.

</details>


### [179] [Adaptive Phase-Switching for Communication-Efficient Federated LoRA Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13512)
*Jerry Adams Franklin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Federated LoRA communication costs are reduced using adaptive phase-switching with ReverseAdaptive, achieving 40.5% round-trip savings over FLoRA with minimal quality loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current federated LoRA protocols have high client-to-server communication costs, and existing accounting ignores asymmetric transition rounds and grouped-query attention shapes, leading to inaccurate savings estimates.

Method: Proposed ReverseAdaptive, an adaptive phase-switching aggregator that monitors relative improvement in global training loss against a dimensionless threshold to locate the optimal switching point, rather than fixing phase boundaries in advance.

Result: ReverseAdaptive achieves 40.5% measured round-trip savings over FLoRA with only 0.0063 held-out instruction-following loss cost, and outperforms FFA-LoRA by 0.0182 in held-out loss (20x larger than per-method seed standard deviation).

Conclusion: Adaptive phase-switching with threshold monitoring effectively reduces federated LoRA communication costs while maintaining model quality; learning LoRA factors before freezing produces better adapters, and the approach transfers across model scales without retuning.

Abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models with low-rank adaptation reduces per-client trainable parameters, but client-to-server communication remains the dominant cost. Existing accounting for federated LoRA protocols omits the asymmetric transition round when a protocol changes aggregation mode, and reports savings that ignore grouped-query attention shapes. This paper measures per-round upload and download bytes for a bidirectional B-only federated LoRA protocol and places five methods, three from prior work, on a single communication-quality frontier. The frontier has a knee, which an adaptive phase-switching aggregator, ReverseAdaptive, locates by monitoring the relative improvement in global training loss against a dimensionless threshold rather than by fixing a phase boundary in advance. On TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat with Alpaca, ReverseAdaptive attains 40.5 percent measured round-trip savings over FLoRA at a held-out instruction-following loss cost of 0.0063. It outperforms FFA-LoRA, which freezes the first of the two LoRA factors at initialization, by 0.0182 in held-out loss, more than twenty times the largest per-method seed standard deviation on that metric, so learning that factor before freezing it produces better adapters. The same threshold transfers across model scales without retuning, and the quality cost of the transition is stable across the two datasets tested.

</details>


### [180] [Operational Range Bounding in Spectroscopy: A Safety Cage Framework for Machine Learning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13514)
*Nikki Grens,Luís F. Simões,Kai Hou Yip,Theresa Lueftinger*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Safety cage architecture for monitoring black-box ML models in space missions detects unreliable predictions using multiple runtime indicators and rejection strategies to reduce errors by 45-65% with only 20% data coverage reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensuring reliability of black-box ML models in safety-critical space missions is challenging, especially when ground-truth validation is unavailable. ML models for analyzing exoplanetary data are susceptible to instrument anomalies, stellar activity, and domain shifts, creating unquantified risks.

Method: Modular safety cage architecture operating as parallel monitoring layer without modifying underlying estimator. Monitors runtime indicators: uncertainty quantification, out-of-domain detection, and influence functions. Controlled evaluation under in-domain and cross-domain conditions using Ariel Data Challenges datasets (2019, 2021). Uses safety-driven rejection strategies and formal coverage-risk framework.

Result: Model failure is multifaceted - no single indicator captures all failure modes, demonstrating need for indicator fusion. Safety-driven rejection strategies achieve 45-65% error reduction across domains with only 20% reduction in data coverage. Systematic analysis identifies indicator combinations that maximize risk-ranking accuracy and optimize trade-off between data coverage and scientific performance.

Conclusion: Safety cages provide transparent mechanism for detecting unreliable predictions and represent critical step toward safe deployment of data-driven models in scientific applications like astrophysics where ground truth is seldom available.

Abstract: Ensuring the reliability of black-box machine learning models in safety-critical space missions remains a significant challenge, particularly when ground-truth is unavailable for validation. Although machine learning models offer a powerful means to augment standard pipelines by extracting transmission spectra from complex exoplanetary light curves, their susceptibility to unmodelled instrument anomalies, stellar activity, and domain shifts introduces unquantified risks. This study evaluates a modular safety cage architecture that operates as a parallel monitoring layer to assess the validity of a prediction without modifying the underlying estimator. By monitoring different runtime indicators, including uncertainty quantification, out-of-domain detection, and influence functions, the framework constrains the model's operational domain to a verified region. A controlled evaluation is conducted under both in-domain and cross-domain conditions, using datasets from the 2019 and 2021 editions of the Ariel Data Challenges. The results reveal that model failure is multifaceted and that no single indicator captures all failure modes, demonstrating the need for indicator fusion. The application of safety-driven rejection strategies shows that a modest 20% reduction in data coverage results in error reductions between 45% and 65% across different domains and evaluation metrics. Using a formalised coverage-risk framework, a systematic analysis of indicator combinations is performed to identify configurations that maximise risk-ranking accuracy and optimise the trade-off between data coverage and scientific performance. Safety cages provide a transparent mechanism for detecting unreliable predictions and represent a critical step towards the safe deployment of data-driven models in scientific applications, such as astrophysics, where ground truth is seldom available.

</details>


### [181] [GeoTTER: Leveraging Local Geometry of Optimal Transport for Zero-Shot Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13518)
*Wei-Yang Alex Lee,Rudrasis Chakraborty,Vishnu Lokhande*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GeoTTER is a novel optimal transport framework for zero-shot classification that addresses miscalibration and adaptability issues by incorporating geometric structure smoothing and clustering-guided cost correction, achieving significant accuracy improvements over existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional optimal transport methods for zero-shot classification suffer from miscalibration and lack of adaptability because they rely on fixed cost matrices derived solely from pre-trained model embeddings, without considering local geometric structure or correcting systematic biases.

Method: GeoTTER introduces two key techniques: 1) Graph-Laplacian smoothing to incorporate local geometric structure into optimal transport, addressing high-frequency label jaggedness by enforcing neighborhood consistency. 2) Clustering-guided cost components fused with globally adjusted transport cost to correct coherent angular drift (low-frequency orientation bias), achieving multi-objective optimization that respects both global constraints and latent data structure.

Result: GeoTTER achieves a median improvement of +6.82% compared to standard zero-shot classification and +2.13% compared to OTTER (a previous optimal transport approach), showing robust improvements across diverse benchmarks.

Conclusion: GeoTTER successfully redefines optimal transport for zero-shot classification by addressing both high-frequency label inconsistencies and low-frequency systematic biases through geometric structure integration and clustering guidance, demonstrating superior performance and adaptability compared to conventional methods.

Abstract: We present GeoTTER, a novel framework that redefines optimal transport in the realm of zero-shot classification. Conventional methods often suffer from miscalibration and a lack of adaptability, as they rely on fixed cost matrices derived solely from pre-trained model embeddings. In contrast, GeoTTER addresses these limitations by incorporating two key techniques. First, to alleviate high-frequency label jaggedness (sample-level manifold jitter that assigns neighboring embeddings to different classes), GeoTTER integrates local geometric structure into the optimal transport formulation via graph-Laplacian smoothing, a technique grounded in spectral graph theory that enforces neighborhood consistency. Second, to correct coherent angular drift (a low-frequency orientation bias in which large groups of samples share the same angular offset from their true label prototypes), we fuse clustering-guided cost components with a globally adjusted transport cost, achieving a multi-objective optimization that respects both global distribution constraints and latent data structure. With a median improvement of +6.82% compared to zero-shot and +2.13% compared to OTTER, GeoTTER shows robust improvements across a diverse set of benchmarks.

</details>


### [182] [Rolling Day-Wise Mortality Prediction in Critically Ill Patients With AKI on CRRT Utilizing Machine Pressure Waveforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13524)
*Shehan Irteza Pranto,Joanna Yang,Joshua Lambert,Stuart L. Goldstein,Lili Chan,Girish N. Nadkarni,Tiago K. Colicchio,Javier A. Neyra,Jin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel machine learning approach that combines CRRT machine waveform data with EHR clinical data to predict one-day mortality in critically ill AKI patients on continuous renal replacement therapy, achieving AUROC of 0.766.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current mortality risk assessment for AKI patients on CRRT relies only on clinical EHR data while discarding continuous minute-level circuit pressure waveforms from CRRT machines, preventing real-time detection of deterioration. These machine data streams are contaminated and unusable in raw form.

Method: Cleaned CRRT machine data by aligning with charted therapy intervals, removing non-physiological minutes, denoising using synthetic spike-injection benchmarks, and masking unobserved intervals. Developed a transformer-based stacked ensemble that late-fuses a window-reduced sequence transformer with classical models using circuit-instability features and clinical EHR variables.

Result: On CRRTnet cohort (976 patients, 4,585 days), machine-only model achieved AUROC 0.625, EHR-only 0.717, while integrated model reached 0.766 for one-day mortality prediction. SHAP analysis showed machine features increased from 20% to 46.7% of top features when including circuit-instability descriptors (filter pressure, TMP, ARD).

Conclusion: This is the first patient-level mortality prediction incorporating CRRT machine data, transforming a previously discarded bedside data stream into a continuous risk signal that provides valuable prognostic information beyond clinical EHR data alone.

Abstract: Critically ill patients with acute kidney injury (AKI) on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) face high mortality, yet current risk assessment relies primarily on clinical parameters from electronic health records (EHR) and ignores minute-level circuit pressure waveforms generated by CRRT machines that track the extracorporeal circuit's interaction with the patient. Clinicians therefore cannot see deterioration as it develops. Risk is reassessed only when labs are drawn, while this continuous record is discarded because it is contaminated by shared-device records, non-physiological minutes, and sensor artifacts. To make the stream usable, we aligned machine records to charted therapy intervals to prevent cross-patient leakage, removed priming and downtime minutes, tuned denoising on a synthetic spike-injection benchmark, and masked unobserved intervals rather than imputing them. On this cleaned stream, we define a rolling day-wise task and a transformer-based stacked ensemble that late-fuses a window-reduced sequence transformer with classical models using circuit-instability features and clinical EHR variables. In a leak-safe benchmark on the multi-center CRRTnet cohort (976 patients, 4,585 treatment days), the machine-only model had the lowest standalone prognostic value (AUROC 0.625), followed by the EHR-only model (0.717). Integrating EHR and machine streams reached a one-day mortality AUROC of 0.766. SHAP attribution showed that circuit-instability descriptors raised the machine share of the top 15 combined-model features from 3 to 7 (20.0% to 46.7%), highlighting filter pressure, transmembrane pressure (TMP), and access-to-return difference (ARD). To our knowledge, this is the first patient-level mortality prediction incorporating CRRT machine data, turning a discarded bedside stream into a continuous risk signal.

</details>


### [183] [Generative Interpretability via Scalable Neuro-Symbolic Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13529)
*Xiaocong Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper argues for a shift from post-hoc interpretability to "generative interpretability" for safer LLM deployment in agentic systems, proposing neuro-symbolic models as a concrete implementation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs move from chatbots to agentic systems where outputs have irreversible real-world consequences, current post-hoc interpretability approaches are structurally inadequate for safe deployment because they only explain behavior after the fact and cannot audit or intervene during inference.

Method: Proposes generative interpretability as an architectural property where models natively expose semantically meaningful checkpoints during inference that are human-understandable and amenable to causal intervention. Suggests neuro-symbolic models as a concrete instantiation of this paradigm.

Result: The paper demonstrates the merits of generative interpretability compared to other interpretability research paradigms, showing how it enables auditing and intervention before outputs are committed.

Conclusion: A fundamental shift to generative interpretability is necessary for safe and trustworthy LLM deployment in agentic systems, with neuro-symbolic models serving as a practical implementation pathway.

Abstract: As the use of Large Language Models moves from chatbots into agentic systems, where outputs become actions with irreversible consequences on reality, the existing paradigm on AI Interpretability research, post-hoc interpretability, is structurally inadequate for safe and trustworthy model deployment: it explains behavior after the fact but cannot audit or intervene in an inference computation before it commits to an output. We therefore argue for a shift toward \emph{generative interpretability}, an architectural property under which a model's inference pass natively exposes semantically meaningful checkpoints that are human-understandable and amenable to causal intervention. We show the merits of generative interpretability as comparison to other interpretability research paradigms, and propose Neuro-Symbolic Models as a concrete instantiation.

</details>


### [184] [Attention Is All You Need (to Avoid Spurious Oscillations)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13531)
*Jinyoung Jeong,Joseph B. Choi,Xinlun Cheng,H. S. Udaykumar,Sanghun Choi,Stephen S. Baek*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A conservative finite-volume scheme using attention-based flux selection enables large time steps for shock transport without breaking shocks, showing attention can serve as a learnable information stencil for conservative large-step simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses whether attention mechanisms can enable large time steps in shock transport simulations without breaking shocks across multiple cells in a single update, aiming to overcome conventional CFL constraints.

Method: Develops a conservative fixed-grid finite-volume scheme with CFL-conditioned attention flux that selects upstream information based on transport requirements. Uses 1D inviscid Burgers transport as test case, compares with WENO-5+SSP-RK3 and Forward Euler, and extends to 2D scalar Burgers and 1D shallow-water systems.

Result: The learned attention flux reliably preserves sharp shocks with time steps 4x larger than conventional methods while using only one stage per update. Attention shifts upstream with local transport reach and becomes more selective near shocks, showing transport-scale information and state-dependent selection directly contribute to performance.

Conclusion: Attention can serve as a learnable information stencil for conservative large-step shock transport, though current limitations include finite candidate reach and problem-dependent robustness. The conservation-scale-selection principle transfers beyond the original scalar setting to more complex systems.

Abstract: Can attention move a shock across several cells in one update without breaking it? We develop a conservative, fixed grid finite-volume scheme in which a CFL-conditioned attention flux selects upstream information according to the transport required by the current time step. One-dimensional inviscid Burgers transport is used as the central mechanism test: the same learned flux remains reliable in the conventional small-step regime and, with a time step four times larger, preserves sharp shocks while using one stage per update. A standard fifth-order WENO scheme with third-order strong-stability-preserving Runge-Kutta time integration (WENO-5+SSP-RK3) is included alongside controlled Forward Euler comparisons to separate flux selection from time integration. The learned attention shifts upstream with the local transport reach and becomes more selective near shocks; inference-time interventions and retrained ablations show that transport-scale information and state-dependent selection contribute directly to performance. Directional two-dimensional scalar Burgers transport and the one-dimensional shallow-water system then test whether the conservation-scale-selection principle transfers beyond the original scalar setting. The results support attention as a learnable information stencil for conservative large-step shock transport, while identifying finite candidate reach and problem-dependent robustness as the present limits.

</details>


### [185] [Toward Optimal Switching Regret for Multi-Armed Bandits with Oblivious Adversary](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13547)
*Mengxiao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A single algorithm achieves optimal switching regret in adversarial bandits with unknown number of switches against oblivious adversaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When the number of comparator switches S is known, optimal regret Õ(√(S+1)KT) is achievable. However, when S is unknown, this guarantee was previously shown to be impossible under adaptive adversaries, but it remained an open problem whether it could be achieved against oblivious adversaries.

Method: Combines a fixed-share learner with dyadic-interval subroutines. Uses non-uniform prior to favor following the main learner, keeping costs small. Subroutines search for local improvements using randomized learning rates and implicit exploration. When subroutines accumulate enough improvement, the main learner's learning rate doubles to adapt to unknown S.

Result: The algorithm achieves Õ(√(S+1)KT) expected regret for every S against an oblivious adversary, resolving the open problem from Auer et al. [2019b].

Conclusion: A single algorithm can achieve optimal switching regret even when the number of comparator switches is unknown, provided the adversary is oblivious rather than adaptive.

Abstract: We study switching regret in adversarial multi-armed bandits, where the learner competes with an arm sequence that changes at most $S$ times. When $S$ is known, an optimal expected regret of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{(S+1)KT})$ is obtainable [Auer et al., 2002]. However, when $S$ is unknown, Marinov and Zimmert [2021] show that this guarantee is impossible under an adaptive adversary. In this paper, we show that a single algorithm achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{(S+1)KT})$ expected regret for every $S$ against an oblivious adversary, resolving an open problem of Auer et al. [2019b]. Our algorithm combines a fixed-share learner initialized with a small learning rate and dyadic-interval subroutines that search for local improvements using randomized learning rates and implicit exploration. Importantly, a non-uniform prior favors following the main learner, keeping the cost of maintaining many subroutines small. When the subroutines accumulate sufficient improvement over the main learner, its learning rate doubles, allowing adaptation to the unknown number of comparator switches $S$.

</details>


### [186] [When Greedy Sampling Explores: KL-Regularized Contextual Bandits without Eluder-Dimension Dependence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13564)
*Zichen Wang,Haoyang Hong,Huazheng Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Greedy sampling achieves logarithmic regret in KL-regularized contextual bandits without eluder dimension dependence, with trade-offs between greedy and UCB-style exploration based on regularization strength.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to understand KL-regularized contextual bandits under both reward and preference feedback, seeking to show that simple greedy sampling can achieve strong regret bounds without relying on the eluder dimension, which is a complex structural parameter.

Method: The authors analyze a simple greedy algorithm that directly samples from the Gibbs policy induced by the estimated reward. They extend this analysis to preference feedback under both general preference and Bradley-Terry models, comparing greedy sampling with upper confidence bound (UCB)-style exploration approaches.

Result: The main results show that greedy sampling can achieve logarithmic regret without explicit dependence on the eluder dimension for both reward and preference feedback. Additionally, they establish a trade-off: greedy sampling performs better with strong KL regularization, while additional exploration becomes preferable as regularization weakens.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that simple greedy algorithms can achieve strong theoretical guarantees in KL-regularized contextual bandits, particularly when regularization is strong, providing insights into the exploration-exploitation trade-off in these settings.

Abstract: We study KL-regularized contextual bandits under both reward and preference feedback. We show that greedy sampling can achieve logarithmic regret without explicit dependence on the eluder dimension. For reward feedback, we establish an eluder-dimension-independent regret bound for a simple greedy algorithm that directly samples from the Gibbs policy induced by the estimated reward. We further extend this result to preference feedback under both the general preference and Bradley--Terry models, while also sharpening existing dimension-dependent guarantees. Our analysis reveals a trade-off between greedy sampling and upper confidence bound-style exploration: greedy sampling enjoys stronger guarantees when KL regularization is sufficiently strong, whereas additional exploration becomes preferable as the regularization weakens.

</details>


### [187] [AttnFuse: A Composable DSL for Compiling Attentions to Fused GPU Kernels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13612)
*Varun Kumar Dasoju,Tian Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AttnFuse is a domain-specific language and compiler that enables researchers to describe custom attention variants with pre-multiplication operations like Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) and generates optimized fused GPU kernels, achieving near-hand-tuned performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing tools like PyTorch's flex_attention can't handle pre-multiplication transformations like RoPE (used by all major LLMs), forcing researchers to write custom GPU kernels for new attention variants, which is time-consuming and requires expert knowledge.

Method: AttnFuse introduces a small DSL with ten high-level building blocks for describing attention variants, including pre-multiplication operations like RoPE. The compiler automatically generates a single fused GPU kernel for the entire computation, with optimization decisions based on GPU characteristics.

Result: AttnFuse achieves 2.10× speedup over flex_attention on RoPE+causal patterns on RTX 3090, and runs Llama-3-8B training steps within 5% of PyTorch's hand-tuned backend on H100. The research reveals the "Rotation Calculus" - a formula determining when to fuse RoPE vs apply separately based on GPU compute-to-bandwidth ratio.

Conclusion: A small, attention-specific compiler like AttnFuse can bridge the gap between flexible research code and production kernels, enabling researchers to experiment with attention variants without sacrificing performance or requiring GPU programming expertise.

Abstract: Modern AI systems are built on the Transformer architecture, whose core operation, attention, accounts for the majority of computation and memory cost. Researchers continually propose new attention variants to improve quality, efficiency, or context length, but each variant currently requires expert-written GPU code to run at usable speeds. PyTorch's recent flex\_attention lets researchers describe custom attention patterns in Python and compile them to fused kernels, but its design is limited to modifications applied after the central matrix multiplication, excluding Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), the positional encoding used by every major LLM.
  We introduce AttnFuse, a small DSL for attention that makes pre-multiplication transformations like RoPE first-class operations. Researchers compose ten high-level building blocks to describe a variant, and AttnFuse's compiler emits a single fused GPU kernel for the entire computation. On an RTX 3090, AttnFuse achieves a 2.10$\times$ speedup over flex\_attention on the RoPE+causal pattern. On an H100, it runs a full Llama-3-8B training step within 5\% of PyTorch's hand-tuned backend. Our investigation reveals the Rotation Calculus: whether to fuse RoPE or apply it separately depends on the GPU's compute-to-bandwidth ratio, with a derived crossover that matches measurement. AttnFuse demonstrates that a small, attention-specific compiler can close the gap between flexible research code and production kernels.

</details>


### [188] [An Efficient and Modular Framework for Targeted Harm Mitigation in LLMS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13624)
*Roberto Campbell,Momin Abbass,Muneeza Azmat,Michal Ulewicz,Raya Horesh,Kristjan Greenewald,Rogério Abreu de Paula,Nathalie Baracaldo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A modular correction framework using Activated LoRA adapters and context-aware routing to eliminate harmful outputs from pretrained LLMs during generation, enabling low-latency targeted safety improvements without compromising task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large Language Models are powerful zero-shot learners but remain prone to misalignment with human preferences, producing biased, toxic, or harmful outputs. Existing alignment methods are costly, tightly coupled to models, and lack flexibility and scalability.

Method: Proposes a modular correction framework that augments pretrained LLMs with Activated LoRA (aLoRA) adapters and a context-aware routing mechanism. Expert adapters activate mid-sequence without invalidating the KV cache, enabling low-latency targeted correction. Each expert is trained to detect and mitigate specific harms, while a learned router dynamically selects appropriate experts based on model's intermediate outputs.

Result: The system improves alignment on standard safety benchmarks while preserving task performance. It offers a lightweight and efficient solution for safer and more controllable LLM deployments.

Conclusion: The proposed modular correction framework provides a flexible, scalable, and efficient approach to improving LLM safety without the drawbacks of existing alignment methods, enabling safer deployment of large language models with targeted harm mitigation during generation.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful zero-shot learners but remain prone to misalignment with human preferences, often producing biased, toxic, or otherwise harmful outputs. Existing alignment methods, while effective, are costly and tightly coupled to the model, limiting flexibility and scalability. We propose a modular correction framework that augments pretrained LLMs with Activated LoRA (aLoRA) adapters and a context-aware routing mechanism to eliminate harms from misaligned model responses. Our approach enables expert adapters to activate mid-sequence without invalidating the KV cache, allowing low-latency, targeted correction during generation. Each expert is trained to detect and mitigate specific harms, such as bias or toxicity. A learned router dynamically selects appropriate experts based on the models intermediate outputs. We demonstrate that our system improves alignment on standard safety benchmarks while preserving task performance, offering a lightweight and efficient path toward safer and more controllable LLM deployments.

</details>


### [189] [FlowTSFM: Turning Encoder Depth into Quantile Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13640)
*Bahaeddine Abdessalem,Shifeng Xie,Zehao Xiao,Youssef Attia El Hili,Ambroise Odonnat,Jianfeng Zhang,Lujia Pan,Keli Zhang,Malik Tiomoko*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FlowTSFM introduces a recurrent encoder architecture where a single Transformer block is applied iteratively with shared parameters, supervised by a quantile-flow objective that guides intermediate states toward the final forecast, achieving competitive performance with significantly fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current encoder-based time series foundation models use deep stacks of independently parameterized Transformer layers where only the final forecast is supervised, leaving intermediate representations without explicit predictive roles and resulting in inefficient parameter usage.

Method: FlowTSFM interprets depth as a recurrent transport process using a single Transformer block applied iteratively with shared parameters. It employs a quantile-flow objective combining pinball forecasting loss with path-level position matching to supervise intermediate states along a trajectory from prior distribution to final forecast.

Result: With only 38.8M parameters, FlowTSFM achieves competitive performance on GIFT-Eval and TIME benchmarks, staying within 1.8-4.6% MASE of stronger baselines while using ~3x fewer parameters than Chronos-2 (119.5M). It also achieves a CosMean score of 0.919 vs 0.350 for Chronos-2, showing more structured predictive trajectories.

Conclusion: Recurrent parameter sharing combined with path supervision enables more structured predictive trajectories at favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs, suggesting a promising alternative to deep independent-layer architectures for time series foundation models.

Abstract: Encoder-based time series foundation models (TSFMs) typically rely on deep stacks of independently parameterized Transformer layers, where only the final forecast is supervised and intermediate representations have no explicit predictive role. We introduce FlowTSFM, an encoder architecture that interprets depth as a recurrent transport process: a single Transformer block is iteratively applied with shared parameters, while a quantile-flow objective supervises intermediate states along a prescribed trajectory from a prior distribution toward the final forecast. The objective combines pinball forecasting loss with path-level position matching. With only 38.8M parameters, FlowTSFM achieves competitive performance on GIFT-Eval and TIME, remaining within 1.8-4.6% MASE of stronger baselines while using approximately $3\times$ fewer parameters than a 12-layer Chronos-2 model (119.5M). Beyond accuracy, we introduce CosMean, a scale-free diagnostic measuring whether recurrent updates consistently align toward the final prediction. Under a matched intermediate-state probing protocol, FlowTSFM achieves a CosMean score of 0.919 compared with 0.350 for Chronos-2, suggesting that recurrent parameter sharing combined with path supervision is associated with substantially more structured predictive trajectories at a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

</details>


### [190] [When Compliance Data Masquerades as Evaluation: Measurement Validity for Deployed AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13642)
*Hung-Yu Lin,Xingran Huang,Qiming Guo,Jinwen Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper warns that using operational monitoring data (like automated driving crash reports) as if they were designed for comparative evaluation leads to flawed AI system assessments, and proposes an explicit "evaluation contract" to align measurement with intended claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a recurring problem where data collected for operational monitoring or regulatory compliance (e.g., automated driving disengagement and crash reports) are misinterpreted as if they were designed for comparative evaluation, leading to invalid safety claims about deployed AI systems.

Method: The paper frames this as a measurement-validity problem in AI evaluation, analyzes automated driving safety evaluation as a case study, and identifies key misalignments in reporting scope, exposure, deployment domain, event capture, and comparator construction. It then proposes an "evaluation contract" framework that makes assumptions explicit before operational data are interpreted as evidence.

Result: The analysis reveals that operational monitoring data (like U.S. disengagement and crash reports) have fundamental limitations for making comparative safety claims due to differences in reporting scope, exposure, deployment domains, event capture methods, and comparator construction. The proposed evaluation contract provides a structured approach to align measurements with intended claims.

Conclusion: Data useful for monitoring deployed AI systems are not automatically valid benchmarks for evaluating them. Comparative claims about AI systems require explicit alignment between capability intent, measured outcomes, exposure opportunities, deployment domains, data-generation processes, and evaluation comparators - a framework that should be formalized before operational data are interpreted as evidence of performance.

Abstract: We argue that a recurring failure in the evaluation of deployed AI systems occurs when data collected for operational monitoring or regulatory compliance are interpreted as if they were designed for comparative evaluation. Automated driving provides a concrete example of this problem. U.S. disengagement and crash-reporting regimes produce valuable operational evidence, but differences in reporting scope, exposure, deployment domain, event capture, and comparator construction limit the safety claims that can be supported from these measurements alone. We frame this issue as a measurement-validity problem in AI evaluation rather than as a transportation-specific data limitation. We argue that comparative claims about deployed AI systems require alignment between the intended capability, measured outcome, exposure opportunity, deployment domain, data-generation process, and evaluation comparator. Using automated-driving safety evaluation as a case study, we propose an evaluation contract that makes these assumptions explicit before operational data are interpreted as evidence of comparative performance. The broader implication is that data useful for monitoring deployed AI systems are not automatically valid benchmarks for evaluating them.

</details>


### [191] [Curvature-Independent Regret Bounds for Distributed Online Optimization on Hadamard Manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13646)
*Zhanyuan Cai,Emre Sahinoglu,Shahin Shahrampour*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Distributed Riemannian Online Gradient Descent (D-ROGD) achieves curvature-independent regret bounds for decentralized online optimization on Hadamard manifolds using horospherical convexity instead of geodesic convexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous decentralized Riemannian optimization methods under geodesic convexity often require curvature information, either for analysis (finite lower bound on sectional curvature) or in algorithm parameters (step sizes, consensus contraction factors). This curvature dependence is limiting and may degrade performance.

Method: The authors propose Distributed Riemannian Online Gradient Descent (D-ROGD) which combines local Riemannian h-subgradient updates with implicit Fréchet-mean consensus. They focus on horospherical convex (h-convex) functions instead of geodesic convex (g-convex) functions to relax curvature dependence.

Result: For h-convex objectives: O(√T) static regret. For strongly h-convex objectives: O(log T) static regret. These bounds match corresponding Euclidean rates in T-dependence, with network dependence governed only by the spectral gap. Experimental results on hyperbolic embeddings confirm these rates without observable curvature degradation.

Conclusion: This work provides the first curvature-independent regret guarantees for decentralized online optimization on Hadamard manifolds by using horospherical convexity rather than geodesic convexity, eliminating the need for curvature information in both analysis and algorithm parameters.

Abstract: This work addresses decentralized online Riemannian optimization on Hadamard manifolds. Prior work under geodesic convexity (g-convexity) may require curvature information in the optimization analysis, typically through a finite lower bound on the sectional curvature. Curvature may also enter the step size or contraction factor of tangent-space Riemannian consensus schemes. In this work, we relax the curvature dependence for a narrower class of horospherical convex (h-convex) functions. We study Distributed Riemannian Online Gradient Descent (D-ROGD), which combines local Riemannian h-subgradient updates with an implicit Fréchet-mean consensus. For h-convex and strongly h-convex local objectives, we establish $O(\sqrt{T})$ and $O(\log T)$ static regret, respectively, matching the corresponding Euclidean rates with respect to $T$, with network dependence governed solely by the spectral gap. To our knowledge, these are the first curvature-independent regret guarantees for decentralized online optimization on Hadamard manifolds. Experiments on hyperbolic embeddings corroborate the predicted rates, with no observable degradation due to curvature.

</details>


### [192] [Online Bayesian Node Classification on Inductive Graphs under Distribution Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13655)
*Jinwen Xu,Gonzalo Mateos Buckstein,Qin Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VBLL (Variational Bayesian Last-Layer) is a method that combines a deterministic GNN encoder with Bayesian last-layer parameters for node classification on evolving graphs, enabling both inductive generalization under distribution shift and calibrated uncertainty quantification through online Laplace updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Node classifiers on evolving graphs need to handle two critical challenges: inductive generalization to new nodes under distribution shift, and calibrated uncertainty for safety-sensitive applications. Standard GNNs are typically trained once and fail to address either requirement.

Method: Adapts Bayesian last-layer model by placing random last-layer parameters on top of a deterministic GNN encoder. Uses variational Bayesian last-layer (VBLL) objective that jointly trains encoder and approximate last-layer posterior via evidence lower bound with Monte Carlo expected log-likelihood. At test time, freezes encoder and applies online Laplace update to last-layer posterior.

Result: Across five node-classification benchmarks under distribution shift, online GVBLL is the only method achieving best accuracy and negative log-likelihood on every dataset. Improves accuracy by up to 17 percentage points on Cora and 14 percentage points on ogbn-arxiv over strongest non-GVBLL baseline, while remaining competitive in calibration.

Conclusion: The VBLL approach effectively addresses both inductive generalization and uncertainty calibration for evolving graph node classification, outperforming existing methods in accuracy and likelihood while maintaining competitive calibration performance.

Abstract: On evolving graphs, node classifiers must satisfy two key requirements: inductive generalization to newly arriving nodes under distribution shift and calibrated uncertainty for safety-sensitive applications. Standard graph neural networks (GNNs) are typically trained once and address neither requirement. We adapt the Bayesian last-layer (BLL) model by placing random last-layer parameters on top of a deterministic GNN encoder for uncertainty quantification. The categorical softmax likelihood required for classification breaks Gaussian conjugacy, so neither the training posterior nor the test-time streaming update has a closed-form solution. To address both challenges, we introduce a variational Bayesian last-layer (VBLL) objective that jointly trains the encoder and an approximate last-layer posterior by maximizing an evidence lower bound with a Monte Carlo expected log-likelihood. At test time, we freeze the encoder and apply an online Laplace update to the last-layer posterior. This update corresponds to a power-prior Bayesian model with exponential forgetting and a Kullback-Leibler anchor to the training posterior. Across five node-classification benchmarks under distribution shift, online GVBLL is the only method to achieve the best accuracy and negative log-likelihood on every dataset. It improves accuracy by up to 17 percentage points on Cora and 14 percentage points on ogbn-arxiv over the strongest non-GVBLL baseline, while remaining competitive in calibration with MC Dropout, Deep Ensembles, Temperature Scaling, and Gaussian-process classifiers.

</details>


### [193] [Leakage-Safe and Scheduler-Aware Machine Learning for Grid Job Runtime Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13701)
*Ashfaq Ali Shafin,Khandaker Mamun Ahmed*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Job runtime prediction for grid computing using CatBoost with temporal validation achieves R²=0.239 and reduces average waiting time by 50.92% in scheduling simulations, but random-split evaluation overestimates performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate job runtime prediction can improve scheduling-aware resource management in grid and distributed computing environments, but existing prediction models need evaluation under realistic deployment constraints rather than just random cross-validation.

Method: Reformulated CPU burst time prediction as leakage-safe pre-execution job runtime prediction using only submission-time attributes. Compared standard regressors, chronological baselines, categorical encoding strategies, and CatBoost with native categorical handling. Added temporal hyperparameter tuning, runtime predictability analysis, feature ablation, error analysis by job length, and a minimal scheduling simulation.

Result: CatBoost achieved strongest deployment-oriented result with R²=0.239, MAE=27,019, RMSE=46,587, and LogMAE=2.646 on held-out temporal test set. Single-server simulation over 69,523 jobs showed prediction-informed SJF reduces average waiting time by 50.92% relative to FCFS.

Conclusion: Random-split evaluation overestimates performance, categorical-native boosting improves temporal generalization, and long-job underestimation remains a scheduler-relevant challenge despite improved prediction accuracy.

Abstract: Accurate job runtime prediction can improve scheduling-aware resource management in grid and distributed computing environments, but prediction models must be evaluated under realistic deployment constraints. This paper revisits CPU burst time prediction on the GWA-T-4 AuverGrid workload trace and reformulates it as leakage-safe pre-execution job runtime prediction. We define the target as job-level runtime, use only submission-time attributes, exclude post-execution variables, and evaluate models under temporal and cold-start settings rather than relying only on random cross-validation. We compare standard regressors, chronological historical baselines, categorical encoding strategies, and CatBoost with native categorical handling. We further add temporal hyperparameter tuning, runtime predictability analysis, feature ablation, error analysis by job length, and a minimal scheduling simulation. After temporal-validation tuning, CatBoost achieves the strongest deployment-oriented result with R^2=0.239, MAE=27,019, RMSE=46,587, and LogMAE=2.646 on the held-out temporal test set. A single-server simulation over all 69,523 held-out temporal test jobs shows that prediction-informed SJF reduces average waiting time by 50.92% relative to FCFS. The results show that random-split evaluation overestimates performance, categorical-native boosting improves temporal generalization, and long-job underestimation remains a scheduler-relevant challenge.

</details>


### [194] [Certifying Model Upgrades with Slice-Wise Non-Regression and Incumbent Fallback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13714)
*Shengwei Zhang,Tao Wu,Fei Qian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a reproducible release procedure for model updates that certifies non-inferiority across slices rather than just avoiding detected harm, with finite-sample guarantees for different candidate selection scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model updates can improve aggregate metrics while degrading performance on specific slices that matter to downstream users, and current approaches that only avoid "detected harm" can still release harmful updates with high probability when evaluation is noisy.

Method: Develops a reproducible release procedure that separates candidate search from independent, paired evaluation, returning the incumbent when certification fails. Uses established intersection-union and Learn-then-Test principles to provide finite-sample guarantees for different scenarios: one frozen candidate, finite candidate library, and prespecified testing order.

Result: In simulations, a "no-detected-harm" gate released harmful candidates in 99.7% of trials in a 32-slice setting, compared to 2.6% for an exact non-inferiority gate. A constructed two-block family achieved larger certified utility than a scalar path. Public digits experiments consistently returned the incumbent due to underpowered certification.

Conclusion: Establishes an auditable protocol for model release with slice-level non-regression guarantees and identifies its limitations, but does not demonstrate benefits on foundation models or multilingual translation upgrades.

Abstract: An updated model can improve an aggregate metric while degrading a slice that matters to a downstream user. We study checkpoint selection subject to non-regression tolerances relative to a retained incumbent. The central distinction is between failing to detect harm and certifying non-inferiority: the former can release harmful updates with high probability when evaluation is noisy. We give a reproducible release procedure that separates candidate search from independent, paired evaluation and returns the exact incumbent when certification fails. Applying established intersection-union and Learn-then-Test principles, we state finite-sample guarantees for one frozen candidate, a finite candidate library, and a prespecified testing order. A joint release decision does not require a slice-count Bonferroni penalty, although certification power can still decrease with the number of slices. In bounded-score simulations, a no-detected-harm gate releases a harmful candidate in 99.7% of trials in one 32-slice setting, compared with 2.6% for an exact non-inferiority gate at a 5% target. A constructed two-block family yields larger certified utility than a scalar path under matched candidate counts. Public digits experiments, including a subsequent continuation that improves average aggregate accuracy, return the incumbent in every run because certification is underpowered. These results establish an auditable protocol and its limitations; they do not establish benefits on foundation-model or multilingual translation upgrades.

</details>


### [195] [A Variational Optimal Transport Operator on Incompressible Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13729)
*Jinjin He,Shenyifan Lu,Sinan Wang,Zhiqi Li,Duowen Chen,Bo Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VIOT is a neural operator for amortized incompressible density transport that predicts divergence-free velocity fields in real-time, replacing hour-scale optimization with feed-forward inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional adjoint fluid solvers and differentiable simulations require hour-scale optimization for each new source-target density pair, which is computationally expensive and impractical for real-time applications.

Method: Three-component system: 1) stream-function/vector-potential representation ensuring incompressibility by construction, 2) regularized transport objective balancing endpoint accuracy and flow smoothness, and 3) Fourier Neural Operator backbone amortizing solutions across new pairs and grid resolutions.

Result: VIOT achieves approximately 10^4× speedup compared to per-instance baselines, completing 2D/3D rollouts in seconds per pair versus hours for traditional methods. It generalizes beyond training distribution to user-drawn pairs in real-time interactive systems.

Conclusion: VIOT successfully transforms incompressible transport into a reusable neural operator that enables real-time generative capability for various transport processes while maintaining incompressibility constraints.

Abstract: We present the Variational Incompressible Optimal Transport (VIOT) operator, a generative neural operator for amortized incompressible density transport. Given a new source-target density pair, VIOT predicts a divergence-free velocity field and generates the full transport trajectory by feed-forward inference, replacing the hour-scale per-pair optimization used by adjoint fluid solvers and differentiable simulation baselines. The system consists of three components: a stream-function or vector-potential representation that enforces incompressibility by construction, a regularized incompressible transport objective that balances endpoint accuracy and flow smoothness, and a Fourier Neural Operator backbone that amortizes the solve across new pairs and grid resolutions. Together, these components make incompressible transport a reusable neural operator that facilitates various transport processes. Further, the generative capability extends beyond the training distribution, with VIOT producing incompressible transports for user-drawn source-target pairs in a real-time interactive system. We demonstrate VIOT on 2D and 3D density-transport benchmarks. Both 2D and 3D rollouts complete in seconds per pair, while per-instance baselines in our 2D comparisons optimize each new pair from scratch and require on the order of an hour, a roughly $10^4\times$ online speedup.

</details>


### [196] [JumpStart Your Policy Learning with Lessons from 160,000 Training Runs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13730)
*Nabil Omi,Eric Bae,Chung Yik Edward Yeung,Siddhartha Sen,Ali Farhadi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Large-scale study of offline RL and imitation learning showing that no single algorithm dominates across 114 datasets, proper hyperparameter tuning reshuffles rankings, and benchmark composition affects conclusions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work shows offline policy learning results are sensitive to reporting choices, hyperparameter tuning, and dataset properties, but these sources of variability haven't been systematically investigated together at scale to understand how they shape conclusions.

Method: Conducted large-scale empirical study training over 160,000 policies across 114 datasets, analyzed hyperparameter tuning effects, studied hyperparameter sensitivity and transfer across environments, and developed dataset-conditioned recommender system.

Result: No algorithm dominates across all environments - aggregate performance among strongest methods is often close but leaders differ substantially by environment. Hyperparameter tuning frequently reshuffles algorithm rankings, and benchmark composition can produce conflicting conclusions.

Conclusion: Offline policy learning research requires careful consideration of hyperparameter tuning, benchmark composition, and environment diversity. The JumpStart resource suite (policies, scores, hyperparameters, code, website) aims to make research more reliable and enable future work.

Abstract: Reliable progress in offline policy learning depends on careful reporting, well-tuned baselines, and evaluation across diverse conditions. Prior work has shown that results can be sensitive to reporting choices, hyperparameter tuning, and dataset properties, but these sources of variability have not been systematically investigated together at the scale needed to understand how they shape conclusions. To address this gap, we present a large-scale empirical study of offline reinforcement and imitation learning, training over 160,000 policies across 114 datasets. At this scale, no algorithm dominates: aggregate performance among the strongest methods is often close, but the leaders differ substantially across environments. We find that proper hyperparameter tuning frequently reshuffles perceived algorithm rankings and that benchmark composition can produce conflicting conclusions. We also study hyperparameter sensitivity and transfer across environments, identifying a simple strategy for deriving strong default configurations. We use our findings to develop a dataset-conditioned recommender that provides task-specific algorithm recommendations for practitioners. Finally, we release JumpStart: a resource suite containing every trained policy, per-model scores and hyperparameters, strong baselines across all environments, training and evaluation code, and an extensible website for retrieving, analyzing, and contributing results. Together, these resources aim to make offline policy-learning research more reliable and enable future work beyond the scope of this study.

</details>


### [197] [HarnessBandit: Joint Learnability-Transferability Scheduling for Multi-Harness Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13739)
*Hongliang Wei,Xiaobing Tu,Yinggui Wang,Zhengxi Liu,Rongkun Xue,Jinkui Ren,Xiantao Zhang,Debin Zhao,Xiaopeng Fan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HarnessBandit is an online scheduler that selects optimal training harnesses per step to improve robustness of language-model agents across diverse interfaces, outperforming mixed-batch training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language-model agents are deployed through diverse harnesses (system prompts, tool schemas, control loops, trajectory formats) with uneven performance across interfaces. Robustness to harness variation is important, but training across multiple harnesses introduces scheduling challenges for optimal learning signals.

Method: HarnessBandit: an online scheduler that selects one harness per optimizer step. After group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), it observes learnability (mean absolute advantage) and transferability (cosine similarity between gradient sketches). Signals are fused after normalization and sampled with visit-dependent bonus and exploration floor.

Result: Training Qwen3.5-2B across six harnesses on ClawGym shows HarnessBandit improves over mixed-batch multi-harness training on PinchBench (held-out tasks, in-distribution OpenClaw) and ClawEval (held-out tasks and harness). Diagnostics indicate learnability and transferability provide distinct, evolving signals.

Conclusion: HarnessBandit successfully addresses the harness scheduling problem for training robust language-model agents, demonstrating improved performance through intelligent harness selection based on learnability and transferability metrics.

Abstract: Language-model agents are increasingly deployed through diverse harnesses that differ in system prompts, tool schemas, control loops, and trajectory formats. The same model can perform unevenly across these interfaces, making robustness to harness variation an important objective. A natural approach is to train a shared policy through multiple harnesses, but doing so introduces a scheduling problem: each training step should favor a harness that currently provides a useful learning signal while also producing an update that benefits the other harnesses. We develop HarnessBandit, an online scheduler that selects one harness per optimizer step. After a group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) update, it observes learnability -- the mean absolute advantage on the batch -- and transferability -- the cosine between a low-dimensional gradient sketch of the current harness and exponential moving averages of the remaining harnesses. The two signals are fused after pooled sliding-window min-max normalization and sampled with a visit-dependent bonus and an explicit exploration floor. We train Qwen3.5-2B across six harnesses on ClawGym and evaluate on PinchBench (held-out tasks, in-distribution OpenClaw) and ClawEval (held-out tasks and harness). HarnessBandit improves over mixed-batch multi-harness training on both benchmarks, while training diagnostics indicate that learnability and transferability provide distinct, evolving signals.

</details>


### [198] [Training Specialist Models without Reasoning Trajectories for Domain Expert Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13770)
*Yilei Tu,Zihao Li,Shaoxiong Ji,Jörg Tiedemann,Fei Yuan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Specialist models trained without explicit reasoning supervision implicitly select reasoning trajectories, and these latent distributions directly control the specialization-generalization trade-off inherited by distilled students.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand what governs the reasoning trajectories generated by specialist models when they are trained only on question-answer pairs without explicit reasoning supervision, and to determine how these latent trajectories affect downstream distillation.

Method: Use student distillation as an agnostic probe to isolate and observe latent trajectory distributions from specialists. Analyze 27 specialist-student pairings and explicitly control the specialist's distributional drift to systematically shift both teacher and student along specialization-generalization trade-offs.

Result: Specialist optimization implicitly selects from latent trajectory space, and specialist-student specialization-generalization profiles correlate exceptionally strongly. Explicitly controlling specialist distributional drift systematically shifts both teacher and distilled student along a controllable trade-off between domain precision and general-capability retention across chemistry, physics, and multilingual settings.

Conclusion: When gold reasoning supervision is absent, tuning choices during specialist training directly control the latent supervision passed to downstream models via distillation, establishing a new view of specialist training as controlling latent reasoning distributions.

Abstract: Specialist distillation effectively transfers domain expertise to student models via teacher-generated reasoning trajectories. However, when these specialists are trained solely on question--answer pairs without explicit reasoning supervision, what governs the trajectories they generate? In this work, we show that specialist optimization implicitly selects from this latent trajectory space.
