In particular, we assess downstream performance and fairness, where fairness refers to reduced sensitivity to dataset biases across sensitive subgroups. Our experiments demonstrate that using a causal approach to synthetic training data generation can lead to tangible benefits, with these insights offering valuable guidance to machine learning practitioners for the effective design of data generation protocols.

</details>


### [224] [LIMBO: Lifelong Inference-Time Memory and Budget Optimization for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14138)
*Siddharth Sharma,Nilesh Prasad Pandey,Onat Gungor,Tajana Rosing*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LIMBO is an online framework that treats memory as a controllable inference-time resource for LLM agents, jointly optimizing memory allocation and inference budget for each task without modifying the underlying agent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lifelong LLM agents need to continually learn new capabilities while retaining competence on previous tasks, using experience replay. However, replay consumes limited prompt and compute resources that compete with other essential components like retrieval, reasoning, and tool use. Existing approaches use fixed replay policies regardless of whether replay benefits the current task, making effective resource allocation crucial.

Method: LIMBO introduces inference-time memory allocation as a distinct problem class and provides the first online framework that learns to optimize memory strategy and inference budget for each incoming task. Unlike prior approaches, it learns allocation online in a single pass, explicitly balancing task performance and inference cost without requiring model weight modifications, teacher supervision, or offline retraining.

Result: Across three LLM backbones on LifelongAgentBench, LIMBO achieves better cost-accuracy tradeoffs than state-of-the-art memory-augmented baselines. It nearly matches all strongest baselines while achieving up to ~83% lower inference cost (~53% on average). LIMBO adapts its policy across models and environments without retraining.

Conclusion: Effective memory allocation for lifelong LLM agents can be learned online rather than manually specified. LIMBO demonstrates that treating memory as a controllable inference-time resource and jointly optimizing memory strategy with inference budget enables significant computational savings while maintaining strong task performance.

Abstract: As LLM agents become integrated into increasingly complex workflows, they must continually acquire new capabilities while retaining competence on previously learned tasks. Lifelong agents address this through experience replay, injecting past interactions into the prompt to leverage prior experience during inference. However, replay is not free: every replayed trajectory competes with retrieval, reasoning, tool use, and verification for the same limited prompt and compute budget, making effective resource allocation essential. Existing approaches allocate these resources using fixed replay policies, regardless of whether replay is beneficial for the current task. We identify this as inference-time memory allocation, a distinct problem class for lifelong agents, and introduce LIMBO: the first online framework to our knowledge that treats memory as a controllable inference-time resource and jointly optimizes memory strategy and inference budget for each incoming task. Unlike prior approaches that fix the replay policy or require model weights, teacher supervision, or offline retraining, LIMBO learns this allocation online in a single pass, explicitly balancing task performance and inference cost without modifying the underlying agent. Across three LLM backbones on LifelongAgentBench, LIMBO achieves better cost-accuracy tradeoffs than state-of-the-art memory-augmented baselines and nearly matches all strongest such baselines at up to ~83% lower inference cost (~53% on average). LIMBO adapts its policy across models and environments without retraining, demonstrating that effective allocation can be learned online rather than manually specified.

</details>


### [225] [T-SMART: Mechanism-Level Attribution for Tool-Augmented Time-Series Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14142)
*Ivan Delgado,Himansi Gupta,Bishal Khatri,Niharika Sapre,Lameta Shamoon,Onat Gungor,Tajana Rosing*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: T-SMART is a neurosymbolic framework that separates LLM reasoning, deterministic computation, and structured perception for time-series QA, showing that deterministic computation provides the dominant benefit over language reasoning alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs struggle with time-series question answering, especially when numerical signals are serialized as text. Existing tool-augmented systems intertwine language reasoning, computation, and perception, making it hard to determine which components drive performance improvements.

Method: T-SMART framework uses a frozen LLM to interpret questions and select operations, deterministic tools for numerical computation, and structured perception invoked only when needed. The approach enables controlled paired ablations to isolate component contributions.

Result: Deterministic computation improves accuracy by 31.7 percentage points over direct LLM reasoning on serialized time series. Language understanding and perception offer smaller complementary gains, showing reliable numerical execution is the primary driver of performance.

Conclusion: Tool-augmented TS-QA benefits primarily from reliable numerical execution rather than additional language-model reasoning. T-SMART provides a controlled framework for analyzing component contributions in neurosymbolic time-series systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can struggle with time-series question answering (TS-QA), especially when numerical signals are serialized as text and require explicit computation. Tool-augmented approaches improve performance, but existing systems often intertwine language reasoning, computation, and perception, making it difficult to determine which components drive the gains. We present T-SMART, a neurosymbolic framework that separates these roles: a frozen LLM interprets questions and selects operations, deterministic tools perform numerical computation, and structured perception is invoked only when needed. Controlled paired ablations show that deterministic computation provides the dominant benefit, improving accuracy by 31.7 percentage points over direct LLM reasoning on serialized time series, while language understanding and perception offer smaller complementary gains. These results indicate that tool-augmented TS-QA benefits primarily from reliable numerical execution rather than additional language-model reasoning and provide a controlled framework for analyzing component contributions in neurosymbolic time-series systems.

</details>


### [226] [Signatures of Steerability in Activation Space of Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14151)
*Prajjwal Bhattarai,Tuka Alhanai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Simple separability metrics strongly correlate with downstream steerability of language models, serving as practical diagnostics for when contrastive activation steering vectors will work effectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While activation steering is a canonical and computationally efficient method for controlling language model behavior, its effectiveness varies markedly across concepts and depends heavily on the dataset used. There's a need to better understand when steering vectors will generalize and be effective.

Method: The authors analyze the relationship between simple separation metrics and downstream steerability across diverse settings. They provide evidence from synthetic superposition experiments showing correlation between separation metrics and alignment between empirical and true feature directions.

Result: Simple separation metrics strongly correlate with downstream steerability of language models, even after controlling for layers and dataset effects. Separation metrics also correlate with alignment between empirical and true feature directions in synthetic superposition experiments.

Conclusion: Simple separability statistics can serve as practical diagnostics for predicting when steering vectors are likely to work effectively, making it easier to anticipate the success of contrastive activation steering methods.

Abstract: Steering language models using a set of contrastive representations has been a canonical and computationally efficient method for controlling model behavior. Despite this success in controlling certain model behaviors, the effectiveness of activation steering varies markedly across concepts; the generalization properties of steering vectors are often considered a function of the dataset used to construct them. We make this dataset-dependence claim more rigorous and show that simple separation metrics strongly correlate with the downstream steerability of language models across diverse settings, even after controlling for layers and dataset effects. Beyond prediction, we provide evidence from a synthetic superposition experiment that separation metrics are strongly correlated with alignment between the empirical and true feature direction. Our results suggest that simple separability statistics can serve as practical diagnostics for when steering vectors are likely to work.

</details>


### [227] [CyFM: Cylindrical Optimal Transport for Few-Step Complex-Valued Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14171)
*Marcel Musiałek,Iga Wolanin,Damian Ryczko,Anna Grelewska,Oleksii Furman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CyFM uses cylindrical geometry for complex signals, computes optimal transport coupling in cylindrical metric, and outperforms Cartesian baselines in few-step generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Complex-valued signals like MRI and audio are typically modeled as flat two-channel Euclidean data, but their natural geometry is cylindrical (amplitude-phase). The paper investigates the cost/benefit of using cylindrical geometry instead of inherited metrics.

Method: 1) Replace inherited cylindrical metric with decoupled product metric; 2) Analyze Cylindrical Flow Matching (CyFM) with bounded regression targets; 3) Couple noise and data by exact minibatch Optimal Transport computed jointly over whole fields in cylindrical metric; 4) Expose limitations of factorized couplings.

Result: 1) Cartesian paths induce heavy-tailed angular velocity distribution (power law index ≈1.0); 2) Cylindrical OT coupling reduces few-step error by 3-60% across resolutions; 3) CyFM beats Cartesian baselines at every step count up to k=8; 4) At convergence, no significant geometry difference; 5) Transport-cost reduction collapses with dimension (86% to 3%).

Conclusion: CyFM with cylindrical OT coupling improves few-step generation quality despite dimensional collapse of transport-cost reduction. Factorized couplings can silently destroy joint data distributions. Cylindrical geometry offers practical benefits for complex signal modeling.

Abstract: Complex-valued signals, such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and audio spectrograms, are almost always modelled as flat two-channel Euclidean data. For nonzero values the amplitude-phase chart $z \mapsto (|z|, z/|z|)$ identifies the signal domain with the cylinder $(0, \infty) \times S^1$, on which we deliberately replace the inherited metric $dA^2 + A^2 dθ^2$ by the decoupled product metric $dA^2 + dθ^2$. In this empirical study we measure what that substitution costs and what it buys. By computing exact analytical bridges, we demonstrate that Cartesian paths induce a heavy-tailed distribution of angular velocity (power law index $\approx 1.0$), with nearly half of the probability paths exceeding an angular speed of $π$ under independent coupling, a rate no cylindrical path ever exceeds. To resolve this, we analyze Cylindrical Flow Matching (CyFM), which strictly bounds the regression target, and couple noise and data by exact minibatch Optimal Transport computed jointly over whole fields in the cylindrical metric. Although the transport-cost reduction of this coupling collapses with field dimension (from 86% for scalar pairs to 3% for $64\times64$ fields), its benefit to few-step generation does not: it lowers the few-step error of the cylindrical model by 3-60% at every evaluated resolution. With this coupling, CyFM has a lower error than the best Cartesian baseline at every step count up to $k = 8$ and every evaluated resolution, with all five seeds separated and without distillation, and at convergence we detect no significant difference between the two geometries. Finally, we expose the "Factorized Coupling Trap," showing that dimension-wise or patch-wise transport factorizations silently destroy the joint distribution of the data. All experiments are on synthetic complex fields.

</details>


### [228] [Inherited Heads: Audio language models track speakers with their text backbone's attention, and an attention-mass ranking retrieves a different set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14174)
*Bojro Das*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Fixed bias added to attention heads in audio language models redirects speaker focus from random guess levels (6-16%) to near-perfect accuracy (90.7-99%), using text-only model heads without audio-specific training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Audio language models perform poorly at speaker attribution tasks (below random chance), suggesting they lack proper mechanisms for tracking and attributing speech to specific speakers in multi-speaker recordings.

Method: Researchers added fixed bias to attention logits of selected heads without training. Heads were identified by: 1) ranking text-only language models on written versions of the task, 2) measuring attention placement on target segments, and 3) using normalized variants measuring how attention moves with questions. These heads were then transferred to audio models unchanged.

Result: Adding bias to top 100 heads redirects audio model output to specified speakers with 90.7-99% accuracy. Text-only model heads transferred to audio models achieve 80.8-95% accuracy without audio-specific selection. Shared heads between audio and text models (66-74/100 vs chance ~20) reproduce most steering effect. Normalized attention scoring outperforms established methods, reducing unplaceable outputs from 69.7% to 1.0% in Ultravox model.

Conclusion: Attention heads in language models contain transferable mechanisms for tracking entities across modalities, even without modality-specific training. Current scoring methods for identifying effective heads are suboptimal, with normalized attention movement scoring significantly outperforming established approaches for speaker attribution tasks.

Abstract: Asked to describe what one of six speakers in a recording talks about, audio language models describe the right one on 6 to 16% of trials, below the 16.7% a guess would give. Adding a fixed bias to the attention logits of a hundred heads, under a tenth of the model's and with no training, redirects the description to whichever speaker we choose, on 90.7% to 99.0% of trials. Those heads are largely not specific to audio. Rank the text-only language model an audio model was built from, or a released model of the same family, on a written version of the task, take its top hundred heads, and carry them over unchanged: they redirect the audio model on 80.8% to 95.0% of trials, with nothing about audio entering the selection. The audio and text head sets share 66 to 74 of 100 where chance would give about 20, and the shared part alone reproduces almost all of the steering. What that does not show is that sharing is what makes the heads work: an equal-sized draw from the same discovered hundred does nearly as well, and none of our three models separates the two explanations. A second finding concerns how such heads are found. Ranking heads by how much attention they place on the segment asked about, as an established score does, or by how much of their attention moves with the question, as a per-head normalised variant does, gives top hundreds that share 69, 37 and 4 heads across our three models. In Ultravox, where they share 4, the established score's heads leave output the judge cannot place on any segment on 69.7% of trials, against 40.0% with no intervention and 1.0% for the normalised variant. That is one arm of six; on the other five the established score steers above a random draw.

</details>


### [229] [A Machine Learning Framework for Fault Detection, Isolation, and Severity Prediction of Autonomous VTOL Aircraft](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14180)
*Ripon C. Sarker,Pedram H. Dabaghian,Raman Goyal,Atanu Halder*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CNN-based ML framework detects, isolates, and predicts rotor fault severity in VTOL aircraft with high accuracy using real flight data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fault detection in autonomous VTOL aircraft is critical because minor component degradations can rapidly destabilize multirotor vehicles in complex safety-critical environments, while real-flight detection remains challenging due to sensor noise, environmental disturbances, and nonlinear aerodynamics.

Method: Develops a comprehensive machine-learning framework using convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture to learn spatio-temporal patterns from multivariate flight dynamics for direct inference of both faulted rotor and damage level; validated first with simulated data from a data-generative model, then experimentally on a hexacopter with controlled blade-tip breakage.

Result: Achieves rotor-wise fault classification accuracies above 99% and severity estimation accuracy of 96% within 1% tolerance in experimental data, demonstrating strong generalization capabilities.

Conclusion: The framework supports real-time health monitoring for autonomous VTOL systems, providing robust fault detection, isolation, and severity prediction that can enhance safety and reliability in complex operational environments.

Abstract: Fault detection in autonomous VTOL aircraft is critical because even minor component degradations can rapidly destabilize multirotor vehicles operating in complex, safety-critical environments, motivating robust fault detection and estimation strategies capable of identifying early signs of rotor damage; however, real-flight fault detection remains challenging due to sensor noise, environmental disturbances, and the nonlinear aerodynamics of multirotor platforms. This study proposes a comprehensive machine-learning framework for rotor fault detection, isolation, and severity prediction using real flight data. A convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture is developed to learn spatio-temporal patterns from multivariate flight dynamics, enabling direct inference of both the faulted rotor and its damage level. The framework is first validated using simulated data generated by a data-generative model, and experimental validation is then performed on a hexacopter by introducing controlled blade-tip breakage. The trained model achieves rotor-wise fault classification accuracies above 99% and severity estimation accuracy of 96% within a 1% tolerance in experimental data, demonstrating strong generalization and supporting real-time health monitoring for autonomous VTOL systems.

</details>


### [230] [ZAPS: Zero-Cost Active Proxy Search for Neural Architecture Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14184)
*Hassan Touayouch,Rabie Najem,Mohammed Benjelloun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ZAPS: A zero-cost active proxy search framework that combines proxy signals with architectural topology in active learning to efficiently identify top neural architectures under constrained evaluation budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Zero-cost proxies for Neural Architecture Search are noisy individually, and existing methods fail to effectively combine multiple correlated proxies with architectural topology in a unified active learning framework for efficient architecture evaluation.

Method: Four-stage pipeline: (1) ProxyFit selects compact non-redundant proxy subset offline via greedy anti-redundancy criterion; (2) Hybrid K-means seeding for balanced exploitation-exploration; (3) Dynamic proxy re-selection via bootstrapped voting; (4) XGBoost ensemble ranking combining proxy ranks and topological encodings with UCB acquisition function.

Result: ZAPS recovers 52.3% of true top-100 architectures on CIFAR-10 and 65.8% on CIFAR-100 with B=200 evaluations, outperforming all baselines (Random Search, Local Search, REA, BANANAS, TPE) with lower run-to-run variance. Performs best under scarce evaluations where other methods struggle.

Conclusion: ZAPS effectively integrates proxy signals and architectural topology within active learning, significantly improving architecture search efficiency under constrained evaluation budgets, particularly in challenging search spaces where evaluations are scarce.

Abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) automates network design, but evaluating a single candidate requires training it to convergence, making exhaustive search intractable. Zero-cost proxies estimate architecture quality at initialization in seconds, yet a single proxy is noisy, and combining several does not straightforwardly help: proxies are strongly correlated, so naive aggregation compounds their shared errors instead of averaging them out. Existing methods exploit either proxy signals or architectural topology - never both within a single active-learning framework. We introduce ZAPS (Zero-cost Active Proxy Search), a four-stage pipeline that closes this gap. ZAPS (i) selects a compact, non-redundant proxy subset offline via ProxyFit, a greedy anti-redundancy criterion; (ii) seeds the search with a hybrid K-means strategy that balances exploitation and exploration; (iii) re-selects proxies at every iteration by a bootstrapped vote as the labeled set grows; and (iv) ranks candidates with an XGBoost ensemble trained jointly on proxy ranks and one-hot topological encodings, queried through an Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) acquisition function. On NAS-Bench-201 under a budget of B=200 evaluations, ZAPS recovers 52.3% of the true top-100 architectures on CIFAR-10 and 65.8% on CIFAR-100, ahead of every baseline we consider - Random Search, Local Search, REA, BANANAS and TPE - and, on CIFAR-10, with less than half the run-to-run standard deviation of the strongest of them. The advantage is largest where evaluations are scarce: on NAS-Bench-201 it narrows as the budget grows, whereas on the harder NAS-Bench-101, which no method comes close to saturating, it widens instead. All methods are scored by a single criterion: how much of the true top-100 lies among the architectures they actually evaluated.

</details>


### [231] [Entropy-Punctured Bloom Filters for Memory-Efficient Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14187)
*John Cartmell,Mihaela Cardei,Ionut Cardei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Bloom Filter encodings with entropy-based bit removal provide memory-efficient feature representations for regression tasks, achieving better predictive efficiency than traditional compression methods while maintaining competitive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory-efficient feature representations are crucial for ML applications with storage, transmission, bandwidth, or privacy constraints. While Bloom Filter encodings offer compact probabilistic representations, their behavior under structural compression and applicability to regression tasks remain underexplored.

Method: Proposed entropy-punctured Bloom Filters: starting from fixed-length BF encodings of quantized features, remove low-variability bit positions identified using empirical entropy. Evaluated on diverse regression datasets comparing raw features, PCA, Random Projection, and BF variants under leakage-free protocols with matched representation sizes using ridge regression, XGBoost, and neural networks.

Result: Bloom Filter encodings remain competitive with classical compressed representations (PCA, Random Projection) while achieving substantial storage savings. Entropy-based puncturing further reduces representation size with minimal loss in predictive fidelity, yielding improved predictive efficiency (R2 relative to encoded representation size per sample).

Conclusion: Entropy-punctured Bloom Filters provide an effective representation-level compression approach for memory-constrained machine learning, offering a practical solution for scenarios where memory efficiency is critical while maintaining predictive performance.

Abstract: Memory-efficient feature representations are increasingly important in machine learning settings where storage, transmission cost, bandwidth, or privacy constraints limit access to raw data. Bloom Filter (BF) encodings provide compact probabilistic representations of engineered features, but their behavior under structural compression and their applicability to regression tasks remain underexplored.
  In this work, we propose entropy-punctured Bloom Filters, a memory-aware encoding strategy that removes low-variability bit positions identified using empirical entropy. Starting from fixed-length BF encodings of quantized features, the proposed approach produces reduced representations that preserve predictive structure while improving predictive efficiency relative to encoded representation size.
  We evaluate the approach on diverse regression datasets, comparing raw features, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Random Projection (RP), and Bloom Filter variants under leakage-free evaluation protocols and approximately matched representation sizes. Performance is assessed using ridge regression, XGBoost, and neural networks, with predictive efficiency measured as R2 relative to encoded representation size per sample.
  Results show that Bloom Filter encodings remain competitive with classical compressed representations while achieving substantial storage savings. Entropy-based puncturing further reduces representation size with minimal loss in predictive fidelity, yielding improved predictive efficiency. These findings demonstrate that entropy-punctured Bloom Filters provide an effective representation-level compression approach for memory-constrained machine learning.

</details>


### [232] [Data-free On-policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14193)
*Gengsheng Li,Mao Zheng,Mingyang Song,Jie Sun,Zeyuan Liu,Ruiqi Liu,Qiyong Zhong,Haiyun Guo,Junfeng Fang,Jinqiao Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OPD requires almost no external data - just 8 prompts can match performance of 17k problems, and self-generated questions perform as well as or better than real data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy distillation is widely used in post-training but its actual data efficiency hasn't been examined - there's an opportunity to understand what data OPD actually needs and potentially eliminate external data requirements.

Method: Analyzed OPD training dynamics across different datasets, identified that the unit of data is states not prompts, introduced Data-free OPD where teacher writes its own questions, and tested on multi-teacher distillation.

Result: Found OPD insensitive to data: 8 prompts ≈ 17k problems; Data-free OPD matches/exceeds real data performance; 1k self-generated questions achieve 98.5% of multi-teacher distillation headroom; Data transfers reasoning patterns not domain knowledge.

Conclusion: OPD fundamentally transfers the teacher's reasoning mode rather than domain knowledge, enabling data-free distillation that matches real data and questioning the necessity of large external datasets for OPD.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a standard component of frontier post-training pipelines, yet how much its training data actually contributes has gone largely unexamined. On the two teacher-student pairings most common in practice, we find OPD almost indifferent to its data: eight prompts already match a 17k-problem dataset, and three independently built datasets whose difficulty and teacher-student KL differ several-fold produce nearly indistinguishable training curves. Two causes account for this. First, the unit of data in OPD is the state a prompt leads to, not the prompt itself: a single prompt keeps exposing new teacher correction as sampling continues, while the marginal value of additional prompts collapses after eight. Second, replacing mathematics with competitive programming still recovers over ninety percent of the in-domain gain, indicating that OPD transfers the teacher's mode of reasoning rather than knowledge related to the data. We take this to its limit with Data-free On-policy Distillation (DF-OPD), in which the teacher writes its own training questions under a simple prompt -- no external data, no filtering -- leaving a system of just two policies. DF-OPD matches and even surpasses real data, and the questions it produces track the teacher's own post-training data on three key diagnostics of training dynamics, which other real datasets do not. Applied to multi-teacher distillation, where the (prompt, domain) pairs normally have to be derived from post-training data that is often out of reach, 1k self-generated questions close 98.5% of the available headroom, even surpassing the 96.6% reached with 7k real examples. Moreover, together these results invite a reassessment of the role data plays in OPD.

</details>


### [233] [Graph-Transformer Fraud Detection with Self-Supervised Pretraining and Conformal Risk Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14234)
*Sergei,Komarov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GTFD is a graph-transformer fraud detector that combines graph structure and transaction sequences with conformal risk control to detect coordinated financial fraud with high accuracy and robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Financial fraud in corporate transaction networks has become more coordinated and harder to detect using traditional rule-based engines or classical learning models that treat transactions in isolation. There's a need for methods that can capture both structural relationships and temporal patterns in transaction networks.

Method: GTFD uses a multi-head graph attention network to encode graph structure, a gated transformer to encode ordered transaction sequences, and combines both views through a cross-modal gating layer. It includes a conformal risk-control head for threshold-free anomaly scores with finite-sample coverage guarantees. The network is trained with self-supervised link-mask pretraining plus adversarial augmentation for stability under scarce labels and adversarial perturbations.

Result: GTFD achieves AUROC of 0.990, F1-score of 96.1% (precision 96.3%, recall 95.9%), and accuracy of 98.4%. It reduces false-positive rate by about 29% relative to the strongest baseline while raising coordinated fraud-ring recall from 85.1% to 96.5%. Ablations show self-supervised pretraining contributes ~2.0 AUROC points and conformal head contributes ~1.9 AUROC points. GTFD maintains 89.2% accuracy at perturbation magnitude 0.20 where the next-best model falls to 76.4%.

Conclusion: GTFD effectively detects coordinated financial fraud by fusing structural and temporal evidence with robust training techniques, significantly outperforming existing methods while providing formal statistical guarantees through conformal risk control.

Abstract: Financial fraud in corporate transaction networks has grown more coordinated and harder to detect with rule-based engines and with classical learning models that treat each transaction in isolation. This paper presents GTFD, a graph-transformer fraud detector that fuses structural and temporal evidence from a corporation's payment graph. GTFD encodes the graph with a multi-head graph attention network, encodes ordered transaction sequences with a gated transformer, and combines both views through a cross-modal gating layer. A conformal risk-control head converts the fused representation into threshold-free anomaly scores with finite-sample coverage guarantees, and the network is trained with self-supervised link-mask pretraining plus adversarial augmentation so it remains stable under scarce labels and under adversarial perturbation. On a corporate transaction benchmark enriched with coordinated fraud rings, GTFD reaches an AUROC of 0.990, an F1-score of 96.1% (precision 96.3%, recall 95.9%), and an accuracy of 98.4%. It reduces the false-positive rate by about 29% relative to the strongest baseline while raising coordinated fraud-ring recall from 85.1% to 96.5%. Ablations attribute roughly 2.0 AUROC points to self-supervised pretraining and 1.9 AUROC points to the conformal head, and adversarial stress tests show GTFD retains 89.2% accuracy at perturbation magnitude 0.20 where the next-best model falls to 76.4%.

</details>


### [234] [CoArena: Evaluating Computer-Use and Multi-Agent Systems in Real Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14239)
*Nitish Kovuru,Prateek Jannu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoArena is a real-time benchmark platform for computer-use agents where real users submit tasks, two systems execute them concurrently in identical sandboxed desktops, users judge outcomes blindly, and a public leaderboard is continuously updated from these judgments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static benchmarks for computer-use agents have limitations: they age, leak into training data, and cannot capture evolving user needs and weekly usage patterns. They measure capability on a fixed task set rather than what users actually want from agents in practice.

Method: 1) Real users submit tasks; 2) Two systems (single model or multi-agent pipelines) execute the same task concurrently in identical sandboxed desktops; 3) Users judge outcomes blindly; 4) Continuous public leaderboard updated from judgments. Formalizes real-time evaluation with five measurable properties: continuous task arrival, live concurrent execution, online rating updates, freshness with contamination resistance, and bounded feedback latency.

Result: Provides complete rating methodology using Bradley-Terry pairwise model with weighted observations and ties, penalized maximum-likelihood estimator, streaming updates (stochastic-gradient steps), confidence intervals, rank bands from parametric bootstrap, rules for new system entry, and convergence rate analysis. Includes vote quality management with inter-judge agreement statistics, redundant judging, and handling of ties/abstentions. Demonstrates with a five-system example (211 votes) showing full derivation from vote matrix to ratings, intervals, and rank bands.

Conclusion: CoArena addresses fundamental limitations of static benchmarks by creating a real-time, user-driven evaluation platform that continuously measures how people actually use computer-use agents, ensuring relevance, freshness, and contamination resistance while providing robust statistical methodology for ranking systems.

Abstract: Static benchmarks for computer-use agents fix a task set at release and score every system against it once. That makes them reproducible, and it lets them drift from what they should measure: a fixed task set ages, leaks into training corpora, and cannot follow how people actually use agents from week to week. CoArena measures use directly. Real users submit tasks; two systems, each a single model or a multi-agent pipeline behind the same tool interface, execute the same task concurrently in identical sandboxed desktops; users judge the two outcomes without knowing which system produced them; and a public leaderboard is refit from those judgments. The central contribution is a formal account of what makes such an evaluation real-time. We define real-time as five measurable properties, each with an equation and a worked example: continuous task arrival, live concurrent execution, online rating updates, freshness with contamination resistance, and bounded feedback latency from a failed run to a reusable training environment. The rating methodology follows in full: the Bradley-Terry pairwise model, its likelihood with weighted observations and ties, the penalized maximum-likelihood estimator, and the streaming update applied when a single vote arrives (a stochastic-gradient step on the same likelihood, recovering Elo). It gives confidence intervals from the observed information and a cluster-robust sandwich, rank bands from a parametric bootstrap, the rule by which a new system enters the board, and the convergence rate of the estimate. Vote quality is treated with inter-judge agreement statistics, redundant judging, and explicit handling of ties and abstentions. A five-system example with 211 votes is carried from the vote matrix to ratings, intervals, and rank bands. Every number is derived from stated inputs or labeled illustrative; none is a measurement of a deployed system.

</details>


### [235] [Bayesian optimization with kernel ensembles and disagreement-based acquisition for source localization and acoustic inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14262)
*Heng Zhang,Haotian Xiang,Florian Meyer,Qin Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Bayesian optimization with a weighted ensemble of Gaussian processes using different kernel families improves source localization and geoacoustic inversion by reducing dependence on single kernel choice and achieving better optimization performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Joint source localization and geoacoustic inversion requires optimizing an expensive objective function using normal mode propagation models. Traditional Bayesian optimization with Gaussian processes depends heavily on kernel choice, and in high-dimensional search spaces with few observations, no single kernel performs consistently well across different inversions.

Method: Proposes using a weighted ensemble of Gaussian processes with different kernel families instead of committing to a single kernel. Combines this ensemble with an optimum-conditioned acquisition function that determines where to evaluate the expensive objective next. The method adapts the surrogate model to the observed objective without prior commitment to specific kernel structure.

Result: Experiments on simulated and measured SWellEx-96 data show the method achieves the lowest mean final objective among considered Bayesian optimization strategies and reduces parameter estimation error on most coordinates. Ablation studies reveal the ensemble provides robustness to kernel choice, while the acquisition function accounts for most of the optimization gains.

Conclusion: The weighted ensemble approach with multiple kernel families combined with an optimum-conditioned acquisition function improves Bayesian optimization performance for joint source localization and geoacoustic inversion by reducing dependence on kernel selection and achieving better parameter estimates with limited expensive model evaluations.

Abstract: Joint source localization and geoacoustic inversion requires optimizing an objective built from an expensive normal mode propagation model. Bayesian optimization (BO) with a Gaussian process (GP) surrogate can obtain accurate parameter estimates within a limited number of forward model evaluations, but its performance depends on the choice of kernel family. With few observations in a seven-dimensional search space, no single kernel can be expected to perform consistently well across individual inversions. To reduce this dependence, we use a weighted ensemble of GPs with different kernel families, allowing the surrogate to adapt to the observed objective without committing to one kernel in advance. The ensemble is combined with an optimum-conditioned acquisition function that determines where the expensive objective should be evaluated next. Experiments on simulated and measured SWellEx-96 data show that the resulting method achieves the lowest mean final objective among the considered BO strategies and reduces parameter estimation error on most coordinates. Ablation results further show that the ensemble provides robustness to kernel choice, while the acquisition function accounts for most of the optimization gain.

</details>


### [236] [Biquaternionic Space with Complex-valued Attention for Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14279)
*Rushan Geng,Cuicui Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BSCA: A temporal knowledge graph embedding model using biquaternionic space with complex-valued attention for better representation of diverse relational patterns and time-varying entities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing temporal knowledge graph embedding models often use single geometric spaces that limit representation of diverse relational patterns, and treat entity representations as static despite temporal evolution of knowledge graphs.

Method: Combines circular and hyperbolic rotations within unified biquaternionic framework with complex-valued attention mechanism that adaptively fuses time-conditioned and relation-conditioned entity representations, allowing them to vary with temporal and relational context.

Result: Achieves competitive performance across five benchmark datasets, with largest improvement on GDELT: achieves MRR of 52.1% compared to 38.1% for strongest baseline.

Conclusion: Biquaternionic space with complex-valued attention effectively addresses limitations of single-space models by enabling more flexible representation of diverse relational patterns and context-varying entity representations in temporal knowledge graphs.

Abstract: Temporal knowledge graph embedding (TKGE) models infer missing facts in knowledge graphs that evolve over time. Many existing models use a single geometric space, which can limit their ability to represent diverse relational patterns, or treat entity representations as static. We propose Biquaternionic Space with Complex-valued Attention (BSCA), a TKGE model that combines circular and hyperbolic rotations within a unified biquaternionic framework. A complex-valued attention mechanism adaptively fuses time-conditioned and relation-conditioned entity representations, allowing them to vary with temporal and relational context. Experiments on five benchmark datasets show competitive performance across datasets, with the largest improvement on GDELT: BSCA achieves an MRR of 52.1\%, compared with 38.1\% for the strongest baseline in our comparison.

</details>


### [237] [Learning Source Acquisition Policies by Offline Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14299)
*Ziqi Zhao,Run Xu,Qingjian Ni*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: O-MPAC is a method for predicting under acquisition budgets that transfers risk-cost targets from complete training records into a shared source-action scorer, enabling dynamic feature group selection during inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of prediction under acquisition budgets where feature groups need to be chosen dynamically, and their value can depend on later queries. Existing methods struggle with these sequential decision-making problems with cost constraints.

Method: O-MPAC transfers finite-horizon risk-cost targets from complete training records into a shared source-action scorer. At inference time, it uses partial observations and source metadata, re-scores after each query, and applies a hard cost mask. The method analyzes how tied teacher targets and remaining planning horizon affect learned decisions.

Result: In experiments: 1) 0.965 accuracy in five-seed routing experiment under both original and context-last orders, 2) Validation selects H1 without action cross-entropy in all thirty splits across six real tasks, 3) O-MPAC achieves highest mean budget-integrated accuracy on five tasks against source-adapted GDFS, DIME, AACO+NN and a static policy.

Conclusion: O-MPAC provides an effective approach for acquisition budget prediction that can adaptively select feature groups by transferring complete record knowledge to partial observation scenarios, demonstrating strong performance against state-of-the-art baselines.

Abstract: Predicting under an acquisition budget requires choosing feature groups whose value can depend on later queries. O-MPAC transfers finite-horizon risk-cost targets from complete training records into a shared source-action scorer. At inference time, the scorer uses partial observations and source metadata, re-scores after each query, and applies a hard cost mask. We analyze how tied teacher targets and the remaining planning horizon affect the learned decisions. Uniform supervision over tied minima preserves the target distribution under source relabeling. In a five-seed routing experiment, it achieves 0.965 accuracy under both original and context-last orders. On six real tasks, validation selects H1 without action cross-entropy in all thirty splits. O-MPAC has the highest mean budget-integrated accuracy on five tasks against source-adapted GDFS, DIME, AACO+NN and a static policy.

</details>


### [238] [Nonparametric Variance-Penalized Actor-Critic: Statistical Inference for Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14327)
*Saunak Kumar Panda,Tong Li,Yisha Xiang,Ruiqi Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Nonparametric variance-penalized actor-critic framework replaces dedicated variance critics with bootstrapping/random scaling estimators, enabling single-critic architecture with bounded variance penalties and proven convergence, while matching or exceeding baseline performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing variance-penalized RL methods require a dedicated second critic to estimate return variance, which adds architectural complexity and compounds estimation error during learning. There's a need for simpler, more robust approaches to risk-sensitive RL.

Method: Proposes nonparametric variance-penalized actor-critic (VPAC) framework using statistically grounded online estimators based on bootstrapping and random scaling techniques from statistical inference literature. These estimators require no auxiliary network, maintain single-critic architecture, and produce bounded variance penalties. Developed both Q-learning and two-timescale actor-critic variants with convergence analysis.

Result: Established almost-sure convergence for both algorithms requiring only bounded variance estimates rather than consistency. Empirically matched or exceeded variance reduction of dual-critic VPAC baseline across discrete/continuous environments. On HTS manufacturing case study, VPAC-RS achieved 74% reduction in steady-state critical current variability and 63% reduction in episode return standard deviation, improving yield consistency.

Conclusion: Nonparametric statistical inference provides a practical and theoretically sound alternative to auxiliary critics for risk-sensitive RL, eliminating architectural overhead while maintaining or improving performance in reducing variance and improving policy stability.

Abstract: Variance penalization is a principled approach to risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) that explicitly trades expected return for policy stability. Existing methods require a dedicated second critic to estimate return variance online, adding architectural complexity and compounding estimation error during learning. We propose a nonparametric variance-penalized actor-critic (VPAC) framework that replaces the variance critic with statistically grounded online estimators based on bootstrapping and random scaling, techniques drawn from the statistical inference literature for stochastic approximation. These estimators require no auxiliary network, maintain a single-critic architecture, and produce variance penalties that are bounded by construction, enabling clean convergence analysis. We establish almost-sure convergence for both a variance-penalized Q-learning algorithm and a two-timescale actor-critic variant via the ordinary differential equation (ODE) method, requiring only that variance estimates remain bounded rather than consistent. Empirically, we evaluate across discrete and continuous stochastic environments, demonstrating that the proposed methods match or exceed the variance reduction achieved by the existing dual-critic VPAC baseline while eliminating the overhead of a second critic. We further validate on a high-temperature superconductor (HTS) manufacturing case study, where VPAC-RS (Random Scaling) achieves a 74% reduction in steady-state critical current variability and a 63% reduction in episode return standard deviation, translating directly to improved yield consistency. Our results establish nonparametric statistical inference as a practical and theoretically sound alternative to auxiliary critics for risk-sensitive RL.

</details>


### [239] [Communication-Efficient LLM Adaptation over Decentralized GPU Meshes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14339)
*Sameera Ramasinghe,Shamane Siriwardhana,Thalaiyasingam Ajanthan,Hadi Mohaghegh Dolatabadi,Chamin P Hewa Koneputugodage,Gil Avraham,Violetta Shevchenko,James Snewin,Karol Pajak,Harry Xi,Alexander Long*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes an asynchronous two-circuit system with spectral correction optimizer for decentralized training, achieving 9-40x throughput gains while matching dense uncompressed performance through pipeline and data parallel compression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Decentralized training enables large-model training on low-end GPUs and internet connections, but communication along both data-parallel and pipeline-parallel axes becomes the primary bottleneck, especially for post-pretraining adaptation scenarios.

Method: Proposes an asynchronous two-circuit system: 1) fast compressed training circuit using activation masking for pipeline-parallel transfer and compressed data-parallel synchronization, and 2) slow anchor circuit running occasional unmasked forward-backward passes off the critical path. Also introduces a spectral correction optimizer that uses delayed anchor priors to denoise masked gradients without blocking the fast stream.

Result: Pipeline-parallel compression alone yields up to 9x throughput gain, and combining it with data-parallel compression increases beyond 40x over internet-grade ~200Mbps connections, while matching dense uncompressed performance across domain adaptation and continual pretraining tasks.

Conclusion: Activation masking with asynchronous two-circuit anchoring enables reliable high-compression post-pretraining adaptation, overcoming prior limitations of aggressive activation compression and significantly improving decentralized training throughput without sacrificing performance.

Abstract: Decentralized training enables large-model training over low-end GPUs and internet-grade connections, but communication along both data-parallel and pipeline-parallel axes becomes the primary bottleneck. We study post-pretraining adaptation in this setting. We propose an asynchronous two-circuit system: a fast compressed training circuit drives throughput using activation masking for pipeline-parallel (PP) transfer and compressed data-parallel (DP) synchronization, while a slow anchor circuit runs occasional unmasked forward--backward passes off the critical path. Then, we introduce a spectral correction optimizer that uses these delayed anchor priors to denoise masked gradients without blocking the fast stream. Although prior work has found aggressive activation compression unreliable, we show that masking supports post-pretraining adaptation at high compression rates when anchored this way. Pipeline-parallel compression alone yields up to a $9\times$ throughput gain, and combining it with data-parallel compression increases beyond $40\times$ over internet-grade $\sim 200$Mbps connections, while matching dense uncompressed performance across domain adaptation and continual pretraining.

</details>


### [240] [Multimodal deep learning from spectra for small-molecule structure identification: enhancing robustness with mixed-condition training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14360)
*Bowen Gao,Lei Zhu,Yiying Wang,Wenjie Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Mixed-condition training with MoE fusion improves small-molecule structure identification robustness by incorporating spectroscopy/chemistry domain knowledge into training protocol.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world molecular characterization faces challenges with missing, degraded, or mismatched spectra, making multimodal models vulnerable to practical deployment issues.

Method: Used mixed-condition training incorporating domain knowledge with MoE fusion on Multimodal Spectroscopic Dataset (MS, IR, NMR). Evaluation protocol included modality-specific perturbations and chemically informed spectrum replacements across 30 conditions.

Result: Mixed-condition training provided main performance gains: MRR increased from 0.9203 to 0.9763 (6.08% relative), R@1 from 89.50% to 96.36% (7.67% relative). IR-only MRR increased 2.15x, MS/MS-only 2.31x while maintaining high complete-input performance.

Conclusion: Integrating domain knowledge into training-condition design improves robustness of molecular structure identification, with additional gains from MoE fusion under mixed-condition training.

Abstract: In practical molecular characterization, small-molecule structure identification benefits from complementary spectroscopic evidence, but missing, degraded, or mismatched spectra challenge multimodal models. Herein, we incorporate domain knowledge from spectroscopy and chemistry into mixed-condition training for candidate structure reranking, using a reproducible evaluation protocol and mixture-of-experts (MoE) fusion. The protocol incorporates perturbations tailored to each spectroscopic modality and chemically informed spectrum replacements to cover variations in spectral availability, quality, and consistency. A total of 79,462 test samples were evaluated across 30 predefined conditions using simulated spectra from the Multimodal Spectroscopic Dataset (MSSD) for mass spectrometry (MS), infrared (IR) spectroscopy, and 1H and 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), with up to 128 hard candidate structures per sample. A controlled two-by-two factorial comparison of complete-input training versus mixed-condition training and vanilla concatenation versus MoE fusion, with matched evaluation conditions, showed that mixed-condition training provided the main gains in both architectures. For MoE, mean reciprocal rank (MRR), averaged equally across conditions, increased from 0.9203 to 0.9763, a relative increase of 6.08%. Recall at rank 1 (R@1), averaged over the same conditions, increased from 89.50% to 96.36%, an increase of 6.86 percentage points and a relative increase of 7.67%. IR-only and MS/MS-only MRR increased from 0.4337 to 0.9307 and from 0.3711 to 0.8575, reaching 2.15 and 2.31 times their respective baseline values, while complete-input performance remained high. These results support integrating domain knowledge into training-condition design to improve robustness, with further gains from MoE under mixed-condition training.

</details>


### [241] [Towards Identifying the Dataset Biases Causing Phantom Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14449)
*Jonas Jürß,Pietro Liò*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A simple SBERT-based signature can identify hidden biases transferred from teacher to student models, achieving MCC of 0.83 when teacher is known and 0.46 when unknown.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent research shows teacher models can transfer biases to students through datasets where explicit bias references have been filtered out, and existing data-level defenses fail to reliably detect or remove these biases even when knowing what to look for.

Method: The authors propose using a simple signature based on Sentence BERT (SBERT) embeddings to identify the topic of hidden biases in model transfers.

Result: The SBERT signature achieves Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.83 when the teacher model used by the attacker is known, and 0.46 when it is unknown. Different teacher models express the same bias through different vocabulary.

Conclusion: Hidden biases can be identified using SBERT embeddings, with effectiveness depending on knowledge of the teacher model, and biases manifest differently across models despite representing the same underlying bias.

Abstract: Recent work has shown that a teacher model can transfer a bias to a student through a dataset from which every explicit reference to that bias has been filtered out, and that no data-level defense reliably removes or detects it even when knowing what bias to look for. Aiming to shed light on the hidden traces of these biases, we show that a simple signature based on Sentence BERT embeddings can identify the topic of such a bias with a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.83 if the teacher model used by the attacker is known and 0.46 if it is not. Additionally, we observe that different teacher models appear to express the same bias through different vocabulary.

</details>


### [242] [Follow the Geometry, Not the Model: Cold Start Semi-Supervised Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14451)
*Itai David,Daphna Weinshall*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VAST decouples pseudo-label generation from classifier training in cold-start SSL by using frozen self-supervised embeddings and a Veracity Matrix to aggregate label evidence across data manifolds, outperforming graph-based baselines and conventional confidence-gated methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard SSL methods that couple pseudo-label generation with classifier training fail in cold-start regimes where only a few labels per class are available, because the classifier cannot properly supervise itself before learning meaningful representations.

Method: 1) Use frozen self-supervised embeddings to infer probabilistic beliefs over unlabeled data based on data geometry 2) Introduce Veracity Matrix (kernel-based structure) to aggregate label evidence across data manifold 3) Add Veracity Propagation for self-terminating belief spreading beyond kernel neighborhood 4) Distill beliefs into an inductive classifier rather than requiring transductive inference.

Result: VAST outperforms strongest graph-based SSL baselines across three datasets, with statistically significant gains in 7 of 9 comparisons. It also produces deployable inductive classifiers. Conventional confidence-gated SSL methods underperform in cold-start settings and don't consistently exceed labeled-only performance.

Conclusion: Decoupling label inference from classifier training via geometry-aware probabilistic reasoning is crucial for cold-start SSL. The Veracity Matrix and propagation approach effectively leverages self-supervised embeddings to overcome the limitations of coupled SSL methods in low-label regimes.

Abstract: Modern semi-supervised learning (SSL) couples pseudo-label generation and classifier training, using the classifier's own confidence to select the pseudo-labels that are then used to update the model. In the cold-start regime, where at most a few labels per class are available, this coupling is ill-posed, since the classifier cannot supervise itself before it has learned.
  To address this problem, we propose VAST (Veracity-Aware Semi-Supervised Training), which decouples these two stages. Probabilistic beliefs over the unlabeled set are first inferred directly from the geometry of a frozen self-supervised embedding and only then distilled into an inductive classifier.
  The construction rests on the Veracity Matrix, a kernel-based structure that aggregates label evidence across the data manifold and admits an interpretation as a Dirichlet posterior under a per-observation powered-likelihood model. Additionally, we introduce Veracity Propagation, a self-terminating belief-spreading step that extends coverage beyond the kernel neighborhood of the labeled set.
  Under a controlled protocol in which all methods receive identical frozen embeddings and labeled sets, VAST outperforms the strongest graph-based SSL baselines at every operating point across three datasets, with statistically significant gains in 7 of 9 comparisons, while producing a deployable inductive classifier rather than requiring transductive graph inference. Compared with end-to-end confidence-gated SSL, we further find that these methods underperform in this setting and, in our experiments, do not consistently exceed labeled-only performance.

</details>


### [243] [Retrieval-Guided Fine-Tuning as Noisy Estimation: Risk bounds and Architectural Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14485)
*Bhargav Lad,Yifan Hao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RAG-FT's statistical properties are analyzed through a multi-task linear regression framework, showing retrieval failure decays exponentially with task separation, and revealing instability in uniform-weight attention aggregation that reweighting can fix.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retrieval-Guided Fine-Tuning (RAG-FT) incorporates retrieved data into training, but the statistical consequences of noisy retrieval during training remain theoretically undercharacterized, creating a gap in understanding when and why RAG-FT works or fails.

Method: Models RAG-FT as an estimation problem in a multi-task linear regression framework using OLS proxy for single-layer linear self-attention to obtain finite-sample risk bounds. Introduces Distance-Proportional Noise (DPN) model where retrieval quality degrades with rank, comparing OLS proxy with literal uniform-weight forward pass of linear self-attention.

Result: Under homoscedastic retrieval noise: retrieval failure decays exponentially with task separation relative to noise, and explicit finite-sample conditions show RAG-FT achieves lower risk than target-only and full-corpus training. Under DPN: attention estimator's bias diverges as Θ(n^{2q}) even under exact retrieval, while OLS risk remains Θ(d/n) for every noise exponent q>0, locating instability in fixed unweighted aggregation rather than noisy retrieval itself.

Conclusion: The instability in RAG-FT comes not from noisy retrieval itself but from the fixed, unweighted aggregation of the literal linear self-attention forward pass; reweighting by reliability can remove this instability, which is validated through simulation of the DPN model.

Abstract: Retrieval-Guided Fine-Tuning (RAG-FT) incorporates retrieved data directly into the training objective, but the statistical consequences of noisy retrieval during training remain theoretically undercharacterized. We study this question by modeling RAG-FT as an estimation problem in a multi-task linear regression framework, using an OLS proxy for single-layer linear self-attention to obtain finite-sample risk bounds. Under homoscedastic retrieval noise, we show that retrieval failure decays exponentially with task separation relative to noise, and derive explicit finite-sample conditions under which RAG-FT achieves lower risk than both target-only and full-corpus training. We then introduce a Distance-Proportional Noise (DPN) model, in which retrieval quality degrades with rank, and compare two estimators under the same retrieval process: the OLS proxy and the literal, uniform-weight forward pass of linear self-attention. We prove that the attention estimator's bias diverges as $Θ(n^{2q})$ even under exact retrieval, while OLS risk remains $Θ(d/n)$ for every noise exponent $q>0$. These results locate the instability not in noisy retrieval itself, but in the fixed, unweighted aggregation of the literal LSA forward pass, which reweighting by reliability empirically removes. We validate the predicted rate separation through direct simulation of the DPN model.

</details>


### [244] [EdgeHAR: An Edge-Native Compact Sensor Foundation Model for Human Activity Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14498)
*He Zhang,Siyu Yuan,Siyu Liu,Sizhen Bian,Bin Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EdgeHAR is an edge-native compact sensor foundation model for wearable intelligence that learns transferable representations by factorizing sensor signals into three disentangled latent codes for efficient adaptation to real-world sensing shifts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing foundation models for human activity recognition (HAR) are designed for cloud-scale deployment and struggle with real-world sensing shifts including unseen users, devices, sampling rates, and sensor placements.

Method: EdgeHAR learns transferable representations by factorizing sensor signals into three latent codes: Activity-Semantic Code (reusable activity knowledge), Motion-Dynamics Code (temporal patterns), and Acquisition-Context Code (sensor-specific variations), enabling efficient adaptation through lightweight adaptation modules.

Result: EdgeHAR maintains competitive recognition performance under distribution shifts with substantially reduced deployment cost, achieving foundation-model-level transferability while satisfying edge constraints in computation, memory, latency, and privacy.

Conclusion: EdgeHAR establishes a practical paradigm for compact, edge-first foundation models for ubiquitous sensing systems, addressing the limitations of cloud-scale models for wearable intelligence applications.

Abstract: Sensor-based human activity recognition (HAR) is fundamental to ubiquitous and wearable computing, yet existing foundation models are largely designed for cloud-scale deployment and struggle with real-world sensing shifts, including unseen users, devices, sampling rates, and sensor placements. We present \textbf{EdgeHAR}, an edge-native compact sensor foundation model designed for wearable intelligence. Unlike conventional models that entangle activity knowledge with acquisition variations, EdgeHAR learns transferable representations by factorizing sensor signals into three latent codes: an \textbf{(i)Activity-Semantic Code} capturing reusable activity knowledge, a \textbf{(ii)Motion-Dynamics Code} modeling temporal patterns, and an \textbf{(iii)Acquisition-Context Code} representing sensor-specific variations. This disentangled design enables efficient adaptation to new users, devices, placements, and activity classes with limited target-domain data. By incorporating lightweight adaptation modules, EdgeHAR achieves foundation-model-level transferability while satisfying edge constraints in computation, memory, latency, and privacy. Experiments across heterogeneous HAR datasets demonstrate that EdgeHAR maintains competitive recognition performance under distribution shifts with substantially reduced deployment cost. EdgeHAR establishes a practical paradigm for compact, edge-first foundation models for ubiquitous sensing systems.

</details>


### [245] [Should All Noises Be Treated Equally: Impact of Input Noise Variability on Neural Network Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14504)
*Salma Alsinan,Maksim Makarenko,Sixiu Liu,Ali Aldawood,Ibrahim Hoteit*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Investigates how noise parameter variations affect neural network generalization and robustness for seismic data processing tasks like first break picking and denoising, showing that larger noise scales improve generalization and compound noise training enhances robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Geophysical field data contains complex heterogeneous noise that obscures weak seismic events and complicates automated interpretation. Deep learning performance is sensitive to training noise characteristics, especially under out-of-distribution conditions.

Method: Simulate seismic-while-drilling data and apply controlled noise augmentation using stochastic generators to vary noise characteristics. Train different neural networks on fixed noise types and scales, then evaluate across seen/unseen noise scenarios. Incrementally increase noise complexity with compound mixtures and assess performance under challenging OOD conditions.

Result: Larger noise scales boost generalization, and alignment between noise type, task complexity, and architecture is key for maximizing generalization gains. Training with compound noises mitigates weaknesses of single-noise training, acting as implicit regularization to improve robustness.

Conclusion: Provides guidance for developing deep learning models that generalize effectively across diverse and unpredictable noise conditions, highlighting key factors influencing model resilience in noisy geophysical environments.

Abstract: Geophysical data collected from active field sites are often contaminated by complex and heterogeneous noise, obscuring weak seismic events, and complicating automated interpretation. Although deep learning offers promising solutions for seismic processing, its performance is highly sensitive to the nature of training noise, especially under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions. This study investigates the influence of noise parameters, such as type, scale, and complexity on the performance, generalization and robustness of neural networks in two geophysical tasks: first break picking and denoising. We simulate seismic-while-drilling data and apply controlled input source noise augmentation using stochastic generators to vary the noise characteristics. Different neural networks are trained on fixed noise types and scales, then evaluated across both seen and unseen noise scenarios. We incrementally increase the complexity of the noise by introducing compound noise mixtures and assess the performance of the model under increasingly challenging OOD conditions. This yields a robustness matrix that captures the generalizability of each model relative to its training configuration. Results indicate that larger noise scales boost generalization, and that effective alignment between noise type, task complexity, and architecture is key for maximizing generalization gains. In addition, training with compound noises mitigate weaknesses associated with single-noise training, acting as an additional implicit regularizer to improving robustness. These findings highlight key factors influencing model resilience in noisy geophysical environments and offer guidance for developing deep learning models that generalize effectively across diverse and unpredictable noise conditions.

</details>


### [246] [GNN4PPM: Multi-Target Predictive Process Monitoring with Relational Graph Convolutional Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14534)
*Ana Costa,Johannes Mäkelburg,Luise Pufahl*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GNN4PPM uses graph neural networks and knowledge graphs to predict complete next events in predictive process monitoring, capturing more event log information than traditional methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing predictive process monitoring approaches only consider basic event information (activities, timestamps, case IDs) while ignoring the rich additional data recorded in real-life event logs. This leads to incomplete predictions and missed opportunities to leverage full event information.

Method: The authors introduce GNN4PPM, which represents event information in a heterogeneous knowledge graph capturing event log semantics as RDF. They train embeddings using a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (R-GCN) to predict all next events along with their complete data payload simultaneously.

Result: Experiments with state-of-the-art solutions show that GNN4PPM is promising, proving its accuracy and applicability in complex predictive process monitoring settings.

Conclusion: GNN4PPM effectively addresses the limitation of traditional PPM approaches by leveraging graph neural networks and knowledge graphs to capture comprehensive event log information, enabling more complete and accurate next event predictions including full data payloads.

Abstract: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) aims at predicting at runtime and as early as possible the future states of a process execution. Common tasks include predicting the next event, the time to completion of a trace, and outcomes. Existing approaches typically consider an event from the perspective of the executed activities along with their timestamps and case identifiers. This leads to the disadvantage that in real-life settings, there is much more information recorded in the event log that is not captured or completely ignored when performing prediction tasks. We introduce GNN4PPM, an approach that predicts all next events along with their complete data payload at once. We represent event information in a heterogeneous knowledge graph that captures the event log as an RDF semantics, and train the embeddings with a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (R-GCN). Our approach is promising in comparison to existing solutions, and experiments with state-of-the-art solutions prove the accuracy and applicability of GNN4PPM in complex settings.

</details>


### [247] [Selecting k Paths with the Minimum Longest Path Length in the Stochastic Semi-Bandit Setting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14557)
*Shunsuke Aoki,Atsuyoshi Nakamura*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents an online algorithm for selecting k parallel paths in a network to minimize maximum transmission time, considering edge capacity constraints and stochastic transmission times.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When performing parallel data transmission through networks using multiple paths, minimizing the maximum transmission time among selected paths is practically important for efficient data transfer and network optimization.

Method: The authors formulate this as a semi-bandit problem where k paths must be selected from origin to destination in a directed graph at each time step, with edge capacity constraints limiting how many paths can go through each edge. They propose an algorithm to solve this online optimization problem with stochastic transmission times.

Result: The paper presents a proposed algorithm for solving the formulated semi-bandit problem of selecting optimal path sets to minimize maximum traversal time in the presence of capacity constraints and stochastic transmission times.

Conclusion: This work addresses the important practical problem of optimizing parallel data transmission in networks by formulating it as an online semi-bandit problem and providing algorithmic solutions to minimize maximum transmission time under realistic constraints.

Abstract: When performing parallel data transmission through a network using multiple paths, it is practically important to minimize the maximum transmission time among the selected paths. This study addresses an online problem in which $k$ paths from an origin vertex to a destination vertex must be selected at each time step within a network represented as a directed graph. Here, the number of paths going through each edge in each parallel data transmission is limited to its capacity, and the time required for transmission is determined stochastically. We formulate the semi-bandit problem of selecting a set of paths to minimize the maximum traversal time among the selected paths and propose an algorithm to solve it.

</details>


### [248] [Pathwise Individual Rationality in Federated Learning: A Mechanism-Architecture Co-Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14591)
*Amin Meghrazi,Srinivasan Parthasarathy,Andrew Perrault*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Federated Learning clients face tradeoffs between privacy/communication costs and model benefits; the paper introduces individual rationality constraints to ensure clients don't do worse than local training, proposes a new design with short-term guarantees and personalized evaluation to prevent extended periods of underperformance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clients in Federated Learning face real costs (privacy, communication, computation) and need guarantees that federation provides better utility than local training alone. Current FL approaches lack short-term participation guarantees, causing clients to remain below their local baseline for extended periods (hundreds of rounds).

Method: The paper first examines pathwise FL performance with individual rationality constraints, showing capping client contributions backfires. Then proposes a novel design combining: 1) short-term participation guarantees, 2) personalized model evaluation, 3) fair incentive maintenance. Provides theoretical basis and empirical validation under different heterogeneity levels.

Result: Analysis shows clients can stay below local baseline for hundreds of rounds in standard FL. Capping contributions collapses learning even with low heterogeneity. The proposed design enables clients to avoid short-term losses without harming overall performance in moderate heterogeneity; under severe heterogeneity, shows promising outcomes compared to local baseline with some accuracy cost.

Conclusion: Individual rationality constraints are crucial for practical FL adoption. The proposed framework combining short-term guarantees with personalized evaluation provides a viable solution to the participation-cost tradeoff, ensuring clients benefit throughout training while maintaining fair incentives, addressing a critical limitation in current FL approaches.

Abstract: Participation in federated learning (FL) comes at a cost. Clients trade off privacy, communication, and compute costs for potentially greater gains in model efficacy. This paper explores this tradeoff under the aegis of individual rationality (IR) versus autarky, the basic game-theoretic requirement that the federation provide utility no worse than local training. Using the above as the design target, we examine pathwise performance of FL, as a per-round bound on cumulative surplus, not just as an asymptotic equilibrium guarantee under different models of client data distribution heterogeneity. Along this path, clients can remain below their local-training baseline for hundreds of rounds. The natural remedy is to cap each client's per-round contribution so that this shortfall stays bounded, and we prove that it backfires, collapsing learning even at low-to-modest heterogeneity.
  We then propose a novel design that combines short-term participation guarantees with personalized model evaluation, while maintaining fair incentives. We provide a theoretical basis for this new approach and empirically demonstrate that clients can avoid short-term losses without harming overall performance, even under moderate data distribution heterogeneity; under severe heterogeneity, the design shows promising outcomes for clients compared to their local baseline at some cost in accuracy.

</details>


### [249] [Diagnosing Temporal Misalignment in Multichannel Time-Series Classification with Minimum Description Length](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14595)
*Sebastian Buschjäger,Michael Frichert,Daniel Kuhe,Jian-Jia Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel diagnostic method using Minimum Description Length (MDL) to detect and correct temporal misalignment in multichannel time-series data without requiring retraining, reference data, or labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
