The objective is to develop theoretically grounded, efficient and scalable RL algorithms to learn both the optimal value functions (which also solve the exploratory HJB equation) and optimal exploratory feedback control policies. When the diffusion coefficients do not contain control, we employ probabilistic representations of both the optimal value function and its gradient based on an auxiliary state process depending only on the diffusion part of the original dynamics. With a delicate analysis on some properly defined mappings and their fixed points, this leads to the introduction of our policy iteration algorithms and their convergence. We demonstrate the performance of our algorithms through various numerical examples. Finally, we study a special control-dependent diffusion case where probability representation of the Hessian is called for.

</details>


### [273] [LiftGCN: Efficient Energy-Preserving Graph Learning via Joukowski Spectral Lifting for Finite Element Stress Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14977)
*Chen Zeng,Qiao Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LiftGCN is an efficient spectrally stable graph network for finite element stress prediction that preserves high-frequency information using Joukowski spectral lifting, avoiding expensive matrix functions while maintaining low computational complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Finite element stress fields exhibit strong local non-smoothness with stress concentrations near geometric features, causing sharp spatial gradients and high-frequency components. Conventional graph neural networks using message passing are inherently smoothing and attenuate high-frequency information, making them unsuitable for capturing stress concentrations accurately.

Method: LiftGCN uses Joukowski spectral lifting to map the real spectrum of a normalized graph operator onto the unit circle. This spectral transformation is realized as a simple second-order recurrence, avoiding matrix exponentials, eigendecomposition, and high-order polynomial truncation. The linear Joukowski backbone has unit-modulus characteristic roots and an energy-preserving structure under positive-definite metric, preventing exponential attenuation of graph-frequency components. Each layer requires only one sparse neighborhood aggregation with O(ed) complexity, plus lightweight local nonlinear residuals for expressive feature transformations.

Result: Experiments on finite element stress prediction show that LiftGCN achieves competitive overall accuracy while significantly improving reconstruction of stress concentrations and local high-gradient structures. It also provides substantially reduced computational cost compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: LiftGCN provides an efficient spectrally stable graph network that effectively captures stress concentrations in finite element analysis while maintaining low computational complexity, making it suitable for applications requiring preservation of high-frequency information in graph-structured data.

Abstract: Finite element stress fields often exhibit strong local non-smoothness, where stress concentrations near holes, notches, and loading regions induce sharp spatial gradients and high-frequency graph components. Although graph neural networks naturally operate on irregular finite element meshes, conventional message passing is inherently smoothing and progressively attenuates such high-frequency information. Unitary propagation alleviates this problem by preserving spectral magnitudes, but typically relies on matrix functions and high-order approximations with $O(Ked)$ propagation complexity. We propose LiftGCN, an efficient spectrally stable graph network based on Joukowski spectral lifting. LiftGCN maps the real spectrum of a normalized graph operator onto the unit circle through the Joukowski relation and realizes the resulting spectral transformation as a simple second-order recurrence, avoiding matrix exponentials, eigendecomposition, and high-order polynomial truncation. We show that the linear Joukowski backbone has unit-modulus characteristic roots and admits an energy-preserving structure under a positive-definite metric, preventing exponential attenuation of graph-frequency components with depth. Each layer requires only one sparse neighborhood aggregation, yielding $O(ed)$ propagation complexity, while lightweight local nonlinear residuals provide expressive feature transformations. Experiments on finite element stress prediction demonstrate that LiftGCN achieves competitive overall accuracy while improving reconstruction of stress concentrations and local high-gradient structures with substantially reduced computational cost. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChenZeng001/LiftGCN.

</details>


### [274] [HGTO: A Unified Graph-Based Physics-Informed Formulation for Structural Topology Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15001)
*Kangzheng Liu,Uday Kumar Punna,Leixin Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HGTO introduces a unified graph-based topology optimization method that parameterizes element densities on element graphs and determines structural states on node-element hypergraphs, achieving comparable compliance to conventional methods with lower computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing neural topology optimization methods mainly use coordinate field representations and make limited use of the discrete relationships inherent in finite element meshes, despite density-based topology optimization being naturally structured around nested material updates, structural analyses, and sensitivity assessments.

Method: HGTO extends neural topology optimization from coordinate space to finite-element graph space by parameterizing element densities on the element graph from the mesh and determining structural state on corresponding node-element hypergraphs, while keeping finite element operations (kinematics, quadrature, constitutive response, force assembly) as explicit differentiable computations.

Result: Numerical studies demonstrate compliance comparable to conventional density-based optimization at substantially lower computational cost than representative coordinate-based dual-field neural methods, with the formulation accommodating high-resolution/irregular meshes, 3D structures, finite deformation, and elastoplastic response.

Conclusion: The graph-based formulation provides a unified approach that couples material field and equilibrium state through finite-element incidence structures, enabling efficient and flexible topology optimization across various mesh types and material behaviors.

Abstract: Density-based topology optimization is typically structured as a nested sequence of material updates, structural analyses, and sensitivity assessments. While neural density parameterization and dual-field physics-informed approaches provide data-free alternatives, most existing methods represent density and displacement as coordinate fields and make limited use of the discrete relationships inherent in the finite element mesh. The present study introduces HGTO, a unified graph-based formulation that extends complete neural topology optimization from coordinate space to finite-element graph space. Element densities are parameterized on the element graph derived from the mesh, and the structural state is determined on the corresponding node--element hypergraph. Finite element kinematics, numerical quadrature, constitutive response, and force assembly remain explicitly defined operations within the differentiable computation. The material field and equilibrium state are therefore coupled through a common finite-element incidence structure. Numerical studies show compliance comparable to conventional density-based optimization at substantially lower computational cost than a representative coordinate-based dual-field neural method. The same coupled formulation accommodates high-resolution and irregular meshes, three-dimensional structures, finite deformation, and elastoplastic response.

</details>


### [275] [Pick Your Poison: Learning to Select Poison Sets for Stronger LLM Backdoor Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15029)
*Aashiq Muhamed,Mona T. Diab,Virginia Smith,Andrew Ilyas,Matthew Jagielski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAILS is a method for selecting optimal poison sets in backdoor attacks that significantly improves attack success rates by using learned set scoring from limited evaluations, outperforming existing influence-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing backdoor poisoning evaluations typically use random poison selection from candidate pools, which can severely underestimate worst-case vulnerability. There's a need for systematic poison selection methods that can identify more effective poison sets to better assess model vulnerabilities.

Method: The authors formalize poison selection as oracle-budgeted set optimization and introduce SAILS (Set-level Audit-Informed Iterative Learned Selection). SAILS learns a set scorer from a few hundred finetune-and-evaluate runs, then ranks millions of candidate sets and audits only a small shortlist of the most promising ones.

Result: SAILS improves held-out attack success by 30 percentage points on average over the strongest influence baselines. The method transfers from small-scale to full-scale finetuning and extends to code-generation, agentic, and API-only backdoors. Across three LLaMA-3-8B backdoor settings, attack success ranged from 3% to 80% depending on poison set selection.

Conclusion: Poison selection significantly impacts backdoor attack effectiveness, and SAILS provides an effective method for identifying optimal poison sets, demonstrating that random sampling underestimates model vulnerability and that systematic selection is crucial for accurate security assessments.

Abstract: Backdoor poisoning attacks add poisoned examples to otherwise-clean finetuning data, pairing a trigger with a target behavior that the model learns to produce when the trigger appears. Existing evaluations typically fix the number of poisoned examples and sample them at random from a candidate pool. We show that this can severely underestimate worst-case vulnerability: across three LLaMA-3-8B backdoor settings, holding the model, clean data, and poison count fixed, attack success ranges from 3% to 80% depending only on which poison set is chosen.
  We formalize poison selection as oracle-budgeted set optimization and introduce SAILS (Set-level Audit-Informed Iterative Learned Selection), which learns a set scorer from a few hundred finetune-and-evaluate runs, ranks millions of candidate sets, and audits only a small shortlist. SAILS improves held-out attack success by 30 percentage points on average over the strongest influence baselines, transfers from small-scale to full-scale finetuning, and extends to code-generation, agentic, and API-only backdoors.

</details>


### [276] [MoARa: Module-Aware Rank Allocation and Structure-Preserving Decomposition for Low-Rank LLM Pre-training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15037)
*Keunyoung Kim,Nojun Kwak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MoARa improves low-rank gradient projection for LLM pretraining by using module-aware rank allocation and magnitude-direction decomposition, achieving 37% faster training with minimal memory overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing low-rank gradient projection methods allocate projection-rank budget uniformly across Transformer modules, ignoring heterogeneous projection sensitivity. Additionally, projecting raw gradients attenuates both magnitude and direction jointly, limiting training efficiency and wall-clock time improvements.

Method: MoARa combines two key components: 1) Static profiling-based module-aware projection-rank allocation that adaptively allocates rank budget based on each Transformer module's sensitivity, and 2) Block-wise magnitude-direction decomposition where gradients are decomposed (default block size near attention head dimension) before projection to preserve both aspects separately.

Result: On Llama 2 7B, MoARa reaches standard GaLore's final perplexity in 37% fewer steps and 34% less wall-clock time with only 0.2% peak reserved memory overhead. Across five Transformer architectures (300M to 7B scales), the method shows consistent improvements. Module-aware rank allocation alone provides directionally consistent step reductions on all six evaluated low-rank pretraining methods.

Conclusion: MoARa significantly accelerates low-rank LLM pretraining by addressing suboptimal uniform rank allocation and joint gradient attenuation. The module-aware approach with magnitude-direction decomposition represents an effective way to improve training efficiency while maintaining the memory benefits of low-rank gradient projection methods.

Abstract: Low-rank gradient projection reduces the optimizer-state memory cost of large language model (LLM) pretraining, but the steps and wall-clock time needed to reach a target quality remain a meaningful axis for improvement. We attribute this to two design choices in existing methods: the projection-rank budget is allocated uniformly across Transformer modules with heterogeneous projection sensitivity, and projecting a raw gradient attenuates its magnitude and direction jointly. We propose MoARa, which combines a static profiling-based module-aware projection-rank allocation with a block-wise magnitude-direction decomposition; the default block size is set in the neighborhood of the attention head dimension. Across five Transformer architectures spanning Llama, Qwen, and DeepSeek at 300M to 7B scales, GaLore with MoARa reaches standard GaLore's final perplexity in 37% fewer steps and 34% less wall-clock time on Llama 2 7B, with only 0.2% peak reserved memory overhead under standard graph compilation. Across the six low-rank pretraining methods we evaluate, module-aware rank allocation alone delivers directionally consistent step reductions on all six. On compatible hosts, the two-component design reaches up to 41.7% step reduction and 37.1% wall-clock reduction.

</details>


### [277] [Structured Features Overfit Where Random Features Grok](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15047)
*Chon-Fai Kam,Miloud Bessafi,Frederic Cadet*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Over-parameterized ridge regression with structured Fourier features doesn't show the memorize-then-generalize behavior seen with random Gaussian features; instead, increasing feature capacity degrades performance without a phase transition, controlled by active feature modes rather than capacity ratio.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous work (Xu, Vardi & Safran 2026) showed that over-parameterized ridge regression with unstructured random Gaussian features exhibits "grokking" - a delay between memorization and generalization where the delay grows with 1/λ (inverse weight decay). The authors want to investigate whether this behavior persists with structured feature maps.

Method: The study uses a band-limited Fourier feature map over ℤₚ² with a single-character target function within the expressible class. They analyze ridge regression with fixed positive weight decay while varying the band width (number of Fourier modes). They examine performance degradation by comparing 1089 active modes versus 4225 full modes.

Result: With structured Fourier features, there is no memorize-then-generalize regime. Increasing the band width drives peak held-out accuracy monotonically from 1.00 to 0.07. Performance degradation occurs at capacity ratio q/n = 0.638, far below interpolation threshold. The critical factor is the number of active modes through the teacher-weighted spectrum of the empirical Gram matrix, not the capacity ratio. Masking to 1089 active modes yields perfect accuracy (1.000), while the full 4225-mode band collapses to 0.185.

Conclusion: Structured feature geometry fundamentally changes the learning dynamics compared to unstructured random features. The absence of grokking behavior in structured Fourier features reveals that the memorize-then-generalize phenomenon is not universal but depends on feature structure. Performance is controlled by the number of active modes and their spectral properties rather than overall capacity ratio, distinguishing this from double descent phenomena.

Abstract: Xu, Vardi and Safran (ICML 2026) prove that over-parameterized ridge regression over an unstructured random Gaussian feature map groks, with the delay between memorization and generalization growing as $1/λ$ in the weight decay. We show that on a structured feature map the same delay does not appear. For a band-limited Fourier feature map over $\mathbb{Z}_p^2$ carrying a single-character target that lies inside the expressible class, enlarging the band at fixed positive weight decay drives peak held-out accuracy monotonically from $1.00$ to $0.07$, with no memorize-then-generalize regime anywhere along the sweep. The degradation is not an interpolation effect. It sets in at capacity ratio $q/n = 0.638$, far below the interpolation threshold, on separate grounds from the exact null space that appears above it. What does have a sharp boundary is the active support. Holding the nominal dimension fixed and masking the band back to $1089$ active modes restores held-out accuracy of $1.000$ with zero variance across seeds, while the full $4225$-mode band collapses to $0.185$. The number of active modes acts through the teacher-weighted spectrum of the empirical Gram matrix and not through the capacity ratio, which makes this a statement about feature geometry and not a restatement of double descent.

</details>


### [278] [Ensemble Complexity in Photovoltaic Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15049)
*Sun Ze,Zhou Liguo,Xu Yuqing,Yu Lei,Jiang Mingming*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Ensemble forecasting can improve PV predictions but some components add little value or increase computational cost. Analysis shows selective component evaluation is needed with careful consideration of weather data availability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the problem that while ensembles can improve photovoltaic (PV) forecasting accuracy, some ensemble components contribute little predictive value while potentially increasing computational cost. The authors seek to systematically evaluate which components are truly valuable versus redundant.

Method: The researchers used matched comparisons and ablation studies of a fixed heterogeneous predictor bank. They conducted hourly experiments using GEFCom2014 and three additional public datasets (PVDAQ, OPSD, Ausgrid) with chronological partitions and three random seeds. They employed retrospective ERA5 weather data assistance and examined static fusion versus boosting. They also performed exploratory component removal analyses to identify group-level dependencies and individual redundancies, and conducted a separate 15-minute frequency experiment replacing a neural network component with a tree predictor.

Result: Static fusion reduced scaled mean absolute error by 1.11% (PVDAQ), 4.41% (OPSD), and 1.63% (Ausgrid) compared to matched boosting, but only OPSD's improvement remained statistically significant after multiple-comparison correction. Weather gating provided no consistent incremental benefit. Component removal analysis revealed group-level dependencies alongside individual redundancy. In the 15-minute experiment, replacing a neural component with a tree predictor reduced normalized error by 1.72% but increased inference time.

Conclusion: The findings support component-wise evaluation of ensemble methods with explicit limits on weather data availability and test-set reuse. Not all ensemble components provide meaningful benefits, and computational cost should be considered alongside accuracy improvements. The research emphasizes the importance of selective, systematic component assessment rather than indiscriminate ensemble building.

Abstract: An ensemble can improve photovoltaic forecasts while adding components that contribute little or increase computation. We assess these effects through matched comparisons and ablations of a fixed heterogeneous predictor bank. Hourly experiments use GEFCom2014 and three additional public datasets, with chronological partitions and three seeds. Under retrospective ERA5 assistance, static fusion reduces scaled mean absolute error against matched boosting by 1.11%, 4.41%, and 1.63% on PVDAQ, OPSD, and Ausgrid; only OPSD remains supported after multiple-comparison correction. Weather gating offers no consistent incremental benefit. Exploratory member removals show group-level dependence alongside individual redundancy. A separate, previously inspected fifteen-minute case replaces one neural member with a tree predictor: normalized error falls by 1.72%, but measured inference is slower. These findings support component-wise evaluation with explicit limits on weather availability and test-set reuse.

</details>


### [279] [Not All Prompts Are Equal: Exploration-Guided Prompt Scaffolding for Multimodal Reinforcement Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15051)
*Yuanhao Yue,Qianli Ma,Chengyu Wang,Haoting Wang,Lei Shen,Jun Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Exploration-guided prompt scaffolding framework that dynamically adapts training prompt distribution during RL post-training of multimodal LLMs, using Exploration Potential Score to identify useful prompts and teacher models to rewrite low-utility prompts for better learning efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In online RL training, prompts vary significantly in their informativeness for current policy - some are already saturated while others are too difficult, but standard training allocates equal rollout budget to all prompts regardless of utility, leading to inefficient training.

Method: Proposes a framework with Exploration Potential Score (EPS), a lightweight rollout-based proxy for prompt utility derived from KL-regularized policy improvement theory. Instead of discarding low-utility prompts, uses teacher models to generate scaffolded rewrites that preserve task intent while making training more informative. This reframes teacher supervision as training-data refinement rather than output imitation.

Result: Integrated with GRPO on Geo3K and MMK12, the method consistently outperforms baselines on both in-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks: achieves up to 9.7% relative improvement in-domain, gains of 11.5% on MathVision, and 11.1% on MMMU-Pro.

Conclusion: Dynamic adaptation of training prompt distribution through exploration-guided scaffolding significantly improves RL post-training efficiency and effectiveness for multimodal LLMs, achieving substantial performance gains across diverse benchmarks by focusing rollout budget on more informative prompts and refining less useful ones.

Abstract: Training prompts in online reinforcement learning (RL) differ substantially in how informative they are for the current policy: some are already saturated while others are too difficult to yield reliable learning signals, yet both receive equal rollout budget under standard training. We propose an exploration-guided prompt scaffolding framework that adapts the training prompt distribution dynamically throughout RL post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Central to our approach is the $\textit{Exploration Potential Score} (EPS)$, a lightweight rollout-based proxy for prompt utility derived from KL-regularized policy improvement theory, computable directly from on-policy rollout statistics without additional overhead. Rather than discarding low-utility prompts, we use a teacher model to generate scaffolded rewrites that preserve the original task intent while making subsequent training more informative, reframing teacher supervision as training-data refinement rather than output imitation. Integrated with GRPO on Geo3K and MMK12, our method consistently outperforms the baseline on both in-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks, achieving up to 9.7\% relative improvement in-domain and gains of 11.5\% on MathVision and 11.1\% on MMMU-Pro.

</details>


### [280] [What Does an LLM Learn from Reinforcement Learning? A Mechanistic Interpretability Perspective with Fixed-SAE Track](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15064)
*Lingheng Du,Yiming Tang,Xufeng Duan,Dianbo Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Fixed-SAE Track is a framework using shared sparse autoencoders across RL training to track representation shifts in LLMs, finding RL mainly enhances existing formatting features rather than creating novel problem-solving capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL is widely used in LLM training but poorly understood at the representation level. While mechanistic interpretability offers sparse autoencoders for analyzing features, current methods can't track feature changes across RL training, leaving unanswered questions about whether RL creates novel features or modifies existing ones.

Method: Fixed-SAE Track trains one shared SAE per layer on activations pooled across the base model and all RL checkpoints, holding feature directions fixed. This allows rigorous tracking of representation shifts through interpretable SAE latents, enabling detection of emerging novel features while maintaining consistent feature definitions across training.

Result: RL-induced representation drift is small, gradual, concept-specific, and concentrated in late layers. RL mainly enhances sampling rates of "ladder tokens" and formatting scaffolding (step breaks, answer delimiters) rather than reshaping problem content. Steering these features into the base model recovers ~80% of RL's performance gain. Synthetic benchmarks confirm RL rarely creates truly novel features.

Conclusion: Fixed-SAE Track provides a principled approach to understanding RL's effects on LLM representations, revealing that RL primarily elicits existing capabilities (like steering does) rather than instilling fundamentally new problem-solving features, offering representational evidence for how RL changes model internals.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely utilized in large language model training to improve targeted capabilities, yet how RL reshapes a model remains poorly understood. Prior attempts to explain how RL works largely offer behavioral perspectives, leaving open what RL gives a model at the representation level: can RL create genuinely novel features, and which existing features does it enhance or suppress? Recent developments in mechanistic interpretability suggest sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as a promising lens to decompose internal activations into human-interpretable features; however, they cannot be directly applied to tracking change across training. In this work, we introduce Fixed-SAE Track, a framework that trains one shared SAE per considered layer on activations pooled across the base model and all RL checkpoints, holding every feature direction fixed so that representation shifts are rigorously defined through the activations of interpretable SAE latents, including the detection of emerging novel features. Validated across multiple datasets and RL algorithms, we find that RL-induced drift is small, gradual, concept specific, and concentrated in late layers, mainly enhancing the sampling rates of a small set of ladder tokens, formatting scaffolding such as step breaks and answer delimiters, rather than reshaping problem content. Steering these features into the base model recovers around 80% of RL's performance gain, suggesting that RL primarily elicits capabilities the model already possesses, much as steering does. We further design a synthetic benchmark with features known by construction to test whether RL can instill genuinely novel features. We believe Fixed-SAE Track provides a principled approach to tracking representation shifts and offers representational evidence for understanding how reinforcement learning changes the inner representation of LLMs.

</details>


### [281] [Sensory Precision Inference for Multimodal Arbitration under Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15065)
*Tin Mišić,Takato Horii*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a multimodal active inference model with joint learning of sensory precision and latent beliefs, demonstrating improved robustness under sensory conflict through dynamic precision inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world autonomous agents face challenges with multisensory data where modalities can be corrupted by noise, missing data, or inter-modal conflicts, requiring adaptive arbitration. Current active inference frameworks don't sufficiently explore the role of dynamically inferred sensory precision in multimodal conflict resolution.

Method: Proposed a multimodal perceptual inference model that jointly updates latent beliefs and modality-specific sensory precisions through iterative free-energy minimization. Introduced a learned prior over sensory precisions that induces class-dependent precision patterns and influences cross-modal inference dynamics. Evaluated using a synthetic multimodal MNIST dataset with visual, auditory, and tactile representations under controlled sensory noise and inter-modal incongruence.

Result: Dynamic precision inference improved reconstruction robustness under corrupted sensory evidence, supported coherent latent inference from reduced sensory evidence, and enabled stable arbitration between conflicting modalities. Learned precision priors generated interpretable precision structures that shaped inference dynamics and cross-modal latent structure.

Conclusion: Sensory precision inference serves as a mechanistic control process for adaptive multimodal belief formation under uncertainty, with precision dynamics functioning as a computational mechanism for robust and interpretable multisensory integration.

Abstract: Autonomous agents operating on multisensory data cannot assume that all sensory modalities remain consistently informative. In real environments, sensory streams are frequently corrupted by noise, missing data, or inter-modal incongruence, requiring adaptive arbitration between competing sensory hypotheses. While active inference provides a principled framework for uncertainty-guided inference, the role of dynamically inferred sensory precision in generative multimodal arbitration under sensory conflict remains comparatively underexplored. We propose a multimodal perceptual inference model in which latent beliefs and modality-specific sensory precisions are jointly updated through iterative free-energy minimization. In our proposed model, sensory precision dynamics not only reflect sensory uncertainty but actively shape the evolution of latent beliefs during multimodal conflict. In addition, we introduce a learned prior over sensory precisions that induces structured, class-dependent precision patterns and influences cross-modal inference dynamics. We evaluate the model using a synthetic multimodal MNIST dataset combining visual, auditory, and tactile representations of digit classes under controlled sensory noise and inter-modal incongruence. Results show that dynamic precision inference improves reconstruction robustness under corrupted sensory evidence, supports coherent latent inference from reduced sensory evidence, and enables stable arbitration between conflicting modalities. Furthermore, learned precision priors generate interpretable precision structures that shape inference dynamics and cross-modal latent structure. These findings support sensory precision inference as a mechanistic control process for adaptive multimodal belief formation under uncertainty, highlighting precision dynamics as a computational mechanism for robust and interpretable multisensory integration.

</details>


### [282] [Branched Optimal Transport Amortization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15072)
*Semyon Semenov,Viktor Kovalchuk,Meir Roketlishvili,Albert Baichorov,Fakhri Karray,Martin Takac,Arip Asadulaev*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel branched flow-matching algorithm that adapts continuous-time optimal transport to learn hierarchical branched generative flows in high dimensions, inspired by the economy-of-scale principle in branched optimal transport.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard continuous-time generative models (like flow matching) fail to capture hierarchical and branching patterns in real-world data, and lack mechanisms for flows to merge or share pathways to minimize transport cost. Branched Optimal Transport principles from natural tree-like structures are understudied for large-scale deep generative model design.

Method: The authors adapt the Benamou-Brenier continuous-time optimal transport formulation to learn branched generative flows. The method uses a scalable branched flow-matching algorithm that parameterizes flows with neural networks, allowing probability mass to aggregate along common pathways before branching to diverse targets.

Result: The method effectively learns complex branched generative processes and demonstrates effectiveness on challenging high-dimensional tasks in biology and image generation.

Conclusion: The work introduces a scalable approach to incorporate branched optimal transport principles into deep generative models, successfully capturing hierarchical patterns in high-dimensional data that standard continuous-time models miss.

Abstract: Methods of Branched Optimal Transport (BOT) mimic the economy and efficiency of natural tree-like structures, such as those found in rivers and biological systems. These methods are widely applicable for designing efficient networks in society, from river basins and blood vessels to mail and gas distribution systems. However, they remain understudied in the context of designing deep generative models, particularly at a large scale. Standard continuous-time generative models, such as the flow matching approach, fail to capture the inherent hierarchical and branching patterns present in real-world data. Current models provide no mechanism for flows to merge or share pathways to minimize total transport cost. Inspired by the "economy of scale" principle in BOT, we introduce a novel, scalable branched flow-matching algorithm designed to solve the branched optimal transport problem in high dimensions. Our method adapts the Benamou-Brenier continuous-time optimal transport formulation to learn branched generative flows. These flows allow probability mass to aggregate along common pathways before branching out to diverse targets. Parametrized by neural networks, our method effectively learns complex branched generative processes. We demonstrate its effectiveness on challenging high-dimensional tasks in biology and image generation.

</details>


### [283] [Ensemble-Conditioned Molecular Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15077)
*Ross Irwin,Alessandro Tibo,Jon Paul Janet,Simon Olsson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A molecular design framework that optimizes both conformational ensemble modes and properties simultaneously using ensemble-conditioned guidance in 3D generative models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional molecular design focuses on finding molecules with single bioactive conformations, but in reality molecules occupy conformational distributions, and many properties depend on the entire ensemble rather than single conformers.

Method: Introduced ensemble-conditioned guidance framework that conditions 3D molecular generative models on both conformational modes (shapes, pharmacophore profiles, protein pockets) and ensemble properties. Features adaptive symmetry learning for composing conditions from different reference frames, flexible-size generation, and allows targeted/avoided conditions across modalities.

Result: Evaluated on new benchmarks for multi-mode conditioning and ensemble property optimization, and demonstrated practical applications in dual-target binder design and active-state-selective agonist design, where conditioning on additional states improves outcomes over single-state conditioning.

Conclusion: Reframing molecular design as optimization of conformational ensemble modes and properties enables more accurate modeling of molecular behavior and allows a wide range of design tasks to be expressed with a single trained model, improving drug discovery outcomes.

Abstract: Molecular design is typically approached as a problem of finding molecules which can adopt a single bioactive conformation. In reality, molecules occupy a distribution over conformations, and many of the properties which determine whether a candidate is viable depend on that distribution rather than on any single conformer. We reframe molecular design as an optimisation of both the modes and properties of molecules' conformational ensembles, where modes can be represented as shapes, pharmacophore profiles or protein pockets, and properties are aggregate scalars computed over the whole distribution. To realise this we introduce ensemble-conditioned guidance, a framework which conditions 3D molecular generative models on both axes simultaneously. Mode conditions are composed adaptively at inference by combining the vector fields produced under each condition. Conditions may be targeted or avoided, mixed across modalities and combined in arbitrary numbers, allowing a wide range of design tasks to be expressed with a single trained model. We introduce adaptive symmetry learning to allow conditions from different reference frames to be composed, and extend our generative framework to enable flexible-size generation. We evaluate on new benchmarks for multi-mode conditioning and ensemble property optimisation, and apply the framework to two practical drug discovery tasks, dual-target binder design and active-state-selective agonist design, where in both cases conditioning on the additional state improves the desired outcome over single-state conditioning.

</details>


### [284] [$\mathbb{SL}(n)$ Representation Learning: An Intrinsic Mixed-Curvature Space with Higher Curvature Capacities and Deeper Order-Aware Composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15083)
*Xingrun Li,Yusuke Mukuta,Xin Yang,Yinyu Ye,Tatsuya Harada*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A new representation space called 𝕊𝕃(n) with det(A)=1 constraint and Schatten-p Finsler structure achieves mixed-curvature learning without manual curvature specification, outperforming existing manifolds on graph benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing mixed-curvature representation learning approaches rely on product manifolds that require manual specification of how different curvature spaces are combined, and separate curvature contributions across factors. There's a need for a more unified approach that naturally captures mixed curvature.

Method: Introduces the 𝕊𝕃(n) space defined by the simple constraint det(A)=1 with a left invariant Schatten-p Finsler structure. This minimal construction provides a noncommutative group structure with inherent order sensitivity and a non-nilpotent Lie algebra that allows nonzero nested Lie brackets at arbitrary depth.

Result: 𝕊𝕃(n) consistently outperforms broad range of representation manifold baselines across graph benchmarks: reduces average distortion by 44.3% on KEGG and 40.5% on HumanCyc, improves Hits@20 by 42.8% on OGBL-PPA. Experiments on Flickr30k-Order show ability to capture higher-order dependencies from ordered composition.

Conclusion: The simple structural constraint det(A)=1 yields unexpectedly rich geometry, capacity, and composition within a unified representation space, demonstrating how minimal construction can achieve maximal mixed-curvature and curvature-coupling capacities relative to intrinsic geometric bounds.

Abstract: Mixed-curvature representation learning seeks to capture rich geometric structures that cannot be adequately modeled by a single curvature regime. Existing approaches largely rely on product manifolds, which require manually specifying how different curvature spaces are combined and separate their curvature contributions across factors. We introduce the $\mathbb{SL}(n)$ space, a representation geometry defined by the simple $\det(A)=1$ constraint and a left invariant Schatten-$p$ Finsler structure. Despite this minimal construction, $\mathbb{SL}(n)$ exhibits pointwise negative, zero, and positive flag curvature around a common flagpole, while its mixed-curvature and curvature-coupling capacities are asymptotically maximal relative to the intrinsic geometric upper bound. Beyond geometry, its noncommutative group structure provides inherent order sensitivity, and its non-nilpotent Lie algebra admits nonzero nested Lie brackets at arbitrary depth, enabling deep order-aware composition. Empirically, $\mathbb{SL}(n)$ consistently outperforms a broad range of representation manifold baselines across graph benchmarks at different scales. It reduces average distortion over the strongest baselines by $44.3\%$ on KEGG and $40.5\%$ on HumanCyc, and improves Hits@20 by $42.8\%$ on OGBL-PPA. Experiments on Flickr30k-Order further support its ability to capture higher order dependencies from ordered composition. Together, these results show how a seemingly simple structural constraint can yield unexpectedly rich geometry, capacity, and composition within a unified representation space.

</details>


### [285] [Beyond Numerical Time Series: A Unified Benchmark for Multimodal Forecasting with Heterogeneous Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15087)
*Peng Chen,Zhihao Zhuang,Hongzhou Chen,Junhao Huang,Aiping Yang,Mengsen Wu,Yiding Liu,Xilin Dai,Zewei Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MUSE-Bench is a comprehensive multimodal time series forecasting benchmark with 14 datasets across 8 domains and 6 context types, addressing limitations of existing numerical-only or fragmented multimodal benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing time series forecasting benchmarks are numerical-centric with limited support for evaluating contextual information, while multimodal benchmarks suffer from limited data/context coverage, fragmented evaluation settings, and overreliance on aggregate evaluation.

Method: Proposed MUSE-Bench with 14 datasets across 8 domains and 6 context types (metadata, events, holidays, news, images, numerical covariates). Evaluated diverse forecasting paradigms (statistical, data-specific, foundation, multimodal, general-purpose LLMs) under shared non-overlapping forecast windows, common target observations, and consistent metrics.

Result: Three main findings: 1) Numerical time series foundation models dominate overall ranking; multimodal foundation model Aurora trails TSFMs but beats data-specific models. 2) External context improves context-aware models, while incorrect/misaligned context degrades performance. 3) General-purpose LLMs perform poorly as direct forecasters, and LLM-guided refinement doesn't yield consistent improvements.

Conclusion: MUSE-Bench enables systematic evaluation of how forecasting models utilize context and provides a foundation for future multimodal forecasting research, addressing critical gaps in current benchmarking practices.

Abstract: Most time series forecasting benchmarks remain numerical-centric and provide limited support for evaluating contextual information that shapes real-world temporal dynamics. Existing multimodal benchmarks also suffer from limited data and context coverage, fragmented evaluation settings, and overreliance on aggregate evaluation. In this paper, we propose \textbf{MUSE-Bench}, a unified benchmark for multimodal time series forecasting with heterogeneous context. It comprises fourteen datasets across eight domains and six types of context: metadata, events, holidays, news, images, and numerical covariates. We evaluate diverse forecasting paradigms, including statistical, data-specific, foundation, multimodal, and general-purpose LLM forecasting methods under shared non-overlapping forecast windows, common target observations, and consistent point and probabilistic metrics. Extensive experiments yield three main findings. First, numerical time series foundation models dominate the overall ranking, while Aurora, the evaluated multimodal foundation model, trails the leading numerical TSFMs but outperforms all evaluated data-specific models. Second, ablations show that external context improves the four evaluated context-aware models, whereas incorrect or temporally misaligned context degrades performance. Third, general-purpose LLMs perform poorly as direct forecasters, and LLM-guided refinement does not yield consistent improvements. MUSE-Bench enables systematic evaluation of how forecasting models utilize context and provides a foundation for future multimodal forecasting research.

</details>


### [286] [Refinement-based Flow Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15123)
*Bumgeun Park,Hyukjun Yang,Donghwan Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RFPO is a novel flow-based policy optimization method for online RL that avoids direct sampling from Q-function-induced distributions by using iterative refinement and flow matching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flow-based policies offer expressive representation for RL, but conventional flow matching requires samples from the target distribution, which is problematic when the desired action distribution is defined implicitly by a Q-function since direct sampling is typically intractable.

Method: RFPO alternates between Q-guided sample refinement and self-target flow matching: 1) generates actions from Gaussian noise using current flow policy, 2) refines them toward Q-induced energy-based distribution via finite-step stochastic refinement, 3) pairs refined actions with initial noise as fixed targets for flow-matching training. The method repeatedly refines its own outputs and learns from resulting targets.

Result: On six continuous-control tasks, RFPO matches or outperforms standard Gaussian-policy baseline on almost every task. On six synthetic 2D target distributions with diverse geometries, RFPO captures complex multimodal structure without mode collapse.

Conclusion: RFPO successfully incorporates Q-guidance into flow policies without requiring direct samples from target distributions, maintains ability to represent multiple action modes, and demonstrates strong empirical performance across various tasks.

Abstract: Flow-based policies offer an expressive representation for online reinforcement learning, but conventional flow matching requires samples drawn from the distribution to be modeled. This poses a challenge when the desired action distribution is defined only implicitly by a Q-function, since directly sampling actions from the resulting distribution is generally intractable. We propose Refinement-Based Flow Policy Optimization (RFPO), a novel framework for training a flow policy in online reinforcement learning by alternating between Q-guided sample refinement and self-target flow matching. RFPO first generates actions from Gaussian noise using the current flow policy and then uses a finite-step stochastic refinement procedure to move them toward an energy-based distribution induced by the Q-function. Each refined action is then paired with its corresponding initial noise sample and used as a fixed target for flow-matching training. By repeatedly refining its own outputs and learning from the resulting targets, RFPO incorporates Q-guidance into the policy without requiring direct samples from the target distribution, while retaining the capacity to represent multiple action modes. We further provide a theoretical analysis of the distributional dynamics induced by RFPO. Across six continuous-control tasks, RFPO matches or outperforms a standard Gaussian-policy baseline on almost every task. Experiments on six synthetic two-dimensional target distributions with diverse geometries demonstrate that RFPO captures complex multimodal structure without mode collapse.

</details>


### [287] [Omni-Streaming Thinking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15128)
*Enjun Du,Siyi Liu,Ziyu Zheng,Jingyu Li,Yiwen Guo,Yongqi Zhang,Difan Zou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OST addresses premature commitment in streaming multimodal models by generating structured outputs with evidence tracking, forecasts, and claim verification with refutation mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Streaming omni-modal models can make premature cross-modal commitments where visual cues cause interpretations to solidify in memory before audio evidence is complete, leading to persistent errors even when later audio contradicts the early interpretation.

Method: Proposes Omni-Streaming Thinking (OST) which generates structured outputs including observed evidence, future evidence forecasts, and claims marked as pending with verification intervals. Stores audio and visual evidence separately, checks claims against specified modality evidence, and implements refutation process when contradictory evidence is detected to reduce influence of incorrect claims and guide state updates.

Result: OST outperforms strongest open baselines by more than 10% relative on average across five streaming and audio-visual benchmarks. On diagnostic benchmark OST-DiagBench, achieves d-prime = 2.95 vs at most 1.38 for baselines while reducing vision-induced auditory hallucinations.

Conclusion: The OST framework effectively addresses premature cross-modal commitment in streaming multimodal models through structured reasoning with evidence tracking, forecasting, claim verification, and refutation mechanisms, significantly improving performance on challenging benchmarks.

Abstract: Streaming omni-modal models must decide what and when to answer from the video chunks and synchronized audio observed so far. Visual cues often support an interpretation before an utterance or sound event is complete. If that interpretation enters memory as a fact, later reasoning can keep relaying it even after audio contradicts it. We call this failure premature cross-modal commitment. We propose Omni-Streaming Thinking (OST), which generates structured outputs that include evidence observed so far, forecasts of future evidence, and claims based on this evidence. Each claim is initially marked as pending and linked to a future verification interval. Audio and visual evidence are stored separately, and OST checks a claim against the evidence from the specified modality at the end of the verification interval. When contradictory evidence is detected, a refutation process reduces the influence of the claim and its dependent states, and then guides a state update using the new evidence. An answer gate decides whether the answer-critical claims meet the conditions for giving a response. Using a frozen Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct backbone with lightweight adaptation, OST outperforms the strongest open baselines on five streaming and audio-visual benchmarks by more than 10% relative on average. We also introduce OST-DiagBench, which holds video fixed and edits audio to test agreement, absence, contradiction, coexistence, and subtitle-speech conflict. OST reaches d-prime = 2.95, compared with at most 1.38 for open baselines, while reducing vision-induced auditory hallucinations.

</details>


### [288] [Multi-source Transfer Learning of Time Series with a Shapelet-based Distance Measure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15148)
*Jiseok Lee,Brian Kenji Iwana*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A training-free source selection method called Shapelet Matching enables efficient multi-source transfer learning for time series classification by comparing discriminative shapelets between datasets, reducing negative transfer risks without expensive pre-training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transfer learning helps with data scarcity in time series classification, but conventional source selection methods require expensive full pre-training for each candidate source dataset. This computational cost makes source dataset selection inefficient, and selecting a single unsuitable source can lead to negative transfer.

Method: The approach has two main components: 1) Shapelet Matching - extracts discriminative shapelets from target and source datasets, then quantifies dataset similarity by comparing shapelet sets without requiring model training. 2) Multi-source transfer learning - selects several top-ranked source datasets based on shapelet similarity, combines them into a single multi-source dataset for pre-training, then fine-tunes on the target task.

Result: Evaluation on 128 UCR Archive datasets using CNN and Transformer backbones shows that multi-source pre-training reduces negative transfer risk on average. Shapelet Matching achieves strongest performance with CNN backbone and remains competitive with patch-based Transformers, while avoiding the cost of pre-training separate models for each candidate source.

Conclusion: Shapelet Matching provides an efficient, training-free method for source dataset selection in time series transfer learning. The multi-source approach effectively mitigates negative transfer risks, making transfer learning more practical by reducing computational overhead while maintaining competitive performance across different model architectures.

Abstract: Transfer learning is an effective technique for addressing data scarcity in deep learning for time series classification, but its success depends on the selection of source datasets. Conventional transferability estimation methods are often computationally expensive, as they require fully pre-training a model on each potential source dataset to assess its suitability. This paper introduces a novel, training-free source selection method named Shapelet Matching. Our approach first identifies discriminative shapelets from the target and potential source datasets. Then, Shapelet Matching quantifies dataset similarity by comparing the extracted sets of shapelets. To mitigate the risk of negative transfer from selecting an unsuitable single source, we introduce a multi-source transfer learning method. We select several source datasets based on their shapelet-based similarity scores, combine them into a single multi-source dataset, and use this aggregated dataset for pre-training. The model is then fine-tuned on the target task. We evaluated our method on 128 datasets from the UCR Archive using both temporal CNN and Transformer architectures. The empirical results demonstrate that our multi-source pre-training reduces the risk of negative transfer on average. Shapelet Matching achieves the strongest performance for the CNN backbone and remains competitive for patch-based Transformer architectures, while avoiding the cost of pre-training a separate model for every candidate source.

</details>


### [289] [Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linear Contextual Bandits with Arbitrary Adaptive Action Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15170)
*Tianyuan Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Matching upper and lower bounds for stochastic linear contextual bandits with arbitrary action menus, improving regret rates by K¹/⁴ or d¹/⁴ factors over previous bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous regret bounds for stochastic linear contextual bandits with arbitrary action menus were suboptimal in their dependence on menu size K and dimension d, motivating tighter analysis.

Method: Establishing matching upper and lower bounds through theoretical analysis of regret rates, analyzing two regimes: K ≤ d and K ≥ d with specific dependency patterns.

Result: For K ≤ d and T ≥ d²: Õ(K¹/⁴√(dT)) upper bound with matching Ω(K¹/⁴√(dT)) lower bound. For K ≥ d: Õ(√(dT)min{√d,(d log K)¹/⁴}) upper bound with matching lower bound. Both improve previous Õ(√(dKT)) bounds.

Conclusion: The paper establishes optimal polynomial dependence on menu size K in stochastic linear contextual bandits, providing matching bounds that improve upon previous results by factors of K¹/⁴ or d¹/⁴.

Abstract: We study stochastic linear contextual bandits with arbitrary action menus that may depend on the fixed parameter and the interaction history. We establish matching upper and lower bounds, up to logarithmic factors. Let $d$ be the dimension, $K$ be the menu size, and $T$ the time horizon. For $2\le K\le d$, we prove an upper bound $\widetilde O(K^{1/4}\sqrt{dT})$. When $T\ge d^2$, we further prove a lower bound $Ω(K^{1/4}\sqrt{dT})$. Thus, for $T\ge d^2$ and $2\le K\le d$, the upper and lower bounds match up to logarithmic factors, and the polynomial dependence on $K$ is optimal. Compared with the previous $\widetilde O(\sqrt{dKT})$ bound, our upper bound improves the dependence on $K$ by a factor of $K^{1/4}$.
  For $K\ge d$, we prove an upper bound $\widetilde O_{d,T}\left(\sqrt{dT}\min\{\sqrt d,(d\log K)^{1/4}\}\right)$ and a lower bound $Ω\left(\sqrt{dT}\min\left\{\sqrt d,\left(\frac{d\log K}{\log(2d)}\right)^{1/4}\right\}\right)$. Here, $\widetilde O_{d,T}$ omits logarithmic factors only in $d$ and $T$. In particular, for polynomially large $K\ge d$, the upper and lower bounds both scale as $d^{3/4}\sqrt T$ up to logarithmic factors, improving the standard $\widetilde O(d\sqrt T)$ rate by a factor of $d^{1/4}$. As $K$ grows further, the regret smoothly recovers the $d\sqrt T$ scale once $\log K$ reaches order $d$.

</details>


### [290] [Temporal Self-Distillation: Faster Inference in Discrete Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15177)
*Shijian Xu,Andrea Miele,Metod Jazbec,Volker Roth,Eric Nalisnick,Ilija Bogunovic*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TSD (Temporal Self-Distillation) trains diffusion language models to make earlier predictions that anticipate final outputs, enabling aggressive parallel decoding without complex multi-stage pipelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion language models can generate multiple tokens in parallel for faster inference, but suffer severe performance degradation when parallel decoding is pushed too aggressively, creating a need for methods that enable faster decoding without sacrificing quality.

Method: Temporal Self-Distillation (TSD) is an on-policy method that trains dLLMs by distilling the model's denoising distribution at earlier timesteps toward its distribution at the final timestep when a token is committed. This encourages earlier predictions to anticipate eventual outputs. It requires no offline teacher generation and works with both base and post-trained policies.

Result: Across seven benchmarks in mathematics, planning, and code, TSD substantially shifts the speed-quality frontier toward the low-compute regime, achieving speedups competitive with offline distillation without needing a complex two-stage pipeline.

Conclusion: TSD provides a simple, single-stage approach to accelerating diffusion language models that enables more aggressive parallel decoding while maintaining performance, avoiding the complexity of traditional multi-stage distillation methods.

Abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) promise fast inference by generating multiple tokens in parallel, but suffer severe performance degradation when parallel decoding is pushed too aggressively. We introduce Temporal Self-Distillation (TSD), a simple on-policy method that trains dLLMs for fast inference by distilling predictions across time. Specifically, TSD distills the model's denoising distribution at earlier timesteps toward its distribution at the final timestep at which a token is committed. This encourages earlier predictions to better anticipate the model's eventual output, enabling much more aggressive parallel decoding. Because its teacher signal comes from the model itself, TSD requires no offline teacher generation and applies seamlessly to both base and post-trained policies. Across seven benchmarks in mathematics, planning, and code, TSD substantially shifts the speed--quality frontier toward the low-compute regime. TSD thus provides a simple, single-stage approach to accelerating dLLMs, achieving speedups competitive with offline distillation while avoiding a complex two-stage pipeline.

</details>


### [291] [Rethinking Correctness for Uncertainty Estimation in Clinical Prediction with Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15180)
*Mingcheng Zhu,Jinning Liang,Tingting Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Correctness criteria in clinical vision-language model evaluation significantly impact uncertainty estimation results; exact matching performs best while LLM-judges sometimes accept erroneous outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models are being explored for clinical predictions, but identifying unreliable predictions is crucial for safe deployment. Uncertainty estimation helps detect unreliable predictions, but its evaluation depends on correctness criteria that may disagree with human judgment or distort UE performance metrics, potentially leading to misleading conclusions about model reliability.

Method: Introduced a two-axis framework evaluating correctness criteria based on: 1) agreement with human judgments, and 2) fidelity to human-referenced UE performance. Assessed eight criteria across three clinical prediction tasks using three models, with 450 predictions annotated by two reviewers. Also evaluated four UE methods across 23,254 clinical predictions.

Result: Exact matching (EM) achieved highest human agreement and lowest UE distortion. BERT-based matching (BEM) and LLM-judge also showed strong human agreement. Criterion choice changed error-detection AUROC by up to 0.146 and reversed relative rankings of UE methods. LLM-judge accepted 16 of 30 human-identified errors, selectively accepting invalid or uncertain outputs.

Conclusion: Correctness assessment is an integral component of clinical uncertainty estimation evaluation and should be validated before UE methods are compared, as criterion choice significantly impacts both absolute performance metrics and relative rankings of uncertainty estimation methods.

Abstract: Vision-language models are increasingly explored for clinical prediction from electronic health records and medical images, where identifying unreliable predictions is important for safe deployment. Uncertainty estimation (UE) enables detecting such predictions, but its evaluation depends on a correctness criterion that determines whether each model output is correct. If this criterion disagrees with human judgement or distorts downstream UE performance, conclusions about model reliability can be misleading. We introduce a two-axis framework that evaluates correctness criteria by their agreement with human judgements and fidelity to human-referenced UE performance. We assess eight criteria across three clinical prediction tasks and three models using 450 predictions annotated by two reviewers. Across the audited tasks, canonical exact matching (EM) achieved the highest observed human agreement and lowest UE distortion, while the BERT-based matching (BEM) and LLM-judge also showed strong human agreement. Across four UE methods and 23,254 clinical predictions, criterion choice changed error-detection AUROC by up to 0.146 and reversed the relative ranking of UE methods. The LLM-judge also selectively accepted invalid or uncertain outputs, accepting 16 of 30 such human-identified errors. These results demonstrate that correctness assessment is an integral component of clinical UE evaluation and should be validated before UE methods are compared.

</details>


### [292] [Convergence rates for generative drifting flows: fixed-scale obstructions and multihead acceleration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15193)
*Arthur Stéphanovitch,Eddie Aamari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Drifting models for one-step generative AI can be accelerated by using multihead scale-normalized approaches instead of fixed resolution, which enables exponential convergence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current drifting models for generative AI perform gradual transport during training but generate samples in a single step. The paper investigates whether the underlying drifting process can achieve rapid convergence to target distributions under ideal conditions, before considering finite-data or optimization constraints.

Method: The paper shows that convergence rate depends critically on spatial scale handling. A single fixed resolution approach makes fine-scale features nearly invisible, leading to extremely slow convergence. The authors introduce a multihead approach that combines scale-normalized information across a continuum of resolutions.

Result: The multihead approach restores exponential convergence near standard reference distributions. The authors prove this mathematically, identifying fixed resolution as a key bottleneck in convergence speed.

Conclusion: Fixed resolution is a key bottleneck for drifting models' convergence. The multihead scale-normalized approach provides a simple route to faster one-step generative models by enabling exponential convergence instead of extremely slow convergence.

Abstract: Drifting models offer a promising route to faster generative AI: they perform gradual transport during training, while generating new samples in a single step. This paper asks whether the underlying drifting process can converge rapidly to a target distribution under ideal conditions, before finite-data or optimization effects are introduced. We show that its convergence rate depends critically on how it handles spatial scale. With a single fixed resolution, fine-scale features of the target can become nearly invisible, leading to extremely slow convergence. We introduce a multihead approach that combines scale-normalized information across a continuum of resolutions. We prove that this multihead approach restores exponential convergence near standard reference distributions. These results identify fixed resolution as a key bottleneck and provide a simple route to faster one-step generative models.

</details>


### [293] [ProtoGuide: Prototype-Driven Guidance for Class-Conditional Graph Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15239)
*Salvatore Romano,Marco Grassia,Pietro Liò,Giuseppe Mangioni*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ProtoGuide is a post-hoc, backbone-agnostic guidance framework for discrete graph diffusion models that enables class-conditional generation without retraining, using frozen prototypes and gradient steering through soft adjacency relaxations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard class-conditional mechanisms in discrete graph diffusion models embed class signals in the denoiser during training, creating coupling between conditioning and model architecture. While classifier guidance works in continuous domains by steering models with classifier gradients, it fails in discrete graph domains because sampled edge states prevent gradient propagation.

Method: ProtoGuide operates at each reverse diffusion step: 1) Relax the denoiser's per-edge output into a differentiable soft adjacency matrix, 2) Embed this soft graph using a frozen Siamese graph neural network, 3) Score embeddings against target-class prototype and nearest competitor class prototype, 4) Compute per-edge gradients damped by a cosine schedule, 5) Inject gradients back into denoiser output. All components (denoiser, Siamese network, prototypes) remain frozen, allowing guidance retargeting by supplying different prototypes.

Result: On five real-world network classes with two different backbones (EDGE and DiGress): ProtoGuide raised macro classification accuracy from 50.7% to 73.5% (EDGE) and from 73.6% to 83.8% (DiGress), outperforming DiGress's built-in conditional training. Gains were largest where unguided models were weakest, with class-dependent improvements. Best-of-N selection matched accuracy only with substantial oversampling at high diversity cost. Additional tests showed effective steering and robustness with very small support sets.

Conclusion: ProtoGuide provides an effective post-hoc guidance mechanism for discrete graph diffusion models that decouples conditioning from model training, enables flexible class steering without retraining, and maintains both accuracy and diversity better than naive oversampling approaches, while demonstrating robustness even with minimal training data.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion models are a prominent family for graph generation, but standard class-conditional mechanisms embed the class signal in the denoiser during training, tying the conditioning mechanism to the trained model. Classifier guidance avoids this coupling in continuous domains by steering a frozen model with a classifier's gradient, but discrete graph diffusion samples discrete edge states, so gradients cannot propagate through the sampled graph. We introduce ProtoGuide, a post-hoc, backbone-agnostic framework that recovers an analogous mechanism. At each reverse step the denoiser's per-edge output is relaxed into a differentiable soft adjacency, embedded by a frozen Siamese graph neural network, and scored against a target-class prototype and its nearest competitor; the resulting per-edge gradient, damped by a cosine schedule, is injected back into the denoiser output. All components stay frozen, so guidance is retargeted by supplying a different prototype. On five classes of real-world networks and two architecturally different backbones, EDGE and DiGress, ProtoGuide raises macro classification accuracy from 50.7% to 73.5% and from 73.6% to 83.8%, and outperforms DiGress's built-in conditional training under our configuration. Gains are largest where the unguided models are weakest, and are not uniform across classes. Per-graph coverage remains high in most settings, while distributional effects are class-dependent. A Best-of-N selection baseline matches this accuracy given enough oversampling, but at a substantial cost in graph diversity. An independently initialized classifier, a directionality test, and a few-shot analysis support target-directed steering and robustness to very small support sets.

</details>


### [294] [Bandits with Probing: Optimal Regret and the Limits of Winner Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15248)
*Yongjie Guan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TLDR: Analysis of multi-armed bandit problem with k-probing per round and maximum reward feedback. Establishes two minimax regret laws: one for independent stochastic rewards with winner feedback, and another for arbitrary sequences with signed contrast between block maxima.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper investigates when the "probing advantage" (probing multiple arms per round) pays off for learning. It examines the fundamental trade-off between probing multiple arms and receiving only the maximum reward feedback, comparing against the best fixed arm benchmark.

Method: The paper establishes two minimax regret laws for different settings: 1) Independent stochastic rewards with winner feedback (maximum reward and winning label), 2) Arbitrary fixed sequences given a single signed contrast between block maxima. The analysis includes anytime upper bounds and allows every adaptive action size for lower bounds.

Result: Two key results: 1) Minimax regret order Φ_{n,k}(T) = min{(n-k)/n T, (n-k)/k} for 2 ≤ k < n under winner feedback. 2) Minimax regret order R_{n,k}(T) = (n-k)/n min{T, (n+T)/k, √(nT/k)} for both i.i.d. rewards and fixed sequences with winner feedback. Both have universal constants and anytime bounds.

Conclusion: The first law reduces regret to pure coverage cost where same-round contrasts absorb stability cost, and independence enables exact resampling whose gains fund sample advancement. The second law adds a learning cost that becomes comparable to coverage at horizon n, and beyond nk, numerical maxima provide advantage over labels alone. The lower bounds accommodate any adaptive action size.

Abstract: A learner probes at most $k$ of $n$ arms each round, receives the maximum of their rewards in $[0,1]$, and competes with the best fixed arm. When does the probing advantage pay for learning? We determine two minimax laws. Under independent stochastic rewards with winner feedback (the maximum and a winning label), or on arbitrary fixed sequences given a single signed contrast between block maxima, the minimax regret has order $Φ_{n,k}(T)=\min\{\frac{n-k}{n}T,\frac{n-k}{k}\}$, $2\le k<n$. Under winner feedback, both arbitrary joint i.i.d. rewards and fixed sequences have minimax regret of order $R_{n,k}(T)=\frac{n-k}{n}\min\{T,\frac{n+T}{k},\sqrt{\frac{nT}{k}}\}$. Both laws have universal constants and anytime upper bounds. The first reduces regret to a pure coverage cost: same-round contrasts absorb the stability cost, and independence permits exact resampling whose gains fund sample advancement. The second adds a learning cost that becomes comparable to coverage at horizon $n$; beyond $nk$, numerical maxima improve over labels alone. The lower bound allows every adaptive action size.

</details>


### [295] [BioDCASE: Active Learning for Bioacoustics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15255)
*Ben McEwen,Rupa Kurinchi-Vendhan,Shiqi Zhang,Lukas Rauch,Marek Herde,Sara Beery*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces and evaluates the 2026 Active Learning for Bioacoustics BioDCASE challenge, testing various active learning sampling methods on bioacoustic datasets, finding that combined acquisition signals and diversity-based selection outperform random and uncertainty-only sampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ecological monitoring relies on machine learning models that need labeled data, but labeling is costly in passive acoustic monitoring where vast data is collected but only small portions can be annotated. Active learning addresses this by prioritizing which samples to label, but progress is difficult to measure due to inconsistent evaluation across different models, budgets, metrics, and datasets.

Method: The paper presents the 2026 Active Learning for Bioacoustics BioDCASE challenge - a systematic evaluation framework for sampling methods. Ten proposed sampling methods from seven teams were evaluated across four subsets of terrestrial and marine bioacoustic data using consistent evaluation protocols.

Result: The top-ranked method achieved an area under the learning curve 26.4% higher than random sampling at the same annotation budget (averaged across four data subsets). Performance varied significantly: 67.1% gain for HSN subset vs random, and 8% gain for ATBFL subset. Top submissions combined multiple acquisition signals, with diversity-based selection outperforming pure uncertainty sampling. Evidence showed that transitioning from diversity to uncertainty selection and reducing redundancy in acquisition batches improves training.

Conclusion: The challenge provides a systematic framework for evaluating active learning methods in bioacoustics. Combined acquisition strategies and diversity-based approaches are most effective, with benefits from transitioning strategies during training and careful batch composition. Larger batch sizes may be beneficial later in the labeling process.

Abstract: Ecological monitoring increasingly relies on machine learning models, whose performance depends on the quality and quantity of labelled data. However, obtaining these labels is costly, particularly in passive acoustic monitoring, where vast amounts of data are collected but only a small proportion can feasibly be annotated. Active learning addresses this bottleneck by prioritizing which samples should be labelled. However, progress is difficult to measure, because published methods are evaluated under different models, budgets, evaluation metrics and datasets. To address this challenge, we present the 2026 Active Learning for Bioacoustics BioDCASE challenge: a systematic evaluation of sampling methods designed to identify effective AL strategies. Participant methods were evaluated across four subsets composed of terrestrial and marine data. Across ten proposed sampling methods from seven teams, the top-ranked method achieved an area under the learning curve 26.4 % higher than random sampling at the same annotation budget, averaged over four data subsets. Significant variation in performance was observed across subsets, with the top-performing submission achieving a 67.1 % gain for the HSN subset over random sampling and a gain of 8 % for the ATBFL subset. Top-ranking submissions combined multiple acquisition signals, and diversity-based selection outperformed pure uncertainty sampling. Furthermore, there is evidence that transitioning from diversity-based to uncertainty-based selection and explicitly reducing redundancy within acquisition batches improve model training. There is also initial evidence that larger acquisition batch sizes may be increasingly beneficial later in the labelling process.

</details>


### [296] [Learning CNF Formulas from Uniform Random Solutions: Near-Tight Sample Complexity for Valiant's Algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15268)
*Weiming Feng,Yixiao Yu,Yiyao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Reanalysis of Valiant's algorithm for learning CNF formulas showing optimal sample complexity bounds with matching lower bounds for different parameter regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Revisit Valiant's classic algorithm from 1984 for learning n-variable CNF formulas with clause size k and variable degree d from random solutions in the local lemma regime, aiming to understand its optimality and establish tight bounds.

Method: Analyze Valiant's original algorithm for learning CNF formulas using i.i.d. uniform random solutions. For different parameter regimes (t≥1 with k≳(1+1/t)log d), study the algorithm's performance and prove matching lower bounds through information-theoretic arguments.

Result: For t≥1, Valiant's algorithm achieves total variation error ε with sample complexity O(n^⌈t⌉/ε). Matching lower bounds are proved for t>1, showing algorithm's optimality. For t=1 (covering 0<t<1), algorithm has optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors (Ω(n/ε) lower bound).

Conclusion: Valiant's 1984 algorithm for learning CNF formulas achieves essentially optimal sample complexity across different parameter regimes in the local lemma setting, with matching lower bounds establishing its fundamental limits.

Abstract: We revisit Valiant's algorithm (Commun. ACM'84) for learning $n$-variable CNF formulas with clause size $k$ and variable degree $d$ from i.i.d. uniform random solutions in the local lemma regime. For fixed $t\geq1$, under $k\gtrsim(1+1/t)\log d$, Valiant's algorithm achieves total variation error $\varepsilon$ with $\widetilde{O}(n^{\lceil t \rceil}/\varepsilon)$ sample complexity. For $t>1$, we prove a matching lower bound for Valiant's algorithm. At $t=1$ (covering $0<t<1$), we show Valiant's algorithm has optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors by an information-theoretic lower bound $\widetildeΩ(n/\varepsilon)$.

</details>


### [297] [Draining Fictitious Knots: Restoring Distance-Awareness Guarantees for High-Dimensional Spline Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15274)
*Masoud Ataei,Mohammad Javad Khojasteh,Vikas Dhiman*

Main category: cs.LG
