TL;DR: DAREK improves Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with distance-aware error bounds, but suffers from fictitious knots in high dimensions. The paper proposes a drainage uncertainty mechanism to fix this, restoring distance-awareness with high performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) show promise for interpretable function approximation, and DAREK adds efficient uncertainty quantification. However, in high-dimensional settings, DAREK's theoretical guarantees weaken due to fictitious knots that appear in the combined input space without corresponding to actual training data, misleading uncertainty estimates.

Method: The paper identifies the fictitious-knot failure mode, characterizes its geometric structure, and proposes a drainage uncertainty mechanism. This mechanism constructs a monotonically decreasing uncertainty path from any fictitious knot region toward the nearest real knot, providing a practical heuristic correction.

Result: Experiments on a 2D synthetic benchmark and a 100-dimensional face dataset show that drainage raises sampled distance-awareness (SDA) from 85% to 98-99%, matching Gaussian processes at lower computational cost.

Conclusion: The drainage method successfully mitigates the fictitious-knot failure mode in DAREK, restoring theoretical distance-awareness in high-dimensional settings while maintaining computational efficiency compared to Gaussian processes.

Abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) with spline activations have recently shown promise for interpretable function approximation. Distance-Aware Error for Kolmogorov Networks (DAREK) introduces a computationally efficient bottom-up approach to uncertainty quantification by equipping KANs with distance-aware error bounds; yet, in high-dimensional settings, the theoretical guarantees can be weakened by the emergence of fictitious knots. Inspired by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, DAREK adopts a componentwise formulation in which each input dimension is treated separately; as a result, induced knot locations may appear in the combined input space without corresponding to actual training data. These fictitious knots mislead the DAREK uncertainty estimator into reporting low uncertainty far from any real observation, violating the distance-awareness guarantee. We identify this failure mode precisely, characterize its geometric structure, and propose a drainage uncertainty mechanism that restores distance-awareness by constructing a monotonically decreasing uncertainty path from any fictitious knot region toward the nearest real knot. The proposed drainage method provides a practical heuristic correction that mitigates the fictitious-knot failure mode while restoring theoretical distance-awareness in high-dimensional settings. Experiments on a 2D synthetic benchmark and a 100-dimensional face dataset show that drainage raises sampled distance-awareness (SDA) from 85% to 98-99%, matching Gaussian processes at lower computational cost.

</details>


### [298] [Impute-EM: Native Mixed-State Diffusion Models for Heterogeneous Data Imputation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15284)
*Sergei Kholkin,Kirill Sokolov,Dmitry Baranchuk,Evgeny Burnaev,Alexander Korotin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Impute-EM: An EM-style framework for mixed-type data imputation using native diffusion models without one-hot relaxations, achieving superior distributional fidelity for heterogeneous tabular data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many existing imputation methods, especially diffusion-based ones, use continuous surrogates like one-hot relaxations for discrete variables, creating a mismatch between model state space and the true mixed discrete-continuous structure of heterogeneous data.

Method: Impute-EM framework alternates between imputing missing entries with current model and refitting diffusion backbone on completed data, using native mixed-state diffusion backbones combining Gaussian and masked categorical components without one-hot relaxations.

Result: Theoretically characterizes updates showing observed mask-indexed marginals match targets at limit, while acknowledging full data distribution non-identifiability. Empirically delivers best distributional fidelity on mixed-type tabular imputation and validates native discrete backbone with text imputation.

Conclusion: Impute-EM provides a principled framework for heterogeneous data imputation that better respects the mixed discrete-continuous nature of real-world data, achieving superior distributional fidelity crucial for downstream modeling tasks.

Abstract: Missing values are ubiquitous in heterogeneous data mining, where numerical, categorical, and binary variables often coexist. Many imputation methods, especially diffusion-based ones, treat discrete variables through continuous surrogates such as one-hot relaxations rather than modeling them natively. This creates a mismatch between the model state space and the mixed discrete and continuous structure of the data. We propose Impute-EM, an Expectation Maximization style framework that alternates between imputing missing entries with the current model and refitting a diffusion backbone on completed data. We instantiate Impute-EM with native mixed-state diffusion backbones for heterogeneous data, combining Gaussian and masked categorical components without one-hot relaxations. In exact settings, we characterize the update and show that the observed mask-indexed marginals match the targets at the limit, while making explicit that the full data distribution is generally non-identifiable from incomplete observations alone. Empirically, Impute-EM delivers the best distributional fidelity on mixed-type tabular imputation, on which downstream modeling relies, with text imputation serving as a controlled validation of the native discrete backbone.

</details>


### [299] [Admissable: Training Reinforcement Learning Agents against Adversarial Missingness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15297)
*Paul Stahlhofen,Luca Hermes,Tim Kochs,Markus Vieth,Barbara Hammer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An adversarial training method that improves reinforcement learning robustness against strategic feature occlusion by adversaries, outperforming random missingness training on MuJoCo tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable safe RL deployment in real-world scenarios where adversaries can strategically occlude observation features to degrade performance, addressing the safety gap in adverse operating conditions.

Method: Formally defines adversarial feature missingness in RL, compares it to related concepts (l∞-norm bounded perturbations and missing data learning), then develops and validates an adversarial training algorithm.

Result: The adversarial training algorithm significantly improves robustness against adversarial missingness across three MuJoCo benchmark environments, outperforming baseline training with random uniform missingness on all tasks.

Conclusion: Adversarial training is effective for increasing RL robustness against strategic feature occlusion attacks, providing a practical approach for safer RL deployment in adversarial environments.

Abstract: In order to make Reinforcement Learning algorithms applicable in real world scenarios, safety must be ensured even under adverse operating conditions. In this work, we consider the challenge of adversarial feature missingness: a scenario in which an adversary occludes features from the agent's observation in order to reduce performance as much as possible. We formally define adversarial missingness for Reinforcement Learning and compare it to the related concepts of $\ell_\infty$-norm bounded adversarial perturbations and learning with missing data. We develop an adversarial training algorithm and show its effectiveness in increasing robustness against adversarial missingness on three MuJoCo benchmark environments. Compared to a baseline trained with random uniform missingness, our method achieves better robustness on all three tasks.

</details>


### [300] [When Correlations Mislead: Confounder-Aware Multi-View Urban Region Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15305)
*Sean Bin Yang,Ying Sun,Zongyi Xu,Tung Kieu,Jilin Hu,Bin Yang,Kristian Torp,Hua Lu,Torben Bach Pedersen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CURE: A confounder-aware framework for multi-view urban region representation learning that separates shared latent components to improve robustness and prevent correlation propagation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-view methods for urban region representation often overlook view-specific regional structures and may propagate correlations induced by shared latent factors, reducing the stability of downstream predictions.

Method: CURE encodes each view with its regional graph structure, estimates a shared latent component, reduces its projected influence before cross-view interaction, and uses hierarchical graph-aware fusion to aggregate residual view representations with local and global regional contexts.

Result: Experiments on three real-world cities show CURE improves predictive performance, remains robust under missing and noisy input views, and provides reliable cross-view integration through shared component separation and context-dependent view weighting.

Conclusion: CURE addresses the limitation of correlation propagation in multi-view urban region representation learning by explicitly separating shared components, leading to more robust and stable embeddings for downstream tasks.

Abstract: Urban region representation learning commonly combines heterogeneous data sources, such as mobility flows, points of interest, and land-use information, to support tasks including mobility analysis, public safety forecasting, and service demand estimation. Existing multi-view methods typically improve region embeddings by strengthening interactions across views. However, such methods often overlook view-specific regional structures and may propagate correlations induced by shared latent factors, which can reduce the stability of downstream predictions. To overcome this major limitation, we propose CURE, a confounder-aware framework for multi-view urban region representation learning. CURE first encodes each view with its regional graph structure, estimates a shared latent component, and then reduces its projected influence before cross-view interaction. A hierarchical graph-aware fusion module subsequently aggregates the residual view representations using local and global regional contexts Experiments on three real-world cities show that CURE improves predictive performance, remains robust under missing and noisy input views, and provides reliable cross-view integration through shared component separation and context-dependent view weighting.

</details>


### [301] [Generalization Can Emerge in Tabular Foundation Models From a Single Table](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.09665)
*Junwei Ma,Nour Shaheen,Alex Labach,Amine Mhedhbi,Frank Hutter,Anthony L. Caterini,Valentin Thomas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In-context learning for tabular data can generalize surprisingly well with minimal pre-training data, including just a single real table, challenging the notion that large synthetic or real datasets are necessary for broad generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper challenges the prevailing assumption in deep tabular modeling that in-context learning requires extensive pre-training on large synthetic corpora (like TabPFN priors) or large collections of real data (like TabDPT training datasets). The authors question whether such massive pre-training is truly necessary for broad generalization across heterogeneous tabular datasets.

Method: The authors systematically pre-train and evaluate on many diverse datasets, analyzing what data aspects are most important for building a Tabular Foundation Model (TFM). They specifically examine how simple self-supervised pre-training on just a single real table can produce transfer learning across benchmarks, and connect this to the shared pre-training procedure of most TFMs, focusing on the number and quality of tasks constructable from a dataset.

Result: The key discovery is that relatively small amounts of data suffice for generalization in tabular in-context learning. Simple self-supervised pre-training on just a single real table can produce surprisingly strong transfer across heterogeneous benchmarks. The number and quality of tasks that can be constructed from a dataset (rather than dataset size alone) is crucial for downstream performance.

Conclusion: The prevailing view that broad generalization in tabular in-context learning requires massive pre-training datasets is challenged. A relatively small amount of data, including potentially just one carefully selected real table with rich task construction possibilities, can yield effective TFMs that generalize well across domains, shifting focus from dataset scale to task diversity and quality.

Abstract: Deep tabular modelling increasingly relies on in-context learning where, during inference, a model receives a set of $(x,y)$ pairs as context and predicts labels for new inputs without weight updates. We challenge the prevailing view that broad generalization here requires pre-training on large synthetic corpora (e.g., TabPFN priors) or a large collection of real data (e.g., TabDPT training datasets), discovering that a relatively small amount of data suffices for generalization. We find that simple self-supervised pre-training on just a \emph{single} real table can produce surprisingly strong transfer across heterogeneous benchmarks. By systematically pre-training and evaluating on many diverse datasets, we analyze what aspects of the data are most important for building a Tabular Foundation Model (TFM) generalizing across domains. We then connect this to the pre-training procedure shared by most TFMs and show that the number and quality of \emph{tasks} one can construct from a dataset is key to downstream performance.

</details>


### [302] [Representing Clinical Conditions on Vital Signs from Healthy Individuals using Latent Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15379)
*Rafael Pina,Varuna De Silva,Mindula Illeperuma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A conditional variational autoencoder model for augmenting healthy vital signs data to mimic clinical condition patterns from ICU data, with evaluation showing improved alignment with clinical labels compared to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine learning for healthcare signal processing applications often requires rich datasets, but access to representative data (especially for clinical conditions) is limited. There's a need to augment existing healthy data to mimic clinical patterns for better model training.

Method: Proposed a deep generative model based on conditional variational autoencoders. Trained the model on publicly available ICU dataset, then applied it to reshape vital signs data collected from healthy individuals to mimic patterns of specific clinical conditions.

Result: The model successfully learned underlying dynamics of ICU data and could reshape healthy individual data to align with vital signs of specific clinical conditions. A proposed distance metric showed the model generates samples more aligned with intended clinical labels compared to tested baselines.

Conclusion: The conditional variational autoencoder approach effectively addresses data scarcity in healthcare ML by augmenting healthy vital signs to mimic clinical conditions, providing a valuable tool for improving model training in data-constrained scenarios.

Abstract: Machine learning can be crucial to help scale complex signal processing applications in scenarios such as healthcare. However, these machine learning models need rich datasets to be trained and there are often cases where it is not possible to access representative datasets. In this paper, we propose a deep generative model based on conditional variational autoencoders with the objective of augmenting the vital signs of healthy individuals in a way that mimics the patterns of a certain clinical condition. More specifically, we use a publicly available ICU (Intensive Care Unit) dataset to train our model and then evaluate it using the vital data that we have collected from healthy individuals. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model can not only learn the underlying dynamics of the ICU data but, more importantly, can reshape our collected data from healthy individuals in a way that is aligned with the vital signs of a certain clinical condition. We propose a distance metric that shows how our model can generate samples that are more aligned with the intended clinical labels when compared to the tested baselines.

</details>


### [303] [CodeTS: Verifiable Text-to-Time Series Generation via Executable Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15393)
*Xudong Yuan,Shunyu Liu,Tongya Zheng,Huiping Zhuang,Mingli Song,Kaixuan Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CodeTS is a verifiable Text-to-Time-Series framework that uses executable code as an intermediate interface, enabling explicit generation logic derivation from textual descriptions through a Text-to-Code-to-TS process with reinforcement learning and verifiable rewards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Text-to-TS methods lack explicit mechanisms to derive generation logic from textual descriptions to guide time series synthesis. There's a need for scenario-specific time series generation when real observations are scarce or costly to acquire, but current approaches don't provide verifiable generation processes.

Method: Proposes CodeTS framework with Text-to-Code-to-TS process: 1) maps textual descriptions to executable code specifying how requirements shape temporal patterns, 2) obtains time series through code execution. Uses aligned Text-Code-TS triplets from structured temporal attributes for supervised initialization, and multi-stage execution-based rewards (format validity, code executability, time series quality) for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR).

Result: Extensive experiments on eight benchmarks across short, medium, and long generation lengths show CodeTS provides strong zero-shot performance, outperforming LLM-based baselines and achieving better averaged results than supervised generative baselines trained on target datasets.

Conclusion: CodeTS effectively bridges textual descriptions and time series generation through code as an interpretable intermediate interface, enabling verifiable and controllable synthesis with improved zero-shot capabilities across various generation scenarios.

Abstract: Text-to-Time Series Generation (Text-to-TS) provides a promising paradigm for synthesizing time series from natural language, enabling scenario-specific generation when real observations are scarce or costly to acquire. However, existing methods typically lack an explicit mechanism for deriving generation logic from textual descriptions to guide time series synthesis. In this paper, we propose CodeTS, a verifiable framework that uses code as an intermediate generation interface, reformulating Text-to-TS generation as a Text-to-Code-to-TS process. CodeTS first maps textual temporal descriptions into an explicit code space, where executable code specifies how textual requirements shape target temporal patterns, and then obtains the time series through code execution. To learn this code generation process reliably without real code annotations, CodeTS constructs aligned Text-Code-TS triplets from structured temporal attributes for supervised initialization. More importantly, we further design multi-stage execution-based rewards that verify format validity, code executability, and time series quality, enabling real Text-TS pairs to provide training signals for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). Extensive experiments on eight benchmarks across short, medium, and long generation lengths demonstrate that CodeTS provides a strong zero-shot solution for Text-to-TS generation, outperforming LLM-based baselines and achieving better averaged results than supervised generative baselines trained on the target datasets.

</details>


### [304] [Single-condition neural solvers encode transferable response spaces for parametric differential equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15432)
*Wenbo Cao,Weiwei Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A method called Linearized Subspace Transfer (LST) enables cross-condition PDE solution transfer using neural solver Jacobians as reusable response spaces, with Active Transfer Modeling (ATM) selectively acquiring additional spaces for improved accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional operator learning for parametric PDEs requires cross-condition data or costly physics-constrained training, and builds global models over prescribed domains which may not be efficient or reusable across different conditions.

Method: 1) Use output Jacobian of neural solution model trained at one condition as reusable response space for cross-condition variations. 2) Linearized Subspace Transfer (LST) minimizes target PDE-system residual over response-space coordinates. 3) Active Transfer Modeling (ATM) uses post-transfer residuals as coverage indicators to selectively acquire additional response spaces from other single-condition models.

Result: Across six systems: 1) Single-condition response spaces supported cross-condition transfer. 2) Enrichment improved accuracy when added spaces expanded representation capacity. 3) ATM reduced error and offline construction cost compared to physics-informed operator baselines. 4) Orders-of-magnitude accuracy gains in representative cases. 5) Millisecond-to-second target adaptation times.

Conclusion: The approach establishes neural solvers as reusable local parametric models, enabling efficient cross-condition PDE solution transfer with reduced training costs and improved accuracy through selective space enrichment.

Abstract: Operator learning for parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) typically builds global models over prescribed domains, requiring cross-condition data or costly physics-constrained training. Here we show that the output Jacobian of a neural solution model trained at one condition defines a reusable response space for cross-condition solution variations. We introduce Linearized Subspace Transfer (LST) to exploit this space and recover target solutions by minimizing the target PDE-system residual over response-space coordinates. Because any single response space has finite coverage, Active Transfer Modeling (ATM) uses post-transfer residuals as coverage indicators to selectively acquire response spaces from additional single-condition models. Across six systems, single-condition response spaces supported cross-condition transfer, with enrichment improving accuracy when added spaces expanded representation capacity. Relative to evaluated physics-informed operator baselines, ATM reduced error and offline construction cost, with orders-of-magnitude accuracy gains in representative cases and millisecond-to-second target adaptation. These results establish neural solvers as reusable local parametric models.

</details>


### [305] [On the role of the tokenizer in ECG transformer models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15433)
*Jiawei Li,Fabio Bonassi,Johan Sundström,Thomas B. Schön,Antônio H. Ribeiro*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ECG Transformer performance is significantly improved by aligning tokens with ECG morphology through physiology-aware tokenization strategies like Median-beat and HeartLang, which boost both predictive accuracy and memory efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tokenization in ECG Transformers affects both the physiological content presented to the model and the sequence length over which attention operates. Understanding how different tokenization strategies impact performance and efficiency is crucial for developing effective ECG analysis models.

Method: The study compared eight tokenization strategies across four Transformer architectures (Transformer, Informer, Reformer, FEDformer) on the nine-label CPSC2018 classification task. Input projection and principal backbone capacity were controlled to isolate the effect of token construction, ensuring fair comparison of tokenization methods.

Result: Median-beat and HeartLang tokenization achieved mean macro-AUCs of 0.893 and 0.889 respectively, significantly outperforming point-wise (0.822) and patch-wise (0.824) tokenization. Pooling these physiology-aware representations yielded an 8.2% relative improvement in macro-AUC while reducing mean sequence length from 1,250 to 158 tokens and mean peak training memory from 5.21 to 0.27 GB.

Conclusion: Aligning tokens with ECG morphology through physiology-aware tokenization strategies significantly improves both predictive performance and memory efficiency without requiring additional backbone capacity. This approach makes ECG Transformers more effective and practical for real-world applications.

Abstract: Tokenization determines both the physiological content presented to an ECG Transformer and the sequence over which attention operates. We compare eight tokenization strategies across Transformer, Informer, Reformer, and FEDformer on the nine-label CPSC2018 classification task. The input projection and principal backbone capacity are controlled to isolate the effect of token construction. Median-beat and HeartLang tokenization achieve mean macro-AUCs of 0.893 and 0.889 across the four backbones, compared with 0.822 and 0.824 for point-wise and patch-wise tokenization. Pooling the two physiology-aware representations yields an 8.2% relative improvement in macro-AUC. They also reduce mean sequence length from 1,250 to 158 tokens and mean peak training memory from 5.21 to 0.27 GB. The results show that aligning tokens with ECG morphology can improve both predictive performance and memory efficiency without increasing backbone capacity. The source code is available on https://github.com/LeeJarvis996/ecg_tokenizer.

</details>


### [306] [GSLAD: Prototype-Regularized Graph Structure Learning for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15483)
*Zepeng Zhang,Fuad Khuri,Keivan Faghih Niresi,Olga Fink*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GSLAD is a graph structure learning framework that detects anomalies in multivariate time series by analyzing structural deviations between variables, using prototype regularization and two-phase training with uncertainty modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial faults often first affect inter-variable structural relationships rather than individual variable trajectories, making them hard to detect with traditional forecasting or reconstruction methods that focus on individual signals.

Method: Two-phase training: (1) train condition-aware graph learner and graph-based forecaster with predictive supervision, (2) cluster inferred normal graphs into structural prototypes representing different normal regimes, then regularize graph learner with deviations from these prototypes. Uses edge-wise variability to characterize structural uncertainty.

Result: Experiments on four industrial benchmarks demonstrate strong overall performance and confirm the effectiveness of structural deviation for both anomaly detection and diagnosis tasks.

Conclusion: GSLAD effectively captures structural deviations in multivariate time series for anomaly detection, addressing the limitation of traditional methods that miss inter-variable structural changes, with practical utility for industrial fault detection and diagnosis.

Abstract: Unsupervised multivariate time series anomaly detection methods typically identify anomalies through forecasting, reconstruction, or representation discrepancies. However, industrial faults may first alter inter-variable structural patterns while individual trajectories remain close to normal, resulting in weak anomaly signals. In this paper, we propose GSLAD, a prototype-regularized graph structure learning framework that uses structural deviations for anomaly scoring. GSLAD adopts a two-phase training strategy. First, a condition-aware graph learner and a graph-based forecaster are optimized with predictive supervision. The inferred normal graphs are then clustered into multiple structural prototypes representing different normal operating regimes, with edge-wise variability characterizing structural uncertainty. Deviations from these prototypes regularize the graph learner in the second phase, encouraging stable and regime-specific structural patterns. During inference, uncertainty-normalized structural deviation is combined with predictive deviation for anomaly scoring. Experiments on four industrial benchmarks demonstrate strong overall performance of GSLAD and confirm the effectiveness of structural deviation for anomaly detection and diagnosis.

</details>


### [307] [Data-driven Prediction of Satellite-observed Avalanche Activity from Snowpack Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15485)
*Jakob Grahn,Filippo Maria Bianchi,Bert Kruyt,Karsten Müller*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Transformer model using SNOWPACK simulation data predicts SAR-detected avalanche activity with moderate success but operational forecasting not yet established.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Avalanche forecasting requires snowpack and activity data, but field observations are sparse across large mountain regions, creating a need for alternative monitoring approaches.

Method: Used SNOWPACK simulations on 20x20 km grid at different elevations and slope angles, combined with five winters of Sentinel-1 SAR avalanche detections across Norway/Sweden. A transformer model used five days of SNOWPACK outputs to predict the following day's SAR-detected Avalanche Activity Index (SAR-AAI). Trained on four winters, validated on one.

Result: Regional mean predicted vs. reference SAR-AAI correlated at r=0.803 after six-day averaging. At 20km cell scale, correlation was weaker at r=0.549. Model followed broad spatiotemporal changes but produced smoother predictions and underestimated strongest activity. Only single training run without independent test.

Conclusion: Results don't establish operational forecast skill but suggest SNOWPACK simulations contain information about broad variations in satellite-observed avalanche activity. Limitations include satellite detection errors, uncertain timing, and need for more rigorous validation.

Abstract: Avalanche forecasting requires knowledge of snowpack conditions and recent avalanche activity, but field observations are sparse across large mountain regions. We explore whether SNOWPACK simulations can predict avalanche activity mapped by synthetic aperture radar (SAR). We compiled five winters of Sentinel-1 avalanche detections across Norway and parts of Sweden, alongside SNOWPACK simulations forced by numerical weather predictions on a 20 x 20 km grid at different elevations and predefined slope angles. A transformer used five days of SNOWPACK outputs to predict the following day's SAR-detected Avalanche Activity Index (SAR-AAI). This index weights larger debris more heavily, spreads detections across possible occurrence dates and normalises by modelled runout area. The model was trained on four winters and evaluated on one validation winter. Regional mean predicted and reference SAR-AAI correlated at r = 0.803 after averaging over complete six-day periods. The model followed broad changes in time and space but produced smoother predictions and underestimated the strongest activity. Agreement at the 20 km cell scale was weaker (r = 0.549) after the same averaging. These results come from a single training run without evaluation on an untouched winter. Satellite observations also contain missed and false detections and uncertain timing. The results therefore do not establish operational forecast skill, but suggest that regional SNOWPACK simulations contain information about broad variations in satellite-observed avalanche activity.

</details>


### [308] [Rotation-Based Subspace Tracking for Robust Kernel PCA on Streaming Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15488)
*Kris Lokere,John Fossaceca*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a rotation-based update mechanism for robust online kernel PCA that enables dynamic tracking of nonlinear subspaces in streaming data with outliers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing online robust kernel PCA algorithms have limitations: they converge to a fixed subspace assumption, gradient-descent-based updates lose effectiveness after initial alignment, and they cannot effectively track dynamic changes in nonlinear data with outliers in streaming scenarios.

Method: Introduces a rotation-based update mechanism that updates the subspace estimate by rotating it toward each new incoming feature vector in RKHS. Presents two complementary rotation strategies moderated by a robust influence function to mitigate outlier effects, enabling dynamic tracking of nonlinear subspaces.

Result: Experiments on synthetic streaming data with known ground-truth subspace show that per-sample rotations converge faster than gradient descent alone, effectively tracking a nonlinear subspace in streaming data.

Conclusion: The rotation-based approach provides an effective mechanism for dynamically tracking nonlinear subspaces in streaming data with outliers, addressing limitations of existing gradient-descent-based robust kernel PCA methods.

Abstract: Machine learning models process large amounts of data, and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a widely used technique to reduce the dimensionality of the data and extract useful features. In practice, datasets often change over time (data drift) and/or arrive one sample at a time (streaming data), making it infeasible to process the entire dataset at once in batch mode. Real-world data also often contains nonlinear patterns, which traditional PCA cannot extract. Kernel PCA addresses this by implicitly mapping samples into a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). Raw data also often contains outliers, which can have an outsized effect on the estimated subspace unless the algorithm is made robust. However, existing online robust kernel PCA algorithms are designed to converge to a subspace that is assumed to be fixed, and gradient-descent-based updates lose their effectiveness at tracking further changes once this initial alignment is achieved. This paper introduces a rotation-based update mechanism, which updates the subspace estimate by rotating it toward each new incoming feature vector in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space, rather than relying on gradient descent alone. We present two complementary rotation strategies, and show that the extent of rotation can be moderated by a robust influence function to mitigate the effect of outliers. Through experiments on synthetic streaming data with a known ground-truth subspace, we show that per-sample rotations converge faster than gradient descent alone, demonstrating an effective mechanism for dynamically tracking a nonlinear subspace in streaming data.

</details>


### [309] [Same path, different: a mechanistic comparison of looped and stacked transformer encoders on 12-lead ECG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15498)
*Pawel Olszowiec,Michal Byra,Grzegorz Gruszczynski,Grzegorz Stefanski,Alberto Presta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Recurrent Transformers (like bViT) achieve equivalent accuracy to standard stacked Transformers (ViT) with 8.9× fewer parameters on ECG classification, constructing similar representations but showing different dynamical behaviors - bViT has smaller step sizes and inter-patient sensitivity while ViT shows collapsing dimensionality and feature expansion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recurrent Transformers that reuse weights rather than stacking distinct layers are gaining popularity for parameter efficiency, but the fundamental differences between looped (recurrent) and stacked architectures remain poorly understood. The paper aims to conduct a controlled comparison of these architectural paradigms.

Method: The study compares bViT (one weight-tied block applied L times) with standard ViT on 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) classification using the PTB-XL dataset. Both models are trained under identical protocols. Geometric similarity metrics are used to analyze latent representations, and various dynamics are measured including step sizes, inter-patient sensitivity, and behavior away from the data manifold.

Result: Despite having 8.9× fewer parameters, bViT achieves accuracy parity with ViT on ECG classification. Both architectures construct comparable latent representations in similar canonical order. However, their dynamics differ significantly: bViT shows smaller step sizes and inter-patient sensitivity, plus near-neutral behavior away from data manifold, while ViT exhibits collapsing dimensionality of representations and out-of-distribution feature expansion.

Conclusion: Recurrent Transformers can match standard stacked Transformers in accuracy with far fewer parameters, suggesting weight tying is an effective parameter efficiency strategy. However, the different dynamical behaviors reveal that while they produce similar final results, they process information differently, which could have implications for generalization, robustness, and interpretability in different applications.

Abstract: Recurrent Transformers reusing their weights rather than stacking $L$ distinct layers are becoming widely adopted due to their parameter efficiency [1,2,3]. However, the exact representational and dynamical differences between looped and stacked architectures remain uncharacterized. This paper presents a controlled study on the example of bViT model [1] applying one weight-tied block $L$ times. We train two models: bViT and standard ViT [4] on 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) classification tasks from the PTB-XL dataset under identical training protocols. Despite an $8.9\times$ parameter reduction, bViT achieves accuracy parity with ViT. Geometric similarity metrics demonstrate that both architectures construct comparable latent representations in an equivalent canonical order. Crucially, their dynamics differ: bViT exhibits smaller step sizes and inter-patient sensitivity, as well as near-neutral behavior away from the data manifold, whereas ViT exhibits collapsing dimensionality of representations and out-of-distribution feature expansion.

</details>


### [310] [End-to-End Verifiable and Robust Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15521)
*Doryan Lesaignoux,Enrique Mármol Campos,Gabriele Spini,José L. Hernández-Ramos,Stephan Krenn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Verifiable federated learning protocol that combines robustness against poisoned updates with public auditability of the aggregation process using cryptographic commitments and zero-knowledge proofs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated learning introduces integrity risks when participants or infrastructure are not trustworthy. Two critical requirements are robustness against Byzantine/poisoned client updates and verifiability of the aggregator's actions. Existing work treats these goals separately, and efficient public verifiability for robust, outlier-excluding aggregation remains limited.

Method: Combines cryptographic commitments with non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs to certify both (1) cosine-similarity-based outlier exclusion and (2) aggregation over the selected set, without revealing individual client updates to verifiers.

Result: Maintains high accuracy under representative poisoning attacks with average accuracy loss below 4% across evaluated configurations. Verification overhead is practical: proof artifacts can be generated and verified within minutes at the studied scale.

Conclusion: Robust outlier exclusion and public verifiability can be jointly achieved in federated learning settings, providing both Byzantine robustness and transparent auditability of the aggregation process.

Abstract: Federated learning enables multiple parties to train a shared model without centralizing raw data with the help of an aggregator, but introduces integrity risks once participants or infrastructure are not fully trustworthy. Two requirements are particularly important: robustness to poisoned or Byzantine client updates, and verifiability of the aggregator so that clients or third parties can audit the reported aggregation without learning individual updates. Existing work has largely treated these goals separately, and efficient public verifiability for robust, outlier-excluding aggregation remains limited. We present a verifiable federated learning protocol that makes a robust aggregation pipeline publicly auditable. Our design combines cryptographic commitments with non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs to certify both (i) cosine-similarity-based outlier exclusion and (ii) aggregation over the selected set, without revealing individual client updates to verifiers. In experiments under representative poisoning attacks, our method maintains high accuracy, with an average accuracy loss below 4\% across the evaluated configurations, while keeping verification overhead practical: proof artifacts can be generated and verified within minutes at the scale studied. In summary, our results show that robust outlier exclusion and public verifiability can be jointly achieved in a federated learning setting.

</details>


### [311] [Beyond Noise: Understanding and Overcoming Temperature Effects in Analog DNN Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15527)
*Niklas Summ,Xiao Wang,Hendrik Borras,Bernhard Klein,Holger Fröning*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Analog computing shows promise for ML on mobile/embedded devices but suffers from temperature-sensitive noise/non-idealities; systematic non-idealities (not stochastic noise) drive temperature degradation; noise-aware training helps, but hardware-in-loop training and temperature-aware calibration provide best accuracy retention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Analog computing offers energy efficiency advantages for deploying ML workloads on resource-constrained platforms like mobile and embedded devices, but analog accelerators are inherently susceptible to noise and non-idealities from physical component variations that are sensitive to environmental factors like temperature, which can significantly degrade inference accuracy.

Method: 1. Comprehensive experimental study on representative analog hardware investigating temperature impact; 2. Characterize behavior of stochastic and systematic non-idealities across operating temperature ranges; 3. Compare simulation-based and hardware-based mitigation strategies for temperature-induced performance degradation; 4. Evaluate noise-aware training, hardware-in-the-loop training, and temperature-aware calibration methods.

Result: Temperature-induced accuracy degradation is driven primarily by systematic non-idealities rather than stochastic noise alone; Noise-aware training improves robustness; Hardware-in-the-loop training and temperature-aware calibration provide the strongest accuracy retention across varying thermal conditions.

Conclusion: Analog ML accelerators face significant temperature-induced performance challenges, with systematic non-idealities being the primary cause; While noise-aware training offers some improvement, the most effective solutions involve hardware-in-the-loop training and temperature-aware calibration techniques to maintain accuracy across thermal variations.

Abstract: The energy efficiency of analog computing makes it one of the most promising candidates for deploying resource-intensive machine learning workloads on constrained platforms such as mobile and embedded devices. However, analog accelerators are inherently susceptible to noise and non-idealities arising from physical component variations, whose behavior is further sensitive to environmental factors. These effects can significantly degrade inference accuracy. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive experimental study on a representative example of analog hardware to investigate the impact of temperature. We first characterize the behavior of stochastic and systematic non-idealities across a range of operating temperatures. Following this, we compare a set of simulation-based and hardware-based mitigation strategies aimed at improving robustness against temperature-induced performance degradation. Our results suggest that temperature-induced degradation is driven primarily by systematic non-idealities rather than stochastic noise alone. Noise-aware training improves robustness, while hardware-in-the-loop training and temperature-aware calibration provide the strongest accuracy retention across varying thermal conditions.

</details>


### [312] [The Misery of Mechanistic Interpretability: A Formal Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15533)
*Tobias Ladner,Matthias Althoff*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: First formal verification framework for interpretable replacement networks (IRNs) in LLMs, showing current IRNs are fragile to input perturbations and proposing verification-aware training to provide certified faithfulness guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current mechanistic interpretability approaches using IRNs are evaluated only empirically on clean data, lacking formal guarantees about their faithfulness when inputs are perturbed. This is problematic for safety-critical applications where auditors need reliable interpretations.

Method: 1) Show IRN fragility by demonstrating semantically minor input perturbations flip dominant IRN features across 5 model families. 2) Propose formal verification framework using reachability analysis to certify sound upper bounds of faithfulness gap in adversarial scenarios. 3) Introduce verification-aware training of IRNs to tighten certified bounds.

Result: Demonstrated IRNs are fragile to small perturbations across GPT-2 small, Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 3 1B, Llama 3.2 1B, R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B. Verification framework provides first formal guarantees for IRN faithfulness, and verification-aware training substantially improves certified bounds, enabling reliable feature-level interpretation.

Conclusion: Provides first formal guarantees for mechanistic interpretability of LLMs, enabling safety auditors to act on feature-level interpretations with certified faithfulness. Verification-aware training of IRNs overcomes fragility issues and makes mechanistic interpretability more robust and trustworthy.

Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability has become the dominant lens for understanding frontier language models, as their inner workings are complex and inherently black boxes. To gain insights into these models, interpretable replacement networks (IRNs) are trained at all layers, exposing interpretable features through sparsely activated neurons. However, the faithfulness of an IRN is usually evaluated only empirically on clean data, and we show that even semantically minor input perturbations flip the dominant IRN features-and thus the human-understandable interpretation-across five open-weight model families (GPT-2 small, Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 3 1B, Llama 3.2 1B, R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B). We propose the first formal verification framework for the faithfulness of an IRN, where reachability analysis certifies a sound upper bound of the faithfulness gap in adversarial scenarios. Moreover, we show that verification-aware training of IRNs substantially tightens this certified bound, restoring a feature-level interpretation that safety auditors can act on. Together, these results give, to the best of our knowledge, the first formal guarantees for mechanistic interpretability of large language models.

</details>


### [313] [Specifying Reward Functions for RL Without Environment Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15544)
*Stephane Hatgis-Kessell,W. Bradley Knox,Emma Brunskill*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EARS (Experience-Free Autonomous Reward Specification) enables learning reward functions from preferences without environment interaction, outperforming LLM-only baselines on long-horizon tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing preference-based methods like RLHF require repeated environment interaction (training policies, sampling real trajectories), which is impractical when environment interaction is computationally expensive or unsafe. There's a need for methods that can specify reward functions without costly real-world interaction.

Method: EARS uses a structured LLM-mediated process to: 1) construct expressive reward features from task description and observation space, 2) strategically sample imagined trajectories in feature space (no real environment interaction), 3) learn feature weights from preferences over imagined trajectory pairs.

Result: EARS outperforms LLM-only baselines (directly prompting LLM for reward functions) on three long-horizon domains (pandemic lockdown regulation, insulin administration, autonomous vehicle control). EARS designs reward functions more aligned with ground truth or LLM context, whether learning from ground-truth preference labels or LLM-labeled preferences.

Conclusion: Preference-based reward specification can remain effective without environment sampling, enabling practical reward design in settings where collecting real trajectories is costly or infeasible. The structured approach of EARS is superior to direct LLM prompting for reward function generation.

Abstract: Enabling human stakeholders to specify reward functions that lead to their desired outcomes is a key challenge in deploying reinforcement learning agents. Preference-based methods such as online RLHF can reduce the burden of manual reward design, but they require repeatedly training policies, sampling trajectories from the real world, and eliciting feedback, making them impractical in settings where environment interaction is computationally expensive or unsafe. We introduce Experience-Free Autonomous Reward Specification (EARS), a method for learning reward functions from preferences without environment interaction. Our approach uses a structured LLM-mediated process to construct a small set of expressive reward features from a task description and the environment observation space, then strategically samples imagined trajectories in this feature space and learns feature weights from preferences over the imagined trajectory pairs. We evaluate on three long-horizon domains: pandemic lockdown regulation design, insulin administration for diabetes patients, and autonomous vehicle control on a highway. We compare EARS to baselines that also enable reward specification without environment interaction--namely, methods that directly prompt an LLM to generate a reward function. When learning from either ground-truth preference labels or preferences labeled by a LLM, EARS designs reward functions that are more aligned with the ground truth reward function that produced the preferences or LLM context than these baselines. These results suggest that preference-based reward specification remains effective without environment sampling, enabling practical reward design in settings where collecting real trajectories is costly or infeasible.

</details>


### [314] [The Token Before the Value Is the Key: How Hybrid Architectures Organize Induction Circuits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15545)
*Ke Cheng,Xin Xu,Yixiao Chen,Lei Xin,Jianbo Zhao,Fanhu Zeng,Yue Liu,Jun Zhang,Jie Jiang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hybrid language models learn complementary computation across layers - Carrying concentrates in efficient layers while Matching focuses in global receivers, with local contributions mainly at lag-one tokens before values.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how architectural complementarity in hybrid language models becomes learned computation, specifically examining how position-sensitive and content-based computations (Carrying predecessor information, Matching sources by content, Copying values) are allocated across heterogeneous layers.

Method: Introduce layer-type-agnostic paired probes tracking Carrying and Matching through common block-update interface; analyze recurrent-global and local-global hybrids; conduct interventions through lag-one masking, convolution removal, early learning-rate reduction; examine varying local windows and induction-enriched training text.

Result: Carrying concentrates in efficient layers and Matching in global receivers; local contribution focuses on lag-one tokens (immediate predecessor); interventions can relocate Carrying/Matching between stages; source-key restoration and fixed-value selection trace receiver's dependence; interventions also change natural-text recall depending on configuration.

Conclusion: The organization of Matching follows how Carrying is learned; the token immediately before the value provides concrete link between hybrid architecture, circuit development, and recall; explanatory focus shifts upstream to how computation is allocated across layers during learning.

Abstract: Hybrid language models can improve capability as well as efficiency, raising the question of how architectural complementarity becomes learned computation. We examine the established induction roles of Carrying predecessor information, Matching a source by content, and Copying its value. How are these position-sensitive and content-based computations allocated across heterogeneous layers? We introduce layer-type-agnostic paired probes that track Carrying and Matching through a common block-update interface. In recurrent--global and local--global hybrids, Carrying concentrates in efficient layers and Matching in global receivers. The measured local contribution concentrates on lag one: the token immediately before the historical value. Changing predecessor support through lag-one masking, convolution removal, or early learning-rate reduction can relocate Carrying and Matching between stages. Source-key restoration and fixed-value selection trace the receiver's dependence on the prepared source. These interventions also change natural-text recall, with outcomes depending on configuration and target. Varying local windows and induction-enriched training text changes the early development of functional Carrying and Matching, connecting architectural priors and training evidence to formation timing. Together, the probes and interventions shift the explanatory focus upstream: the organization of Matching follows how Carrying is learned. The token before the value provides a concrete link between a hybrid's architecture, circuit development, and recall. Code is available in https://github.com/ckpassenger/bind-match-copy/tree/main.

</details>


### [315] [Bayesian Optimisation Using Product-of-Experts Gaussian Process Models with Uncertainty Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15555)
*Yean Hoon Ong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BO-pro-c: Bayesian optimization using product-of-experts Gaussian process model reduces computational cost by 39.4% while maintaining competitive performance with slight regret improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Bayesian optimization uses single global Gaussian process models with cubic computational complexity (O(n³)), limiting scalability to large problems. The GP-pro-c model (product-of-experts with uncertainty calibration) offers benefits like improved uncertainty quantification and reduced cost, but hasn't been thoroughly studied for BO applications.

Method: Developed BO-pro-c algorithm that uses GP-pro-c (product-of-experts Gaussian process with uncertainty calibration) as its surrogate model. This combines multiple local GP experts to preserve global correlations while reducing computational burden compared to single global GP.

Result: Experimental evaluation across diverse BO settings shows BO-pro-c maintains competitive optimization performance with 0.9% reduction in simple regret and 39.4% reduction in computational overhead compared to BO using single global GP model.

Conclusion: BO-pro-c is a promising Bayesian optimization approach that successfully leverages the GP-pro-c model's advantages, achieving significant computational savings while preserving or slightly improving optimization performance, making it suitable for large-scale optimization problems.

Abstract: Bayesian optimisation (BO) typically relies on a single global Gaussian process (GP) model as its surrogate model. However, GP regression has cubic computational complexity in the number of training data points, limiting its applicability to large-scale optimisation problems. The product-of-experts Gaussian process model with uncertainty calibration (GP-pro-c) mitigates this limitation by combining multiple local GP experts, enabling improved uncertainty quantification, reduced computational cost, and preservation of global correlations. Despite these desirable properties, the use of GP-pro-c in BO has not been thoroughly studied. This paper introduces BO-pro-c, a Bayesian optimisation algorithm that uses GP-pro-c as its surrogate model, and evaluate its performance across a diverse range of BO settings. Experimental results suggest that BO-pro-c maintains competitive optimisation performance while achieving a 0.9% reduction in simple regret and a 39.4% reduction in computational overhead relative to a BO algorithm based on a single global GP model.

</details>


### [316] [Multi-View Molecular Representation Learning with Hierarchical Graphs and Contextualized Fingerprints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15611)
*Gwang-Hyeon Yun,Jong-Hoon Park,Bing Hu,Helen Chen,Anita Layton,Young-Rae Cho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HiFi-Mol is a multi-view molecular representation learning framework that combines hierarchical graph encoding with contextualized fingerprint embeddings through separate pretraining and downstream integration, achieving improved performance on molecular property prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current molecular pretraining methods are limited by single-view approaches: graph-based methods focus on atom-bond topology but lack fragment-level supervision, while fingerprint descriptors encode chemical patterns but are typically used as fixed features without learnable representations. There's a need to leverage complementary information from both structural and chemical pattern perspectives.

Method: HiFi-Mol employs a two-branch multi-view framework: (1) Graph branch: hierarchical graph encoder pretrained with fragment-aware masking and multi-resolution supervision to capture substructure-aware representations, (2) Fingerprint branch: contextualized fingerprint encoder that tokenizes active entries from seven fingerprint families and applies masked language modeling. During fine-tuning, the model combines projected multi-resolution graph features with fingerprint embeddings.

Result: On MoleculeNet benchmarks under scaffold split, HiFi-Mol achieves 2.77% improvement in average ROC-AUC over the best baseline across eight classification tasks while maintaining competitive performance on three regression tasks. Analyses show fragment-aware masking improves graph representation quality, and classification results demonstrate dataset-dependent strengths of individual graph and fingerprint variants.

Conclusion: The multi-view approach combining hierarchical graph representations with contextualized fingerprint embeddings provides complementary predictive signals that enhance molecular property prediction. The framework effectively addresses limitations of single-view methods and demonstrates the value of leveraging both structural and chemical pattern information for representation learning.

Abstract: Molecular property prediction requires representations that generalize from limited labeled data to structurally novel compounds. Existing molecular pretraining methods often rely on a single view: graph-based approaches model atom-bond topology but provide limited fragment-level supervision, whereas fingerprint descriptors encode chemical patterns but are typically used as fixed auxiliary features. We propose HiFi-Mol, a multi-view framework that separately pretrains a hierarchical graph encoder and a contextualized fingerprint encoder before downstream integration. The graph branch uses fragment-aware masking with multi-resolution supervision to capture substructure-aware representations, while the fingerprint branch tokenizes active entries from seven fingerprint families and applies masked language modeling to learn contextualized embeddings. During fine-tuning, HiFi-Mol combines projected multi-resolution graph features with fingerprint embeddings for downstream prediction. Evaluated on MoleculeNet benchmarks under the scaffold split, HiFi-Mol achieves a 2.77% improvement in average ROC-AUC over the best baseline across eight classification tasks while maintaining competitive performance on three regression tasks. Further analyses reveal that fragment-aware masking improves graph representation quality, and classification results demonstrate dataset-dependent strengths of the individual graph and fingerprint variants, confirming that the two views provide complementary predictive signals.

</details>


### [317] [Where to Compute and How to Interact: Operator-Readable Adaptation with Gauge-Aware Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15620)
*Zixuan Shen,Quanxu Wan,Bingchuan Wang,Zhi Wang,Biao Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GA-AMNO introduces a gauge-aware neural operator with physics-informed mesh adaptation and geometry-conditioned gauge transport for consistent representation aggregation across adaptive discretizations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adaptive mesh neural operators focus on where to compute but neglect how information should interact after node relocation, potentially entangling physical variation with discretization-induced representation variation.

Method: Proposes Gauge-Aware Adaptive Mesh Neural Operator (GA-AMNO) with physics-informed adaptive allocation for where to compute and geometry-conditioned low-rank gauge transport to map features into target representation contexts before aggregation.

Result: Experiments on five PDE benchmarks show improved predictive accuracy, while controlled interventions verify roles of allocation and interaction, and gauge transport improves cross-discretization representation compatibility under geometric mismatch.

Conclusion: GA-AMNO addresses operator readability by making mesh-to-solver information exchange inspectable and intervenable, providing representation-consistent aggregation for adaptive mesh neural operators.

Abstract: Adaptive meshes enable neural operators for partial differential equations (PDEs) to allocate spatial samples and computation according to local physical structures. Existing approaches, however, mainly address where to compute, with less attention to how information should interact after node relocation. Mesh adaptation changes local sampling scales, neighborhood structures, and geometric contexts, so representations formed at different nodes may not be directly comparable. Direct aggregation can therefore entangle physical variation with discretization-induced representation variation. Because allocation and interaction are jointly optimized through the same output objective, their individual roles are also difficult to distinguish from final errors alone. We introduce operator readability, requiring an adaptive operator to account for and test why computation is allocated to particular locations and how representations interact under the resulting nonuniform discretization. Based on this principle, we propose the Gauge-Aware Adaptive Mesh Neural Operator (GA-AMNO). Physics-informed adaptive allocation answers where to compute, while geometry-conditioned low-rank Gauge transport maps source features into target representation contexts before aggregation, answering how to interact. This makes mesh-to-solver information exchange inspectable and intervenable. We establish sufficient conditions for representation-consistent aggregation and analyze approximate transport errors and continuity under topology-preserving mesh deformations. Experiments on five PDE benchmarks demonstrate improved predictive accuracy, while controlled interventions and geometric-mismatch analyses verify the roles of allocation and interaction and show that Gauge transport improves cross-discretization representation compatibility under strong geometric mismatch.

</details>


### [318] [FedLTLib: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Federated Long-Tail Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15625)
*Changkun Lin,Junxiao Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedLTLib: A standardized benchmark for Federated Long-Tail Learning that addresses data imbalance in mobile edge networks by providing unified evaluation protocols and implementing 13 state-of-the-art algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world mobile computing environments suffer from "Double Heterogeneity" - the combination of global class imbalance and local statistical skew due to heterogeneous mobile devices with varying user behaviors. This creates long-tail distributions where tail classes (representing rare but critical edge-case events) are extremely scarce, leading to severe performance deterioration on these important classes. Prior research lacks consistent experimental configurations and fair comparisons.

Method: The authors introduce FedLTLib, a comprehensive benchmark tailored for Federated Long-Tail Learning (FL-LT). The platform establishes a standardized evaluation framework with diverse benchmark datasets reflecting mobile data characteristics. It implements 13 state-of-the-art algorithms (4 traditional FL algorithms and 9 specialized FL-LT algorithms) to enable fair comparisons under unified experimental protocols.

Result: FedLTLib provides researchers with a standardized platform to perform fair and reproducible evaluations of algorithm robustness and generalization capabilities. The benchmark addresses critical issues of inconsistent experimental configurations and unfair comparisons that plagued prior work in this field.

Conclusion: FedLTLib represents an important contribution to standardizing Federated Long-Tail Learning research, enabling accelerated progress through fair and reproducible evaluations. This advancement will ultimately support the deployment of more robust intelligence in mobile computing ecosystems by addressing the critical challenge of data heterogeneity in federated learning environments.

Abstract: Driven by the escalating demand for privacy-preserving computing, Federated Learning (FL) has witnessed remarkable progress, becoming a cornerstone technology for bridging distributed data silos in mobile edge networks. However, in real-world mobile computing environments, data is generated by heterogeneous mobile devices with varying user behaviors, leading to a significant Long-Tail Distribution. Unlike idealized balanced datasets, data in the wild manifests an acute imbalance where a minority of head classes dominate the sample space while a vast number of tail classes, often representing rare but critical edge-case events, are extremely scarce. This data heterogeneity, which we formally characterize as "Double Heterogeneity", referring to the superposition of global class imbalance and local statistical skew, precipitates severe performance deterioration on tail classes, thereby spurring the vital research direction of Federated Long-Tail Learning (FL-LT). To standardize evaluation and accelerate research in this field, we introduce FedLTLib, a comprehensive benchmark tailored for FL-LT. Addressing the critical issues of inconsistent experimental configurations and unfair comparisons in prior work, FedLTLib establishes a standardized evaluation framework. The platform not only incorporates diverse benchmark datasets reflecting mobile data characteristics but also implements 13 state-of-the-art FL algorithms (4 traditional FL algorithms and 9 FL-LT algorithms). By leveraging FedLTLib, researchers can perform fair and reproducible evaluations of algorithm robustness and generalization capabilities under a unified experimental protocol, ultimately advancing the deployment of robust intelligence in mobile computing ecosystems.

</details>


### [319] [Principal-timestep Restricted Init via Sparse Matrix-decomposition in Flow-matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15643)
*Jiayang Gu,Zheng Fang,Lichaun Xiang,Fanghui Liu,Xu Cai,Hongkai Wen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Prism-LoRA improves diffusion model fine-tuning by using principal timestep selection and channel filtering to address gradient misalignment issues in flow-matching objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flow-matching diffusion models have high fine-tuning costs that limit scalability to downstream tasks. While Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with spectral initialization works well for language models, it fails for diffusion models due to a fundamental mismatch between LoRA's low-rank parameterization and the high-rank gradients induced by flow-matching objectives.

Method: Proposes Prism-LoRA (Principal-timestep Restricted Init via Sparse Matrix-decomposition) with two key components: 1) principal timestep selection - restricts initialization gradients to dominant timesteps to suppress effective gradient rank, 2) principal channel filtering - removes task-irrelevant channels so one-step spectral initialization better aligns with long-horizon optimization trajectory.

Result: The method consistently improves convergence speed and final performance across multiple diffusion fine-tuning benchmarks including subject-driven generation, controllable generation, and deblurring, outperforming baseline LoRA and other spectral-init methods with earlier convergence.

Conclusion: Prism-LoRA successfully addresses the gradient alignment problem in diffusion fine-tuning by adapting spectral initialization to handle the high-rank gradients induced by stochastic timestep sampling in flow-matching objectives, enabling more efficient and effective fine-tuning of diffusion models.

Abstract: Flow-matching diffusion models have recently emerged as a strong paradigm for high-fidelity visual generation. However, their prohibitively high fine-tuning cost limits scalability to downstream tasks. While Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) combined with spectral initialization has demonstrated accelerated convergence and improved performance in autoregressive language models by better aligning gradient directions, we find that it fails to deliver similar gains in diffusion fine-tuning, often yielding marginal or even negative improvements over vanilla LoRA.We attribute this discrepancy to a fundamental mismatch between LoRA's low-rank parameterization and the intrinsically high-rank gradients induced by the flow-matching objective. In particular, stochastic timestep sampling introduces directionally heterogeneous gradient signals across training steps, leading to misaligned updates under low-rank constraints.To address this issue, we propose Prism-LoRA,a Principal-timestep Restricted Init via Sparse Matrix-decomposition framework that improves gradient alignment during fine-tuning. Our method consists of two key components: (i) principal timestep selection, which restricts initialization gradients to a subset of dominant timesteps to suppress effective gradient rank, and (ii) principal channel filtering, which removes task-irrelevant channels, enabling the one-step spectral initialization gradient to better align with the long-horizon optimization trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently improves both convergence speed and final performance across multiple diffusion fine-tuning benchmarks, including subject-driven generation, controllable generation, and deblurring, achieving not only performance improvement but also earlier stages of convergence over baseline LoRA and other spectral-init methods.

</details>


### [320] [Backward SDEs-based Diffusion for Physics-Constrained Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15702)
*Zihao Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A method for physics-consistent inverse problems using terminal-conditioned inversion with score-based diffusion priors, ensuring feasibility guarantees through backward stochastic differential equations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pretrained diffusion models provide strong priors but existing methods for enforcing measurement/physics consistency use heuristics or task-specific training with limited feasibility guarantees at inference time.

Method: Terminal-conditioned inversion for score-based SDE priors: constructs backward SDE from terminal feasibility specification to prior state at chosen noise level, with existence/uniqueness guarantees under regularity conditions. Practical neural BSDE solver composes arbitrary pretrained diffusion priors with constraints without modifying scores.

Result: Validated on toy datasets with stable inversion and distributionally consistent neighborhood sampling. Applied to sparse-view CT reconstruction showing improved quality over baselines while satisfying strict measurement feasibility.

Conclusion: Provides principled framework for enforcing terminal constraints in inverse problems with diffusion priors, offering feasibility guarantees and uncertainty characterization through anchored prior states.

Abstract: Pretrained score-based diffusion models provide strong unconditional priors, yet enforcing measurement or physics consistency in inverse problems is often handled by heuristic guidance, intermittent projections, or task-specific conditional training, with limited guarantees of feasibility at the end of inference. We propose terminal-conditioned inversion for score-based SDE priors. Given a frozen Score-SDE prior and a task-defined terminal feasibility specification, we construct an associated backward stochastic differential equation whose adapted solution defines a principled inverse map from the terminal requirement to a prior state at a chosen noise level. Under standard regularity conditions, we establish existence and uniqueness of the adapted solution and obtain terminal consistency by construction. We further develop a practical neural BSDE solver that composes arbitrary pretrained diffusion priors with domain constraints without modifying the score-defined coefficients, producing an anchored prior state that enables neighborhood sampling for uncertainty characterization. Experiments on toy datasets validate stable terminal-conditioned inversion and distributionally consistent neighborhood sampling. As a real-world case study, we apply the framework to sparse-view CT reconstruction and achieve improved reconstruction quality over representative training-free baselines while satisfying strict measurement feasibility under the prescribed terminal specification. Project is available in: \href{https://laplacelab.github.io/BSDEDiffusion/}{https://laplace.center/icmlbsdeI/}

</details>


### [321] [Knowledge-Enriched Structured EHR Features for 30-Day Hospital Readmission Prediction on MIMIC-IV](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15713)
*Mohamad Najafi,Hongyun Fu,Mathias Brochhausen,Jian Wu,Yaohang Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A knowledge-enriched EHR feature representation method for 30-day hospital readmission prediction that avoids clinical notes, using structured EHR data augmented with medical knowledge sources for interpretable and computationally efficient predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches using pre-trained language models on discharge summaries have limitations: dependence on clinical note availability, high computational costs, and lack of interpretability in the learned representations.

Method: Developed a knowledge-enriched feature representation that augments structured EHR data with four medical knowledge sources: disease ontology mapping, procedure classification, drug ingredient vocabulary, and organ system laboratory aggregation. Creates sparse, interpretable patient representations where each feature corresponds to a named clinical concept.

Result: Achieved AUROC of 0.743 on MIMIC-IV v2.2 cohort under 20-fold cross-validation. Performance is comparable to previously reported methods using structured data or clinical notes, but with significantly lower computational cost. Interpretability analysis revealed demographics, organ system labs, drug ingredients, and first-level disease ontology categories are most predictive.

Conclusion: Knowledge-enriched structured features provide a competitive and efficient alternative to clinical note embeddings for 30-day readmission prediction, offering comparable performance with better interpretability and lower computational requirements.

Abstract: Recent approaches to 30-day hospital readmission prediction rely on pre-trained language models applied to discharge summaries. Although these methods achieve strong performance, they depend on the availability of clinical notes, incur substantial computational costs, and yield representations that lack interpretability. We propose a knowledge-enriched feature representation that augments structured Electronic Health Record (EHR) data with four medical knowledge sources: disease ontology mapping, procedure classification, drug ingredient vocabulary, and organ system laboratory aggregation, without using clinical notes. Each feature dimension corresponds to a named clinical concept, yielding a sparse and interpretable patient representation. The approach is evaluated with six classifiers on a MIMIC-IV v2.2 cohort. Under 20-fold cross-validation, the best configuration achieves an AUROC of 0.743. This performance is comparable to that of previously reported methods on this dataset, including both those using only structured data and those incorporating clinical notes, while requiring considerably less computational cost. Interpretability analysis shows that demographics, organ system labs, drug ingredient features, and first-level ontology disease categories drive prediction, while deeper hierarchy levels contribute negligibly. These findings indicate that knowledge-enriched structured features offer a competitive and efficient alternative to embeddings from clinical notes for 30-day readmission prediction.

</details>


### [322] [Assembling the CREW: A Collaborative Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Automated Related Work Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15721)
*Hai-Dang Dang,Bao-Yen Pham,Bao Nguyen,Tran Thi Huong,Huynh Thi Thanh Binh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CREW proposes a collaborative reinforcement learning framework using LLM agents that dynamically coordinate without predefined workflows, achieving better quality and lower token costs for automatic related work generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
