Motivation: Current multi-agent LLM approaches for automatic Related Work Generation rely on predefined, rigid workflows with static inter-agent coordination, which limits adaptive collaboration needed for synthesizing complex scientific literature.

Method: CREW uses LLM agents that bypass heuristic pipelines to dynamically coordinate by autonomously selecting actions (Retrieve, Disseminate, Compose, Critique) driven by a policy optimized via Independent Proximal Policy Optimization (IPPO).

Result: Extensive experiments on a standard RWG benchmark demonstrate substantial quality improvements over strong existing baselines while significantly reducing token costs.

Conclusion: The CREW framework enables more effective automatic Related Work Generation through dynamic, adaptive collaboration between LLM agents optimized via reinforcement learning, offering both quality gains and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Automatic Related Work Generation (RWG) significantly reduces the human time and effort required to author the Related Work Section (RWS) of a research paper. However, prior methods leveraging multi-agent Large Language Models (LLMs) typically rely on a predefined workflow, where each agent is responsible for a specific step in the entire process. This rigid, static inter-agent coordination limits the adaptive collaboration required to synthesize complex scientific literature. To address this limitation, we propose CREW (Collaborative Reinforcement Learning for Related Work Generation), a novel framework where LLM agents bypass heuristic pipelines to dynamically coordinate by autonomously selecting actions, such as Retrieve, Disseminate, Compose, and Critique, driven by a policy optimized via Independent Proximal Policy Optimization (IPPO). Extensive experiments on a standard RWG benchmark demonstrate that our approach yields substantial quality improvements over strong existing baselines, while significantly reducing token costs. Code is available at https://github.com/YenPBao/CREW-Collaborative-MARL.git

</details>


### [323] [Solving Finite-sum Coupled Compositional Optimization via Multi-block-Single-probe Estimator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15723)
*Wei Jiang,Sifan Yang,Yibo Wang,Lijun Zhang,Zechao Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Novel Multi-block-Single-probe Variance Reduction (MSVR) estimator for finite-sum coupled compositional optimization (FCCO) problems that can track multiple functions while sampling only O(1) functions per iteration, achieving improved sample complexities across various optimization settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional variance reduction methods (SPIDER, SARAH, STORM) maintain estimators for a single function across iterations, but many real-world problems require tracking multiple functions simultaneously. The challenge arises in FCCO problems where we need to track g(w) with m blocks but can only sample O(1) blocks per iteration due to computational constraints.

Method: Proposes Multi-block-Single-probe Variance Reduction (MSVR) estimator that efficiently traces g(w) under partial block sampling. Builds algorithms for FCCO problems based on MSVR to handle non-convex, convex, strongly convex, and Polyak-Łojasiewicz objectives.

Result: Achieves improved sample complexities across various optimization settings. Obtains improved dependence on m when outer function gradients ∇f_i are linear. Empirical studies on multi-task deep AUC maximization demonstrate superior performance compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: MSVR estimator effectively addresses the challenge of tracking multiple functions with limited sampling capacity in FCCO problems, providing theoretical improvements in sample complexity and practical advantages in applications like multi-task deep AUC maximization.

Abstract: Traditional variance reduction methods (e.g., SPIDER, SARAH, STORM) have been extensively investigated for improving the convergence rates of stochastic optimization. These techniques typically maintain a sequence of estimators for a single function (or gradient) across iterations. However, what if we need to track multiple functions, but can only access stochastic samples of $\mathcal{O}(1)$ functions at each iteration? This scenario arises in an important emerging family of finite-sum coupled compositional optimization (FCCO) problems of the form $\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(g_i(\mathbf{w}))$, where each $g_i$ is accessible only through a stochastic oracle. The key challenge is to track $\mathbf g(\mathbf{w})=(g_1(\mathbf{w}), \ldots, g_m(\mathbf{w}))$ over time, where $\mathbf g(\mathbf{w})$ has $m$ blocks but only $\mathcal{O}(1)$ blocks can be probed for their stochastic values at each step. To address this challenge, we propose a novel Multi-block-Single-probe Variance Reduction (MSVR) estimator to efficiently trace $\mathbf g(\mathbf{w})$ under partial block sampling. Building on the MSVR estimator, we develop several algorithms for FCCO problems, achieving improved sample complexities for non-convex, convex, strongly convex, and Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) objectives. We further obtain an improved dependence on $m$ when the outer function gradients $\nabla f_i$ are linear. Empirical studies on multi-task deep AUC maximization further demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed estimators.

</details>


### [324] [A Language-Guided Multimodal Foundation Model for Zero-Shot and Multi-Task Brain Signal Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15740)
*Mingzhi Chen,Yiyu Gui,Guibo Luo,Yuchao Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A new multimodal foundation model called METIS achieves state-of-the-art brain signal analysis with zero-shot capability, outperforming existing models without fine-tuning by aligning brain signals with language representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current brain signal analysis methods face critical limitations: end-to-end models require task-specific retraining and have limited generalization; pre-trained models lack semantic depth and need extensive fine-tuning; general-purpose multimodal foundation models struggle with brain signals due to representational misalignment and lack of domain knowledge.

Method: Introduces METIS, a multimodal foundation model for zero-shot and multi-task brain signal analysis using a unified language-signal alignment framework. Pretrained on the largest and most diverse brain-signal corpus to date (over 70,000 hours from 11,000+ subjects across 20 datasets).

Result: In zero-shot evaluation across 12 datasets, METIS outperformed leading generalist model by 20.9% average accuracy. Without any fine-tuning, METIS matches or exceeds supervised task-specific models. Shows exceptional data efficiency and generalization: 16.0% AUROC advantage in few-shot settings and 15.9% advantage in cross-dataset transfer.

Conclusion: METIS establishes a new paradigm for general-purpose brain signal analysis, enabling zero-shot and multi-task capabilities that overcome current limitations, paving the way for next-generation neurotechnology.

Abstract: Brain signal analysis is essential for both neuroscience research and clinical diagnostics, yet current approaches face critical limitations. End-to-end models require task-specific retraining and exhibit limited generalization, while pre-trained models lack semantic depth and still depend on extensive fine-tuning. Meanwhile, general-purpose multimodal foundation models, though powerful in other domains, struggle to interpret brain signals due to representational misalignment and lack of domain knowledge. This study introduces a multimodal foundation model for zero-shot and multi-task brain signal analysis (METIS) through a unified language-signal alignment framework. METIS is pretrained on the largest and most diverse brain-signal corpus to date, comprising over 70,000 h of recordings from more than 11,000 subjects across 20 datasets. In a comprehensive zero-shot evaluation across 12 datasets, METIS outperformed the leading generalist model by over 20.9% in average accuracy. Remarkably, without any fine-tuning, METIS's performance matches or exceeds that of supervised, task-specific models. Furthermore, METIS demonstrates exceptional data efficiency and strong generalization, achieving an average AUROC advantage of over 16.0% in few-shot settings and 15.9% in cross-dataset transfer. This work establishes a new paradigm for general-purpose brain signal analysis, paving the way for next-generation neurotechnology.

</details>


### [325] [Sylvas: Synergistic Learning Value based Device Scheduling in Federated Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15763)
*Yuxuan Sun,Yuxuan Bai,Tan Chen,Sheng Zhou,Zhisheng Niu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sylvas is a device scheduling framework for federated continual learning at wireless edge that quantifies and selects devices based on learning value considering data distribution quality and pseudo-label reliability under resource constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated continual learning needs to adapt to distributed non-stationary data streams in IoT applications like intelligent transportation and industrial monitoring, but faces challenges in spatio-temporal distribution dynamics, label scarcity, and resource-constrained device scheduling for timely model updating.

Method: Sylvas evaluates learning value from two perspectives: 1) Distributional value (contribution from spatio-temporal distribution perspective) and 2) Label value (quantity-reliability tradeoff of pseudo-labeled data). It integrates these into a synergistic learning value metric to schedule high-value devices while satisfying communication/computation constraints.

Result: Case studies demonstrate that Sylvas supports timely model adaptation under spatio-temporal distribution dynamics and effectively exploits unlabeled data for federated continual learning.

Conclusion: Sylvas provides an effective framework for device scheduling in federated continual learning at wireless edge by quantifying learning value through distributional and label perspectives, enabling efficient model adaptation under resource constraints and data scarcity.

Abstract: Federated continual learning (FCL) enables shared global models to continuously adapt to distributed and non-stationary data streams, making it important for Internet of Things applications such as intelligent transportation, industrial monitoring, and unmanned systems. Under spatio-temporal data distribution dynamics and label scarcity, a key challenge is how to quantify the contribution of each edge device to global learning performance and schedule the most valuable devices under resource constraints for timely model updating. This article presents Sylvas, a synergistic learning value based device scheduling framework for FCL at the wireless edge. Sylvas evaluates the learning value of distributed data from two perspectives: distributional value, which characterizes the contribution of device data to global model learning from a spatio-temporal distribution perspective, and label value, which captures the quantity and reliability tradeoff of pseudo-labeled data. By integrating these factors into a synergistic learning value metric, Sylvas schedules devices with high learning value while satisfying communication and computation resource constraints. Case studies demonstrate that Sylvas supports timely model adaptation under spatio-temporal distribution dynamics and effectively exploits unlabeled data.

</details>


### [326] [Transfer Learning for Socioeconomic Estimation in Forced-Displacement Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15773)
*Steven Ndung'u,Adel Daoud,Ismael Yacoubou Djima,Hai-Anh H. Dang,Patrick Michael Brock*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Satellite data + ML model adapted for refugee/host community socioeconomic monitoring, providing more frequent updates than traditional surveys


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional household surveys for displaced populations are resource-intensive, periodic, and can't capture rapid changes in fragile/conflict settings. Need more frequent, granular data for timely humanitarian decisions.

Method: Adapted a multimodal spatiotemporal vision transformer pretrained on 1.2M households across 36 African countries, then applied to forced displacement settings in South Sudan, Cameroon, Zambia using UNHCR socioeconomic data.

Result: Satellite-derived geospatial covariates explain 66% variance in camp areas (MAE 4.37) and 41% in non-camp areas (MAE 5.41) of socioeconomic outcomes.

Conclusion: The framework complements periodic surveys by filling spatial/temporal gaps with regularly updated socioeconomic estimates, supporting timely humanitarian prioritization and field verification.

Abstract: Progress in inclusive household surveys has strengthened socioeconomic evidence for forcibly displaced populations, providing indispensable benchmarks on living conditions and welfare. However, these surveys remain resource-intensive and periodic, while conditions can change between rounds, particularly in settings affected by fragility, conflict, and violence. More frequently updated, spatially granular complementary evidence is therefore needed to identify where socioeconomic conditions may be changing between survey rounds and to inform operational prioritization. Earth observation and machine learning offer a scalable source of spatially explicit socioeconomic information. However, tools developed for general populations have not been systematically adapted and evaluated in forced displacement settings, where living conditions, settlement patterns, and displacement impacts may differ substantially. We address this gap by adapting a multimodal spatiotemporal vision transformer, pretrained on Demographic and Health Survey data from approximately 1.2 million households across 36 African countries, to forced displacement and host community settings in South Sudan, Cameroon, and Zambia. We develop and evaluate the updated, adapted model using socioeconomic indices derived from UNHCR FDS and RMS data. Our results show that satellite-derived geospatial covariates explain up to 66% of the variation in socioeconomic outcomes in camp-intersecting grids, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 4.37 index points, and 41% in non-camp-intersecting areas, with an MAE of 5.41. The framework complements and adds value to periodic household surveys by filling critical spatial and temporal data gaps with regularly updated, model-based socioeconomic estimates. These estimates sustain insight between survey rounds and support timely humanitarian prioritization and field verification.

</details>


### [327] [MoveBench: A Benchmark for Global-Scale Wildlife Movement Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15780)
*Justin Kay,Shir Bar,Ellen O. Aikens,Martin Becker,Francesca Cagnacci,Juliet Cohen,Scott W. Forrest,Jessica Kendall-Bar,Madeleine Lucas,Macon Overcast,Meredith S. Palmer,Will Rogers,Nicholas J. Russo,Christian Rutz,Larissa T. Beumer,Michael Brown,Ying-Chi Chan,Sarah C. Davidson,Diego Ellis Soto,Anne G. Hertel,Roland Kays,Benjamin Koger,Guram Mikaberidze,Thomas Mueller,Ruth Oliver,Thorsten Papenbrock,Robert Patchett,Jared A. Stabach,Dane Taylor,Scott W. Yanco,Sara Beery*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MoveBench is the first large-scale benchmark for wildlife movement forecasting, featuring 2.6M GPS locations from 800+ animals across 110 species, paired with environmental data. It introduces probabilistic evaluation and shows existing methods generalize better across time than across individuals, with deep learning not consistently outperforming simpler approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wildlife movement prediction is crucial for ecology and conservation but presents unique challenges compared to human/vehicle movement: unconstrained spatial movement, high stochasticity, and strong environmental influences. Current trajectory forecasting methods for humans/vehicles don't adequately address these wildlife-specific challenges, and there's no standardized benchmark for evaluation.

Method: Create MoveBench - a large-scale dataset with 2.6M GPS locations from 800+ individuals across 110 species in 127 countries, paired with 1.6B environmental raster tiles capturing 160 covariates. Develop a probabilistic evaluation protocol for trajectory forecasts to address limitations of point-prediction metrics. Conduct comprehensive empirical evaluation of four method families across multiple temporal and spatial scales.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Existing predictive methods generalize better to future timepoints than to unseen individuals; (2) Deep learning approaches do not consistently outperform simpler baselines; (3) Environmental covariate selection significantly impacts performance. The benchmark enables standardized evaluation and methodological advances.

Conclusion: MoveBench provides the first comprehensive benchmark for wildlife movement forecasting, addressing the need for standardized evaluation in this ecologically important domain. It reveals important insights about method generalization, the performance of deep learning approaches, and the critical role of environmental covariate selection, establishing a foundation for future methodological advancements.

Abstract: Understanding and predicting wildlife movement is critical for ecology and conservation. While trajectory forecasting has advanced for human and vehicle movement, wildlife trajectories present distinct challenges: they are unconstrained in space, highly stochastic, and influenced by environmental conditions. We introduce MoveBench, the first large-scale benchmark for probabilistic wildlife movement forecasting, containing 2.6M GPS locations from 800+ individuals across 110 species in 127 countries, paired with 1.6B environmental raster tiles capturing 160 covariates known or hypothesized to influence movement. We propose a probabilistic evaluation protocol for movement trajectory forecasts, addressing limitations of point-prediction metrics for inherently stochastic phenomena. Through comprehensive empirical evaluation of four method families across multiple temporal and spatial scales, we reveal that: (1) existing predictive methods generalize better to future timepoints than to unseen individuals, (2) deep learning approaches do not consistently outperform simpler baselines, and (3) environmental covariate selection significantly impacts performance. MoveBench enables standardized evaluation of movement forecasting methods and provides a foundation for methodological advances on this ecologically important task.

</details>


### [328] [Sharp Rates and a One-Line Correction for Spectral Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15825)
*Dier Tang,Jing Yee Tan,Guangyue Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper shows that transfer risk in self-supervised learning depends on alignment between task covariance and feature extractor spectrum, not isotropy, provides diagnostic tools to assess and fix misalignment, and proves task diversity forces alignment in high dimensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Practitioners need to know when off-the-shelf self-supervised features are sufficient versus when they need correction for new downstream tasks. Existing theory assumes isotropic task priors, but this is unrealistic and leads to incorrect optimality claims.

Method: Analyzes transfer risk through task covariance alignment with feature extractor's spectral properties. Provides diagnostic statistics costing O(kd_x^2) to measure alignment, proves matching two-sided regret bounds, and introduces a simple reweighting scheme to correct misalignment when detected.

Result: Shows that worst-case regret is exactly 1-1/κ(Λ) with refinements, proves alignment becomes generic in high dimensions with diverse tasks (α=Õ(√d_x/T)), demonstrates diagnostic correctly identifies when correction is needed, and shows one-line reweighting restores optimality.

Conclusion: Isotropy is the wrong hypothesis for self-supervised feature transfer. Alignment between task preferences and feature extractor spectrum determines transfer risk, task diversity forces alignment in high dimensions, and practical diagnostics can guide practitioners on when and how to fix representations.

Abstract: A self-supervised encoder is trained once, frozen, and reused through lightweight probes on tasks nobody named at training time; the practitioner's question is when the off-the-shelf features are good enough and when they need fixing. Canonical correlation analysis, HGR maximal correlation, and the population optimum of the spectral contrastive loss all return the top-$k$ singular subspace of a cross-view dependence operator, justified by isotropy: if the task prior has no directional preference, that subspace is universally optimal. We show isotropy is the wrong hypothesis. The prior enters the transfer risk only through the task covariance $Λ=\mathbb{E}[ΔΔ^\top]$, and only through its compression onto the operator's leading singular directions; what matters is not whether $Λ$ is isotropic but whether its preferred directions are ordered consistently with the operator's spectrum. We prove matching two-sided rates---worst-case regret is exactly $1-1/κ(Λ)$, refines to $1-A_k$ for an alignment coefficient $A_k$, localizes to the top-$2k$ subspace, becomes second order under a spectral gap, and is improvable by no task-agnostic representation---and show why alignment is generic: incoherent preferences cancel in high dimension, and $T$ diverse tasks force $α=\widetilde O(\sqrt{d_x/T})$, a quantitative account of why task diversity, not symmetry, makes self-supervised features transfer. The governing statistics cost $O(kd_x^2)$, and when they signal misalignment a one-line reweighting of the positive-pair term provably restores exact optimality. The result is a diagnostic that answers the practitioner's question from a small labelled budget and refuses when the task bank cannot support the width requested; on controlled data it takes a regret of $0.86$ down to $0.003$, and on a CIFAR-100 encoder it correctly predicts that no correction is needed.

</details>


### [329] [Per-Matrix Optimality Is Not Enough: Three-Level Optimization for Low-Rank LLM Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15838)
*Huicheng Zhang,Xiyao Feng,Ze-Tong Li,Chengkai Zhu,Xiao Shi,Xiwei Pan,Jinguo Liu,Ge Bai,Xin Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A three-level optimization chain (whitened SVD, block-level joint optimization, end-to-end refinement) achieves better Transformer compression with only 256 calibration sequences, significantly reducing perplexity at high compression rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current per-matrix SVD compression is Eckart-Young optimal for individual matrices, but errors compound through nonlinear Transformer blocks. There's a need for optimization methods that consider broader contexts beyond individual matrices to improve compression fidelity.

Method: Three-level chain: L1 - whitened SVD per matrix; L2 - block-level joint optimization across matrices within Transformer blocks; L3 - end-to-end language modeling loss refinement. All use only 256 calibration sequences, no instruction or recovery data.

Result: On LLaMA-7B at 60% compression: WikiText-2 perplexity reduced from 42.1 to 19.1 to 11.4 across chain levels. Block-level stage crucial - skipping it worsens PTB perplexity by 24 points. Improvements hold across 20-80% compression, five architectures up to 13B parameters. With more data, skipping block-level becomes competitive.

Conclusion: The three-level chain significantly improves perplexity and compression fidelity compared to per-matrix SVD alone, though downstream accuracy remains below dense models. Block-level optimization acts as a critical regularizer. There's an offline compute-data trade-off between computation-heavy block optimization and using more calibration data.

Abstract: Per-matrix singular value decomposition (SVD) truncation is Eckart-Young optimal in the whitened Frobenius norm, but errors from independently compressed matrices compound through the block's nonlinear forward pass. Inspired in part by hierarchical variational optimization in quantum many-body methods, we introduce a three-level chain that widens optimization scope from individual matrices to Transformer blocks to the full model: whitened SVD~(L1), block-level joint optimization~(L2), and end-to-end language-modeling loss refinement~(L3), all from 256 calibration sequences, with no instruction or recovery data. On LLaMA-7B at 60% compression, the chain reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 42.1 to 19.1 to 11.4. The block-level stage acts as a regularizer: skipping it worsens Penn Treebank (PTB) perplexity by 24 points, a gap that additional end-to-end training did not close in our experiments. Perplexity gains hold across 20-80% compression, five architectures up to 13B parameters, and both in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks, though the cross-architecture rows use architecture-specific configurations and the ratio sweep was not run under one common protocol. With more calibration data, skipping the block-level stage becomes competitive, revealing an offline compute--data trade-off. We therefore claim improvements only in perplexity and compression fidelity; downstream accuracy remains well below the dense model.

</details>


### [330] [Task-Directed Residual AddUNet:Perfect-Reconstruction Routing for Full-Rate Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15857)
*Vikram R. Lakkavalli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents a perfect-reconstruction interpretation of AddUNet, introduces Residual Full-Rate PR architecture for task-directed representation learning, showing it's equivalent to critically sampled filter banks with exact reconstruction guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To establish a theoretical foundation for U-Net architectures by showing their equivalence to perfect-reconstruction filter banks, and to develop a framework that decouples representation learning from reconstruction requirements, allowing task-directed routing while maintaining exact reconstruction.

Method: 1. Shows AddUNet's survivor-skip structure is exactly equivalent to critically sampled multirate PR filter banks. 2. Develops full-rate formulation removing complementary-subband restrictions while preserving PR. 3. Proposes Residual Full-Rate PR architecture that routes task-irrelevant information away from task-facing survivor. 4. Guarantees exact reconstruction for arbitrary shape-compatible routing operators without requiring invertibility or reconstruction loss.

Result: 1. Verified exact single-channel routing of linearly separable factors to machine precision. 2. On TIMIT dataset, improved test PER from 28.60±2.09% to 25.76±0.41% with fixed recognizer and training protocol while maintaining exact reconstruction. 3. Speaker probing shows structural conservation doesn't imply task-specific invariance.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a solid theoretical connection between U-Net architectures and perfect-reconstruction systems, enabling decoupling of representation design from reconstruction. This allows learning to focus solely on task-directed routing while maintaining structural conservation, providing both theoretical guarantees and practical performance improvements.

Abstract: This paper establishes a perfect-reconstruction (PR) interpretation of AddUNet and its full-rate realization, and introduces a Residual Full-Rate PR architecture for task-directed representation learning. The survivor--skip structure of a constrained additive U-Net is shown to be exactly equivalent to a critically sampled multirate PR filter bank. The full-rate formulation removes the complementary-subband restrictions of the critically sampled system while preserving PR. A Residual Full-Rate PR architecture is then proposed to progressively route task-irrelevant, nuisance, or redundant structure away from the task-facing survivor while retaining the routed information explicitly. Exact reconstruction is guaranteed for arbitrary shape-compatible linear or nonlinear routing operators, without requiring invertibility, a matched synthesis bank, reconstruction loss, or learned decoder. The resulting architecture decouples representation design from reconstruction design: conservation is structural, while learning is devoted to task-directed routing. The same formulation identifies an identity-shortcut ResNet with its residual output retained as a full-rate PR system. Experiments verify exact single-channel routing of linearly separable factors to machine precision. On TIMIT, the proposed front-end improves test PER from $28.60\pm2.09\%$ to $25.76\pm0.41\%$ with the recognizer and training protocol held fixed, while maintaining exact reconstruction. Speaker probing further shows that structural conservation does not itself imply task-specific invariance.

</details>


### [331] [LLM-Based Schema-Aware Split Learning for Privacy-Preserving Mental Distress Prediction Across Heterogeneous Surveys](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15871)
*Md Khalid Syfullah,Alvi Ataur Khalil*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Privacy-preserving framework using LLMs to harmonize and analyze heterogeneous mental health survey data across institutions without sharing raw data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need to collaboratively analyze mental health survey data across institutions while addressing privacy constraints and heterogeneous survey designs (different questions, scales, formats) that prevent direct data integration.

Method: Schema-aware split learning framework: (1) Serialize survey records into natural-language descriptions to unify schemas, (2) Use LLM (LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct) as shared semantic encoder, (3) Fine-tune with LoRA for mental distress assessment, (4) Partition LLM across client (lightweight front-end) and server (resource-intensive backbone), keeping raw data locally.

Result: Achieves average ANLS of 0.708 with only 2,000 training samples, outperforms federated learning in 8 of 9 settings, reduces per-client computation by three orders of magnitude, and generalizes to unseen datasets.

Conclusion: The framework enables accurate, privacy-preserving, and resource-efficient collaborative learning from heterogeneous mental health survey data, addressing key barriers in mental health research.

Abstract: Rising societal and lifestyle complexity has been linked to a growing prevalence of mental distress worldwide. Educational institutions, workplaces, clinics, etc. collect large volumes of mental health survey data to understand and reduce this burden. Collaborative analysis of such data could yield effective generalizable predictive models. Privacy constraints and varied survey designs (i.e., different questions, scales, and formats) hinder direct integration. We propose a schema-aware split learning (SL) framework that preserves privacy, using a large language model (LLM) as a shared semantic encoder to harmonize heterogeneous survey schemas across institutions. We serialize each survey record into a natural-language description, unifying disparate survey schemas into a common format. The LLM is fine-tuned for mental distress assessment via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and partitioned across client and server. Clients retain the raw survey responses locally and run only a lightweight front-end, so original records never leave the institution that collected them. The resource-intensive backbone runs on the server, minimizing client-side computation. Using LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct, the framework attains an average ANLS of 0.708 with only 2,000 training samples, surpasses federated learning (FL) in eight of nine settings, and cuts per-client computation by three orders of magnitude, while generalizing to unseen datasets. Overall, it enables accurate, privacy-preserving, and resource-efficient collaborative learning from heterogeneous mental health survey data.

</details>


### [332] [Learning Multimodal One-step Flow Policy via Value-weighted Optimal Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15883)
*Jaehun Shon,Jinha Choi,Jongwook Jeon,Jongmin Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OptiFlow: A new offline RL method that uses optimal transport to learn one-step flow policies from multimodal datasets, avoiding mode collapse and OOD exploitation while capturing optimal behaviors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline RL learns from fixed datasets with multimodal action distributions. Flow policies can represent multimodal behaviors, but current one-step flow policy learning suffers from mode collapse and exploits overestimation bias in out-of-distribution regions when using standard value guidance.

Method: OptiFlow frames one-step flow policy learning as a structured sample-allocation problem. It jointly trains a value-aware reference flow policy and an efficient one-step policy, coupling their action samples through state-wise entropic optimal transport. Critic-estimated values define distillation target priorities, while action-distance cost ensures geometrically compatible pairings.

Result: OptiFlow effectively captures optimal multimodal behaviors and achieves strong performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the transport-guided approach for in-distribution exploitation.

Conclusion: OptiFlow provides a novel framework for learning one-step flow policies in offline RL that avoids common pitfalls like mode collapse and OOD exploitation by using optimal transport to guide policy distillation towards high-value, dataset-supported modes.

Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning aims to learn a policy solely from fixed datasets, which often contain multimodal action distributions. Flow policies can naturally represent such multimodal behaviors, but learning an efficient one-step flow policy remains challenging: standard value guidance often leads to mode collapse or exploits overestimation bias in out-of-distribution regions. To address this, we introduce One-step Flow policy via Optimal Transport (OptiFlow), a framework for one-step flow policy learning as a structured sample-allocation problem. OptiFlow jointly trains a value-aware reference flow policy and an efficient one-step policy, coupling their action samples through state-wise entropic optimal transport. For each state, critic-estimated values define the priority of distillation target actions, while the action-distance cost ensures geometrically compatible pairings. By avoiding direct critic maximization, our transport-guided approach enables in-distribution exploitation by anchoring the one-step policy to high-value, dataset-supported modes without the risk of out-of-distribution divergence. Experimental results demonstrate that OptiFlow effectively captures optimal multimodal behaviors and achieves strong performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yonsei-DILLab/OptiFlow.

</details>


### [333] [Privacy-enhanced federated learning via asynchronous aggregation and local differential perturbation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15885)
*Zhen Zhong,Shini Yang,Liesheng Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Privacy-enhanced federated learning framework combining Dynamic Differential Privacy, lightweight Homomorphic Encryption, and Local Differential Privacy with asynchronous aggregation for secure distributed training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the need for secure collaborative training in distributed data environments where privacy protection is crucial but traditional federated learning approaches may have privacy vulnerabilities and communication inefficiencies.

Method: Integrates three privacy mechanisms: Dynamic Differential Privacy (DDP), lightweight Homomorphic Encryption (HE), and Local Differential Privacy (LDP). Employs asynchronous aggregation strategy with version control to support distributed training in asynchronous environments.

Result: Achieves high classification accuracy (up to 82.6%) on CIFAR-10 and Purchase-100 datasets even under stringent privacy constraints (ε = 0.1), while reducing communication overhead by 21.3% compared to FedAvg baseline.

Conclusion: The framework effectively balances privacy protection and model performance in distributed machine learning scenarios, providing a scalable technical foundation for large-scale distributed collaborative computing with enhanced security.

Abstract: This study proposes a privacy-enhanced federated learning framework to address secure collaborative training in distributed data environments. The framework integrates Dynamic Differential Privacy (DDP), lightweight Homomorphic Encryption (HE), and Local Differential Privacy (LDP) mechanisms to ensure data privacy protection during model training. Additionally, the framework employs an asynchronous aggregation strategy with version control to support distributed training in asynchronous environments. Experimental validation on the CIFAR-10 and Purchase-100 benchmark datasets demonstrates that the method maintains high classification accuracy (up to 82.6%) even under stringent privacy constraints (ε = 0.1), while reducing communication overhead by 21.3% compared to FedAvg. Experimental results demonstrate that this framework effectively balances privacy protection and model performance in distributed machine learning scenarios, providing a scalable technical foundation for large-scale distributed collaborative computing.

</details>


### [334] [Discrete Beckmann Transport Models for One-Step Language Modeling and Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15903)
*Sophia Tang,Shiyi Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Discrete Beckmann Transport Models (DBTM) enable one- and few-step discrete generation without needing a teacher model or time conditioning, outperforming existing discrete diffusion and flow methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current discrete diffusion/flow models require costly teacher distillation for faster sampling, which limits quality to teacher performance and requires two-stage training.

Method: DBTM uses a time-independent flow with autonomous transport map that moves any point to simplex vertices in one step, minimizing a conservation equation residual directly from data without teacher or time conditioning.

Result: DBTM enables one- and few-step generation that improves quality and accuracy over discrete diffusion and continuous flow baselines on language modeling and reasoning tasks.

Conclusion: DBTM provides an efficient alternative to teacher-distilled discrete models, enabling fast generation without quality trade-offs through novel fixed-point transport dynamics.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion and flow models are a promising alternative to autoregressive language models, but compressing many-step sampling into fewer steps typically requires distilling a pretrained teacher model. This caps the student at the teacher's quality and requires a costly two-stage training pipeline. We introduce Discrete Beckmann Transport Models (DBTM), built on a time-independent flow whose autonomous transport map provably carries any point in the ambient space to a fixed point on the vertices of the simplex in a single step. We show that this fixed-point property is characterized by a conservation equation whose residual can be minimized directly from data, removing the requirement for a teacher flow and time conditioning. Under this construction, a partially trained map corresponds to the flow truncated at finite time, so generation reduces to iterating one map until it reaches a fixed point. We further extend the map to a partial-context interpolant where additional function evaluations act as refinement steps rather than ODE integration steps. On language modeling and reasoning tasks, DBTM enables one- and few-step generation that improves quality and accuracy over discrete diffusion and continuous flow baselines.

</details>


### [335] [Safe Meta-Reinforcement Learning via Information Space Reachability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15915)
*Zeyang Li,Sunbochen Tang,Navid Azizan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Safe meta-RL framework that reasons about safety in information space to enable safe adaptation to unseen tasks with limited experience.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Meta-RL enables adaptation to unseen tasks but real-world applications require safety considerations, which have been underexplored in prior work. There's a need for safe meta-RL frameworks that can account for safety during adaptation.

Method: Introduces reasoning about safety in information space (physical state + agent's belief over underlying task). Develops safety value function that measures probability of avoiding unsafe regions indefinitely. Shows this satisfies self-consistency and Bellman equation, making it learnable via meta-RL. Creates safe meta-RL algorithm learning safety value function for safety filtering and constrained policy optimization.

Result: Experiments on meta-RL benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Conclusion: Proposes a novel safe meta-RL framework that successfully addresses safety concerns in meta-RL adaptation, enabling practical deployment in real-world tasks with safety requirements.

Abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) enables agents to adapt to unseen tasks with limited experience. Despite its promise, the application of meta-RL in real-world tasks is hindered by safety requirements, which have been underexplored in prior work. In this paper, we propose a safe meta-RL framework that explicitly accounts for safety during adaptation. Our key insight is to reason about safety in the information space, which captures both the physical state and the agent's belief over the underlying task. Within this space, we introduce a safety value function that measures the probability of the agent avoiding unsafe regions indefinitely. We show that this function satisfies a self-consistency condition and a Bellman equation, which make it learnable via meta-RL. Based on this formulation, we develop a safe meta-RL algorithm that learns the safety value function and leverages it for safety filtering and constrained policy optimization. Experiments on meta-RL benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

</details>


### [336] [Privacy-Aligned Personalized Federated Learning with Compact Adaptation and Variable-Length Gaussian Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15950)
*Yilin Xu,Chun Hei Michael Shiu,Chih Wei Ling,Linqi Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Record-level DP in personalized FL has structural misalignment between low-dimensional client variation and high-dimensional repeated updates. Proposed method releases private client context once, confines adaptation to fixed coefficient space, uses adaptive optimization geometry, and reduces communication via quantization-as-privacy mechanism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Record-level differential privacy creates a structural misalignment in personalized federated learning when client-specific variation is low-dimensional while training repeatedly releases high-dimensional updates. This misalignment leads to inefficient privacy protection and communication overhead.

Method: 1. Release private client context once and confine repeated adaptation to a fixed coefficient space (dimensionality reduction). 2. Use factorized generator that induces adaptive optimization geometry to reshape noisy updates. 3. Implement Gaussian mechanism for coefficient updates through variable-length quantization where quantization error itself serves as privacy perturbation rather than extra distortion.

Result: Matches or outperforms full-model private adaptation across privacy budgets and client heterogeneity on MNIST and CIFAR-10. Reduces protected uplink by factor of 2.67 at ε=16 on CIFAR-10 with comparable future-client accuracy. Most private-training gain is retained by radial evolution according to controlled ablations.

Conclusion: The proposed approach successfully addresses the structural misalignment in personalized FL with record-level DP by factorizing client variation, using adaptive optimization geometry, and leveraging quantization as privacy mechanism, achieving better privacy-utility-communication trade-offs.

Abstract: Record-level differential privacy exposes a structural misalignment in personalized federated learning when client-specific variation is low-dimensional while training repeatedly releases high-dimensional updates. In this paper, we address this misalignment by releasing a private client context once and confining repeated adaptation to a fixed coefficient space. Beyond dimensionality reduction, the factorized generator induces an adaptive optimization geometry that reshapes noisy updates, and controlled ablations show that most of its private-training gain is retained by radial evolution. To further reduce the communication cost, we realize the Gaussian mechanism for coefficient updates directly through variable-length quantization with finite expected code length, so that the quantization error itself serves as the required privacy perturbation rather than extra distortion. Across MNIST and CIFAR-10, our design matches or outperforms full-model private adaptation across privacy budgets and client heterogeneity, while reducing protected uplink by a factor of 2.67 at \(\varepsilon=16\) on CIFAR-10 with comparable future-client accuracy.

</details>


### [337] [A Chosen Future Can Still Be Rewritten: Causal Writability in Video Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15980)
*Xingyun Wang,Haomin Zheng,Man Yuan,Leqian Yang,Ziming Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Video models contain correct physical motion internally even when generating wrong outputs, and this latent knowledge can be controllably accessed through targeted "edits" in early network layers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to understand why video models generate physically incorrect motion: whether it's a failure to learn correct motion or a failure to use learned knowledge. The authors investigate if correct physical understanding remains available inside trained models despite wrong outputs.

Method: Researchers train models on videos with color-coded mass oscillation speeds (red=slow, blue=fast), then test conflicting cases (red mass with fast motion). They apply low-dimensional "edits" based on simple physical variables to probe internal representations. They analyze writability across network depths and identify sharp boundaries where edits become ineffective.

Result: Models contain correct motion knowledge internally even when generating wrong outputs. Correct motion can be restored via targeted edits in early layers (causal writability). There's a sharp depth boundary where edits stop working, indicating commitment. Early writability predicts which training errors get corrected later. Findings generalize to a pretrained 1.3B parameter video model.

Conclusion: Video models learn correct physical motion but sometimes fail to use it, suggesting the problem is computational rather than representational. The "causal writability" framework provides a method to probe and manipulate internal representations, revealing hierarchical commitment to decisions and offering diagnostic tools for understanding model errors.

Abstract: When a video model generates physically incorrect motion, did it fail to learn the correct motion, or did it learn it but fail to use it? We show the latter: the correct motion remains available inside the model and can still be made to control the generated video. We train on videos where red masses oscillate slowly and blue masses oscillate quickly, then test a red mass with fast observed motion. Even when the model generates slow motion in this conflicting case, a low-dimensional edit predicted from simple physical variables restores the correct fast motion. We call this ability causal writability. At fixed strength, we find a sharp depth boundary: the same edit changes the video before the boundary but not after it. This closure marks commitment for that write. The motion signal nevertheless remains, and a stronger downstream write can restore physical motion, while excessive gain overshoots. Early causal writability predicts which errors training later corrects: those errors are writable at more network depths than errors that persist. We reproduce both causal writability and its sharp closure in a pretrained 1.3B video model, supporting generality across model scale and training regime.

</details>


### [338] [The Router Within: Eliciting Native Skill Routing from a Frozen LLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15982)
*Ruishuo Chen,Xun Wang,Yu Chen,Zhuoran Li,Longbo Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Gavel enables efficient skill routing in LLM agents by reading routing signals from the LLM's own forward passes using just two linear maps, eliminating the need for skill metadata in context and outperforming larger retrieval-based approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current skill routing methods for LLM agents face key limitations: preloading skill metadata into context disperses agent attention and caps library size, while retrieval pipelines move selection out of the agent's capability entirely.

Method: Gavel uses a two-step approach: 1) Glance step projects task and skill mid-layer states through two trained linear maps to score the full library against compact per-skill banks built during installation; 2) Verdict step resumes shortlisted skills' forward passes and reads model's likelihood/yes/no judgments, fused with glance scores as product of experts.

Result: Gavel outperforms progressive disclosure and retrieve-and-rerank pipelines with 1.2B-16B external parameters by up to 13.4 points on written tasks and up to 21.9 when skill needs arise mid-rollout. On Qwen3-32B, it transfers zero-shot to three public benchmarks and new SkillTraj benchmark (372 simulated agent trajectories).

Conclusion: Frozen LLMs already contain routing signals that can be efficiently extracted with minimal parameter overhead (two linear maps), enabling high-accuracy skill selection without skill text in context, with performance scaling with backbone capability and outperforming much larger models in real agent deployments.

Abstract: Skills extend an LLM agent beyond its parametric knowledge, and the gain they promise rests on picking the right one. Deployed harnesses route by preloading every skill's metadata into the context, which disperses the agent's attention and caps the library size. Retrieval pipelines move the selection out of the context, but also out of the agent's capability. We show that the frozen agent LLM already carries the routing signal in its own forward passes, and that two linear maps suffice to read it out with no skill text in the context. Gavel (Glance And Verdict from a frozen LLM) reads it in two steps. A glance projects the task's and each skill's mid-layer states through the two maps, the only parameters trained, and scores the full library against compact per-skill banks that one forward pass builds at installation. A verdict then resumes the shortlisted skills' forward passes and reads the model's own likelihood and yes/no judgment, fused with the glance as a product of experts. Trained once, Gavel transfers zero-shot to three public benchmarks and SkillTraj, our new benchmark of 372 simulated agent trajectories. On Qwen3-32B it outperforms progressive disclosure and retrieve-and-rerank pipelines that add 1.2B to 16B external parameters, by up to 13.4 points on written tasks and up to 21.9 when the need for a skill arises mid-rollout. Routing accuracy improves as the backbone does, and in a bash-agent harness the same 32B triggers the correct skill on Skill-Use more often than far larger frontier models running in Codex.

</details>


### [339] [Bellman Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15987)
*Zhuoqing Song,Haotian Xu,Xikun Zhang,Lidong Bing*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BPO is a new reinforcement learning method for LLMs that improves reasoning without needing a critic network, using trajectory-level optimization instead of state value estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reinforcement learning methods for LLMs often require estimating state values at intermediate steps, which can be challenging. The paper aims to develop a critic-free method that avoids this complexity while improving reasoning capabilities through verifiable rewards.

Method: Introduces Bellman Policy Optimization (BPO), derived from Policy Mirror Descent. It reformulates PMD as a trajectory-level objective using Bellman equations, eliminating the need for state value estimation at intermediate states. The method uses a mismatch-correction weight based on smoothed token probability ratios.

Result: The paper proves BPO has the same unique optimal solution as original PMD. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate BPO's effectiveness in improving LLM reasoning capabilities through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.

Conclusion: BPO provides an effective critic-free RL method for LLMs that simplifies implementation by avoiding intermediate state value estimation while maintaining optimality guarantees, showing promise for improving mathematical reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). We introduce Bellman Policy Optimization (BPO), a critic-free method derived from Policy Mirror Descent (PMD). For autoregressive generation with terminal rewards, BPO uses the Bellman equations to reformulate PMD as a trajectory-level objective. The reformulation avoids estimating state values at intermediate states. We prove that it has the same unique optimal solution as the original PMD objective. We derive the practical BPO loss by approximating this objective. Its mismatch-correction weight is a smoothed ratio of complementary token probabilities. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of BPO.

</details>

### [340] [Machine learning-assisted calibration of Agent-based Models: surrogate-based optimization with Genetic Algorithm and Particle Swarm Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13247)
*Duguma Yeshitla Habtemariam,Jihwan Lee*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Surrogate-assisted evolutionary computation reduces simulation demands for agent-based model calibration by 32-61% while maintaining or improving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent-based models (ABMs) are difficult to calibrate due to stochastic, rugged objective landscapes that require expensive black-box simulations, creating a need for efficient calibration methods.

Method: Adapts inner-loop surrogate-assisted evolutionary computation by embedding machine learning surrogates within GA and PSO algorithms. The surrogate screens candidates, simulator validates only top 50%, reducing simulation demand. Evaluated 48 configurations combining 2 optimizers, 5 surrogates, and 4 calibration objectives on two contrasting ABMs.

Result: Best ML-assisted configurations reduce RMSE by 20.0% on Brock-Hommes and 63.8% on Island models, while reducing computation time by 32.1% and 61.1% respectively. Surrogates significantly reduce time but parameter recovery accuracy gains are best-configuration outcomes rather than average effects.

Conclusion: Surrogate-assisted calibration effectively reduces computational demands for ABMs, but optimal surrogate-optimizer-objective combinations depend on model complexity, indicating no universal default recipe exists.

Abstract: Calibrating an agent-based model (ABM) is difficult because its objective landscape is stochastic and rugged, and can be evaluated only through costly black-box simulations. This study adapts inner-loop surrogate-assisted evolutionary computation (SAEC) to ABM calibration by embedding a machine-learning surrogate within genetic algorithm (GA) and particle swarm optimisation (PSO). At each iteration, the surrogate screens the candidates and the simulator validates only the top 50%, reducing simulation demand while correcting surrogate errors. We evaluate a full factorial of 48 configurations combining two optimisers, five surrogates, and four calibration objectives on two contrasting ABMs, the Brock-Hommes asset-pricing model and the Island growth model. Parameter recovery is measured against pseudo-true values. Relative to the strongest pure-optimiser baseline, the best ML-assisted configurations reduce RMSE by 20.0% on Brock-Hommes and 63.8% on Island, while reducing computation time by 32.1% and 61.1%, respectively. ANOVA with Dunnett's post-hoc tests confirms significant time savings for every surrogate under both Brock-Hommes optimisers and under GA on Island. No surrogate differs significantly from the pure-optimiser baseline in parameter-recovery accuracy on Island; the reported accuracy gains are therefore best-configuration outcomes rather than average effects resolved at this sample size. The best surrogate-optimiser-objective combination changes with ABM complexity, indicating that surrogate-assisted calibration depends on the model and does not admit a universal default recipe.

</details>


### [341] [An Evolutionary Computation Framework for Multi-Agent Q-Learning with Mean-Field Environmental Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13253)
*Lichen Wang,Shijia Hua,Linjie Liu*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Multi-agent reinforcement learning with environmental feedback: a mean-field model describes coupled Q-learning on networks with dynamically changing payoffs, validated against Monte Carlo simulations across various graph types.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the interaction between individual adaptation, local encounters, and changing environmental conditions in networked multi-agent reinforcement learning systems where agents' collective behavior affects their payoff environment.

Method: Formulated a coupled learning-environment model where agents update stateless Q-values on fixed graphs while their population-average behavior drives an environmental variable that dynamically modifies the payoff matrix. Derived a deterministic transport equation for population distribution of Q-values under first-order mean-field closure, coupled with projected discrete update for environmental state.

Result: The mean-field system reproduces main macroscopic cooperation and environmental trajectories compared to finite-network Monte Carlo simulations on random regular, Erdős-Rényi, Barabási-Albert, and random geometric graphs. Trajectory-level RMSE decreases with population size and average degree. Environmental feedback reshapes learned action-value ordering, with reinforcing feedback producing pronounced dependence on initial learning bias and resource level. Environmental timescale crucially affects outcomes.

Conclusion: Provides a population-level description of coupled reinforcement learning and environmental dynamics, characterizing performance of mean-field approximation within tested network and parameter ranges. Environmental feedback significantly influences learning outcomes and cooperation dynamics in networked populations.

Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning in networked populations is governed by the interaction between individual adaptation, local encounters, and changing environmental conditions. To study this interaction, we formulate a coupled learning--environment model in which agents update stateless $Q$-values on a fixed graph, while their population-average behavior drives an environmental variable that dynamically modifies the payoff matrix. Under a first-order mean-field closure, we derive a deterministic transport equation for the population distribution of $Q$-values and couple it with a projected discrete update for the environmental state. The resulting model is evaluated against finite-network Monte Carlo simulations on random regular, Erdős--Rényi, Barabási--Albert, and random geometric graphs. Across the tested parameter ranges, the mean-field system reproduces the main macroscopic cooperation and environmental trajectories, and the trajectory-level root-mean-square error generally decreases with population size and average degree. The analysis further shows that environmental feedback reshapes the learned action-value ordering, while reinforcing feedback can produce pronounced dependence on the initial learning bias and resource level. The environmental timescale also plays an important role: a rapid response can drive the resource state to a boundary before learning adapts, whereas a slower response preserves the interaction between behavioral learning and environmental recovery. These results provide a population-level description of coupled reinforcement learning and environmental dynamics and characterize the performance of the mean-field approximation within the tested network and parameter ranges.

</details>


### [342] [From Process Loss to Assembly Bonus: Human-Grounded Diagnosis of Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13261)
*Ala N. Tak,Teruhisa Misu,Kumar Akash,Zhaobo K. Zheng,Kevin H. Joo,Jonathan Gratch*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: LLM groups can reproduce some outcome-level patterns of human group deliberation but differ significantly in process mechanisms, showing assembly bonus asymmetries similar to humans but with distinct coordination bottlenecks and information-sharing patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used for collaborative problem solving and human-group simulation, making outcome-only evaluation insufficient. Researchers need to know whether LLM groups succeed or fail through human-like deliberative mechanisms when used as models of human groups.

Method: Compared human group chats with matched LLM deliberation traces on Wason-style deductive reasoning tasks, then tested whether the same process signatures generalize to analogical, abductive, and analytical tasks. Analyzed assembly bonus, initial-answer diversity effects, process-level differences, and tested interventions motivated by human group-decision research.

Result: Humans and LLMs show the same assembly bonus asymmetry: discussion improves average member more often than best initial member. Initial-answer diversity accounts for model heterogeneity effects. LLM groups differ process-level by following majorities more often, surfacing less unique information, converging earlier, with correct minority signals succeeding mainly when re-expressed early. Interventions yield modest improvements but don't remove coordination bottlenecks.

Conclusion: LLM groups can reproduce some outcome-level patterns of human deliberation while diverging in mechanisms that generate assembly bonus and process loss, with implications for group simulation and human-AI collaboration.

Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for collaborative problem solving and human-group simulation. This makes outcome-only evaluation insufficient: if LLM groups are used as models of human groups, we need to know whether they succeed or fail through human-like deliberative mechanisms. We compare human group chats with matched LLM deliberation traces on Wason-style deductive reasoning, then test whether the same process signatures generalize to analogical, abductive, and analytical tasks. Humans and LLMs show the same assembly bonus asymmetry: discussion improves the average member more often than the best initial member. Initial-answer diversity accounts for the effect of model heterogeneity, increasing movement in both corrective and destructive directions. The main differences are process-level. Compared with humans, LLM groups follow majorities more often, surface less unique information, and converge earlier; correct minority signals succeed mainly when re-expressed early. Interventions motivated by human group-decision research yield modest improvements in collective outcomes, but do not remove the coordination bottleneck. Together, these results suggest that LLM groups can reproduce some outcome-level patterns of human deliberation while diverging in the mechanisms that generate assembly bonus and process loss, with implications for group simulation and human-AI collaboration.

</details>


### [343] [Conceptualization and experimentation of asset market with price manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13304)
*Pau Fonseca i Casas,Aarón Montero Montero*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: This work reproduces a market manipulation experiment using multi-agent simulation to model human trader psychology and uses formal languages to improve interdisciplinary communication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to model human trader psychological processes to understand decision effects on asset values, and to improve communication between diverse specialists (computing, economics, psychology) through formal language.

Method: Reproduces an existing market distortion experiment using virtual traders in a multi-agent simulation model, employing formal and graphical languages to detail trader behavior.

Result: Shows feasibility of reproducing complex human behaviors in market scenarios and demonstrates convenience of formal/graphical languages for understanding and validating complex economic behaviors.

Conclusion: The approach successfully reproduces human trader psychology in market manipulation scenarios and provides effective tools for interdisciplinary communication and validation of complex economic behaviors.

Abstract: The primary goal of this work is to reproduce the behavior of a human trader, detailing his or her psychological processes to understand the effects of his or her decisions on the final value of an asset. The second goal is to use a formal language to detail this behavior as a tool for improving and simplifying the communication between all actors involved in the project, such as specialists from disciplines as diverse as computing, economics and psychology. As a starting point, we use a paper that shows an experiment that analyzes the influence on other trader's behavior when an agent handler and a trading robot attempt to distort the market. This work reproduces this experiment, using virtual traders that belong to a multi-agent simulation model, showing the feasibility to reproduce complex human behaviors and showing the convenience of use formal and graphical languages to simplify the understanding and the validation of the complex behaviors involved in an economic process.

</details>


### [344] [Learning How Much to Collaborate: Difficulty-Aware Topology Selection for Multi-Agent Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13890)
*Yunsong Hong*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: DATS (Difficulty-Aware Topology Selector) dynamically chooses the optimal multi-agent communication topology for code generation problems based on problem difficulty, achieving better performance at lower cost than fixed topology approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multi-agent code generation systems use a single communication topology for all problems, but problem difficulty varies significantly. The advantage of hierarchical collaboration grows dramatically on harder problems (from 2.4 to 21.1 points gain), while its cost remains 10x higher. There's a need for adaptive topology selection based on problem difficulty and cost considerations.

Method: DATS predicts each topology's probability of solving a problem using a graph network that treats five topologies as nodes of a connectivity order rather than independent labels. It selects the topology maximizing predicted success minus cost, with cost penalty as a single scalar adjustable without retraining. Evaluation uses budget-matched protocol comparing six cost-aware methods on 614 problems from APPS, HumanEval+, and LiveCodeBench datasets.

Result: At 40% of always-hierarchical cost, DATS achieves 77.7% pass@1 vs 73.6% (always-hierarchical) and 74.3% (strongest competitor), with 4.1-point gain. Results hold across four backbones spanning 14 points of capability. Cross-domain study on 400 math problems reproduces the effect (gap widening from 2.5 to 20.9 points). All eleven pairwise McNemar comparisons survive Holm-Bonferroni correction.

Conclusion: DATS demonstrates that dynamic topology selection based on problem difficulty is superior to fixed-topology approaches for multi-agent code generation. The method effectively balances performance and cost, with consistent gains across different model capabilities and problem domains.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems for code generation are deployed with a single communication topology, chosen once for every problem. This is the wrong granularity. Evaluating five topologies on 614 problems from APPS, HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench, we find that the advantage of hierarchical collaboration over a single agent grows from 2.4 points of pass@1 on the easiest third of problems to 21.1 points on the hardest third, while its token cost stays about ten times higher. We propose the Difficulty-Aware Topology Selector (DATS), which predicts each topology's probability of solving a problem and selects the one maximising predicted success minus cost. Its predictor is a graph network that treats the five topologies as nodes of a connectivity order rather than independent labels, worth 1.7 points over a flat multi-label head. Because the cost penalty is a single scalar recalibrable without retraining, routers compare at equal spend: under this budget-matched protocol six cost-aware methods span 21.6 percentage points, and two baselines leading DATS fall behind once calibrated to it. Fixed at 40% of the always-hierarchical cost, DATS reaches 77.7% pass@1 against 73.6% (always-hierarchical) and 74.3% (strongest learned competitor), all eleven pairwise McNemar comparisons surviving Holm-Bonferroni correction. The 4.1-point gain holds across four backbones spanning fourteen points of capability, and replacing the 39 interpretable features with a graph network or a pretrained encoder shifts accuracy by at most 1.3 points, never significantly. A cross-domain study on 400 mathematical reasoning problems reproduces the effect, the gap widening from 2.5 to 20.9 points.

</details>


### [345] [Loop-Back Authority in LLM Agent Teams: A Paired Experiment on Flat and Hierarchical Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14767)
*Burak Agachan,Max van Duijn,Amirhossein Zohrehvand*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Hierarchical orchestration with managerial authority actually reduces output quality compared to flat organizations in multi-agent LLM systems, contrary to classical organizational theory predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether the authority link in hierarchical multi-agent LLM frameworks (where managers can reject and demand revisions) improves or harms output quality on open-ended tasks, given conflicting predictions from classical organizational theory vs. research on LLM sycophancy and Degeneration-of-Thought.

Method: Controlled experiment holding five LLM agents, their roles, prompts, tools, models, and data fixed while varying only whether the Manager can reject worker output and demand revisions. Used 43 paired products across 86 runs of a business-intelligence reporting task, evaluated by a five-model judge panel and deterministic specification check.

Result: Flat organization scored significantly higher on both Utility (d = 0.42, p = 0.009) and Writing Clarity (d = 0.34, p = 0.030). Hierarchical reports hedged 53% more, each revision loop decreased Writing Clarity by 0.14 points, and hierarchical reports cost 51.5% more tokens with no quality gain. Specification accuracy was equally high in both.

Conclusion: Authority in hierarchical LLM agent systems becomes a liability when supervisors can only opine without verifiable criteria. Flat organizations produce higher quality output for open-ended tasks. Supervisors only add value when they can verify outputs against clear specifications rather than making subjective judgments.

Abstract: Hierarchical orchestration, in which a Manager agent reviews worker output and can send it back for revision, is the default coordination pattern in production multi-agent LLM frameworks. Classical organizational theory predicts that the authority link speeds convergence on decisive output; work on sycophancy and Degeneration-of-Thought predicts that authoritative critique makes LLM output worse. Prior comparisons vary whole frameworks on tasks with checkable answers, leaving the authority link untested on open-ended work. We present a paired experiment that holds five LLM agents, their roles, prompts, tools, models, and data fixed and varies one link: whether the Manager may reject a worker's output and oblige a revision. Across 43 paired products and 86 runs of a business-intelligence reporting task, a five-model judge panel and a deterministic specification check score every report. The flat organization scores higher on Utility (d = 0.42, p = 0.009) and on Writing Clarity (d = 0.34, p = 0.030); the classical prediction fails. The reports are the same length, but hierarchical reports hedge 53% more, each revision loop is associated with a 0.14-point drop in Writing Clarity, and the hierarchical Writer's first draft is indistinguishable from the flat report: the gap opens inside the revision loop. Specification accuracy is at ceiling in both organizations, and the supervisory tier costs 51.5% more tokens for no quality gain. A supervisor pays for itself when it can verify and becomes a liability when it can only opine.

</details>
